<meta>Continuing from the previous blank flyleaf, this page marks the transition into the main body or a new section of the manuscript, identified by its physical gathering mark.</meta>

->**C 1**<-

<note>The mark **C 1** is a <term>signature mark</term> (original: *signatura*). These notations were essential guides for bookbinders in the pre-modern era. The letter "C" signifies that this is the third "gathering" or "quire" (a group of sheets folded together), while the number "1" indicates that this is the first leaf of that specific group. This system ensured that the text remained in the correct sequence when the manuscript was sewn into its binding.</note>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page contains a famous exchange between the French philosopher Petrus Ramus and Johannes Kepler. Ramus had challenged the astronomers of his day to create an astronomy without "hypotheses" (mathematical fictions), even offering his own professorship as a prize. Kepler uses this page to "claim" that prize by arguing that his new physics proves Copernicus's theories were not mere fictions, but physical realities.</meta>

# P. RAMUS, Mathematical Schools
## book II, page 50.

<margin>C</margin>The fabrication of *Hypotheses* is therefore absurd. However, the fabrication found in *Eudoxus, Aristotle, Callippus, and Simplicius*, who believed their *Hypotheses* were true—indeed, they worshipped them like the Gods of the <term>unoriginated</term> <note>original: ἀνάρχων (anarchōn). Ramus refers to the ancient belief that the celestial spheres were eternal and had no beginning.</note> spheres. But among their successors, the story is far more absurd: to demonstrate the truth of natural things through false causes. Therefore, *Logic* first, then the *Mathematical* elements of *Arithmetic & Geometry*, will contribute the most help toward establishing the purity and dignity of this most ample art <note>Ramus is referring to astronomy.</note>. And I wish that *Copernicus* had instead devoted his thoughts to that task of establishing an *Astronomy* <note>original: "Astrologiae." In this period, "astrologia" was often used interchangeably with "astronomia."</note> without *Hypotheses*. For it would have been far easier for him to describe an Astronomy corresponding to the truth of his stars, than—like some giant-like labor—to move the Earth so that we might observe the stationary stars according to the Earth's motion. Indeed, let some *Philosopher* and *Mathematician* arise from the many noble schools of *Germany* to seize the palm of eternal praise placed in our midst. And if any fruit of fleeting utility can be offered as a reward for such great virtue, I will promise you the Royal Professorship at *Paris* <note>original: "Lutetiae," the Latin name for Paris.</note> as the prize for an *Astronomy* fashioned without hypotheses; I will fulfill this pledge most gladly, even by the resignation of my own professorship.

# The Author to RAMUS.

<margin>C</margin>You have conveniently abandoned this legal pledge, RAMUS, by departing from your profession <note>Ramus had been killed in the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572, decades before this was published.</note>. If you still held it now, I would indeed claim it as my right; a claim I shall prove by this *Work*, even if your own *Logic* were the judge. While you ask for support for this most ample science from *Logic* and *Mathematics*, please do not exclude the *Physical* aids, which it cannot do without. And unless I am mistaken, you show yourself amenable: since as a *Shaper* [of science] you include *Philosophy* alongside *Mathematics*. With that same openness, then, listen to *Philosophy* itself defending a matter commonly thought most absurd—not with giant-like effort, but with the best reasons. When she does this, she does nothing new, nothing insolent, but performs the duty for which she was invented.

> *It is a most absurd story, I admit, to demonstrate Natural things through false causes; but this story is not found in Copernicus. For he himself also believed his Hypotheses were true, no less than those ancients of yours believed theirs. Nor did he only believe it, but he even demonstrates them to be true; I offer this Work as witness.*

Do you truly wish to know the architect of this story, at which you are so angry? **ANDREAS OSIANDER** is noted in my copy, in the hand of *Hieronymus Schreiber of Nuremberg*. This *Andreas*, therefore, when he was in charge of the edition of *Copernicus*, himself judged that preface (which you call most absurd) to be most prudent (as far as can be gathered from his letters to *Copernicus*), and placed it at the front of the book—while *Copernicus* himself was either already dead or certainly unaware. *Copernicus*, therefore, does not <term>tell myths</term> <note>original: μυθολογεῖ (mythologei)</note>, but seriously <term>argues from demonstration</term> <note>original: ἀποδειξιολογεῖ (apodeixiologei)</note>, which is to say, he <term>philosophizes</term> <note>original: φιλοσοφεῖ (philosophei)</note>; which is what you desired in an *Astronomer*.

<summary>Kepler responds to a challenge by Petrus Ramus, who had criticized Copernicus for using "false" mathematical hypotheses. Kepler reveals that the "fictionalist" preface to Copernicus's work was actually written by Andreas Osiander, not Copernicus himself, and claims he has now provided the physical proof Ramus demanded.</summary>
<keywords>Petrus Ramus, Nicolaus Copernicus, Andreas Osiander, astronomical hypotheses, realism vs fictionalism, physical causes, Royal Professorship of Paris</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of Johannes Kepler's "Astronomia Nova" (New Astronomy) to Emperor Rudolph II. While the previous page provided the intellectual justification for the work by citing Petrus Ramus’s challenge to create an astronomy without "hypotheses," this page shifts to the formal, courtly language of patronage. Kepler presents his scientific breakthrough as a military victory, "capturing" the planet Mars (the god of war) for the Emperor.</meta>

# TO LORD RUDOLPH II
## OF THE ROMANS
### EMPEROR
->Ever August.<-

### OF GERMANY,
### HUNGARY,
### BOHEMIA, etc.
#### KING.
#### ARCHDUKE OF AUSTRIA, etc.

---

**M**OST AUGUST EMPEROR,

**S**o that it may be happy and auspicious for the most serene Name of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty <note>original: "Sæ. Cæ. Mtis. Væ." — an abbreviation for *Sacrae Caesareae Maiestatis Vestrae*</note>, and indeed for the entire House of Austria <note>The Habsburg dynasty, which ruled the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, I finally present to public view, by the commands of Your Majesty, a most Noble CAPTIVE <note>Kepler refers to the planet Mars, the subject of this book. He frames his mathematical discovery as a military triumph where he has "captured" the god of war.</note>, who was acquired by me long ago under the auspices of Your Majesty in a difficult and laborious war. Nor indeed do I fear that he will shrink from the name of Captive, he who long ago was accustomed—having laid aside his shield and weapons for a little while—to [yield] him-

<sig>(**)</sig>
<meta>The catchword "pfum" suggests the next word is "ipsum," meaning "himself."</meta>

<summary>This page is the formal dedication of Kepler's "Astronomia Nova" to Emperor Rudolph II, framing his years of research on the orbit of Mars as a successful "war" resulting in the capture of a noble prisoner.</summary>
<keywords>Rudolph II, Holy Roman Empire, dedication, Mars, patronage, Habsburg, Astronomia Nova</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Rudolph II. The previous page ended mid-sentence, describing how the god/planet Mars used to "yield him-" [self]. This section continues the military metaphor, where Kepler presents his astronomical findings as a captive of war brought to the Emperor's court.</meta>

-self to be conquered and bound, willing and playful; as often as custody, prison, or chains were pleasing [to him]. <note>Kepler alludes to the mythological story of Mars being caught in a net by Vulcan while with Venus; here, it suggests the planet is now "caught" by Kepler’s calculations.</note>

Indeed, no greater celebration could exist for this spectacle than if I were to write a panegyric <term>panegyric: a formal speech or text written in high praise of someone</term> for this most excellent captive and proclaim it with a public voice.

Even though a wonderful brilliance meets one entering this field, turning away and dazzling eyes accustomed to the faint light of Night <note>original: "Noctis"</note> and the shadows of the schoolroom. <note>Kepler contrasts the "brilliance" of the imperial court with the "shadows" of his private life as a mathematician.</note>

Therefore, I leave it to the writers of histories to explain the greatness of our Guest <note>original: "Hospitis" — Kepler refers to Mars as a guest now residing at the Emperor’s court.</note>, acquired through warfare.

Let them surely say that this is he through whom all armies conquer, all military leaders triumph, and all Kings rule; without whose help no one has ever led away any captive with honor. Let them satisfy their eyes by gazing upon him, now captured by my own Mars <note>original: "meo Marte" — a Latin idiom meaning "by my own efforts," but here also a pun on the planet Mars.</note>.

Let the admirers of Roman greatness say that this is the progenitor of the Kings Romulus and Remus, the preserver of the City <note>Rome</note>, the protector of the Romans <term>Quiritium: a formal name for Roman citizens in their civil capacity</term>, the Stabilizer of the Empire <note>original: "Statorem Imperii" — a title usually given to Jupiter, but here applied to Mars as the legendary father of the Roman people.</note>: by whose favor the Romans invented, increased, and perfected military discipline, and subjugated the whole world <note>original: "Orbemque Terrarum"</note>. Let them, therefore, offer congratulations that he has now been hemmed in and acquired for the House of Austria <note>The Habsburg dynasty.</note> under a lucky omen.

I withdraw myself from here to other matters that are better suited to my strengths. Yet I will not plant my foot in that part of my profession where I have a rivalry with my fellow soldiers <note>His fellow astronomers and scholars.</note>.

<summary>Kepler continues his military allegory, framing the planet Mars as a legendary Roman conqueror who has finally been "captured" by Kepler’s mathematical labor and presented to Emperor Rudolph II. He contrasts his own humble scholarly life with the grand history of the Roman Empire and the Habsburg dynasty.</summary>

<keywords>Mars, Rudolph II, panegyric, Romulus and Remus, Roman Empire, House of Austria, military metaphor, patronage</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication of the *Astronomia Nova* to Emperor Rudolph II. Kepler continues the metaphor of the planet Mars as a prisoner of war, captured by the "chains" of his mathematical calculations. He distinguishes between the astrological celebrations of the court and his own astronomical triumph.</meta>

<sig>(**) 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: awaken- (written as suscit-)</meta>

Indeed, let those people enjoy another kind of joy: seeing him bound by the chains of **Calculation** <note>original: "Calculi" — referring to the mathematical computations Kepler used to "trap" the planet's orbit</note>, he who so often escaped their hands and eyes, and was accustomed to making their most important prophecies void—prophecies concerning War, Victory, Empire, military rank, mastery, games, and finally even life itself, whether cut short or prolonged. Let them congratulate Your Majesty <note>original: "M<sup>ti</sup>. V<sup>æ</sup>." — abbreviation for Majestati Vestrae</note> on the Lord of the Nativity <term>Lord of the Nativity: in astrology, the planet that has the most influence over a person's birth chart</term> being brought under power, or rather, reconciled. For, according to their testimony, *Mars* rules over *Scorpio*, which holds the *heart of heaven* <term>heart of heaven: the Midheaven, or the highest point in a chart, representing one's career and public life</term>; he is exalted in *Capricorn*, which is rising; in *Cancer*, where the *Moon* has entered, he is accustomed to play a trigonic game of dice <note>original: "ludere ſolet aſtragalis luſum trigonicum" — a pun on the "trine," a 120-degree astrological aspect, and a game of knucklebones</note>; in *Leo*, where the *Sun* takes up residence, he is a familiar acquaintance. Finally, he is the ruler of *Aries*, under which *Germany* is believed to be subject, and he holds empire in clear agreement with Your Sacred Imperial Majesty <note>original: "S<sup>a</sup>. C<sup>a</sup>. M<sup>te</sup>. V<sup>a</sup>." — abbreviation for Sacra Caesarea Majestati Vestrae</note>.

Therefore, let them take up this part of the triumph; I will give them no cause for quarreling on such a festive day. Let this freedom pass among the military jokes <note>original: "jocos militares" — a reference to the Roman custom where soldiers sang mocking or lighthearted songs during a general's triumphal procession</note>. I myself shall turn to *Astronomy*, and riding in the triumphal chariot, I will explain the remaining glory of our captive—which is known particularly to me—and all the reasons for the war waged and finished.

For we must not hold him without honor, whom the eternal *Architect* of this world, the common Father of the Stars and Men, **JEHOVAH** <note>original: "JOVA"</note>, placed in the front rank of visible bodies; so that in an everlasting course through the ethereal regions, he might serve as a soldier for the glory of his *Creator*. And [he was placed there so that] by a criminal reproach of laziness and ignorance, [he might awaken] the minds of men, which are numbed by a deep lethargy...

<summary>Kepler presents his astronomical discovery as a military triumph, contrasting the astrological predictions of others with his own mathematical "capture" of the planet Mars for the Emperor. He acknowledges Mars's divine placement in the heavens as a challenge meant to stir human intellect from its laziness.</summary>

<keywords>Mars, Rudolph II, astrology, calculation, Astronomia Nova, triumph, trigonic aspect, Germany, Creator, lethargy</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication of Johannes Kepler's "Astronomia Nova" to Emperor Rudolph II. The previous page ended with the catchword "awaken-" (suscit-), referring to how the divine order of the universe incites human curiosity.</meta>

...to awaken him, exercise him with its excursions, and by inciting him, draw him toward the heavens to investigate the praises of his Creator.

This is that most powerful Tamer of human inventions: who, having mocked all the expeditions of astronomers, shattered their machines, and routed their hostile forces, had securely possessed the Secret of his Empire, guarded through all past ages. He had carried out his courses most freely and without restraint, so that that great Priest of Nature, the most famous of the Latins, C. Pliny <note>original: "C. Plinius" — Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the Roman author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*</note>, raised the chief complaint: **THAT THE STAR OF MARS IS UNOBSERVABLE.** <note>original: "MARTIS INOBSERVABILE SIDVS ESSE" — quoting Pliny’s *Natural History*, Book 2, regarding the difficulty of tracking Mars's retrograde motion</note>

The story goes that Georg Joachim Rheticus <note>original: "Georgium Joachimum Rheticum" — (1514–1574) the mathematician and student of Copernicus who was instrumental in the publication of *De revolutionibus*</note>, a famous disciple of Copernicus in the memory of our fathers, and who first dared to desire the restoration of Astronomy and soon strove for it with observations and inventions that were not to be despised: while he stuck fast in wonder at the motion of Mars and could not explain it to himself, he fled to the oracle of his own familiar spirit <term>familiar spirit: a personal guardian or "genius" often invoked by Renaissance thinkers to explain sudden intellectual breakthroughs or divine inspiration</term>. Whether he did this to test the spirit’s learning (if the gods please!) or out of an uncontrollable desire for the truth, they say this cruel patron, becoming exasperated, seized the troublesome questioner by the hair and repeatedly dashed his head against the overhanging ceiling; then, having let him go, he threw his body down onto the floor, adding this response: *"This is the motion of Mars."* 

Rumor is an evil, than which nothing else is more harmful to a good reputation; for it is as tenacious of the false and the wicked as it is a messenger of the truth. Yet it is not incredible that Rheticus himself, when his speculations were not succeeding, rose up in a furor with a disturbed spirit and struck his head against the wall. For what wonder is it if the same thing happened <note>original catchword: "accide-" — beginning the word "acciderit" (happened)</note>

<summary>Kepler discusses the historical difficulty of understanding the orbit of Mars, citing Pliny the Elder's claim that it is "unobservable" and recounting a legend of the astronomer Rheticus's violent frustration with the planet's movements.</summary>
<keywords>Mars, Astronomia Nova, Georg Joachim Rheticus, Pliny the Elder, planetary motion, history of astronomy, astronomical difficulty</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication of Johannes Kepler's *Astronomia Nova* to Emperor Rudolph II. The previous page discussed the difficulties of observing Mars and mentioned the astronomer Rheticus seeking divine or supernatural aid to understand its motion.</meta>

...happened to Rheticus, the challenger of Mars, what once happened to Gaius Octavius Augustus Caesar; when, under the leadership of Quintilius Varus <note>original: "Quintilio Varo" — Publius Quinctilius Varus (46 BC–9 AD), the Roman general who lost three legions at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest</note>, he had lost five legions, which had been surrounded by the enemy Arminius, the fledgling of our Germanic Mars <note>original: "Martis nostri Germanici pullo" — A play on words referring to Arminius (Hermann), the German chieftain who defeated the Romans, and perhaps a nod to the Emperor’s own Germanic territories</note>.

But, as in other empires, so here too the power of our enemy was sustained by nothing more than the popular belief and trepidation of the common people: a feeling which I have always thought should be held in contempt as the way to victory. Indeed, having been moderately well-versed in this theater of Nature, I was convinced—with experience as my teacher—that just as one man does not differ much from another, so neither does one star differ much from another star, nor one enemy from another. For this reason, one should not easily believe the reports of those who rashly spread something unusual about a single individual of the same species.

Above all, however, the diligence of **TYCHO BRAHE** must be praised here—the supreme commander in this <term>military service: Kepler uses "militia" as a metaphor for the rigorous, disciplined work of astronomical observation</term>. Under the auspices of **FREDERICK II** and **CHRISTIAN**, the Kings of Denmark, and finally also of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty, he scouted all the habits of this enemy for us through almost twenty years of continuous nights. He observed every method of its warfare, uncovered all its plans, and, upon his death, left them all written down in his books.

Equipped with these books when I succeeded **BRAHE** in this task, I first ceased to fear an enemy I had already come to know moderately well. Then, having diligently noted the precise moments of time...

<summary>Kepler compares the struggle to understand Mars to a military campaign, praising Tycho Brahe for providing the observational data (the "intelligence") needed to finally conquer the planet's secrets.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Mars, Rheticus, Roman history, military metaphor, celestial observation, Rudolph II</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication of Kepler’s *Astronomia Nova* to Emperor Rudolph II. Kepler is extending the military metaphor, casting himself as a general laying siege to the "enemy" planet Mars using the astronomical data and instruments left to him by Tycho Brahe.</meta>

...to which he <note>Mars</note> was accustomed to return frequently to his former places, as if to his own dens. I directed the **Brahean** machines <note>The high-precision astronomical instruments designed by Tycho Brahe</note> toward that place, equipped with precise <term>sights: "dioptris," the viewing apertures on astronomical instruments used to align them with a star before the invention of the telescope</term>, as if at a certain target. I surrounded every location with a scouting line, while the chariots of the great **Mother Earth** were driven around in a circle <note>A poetic reference to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note>.

However, the business did not succeed without sweat. Often, those machines were missing exactly where their use was most needed; or they were transported by unskilled drivers over muddy roads at a great cost of time and money. At other times, the "discharge" <note>original: "ejaculatus" — likely referring to the projection or sighting of a star's position</note> of certain instruments, not yet fully explored by me, aimed toward locations different from what I had expected. Often the brilliance of the **Sun** or **Moon**, and often a cloudy sky, deceived the eyes of the director. Even more often, the obstruction of the vaporous air <note>A reference to atmospheric refraction, which bends light and makes stars appear in the wrong position</note> deflected the sphere, struck from its straight path. Not infrequently, walls placed at a very oblique angle received the blows in vain, however frequent they were.

To this was added the industry of the enemy in his excursions; his vigilance in ambushes while we were mostly sleeping; and finally his persistence in fighting back. Once one castle was conquered or betrayed, he retreated to another. Nor was the method for conquering all castles the same; nor was the journey from one to the rest easy, but was either intercepted by rivers or hindered by brambles, and for the most part, unknown. Each of these details is written out in its proper place in this commentary.

Meanwhile, in my own camps, what kind of slaughter or calamity did not rage? There was the loss of the most illustrious Leader <note>Tycho Brahe, who died in 1601</note>, mutiny, plague, diseases, and domestic affairs both good and bad, all of which served to drag out the time. Then a new, unforeseen, and terrible enemy appeared from behind, as I reported in my book on the *New Star* <note>Kepler’s work *De Stella Nova* (1606) about the supernova of 1604</note>. At another time, the <term>Tenth Dragon: "Draco decumanus," a play on words referring both to a giant wave (the "decuman" wave) and the "Dragon" (the nodes of the Moon's orbit, where eclipses occur)</term>...

<meta>catchword: -nus</meta>

<summary>Kepler describes the immense practical and theoretical difficulties of observing Mars, comparing his astronomical labor to a grueling military campaign plagued by bad weather, equipment failure, and the death of Tycho Brahe.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Mars, atmospheric refraction, De Stella Nova, astronomical instruments, Earth's orbit, military metaphor</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Kepler’s allegorical dedication to Emperor Rudolph II. Having previously described the difficulty of tracking the planet Mars, Kepler now describes the final stages of the "war" where the planet is finally captured by the laws of mathematics.</meta>

[Typho]nus, with a very long tail, vomiting fires and harassing my camps; the desertion and scarcity of soldiers; the inexperience of recruits; and the head of all troubles, the extreme lack of supplies <note>Kepler likely refers to the chronic lack of funding and the scarcity of reliable observational data</note>.

Finally the enemy, when he saw that I persisted in my purpose and that he was indeed nowhere safe or secure within the circuit of his own kingdom, turned his mind toward plans for peace. Having sent Mother Nature as a mediator, he offered me a confession of victory. Having negotiated for his freedom while remaining within discretionary chains <note>A poetic way of describing how Mars is now "bound" by the mathematical laws Kepler discovered, yet still moves freely in the sky</note>, he shortly after crossed over into my camp with great eagerness, escorted by *Arithmetic and Geometry*.

He did not stop, however—even though after his surrender he has lived in our home under the fair laws of friendship—from spontaneously trying to strike some unknown fears of war into us through hidden deceptions, for he is quite unused to peace. He did this to see if, perhaps, by terrifying us, we might give him an opportunity to laugh at us. But when he saw we were of a brave spirit, he seriously agreed to dwell with us, and having laid aside his pretense of hostility, he proved his loyalty to us.

He asks Your Majesty <note>original: "M^tem. V^am.", abbreviation for "Maiestatem Vestram"</note> for this ONE thing: because he has a great following in the ethereal regions <note>The heavens</note>—for indeed his father is *Jupiter*, his grandfather is *Saturn*, his sister and also his friend (and long ago the chief softener of his bonds) is *Venus*, and his brother and faithful herald is *Mercury*—and because he longs for them and they for him due to the similarity of their characters, he wishes that they too might live among men with him, and become shared participants in the honor with which he himself is treated. May Your Majesty <note>original: "M^tas. V^a.", abbreviation for "Maiestas Vestra"</note> return them to him as soon as possible by means of the remnants of this expedition; for since he has already surrendered, these remnants pose no further danger, [stre-] <note>This is a catchword for the next page, likely "strenue" (strenuously/vigorously)</note>

<summary>Kepler concludes his military allegory by describing the "surrender" of Mars to the tools of Arithmetic and Geometry. He then petitions the Emperor to fund the continued study of the other planets (the "family" of Mars), who remain to be "captured" by science.</summary>

<keywords>Mars, Kepler, Rudolph II, Arithmetic, Geometry, Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, Mercury, celestial mechanics, planetary orbits</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the dedication of the Astronomia Nova. Kepler finishes his extended metaphor of his "war" against the planet Mars by asking for the "sinews of war"—funding—to continue his scientific work, while acknowledging the military environment of the Imperial court in Prague.</meta>

...[and long a constant companion, he wishes to have his affairs] vigorously completed. Regarding this matter, I promptly offer to Your Majesty <note>original: "M^ti. V^ae.", abbreviation for "Maiestati Vestrae"</note> my service, which is not useless (since I am practiced in the most bellicose of matters and knowledgeable of the terrain) and no less faithful than before: praying and beseeching this one thing alone (since frequent conversation with soldiers, captains, and commanders over these past nine years in this court has supplied me with this vocabulary <note>original: "vocem"</note>, just as it has the rest of my speech): that Your Imperial Majesty <note>original: "C^a. M^tas. V^a.", abbreviation for "Caesarea Maiestas Vestra"</note> command the directors of the treasury to think upon the <term>sinews of war</term> <note>original: "nervis belli"; a classical idiom (often attributed to Cicero) meaning that money is the essential strength required to conduct a campaign</note>, and supply me with new funds for the enlisting of soldiers <note>In this metaphor, "enlisting soldiers" refers to hiring assistants or funding the publication of his astronomical research</note>.

I pray for these things as they are matters I know have already been approved by Your Majesty, and I believe they pertain to the glory of God and the immortality of Your August Majesty's Name: to whom I have long ago devoted all my effort, and to whom I now most submissively commend myself.

->The fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Dionysian era 1609.<- <note>March 29, 1609</note>

->To Your Sacred Imperial Majesty,<-

->Your most submissive<-
->Mathematician,<-

->JOHANNES KEPLER.<-

# EPIGRAMS
## ON THESE COMMENTARIES
## REGARDING THE MOTIONS OF MARS.

### URANIA TO KEPLER.

*C E A S E, O son of Kepler, to strive against Mars:*
*Mars submits to no one, unless he submits to himself.*
*In vain, therefore, you attempt to bind him in chains:*
*He who has emerged as a free spirit to countless many.*
<note>Urania is the Muse of Astronomy. Here she begins by warning Kepler that Mars, the god of war and a notoriously "erratic" planet, cannot be conquered.</note>
*So spoke the Muse. But he replied to the Muse thus: What then?*
*Have you forgotten the history of Pallas Athena?*
*Pallas was able to strike down the horrific Mars* <note>original: "Gradivum," a cult name for Mars</note>
*With a stone: at least if you sing the songs of Homer:*
<note>Kepler refers to Book 21 of the Iliad, where the goddess Athena/Pallas knocks Mars down with a heavy boundary stone.</note>
*Why then should he not also now, with the great Minerva assisting,*
*Go under the yoke, however ferocious Mars may be?*
<note>Minerva, like Pallas, represents wisdom and strategic warfare; here she symbolizes scientific intellect.</note>
*Behold this book we have given under the Rudolphine omen,*
*You will say that Mars, even now, endures a hard fate.*
<note>The "Rudolphine omen" refers to the patronage of Emperor Rudolf II, under whose name Kepler’s planetary tables were being prepared.</note>

### ANOTHER.

*T H E Liparean once entangled Mars in nets:*
<note>original: "Lipareius," referring to the god Vulcan, who had his forge on the Lipari Islands.</note>
*When he went into your embraces, O Venus.*
<note>original: "Cytherea," a common epithet for Venus. This refers to the myth where Vulcan caught his wife Venus and Mars in a bronze net.</note>
*Now once again Mars is captured by these same chains:*
*And Venus is not to blame: the fault is yours, Minerva.*
*For indeed Minerva gave these nets to Tycho; and Tycho*
*Gave them to Kepler: who cast them around the legs of Mars.*
<note>This beautifully summarizes the lineage of the discovery: Minerva (Wisdom) inspired Tycho Brahe to collect precise data (the "nets"), which he passed to Kepler to finally "trap" the planet's true path.</note>
*A wondrous thing: Vulcan and the other were great craftsmen:*
*Yet Kepler surpasses both this one and that.*
*The chains of Vulcan lasted only a short time.*
*But on the contrary, these Keplerian chains remain eternal.*

<meta>This page continues the sequence of introductory poems following Kepler's dedication. ### ->AN EXHORTATION<-
# ->BY TYCHO BRAHE,<-
## ->THE GREATEST ASTRONOMER,<-
### ->TO THE DEVOTEES OF ASTRONOMY,<-
### ->APPENDED TO THE RESTORATION OF THE FIXED STARS,<-
### ->*From the Introductory Exercises, Volume 1, Page 295.*<-

**A**nd now the way is paved—a path formerly impassable for many ages, 
At last exhausted by great and watchful labor— 
By which one may climb the peaks of the inaccessible Heaven, 
And penetrate the celestial Houses, the dwellings of the Gods: 
Whether it pleases you to mark the Fixed stars, or those Torches 
Moved in various paths <note>The "Torches moved in various paths" refers to the planets, from the Greek *planētēs* meaning "wanderer."</note>, and to prove the stellar course 
And position, so that the miracles of the Highest **JOVE** <note>original: "JOVÆ"; here Tycho uses the name of the king of the gods to refer to the Creator.</note> might be established. 
Therefore come, O youths, in whom there is a sharp and high vigor 
Of intellect, and the favor of Genius; you into whom, from birth, 
Noble Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy.</note> has inspired a Divine Love of Heaven, 
And granted that you hold the Earth and all earthly things 
Second to ethereal goods: you who do not care for the reckless 
Judgments of the crowd, or the harsh voices of the idle; 
Sending the moles to live in dark caves, 
So that they remain perpetually blind, just as they wish to be: 
Breathe eagerly here; tend toward this goal, leaving the common people behind; 
Nor deprive the Mind—which is a god-like part of Heaven— 
Of this ancestral good; bring your study and labor 
To this cause with one mind; so that it may be allowed to aid the weary King 
**ALFONSO** <note>King Alfonso X of Castile (1221–1284), who sponsored the "Alfonsine Tables," which were the standard for planetary positions before Tycho and Kepler.</note>, who just now, as a successor, carried a weight 
Not equal to his strength—the weight of neighboring **ATLAS** <note>In mythology, Atlas held up the heavens; Tycho implies that Alfonso tried to uphold the science of astronomy but struggled under its inaccuracies.</note>; 
And at the same time, that the great **COPERNICUS** may feel 
Prompt help; lest, while he, trusting, attempts to apply himself 
To the Herculean labor, he should succumb to the unjust burden: 
<margin>* Understand this as the falling of the poles. For here he accuses the imperfection of Astronomy and the ignorance of it; but not indeed the Hypotheses of Copernicus, which make the Earth move.</margin>
And so the poles, deprived of the columns of Atlas and Alcides <note>Alcides is another name for Hercules, who briefly took the weight of the sky from Atlas.</note>, 
Already tottering, may be forced to suffer a huge ruin, 
And at the same time moving the Earth from its station\*, 
A lodging-house of barbarism (which thick ignorance of the sky 
Will produce), disturbing all men, and cattle, and wild beasts 
By a doubtful fall, and mixing the halls of the World 
With blind darkness and ancient Chaos. 
Prohibit this wickedness, and meet the impending loss, 
And with me climb high Olympus with strong 
Forces, so that we may timely close the split cracks, 
And stabilize the ceilings of Heaven with new crossbeams, 
Before the whole Machine <note>original: "Machina"; a common Renaissance term for the structured universe or "World Machine."</note> falls apart.

<summary>A poetic exhortation by Tycho Brahe calling for young astronomers to restore the accuracy of celestial science, which he portrays as a crumbling building supported by overmatched figures like King Alfonso and Copernicus. Tycho emphasizes the divine nature of the mind and the urgent need to stabilize the "Machine" of the world through better observations.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Copernicus, King Alfonso X, Urania, restoration of astronomy, fixed stars, celestial mechanics, Atlas, Hercules, World Machine</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Exhortation" by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, begun on the previous page. Tycho concludes his call for a worthy successor to his astronomical work, which is then followed by a poetic response from Johannes Kepler (the "Author of the Work"). Kepler acknowledges his humbler social standing compared to the noble Tycho but asserts his shared spiritual devotion to the stars.</meta>

Who is present here, then, to earn the beautiful Crown,
Conspicuous with pure gold <note>original: "Obryzo"; referring to gold refined by fire.</note>, gems, ivory, and glowing pyrope <note>original: "Pyropo"; a fiery-red gemstone or gold-copper alloy mentioned by Ovid.</note>,
A crown more firm and lasting through the ages,
Who wishes to join his soul to the heavenly spirits?
Who among the Earth-dwellers, whom the infinite World
Contains, will be granted such sublime things in his heart?
Who yearns to acknowledge the Author of the World, through
The many wonders of the sky beheld in the vast Heavens?
Do you all remain silent alike before such great questions?
Why does it help to mutter? The hand must be applied to the labor:
So that at last the mysteries of the hidden sky may lie open.
If ambition, greed, ignorance, or luxury
Pull some back from such high daring and thrust them to the depths:
At least let them spare others, and not delay the greatest benefits.
I myself, if the gods breathe upon me with a favorable countenance,
<margin>Theu.</margin>
And grant that I may overcome any obstacles on high
With a constant spirit, just as I have until now; I will strive
With all my might to spread open the inner chambers of the great Sky
For those born of earth, and to reveal the hidden recesses.
Only You, wise Founder of wonderful Olympus,
Grant your favor and bring help to one noting your stupendous deeds.

### THE AUTHOR OF THE WORK RESPONDS.

**O** Hero, shining in lineage and high-born descent,
To whom a certain origin of a heavenly mind, above all others,
Has granted both to excel in deeds and to reach out in song,
And by your encouragement to add new life to those who are dying:
Why do you fatigue with flames and wind a soul that is trembling
For what you desire, and which has long nourished such great fires?
For although such great undertakings, surpassing my strength,
Require no other masters than your Muse <note>The "Muse" here refers to Tycho's own inspiration and astronomical expertise.</note> provides;
And Nature, by the law of my birth, gave me a talent
Smaller than my Spirit, and arms weaker than my talent:
Yet the Ninth of the Sisters <note>Urania, the Muse of Astronomy.</note> HAS INSPIRED A DIVINE LOVE OF THE HEAVENS.
What does dire love not compel mortal hearts to do?
That love gave me talent, that love gave me strong arms,
Animating me with an unequal hope. But indeed, because of unjust Juno <note>In this context, Juno likely represents worldly status or the obstacles of fortune that favored the noble Tycho over the commoner Kepler.</note>
We are split into contrary pursuits with an unequal countenance,
Both You and I: to You she gave the material for cultivating
Virtue; to me she denies the hard things: the tide returns to the same place;
To keep me from ethereal places, and, with the theft of Prometheus <note>A reference to Prometheus stealing fire from the gods; Kepler suggests he must "steal" the light of knowledge since he lacks Tycho's wealth and status.</note>
Spurring me on, to guard the sacred Fires more closely.
Therefore she burdens you with large resources, with the glitter of metal
Dazzling your eyes, so that they might be sluggish toward the lights
Of heaven, and might choose to join themselves to purple pageantry,

<summary>Tycho Brahe concludes his call for a successor to master the heavens, after which Johannes Kepler responds, accepting the challenge despite his lack of noble wealth, driven by a "divine love" for astronomy.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Johannes Kepler, Urania, Astronomy, scientific vocation, Prometheus, Juno, celestial crown</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the response of the "Author of the Work" (Johannes Kepler) to Tycho Brahe’s introductory poem. Kepler is responding to Tycho's call for a successor, acknowledging the differences in their social status while asserting their shared intellectual mission.</meta>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;[He] whom the flattering hissing of the common breeze follows,
And whom neglected fortune might threaten with unspeakable grief.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Good luck to your brave spirit, Victor <note>original: "Victor"; here Kepler addresses Tycho as a "conqueror" of the heavens.</note> over both the Divine and the Human,
And over your own affections: you who, having approved with the **eye of Reason** <note>original: "Rationis ocello"; a metaphor for intellectual or mathematical insight.</note>
Those things which must be pursued, and having followed with constant daring,
Were able to scorn the wealth passed down from your father.
Cease to invite companions to this private praise,
Or to write words upon the flowing rivers: Virtue and
Riches do not fit well together; the Pole and the
Earth stand immensely apart, and respect for one is slight in the other.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And as for me, the powerful Goddess <note>Fortune or Nemesis.</note> has so far spurned me and envied me
Immense honor; confining my great vows within narrow
Limits, she has indulged nothing that I could scorn
As being secondary to the Muses, or oppose to my care for the stars:
And her hatred would have conquered, and stood in the way of great daring,
And the envious **Rhamnusia** <note>original: "Rhamnusia"; an epithet for Nemesis, the goddess of retribution/fortune, who had a famous temple at Rhamnus.</note> would have pressed my spirit—though it is
Capable of flying through the heavenly heights—down to the ground; had not,
At the first crossroads of my life, the love of singing
The secrets of the heavens reached me first, following in your footsteps.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, surveying with my mind the orbits worn by the **Wanderers** <note>original: "Erronibus"; a traditional term for the planets.</note>,
And the immense threats and the gaping intervals,
The walls of the World, destined to fall because no columns were placed;
While dark night suppresses the causes, and the crowd of wise men
Sleeps, secure in the truth of the **Prussian Master** <note>original: "Pruteno Magistro"; referring to Erasmus Reinhold, whose "Prutenic Tables" (based on Copernicus) were the standard astronomical reference before Kepler and Tycho.</note>:
I approach, trusting to succeed in so great a burden,
**AND TO STABILIZE THE CEILINGS OF HEAVEN WITH NEW CROSSBEAMS;** <note>This refers to Kepler’s theory in this book that the five Platonic solids act as the structural "beams" or spacers between the planetary spheres.</note>
The **Samian** <note>original: "Samius"; referring to Pythagoras of Samos, who proposed the harmony of the spheres.</note> gave the famous material, the five figures,
**Euclid** gave the Rule, and the renowned Pallas gave the Mind;
**Urania**, redoubling her applause through more than one interpreter,
Sang along to the celebrated triumph, joyful in its success.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You, **Brahe**, wondered at the daring and the sweet labor,
Although, having conceived your own sense of things, you were unwilling to depart from it,
Doubting much concerning the Earth, and much concerning the ether:
Yet it pleased you to enroll me into the number of your own,
To open your nights <note>A reference to Tycho's years of nocturnal observations.</note> to me, and the discoveries of a long
Time; and to let a clear Light shine upon my undertakings.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And would that you had lived! Neither would the Fates have snatched away
The rewards worthy of such great preparation, nor the triumphs so well deserved:
You would have experienced that no other Orbs reveal themselves
To the sight and the subtle instruments—the **INNER SANCTUARIES OF THE GREAT SKY**—
Than those which my crossbeams make firm.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, since the Goddesses have snatched away the Master in his haste;
And since his removal disturbs our festive days and adorned joys—
The patron who ought to have gladdened them—
What shall I do? Except that, having venerated You in the image of my Mind,
I shall bring You back to life, O manifest Hero, through my art.

<summary>Kepler responds to Tycho Brahe, explaining how he pursued astronomy despite his poverty and how his "Mysterium Cosmographicum" (the five solids) provides the structural "beams" for the universe. He laments Tycho's recent death and vows to honor his legacy through his scientific work.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Johannes Kepler, Platonic solids, Prussian Tables, Erasmus Reinhold, Rhamnusia, geometry, planetary orbits, Urania</keywords>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You will stand as a Great Priest in a starry robe.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Here where the altars rise in the blue Temple,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;built for the Creator **G O D**; six paths circle
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;in order, with as many lamps in rapid whirling:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the middle is the Hearth, and the fires of eternal Light.
<margin>The opinion of Aristarchus and Copernicus.</margin>
<note>Kepler describes the heliocentric (Sun-centered) system here, where the Sun is the "Hearth" and the six planets known at the time—Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—circle it.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I approach as a suppliant, and these my labors written in a
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;learned book—the sweetest incense to the **P A R E N T** of **T H I N G S**,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;with your patience; I hand them to you with lifted hands:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I join chaste prayers: **M A Y T H E W I S E F O V N D E R O F O L Y M P V S**

### By the same [author], an Elegy written in a Friendship Book next to the signature and Motto of Brahe,
<note>original: "Philothesio"; a "Book of Friends" or *album amicorum*, a popular 16th-century tradition where scholars signed each others' books with mottos.</note>
->**L O O K I N G &nbsp; U P &nbsp; I &nbsp; L O O K &nbsp; D O W N.**<-
<note>original: "S V S P I C I E N D O &nbsp; D E S P I C I O"; Tycho Brahe's personal motto, suggesting that by contemplating the heavens, one learns to look down upon the vanity of earthly life.</note>

**G**ive place, Noble one, nor disdain the one who follows:
*Whatever I am, they are your gifts; whatever I shall be.*
Hitherto having wondered at the **E M P T Y C A R E S O F M E N**,
In You alone I cease to play my satire.
Your monuments are the rest for my cares:
I was a shadow without you; with you as a father, I shall be a body.
Although the Earth, bound to me, weaves aerial circles;
Let that same Earth stand fixed for you in the place of the Center:
<note>Kepler diplomatically acknowledges their different worldviews: Kepler believed the Earth moved around the Sun, while Tycho believed the Earth remained stationary at the center of the universe.</note>
Indeed, I trace these things back to the ancient Masters:
nor, while I am alive, have they displeased you.
Yet I do not point my weak eyes toward the glowing fires of **Mars** <term>Mavortis</term>
except through your **Nights**, <note>A tribute to Tycho's decades of precise nocturnal observations, which were far superior to any previous data.</note>
<margin>* As if in folio 149 of this work, in the diagram at the letter K, the star of Mars were depicted as an Eye.</margin>
Unless **L O O K I N G U P** you had rightly guided the **sighting-rule** <term>Dioptram</term>,
<note>A dioptra is a classical surveying and astronomical instrument for measuring positions.</note>
I could not from there **L O O K D O W N** upon the course of the Earth;
And I would not measure the swift steps, and the heights meeting the **Goat**,
<note>The constellation Capricorn.</note>
And how great a part of the path the **Sun** <note>original: "Phœbe"</note> gives to the Center:
How it flees and seeks the Sun with equal step,
Yet is not whirled by the same snatching movement;
But toward the fountain it acquires strength by going,
And departing further it becomes weak in turn:
<note>Here Kepler poetically describes what would become his Second Law of Planetary Motion: planets move faster when closer to the Sun ("the fountain") and slower when further away.</note>
From where seven Minds in order carry the seven globes,
And the eighth Spirit from the Father Sun;
And Nature is free with innumerable revolutions,
And nine times five **Gods** perish from the flock.
<margin>* Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book II, Chapter 8.</margin>
<note>Kepler references Aristotle's theory of "Intelligences" or spirits that move the spheres, while subtly moving toward a more physical, mathematical explanation.</note>
Deceive the calculation by ten minutes, Tycho, deceive it:
Which, unless You [do], no one would count; all those things will collapse.
O the cares of men, O how much emptiness there is in things!
If once there is no other way to the stars.

## AN EPIGRAM BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## ON THE STUDIES OF TYCHO 
## BRAHE.

> ->*Tycho described the paths of the Sun and the fixed stars;*<-
> ->*He joined the Moon’s course to them, and then he passed away.*<-
> ->*Phaethon grieves that he climbed into the light-bearing Chariot;*<-
> <note>original: "Phaethon"; in Greek mythology, the son of the Sun god who died when he lost control of his father's chariot. The poet suggests Tycho, unlike Phaethon, mastered the heavenly paths without disaster.</note>
> ->*But this skillful care, Tycho, did you no harm:*<-
> ->*Endymion fell into eternal sleep, loved by the Goddess of the Crossroads;*<-
> <note>original: "Trivia"; an epithet for the goddess Diana or the Moon, who was said to have fallen in love with the mortal Endymion and cast him into an eternal sleep so she could visit him forever.</note>
> ->*An eternal love for the Moon also lulls <term>you</term> to sleep.*<-
> <note>The word "te" (you) is highlighted as a technical term in the original to emphasize the personal connection between the astronomer and his celestial subject.</note>

# TO THE READER
# GREETINGS.

**I** had intended to speak to you at greater length (Reader), were it not that the weight of political duties—with which I am more than usually occupied these days—and the hurried departure of our Kepler, who is at this very moment set to go to Frankfurt, have left me barely even this small opportunity for writing. Therefore, I thought I should advise you in just three words: do not let the freedom Kepler takes in dissenting from Brahe in certain matters—especially physical arguments—disturb you. This in no way harms the work of the <term>RUDOLPHINE TABLES</term> <note>The *Tabulae Rudolphinae*, a massive star catalog and planetary duty list named after Emperor Rudolf II.</note>, and such disagreement has been familiar to all philosophers since the Founding of the World. Furthermore, you will learn from the Work itself that he built upon the foundation of Brahe—that is, upon Brahe's own restoration of the Fixed Stars and the Sun—and that all the material (namely the Observations) was gathered through Brahe's labor. In the meantime, enjoy this remarkable Work of Kepler amidst these tumults of rebellions and wars repeatedly sprouting up (while the Republic of Letters suffers along with the State), as a <term>PRECURSOR</term> <note>original: "Prodromo"; a preliminary publication or scout that comes before the main body of work.</note> of the <term>TABLES</term> and, after them, the <term>OBSERVATIONS</term> which are appearing more slowly under this name. Pray with us to God, Greatest and Best, for more rapid progress of this so greatly desired Work in the future, and for happier times.

->FRANZ GANSNEB TENGNAGEL<-
<note>Tengnagel was Tycho Brahe's son-in-law and a nobleman who took a lead role in managing Tycho's scientific estate after his death.</note>
->OF CAMP, Councilor to His<-
->Sacred Imperial Majesty.<-

Tengnagel's note defends Kepler's right to disagree with Tycho on physics while affirming that the data itself remains rooted in Tycho's observations.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION
## INTO THIS WORK.

<margin>On the difficulty of reading and writing astronomical books.</margin>
**T**he condition for writing mathematical books, especially astronomical ones, is most harsh today. Unless you maintain the genuine subtlety of the propositions, instructions, proofs, and conclusions, the book will not be truly mathematical; but if you do maintain it, the reading becomes extremely tedious, especially in the Latin language, which lacks articles and that particular grace which Greek possesses when it speaks through mathematical symbols. Consequently, there are very few suitable readers today; the rest generally reject such works. How many mathematicians are there who can endure the labor of reading through the *Conics* of <term>Apollonius of Perga</term>?
<note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BCE) was a Greek geometer famous for his work on conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas). Kepler mentions him here because his work is notoriously difficult, much like the astronomy Kepler is about to present.</note>
Yet that material is of the kind that is far more easily expressed by shapes and lines than astronomy is.

**I myself**, who am called a mathematician, while re-reading this work of mine, feel my brainpower wearying as I recall from the diagrams back to my mind the meaning of the proofs—meanings which I myself originally transferred from my mind into these diagrams and text. Thus, while I try to remedy the obscurity of the subject by inserting longer explanations, I now seem to myself to be talkative—a contrary vice in a mathematical matter.

Indeed, the very wordiness of phrases has its own obscurity, no less than concise brevity. The latter escapes the eyes of the mind, while the former distracts them; the one needs light, the other suffers from an excess of glare. In the first, the vision is not moved; in the second, it is plainly blinded.

For that reason, I have decided to assist the reader’s understanding, as much as possible, through a clear introduction to this work.

I wanted this introduction to be twofold. First, I present a Synoptic Table <note>A "synoptic table" is a summary chart or overview intended to show the relationship between all parts of the work at once.</note> of all the chapters of the book. I believe its usefulness will be this: because the material is far from common knowledge, and the terms and methods within it are varied—yet possess great similarity and kinship in their parts—all the terms and methods, when placed next to each other and grasped at a single glance, will explain one another through mutual comparison. For example: I argue about the natural causes which, being unknown, forced the Ancients to posit an <term>Equant</term> circle or "Equating point." 
<note>The Equant was a mathematical tool used by Ptolemy to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down. Kepler will eventually replace this "imaginary" point with physical causes.</note>
I do this in two places: specifically, in the third and fourth parts. A reader engaged with the third part might think I am already dealing with the "first inequality," which resides in the motions of individual planets separately. However, that condition only applies in the fourth part. In the third part, as the Synopsis indicates, I argue about that Equant which, under the name of the "second inequality," commonly varies the motions of all planets and reigns primarily in the Theory of the Sun. Thus, the Synoptic Table will serve to distinguish these matters.

<margin>An introduction into this work for the sake of students of Physics.</margin>
But truly, not even a Synopsis helps everyone equally. For there will be those to whom this table (which I offer as a thread to lead one back out of the labyrinth of this Work) will seem more entangled than the Gordian Knot. For their sake, many things must be gathered here at the front in a heap—things which, being scattered through the work, might not be easily noticed in passing. I will reveal—chiefly for the sake of those who study Physics, and who are angry at ME, or rather at COPERNICUS, and even at the furthest reaches of ANTIQUITY, because the foundations of the sciences have been shaken by the <term>Motion of the Earth</term>—I will, I say, faithfully reveal the purpose of the main chapters that relate to this business. I will set before their eyes all the principles of the proofs upon which my conclusions, so hateful to them, rely.

Once they see this faithfully provided, they will afterwards have a free choice: either to read through and perceive the proofs themselves with the greatest labor; or to trust me, a mathematician by profession, regarding the sincere and geometric method I have applied. They, for their part, should turn to these principles of proof thus placed before their eyes and examine them, certain that unless these principles are overturned, the demonstration built upon them will not fall. I will do the same even when, in the manner of Physicists, I mix probable things with necessary ones, and from these mixtures construct a probable conclusion. Since I have mixed "celestial physics" with astronomy in this work, no one should wonder that some conjectures are also employed. For this is the nature of Physics, of Medicine, and of all sciences which use other axioms besides the most certain indications of the eyes.

<margin>On the sects of Astronomers.</margin>
Thus, let the reader understand that there are two sects of astronomers: one distinguished by its leader PTOLEMY and for the most part by the citation of the Ancients; the other attributed to more recent authors, though it is the most ancient of all. The former treats each of the wandering stars separately and assigns causes of motion to each in its own orbit; the latter compares the planets with each other and deduces whatever is found to be common in their motions from the same common cause. And this sect is again subdivided; for the cause that makes the planets appear...

He provides a guide for readers to navigate his complex proofs, particularly regarding the Motion of the Earth and the use of the Equant.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION.

...stationary and retrograde <note>original: "stationarios retrogradofque"; these are the apparent stops and backward motions planets seem to make in the sky.</note> motions, **COPERNICVS**, along with the most ancient **ARISTARCHO** <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE) was an ancient Greek astronomer who proposed a sun-centered model long before Copernicus.</note>, attributes them to the movement of the Earth, our dwelling place; to which **I** also subscribe. **TYCHO BRAHEVS**, however, attributes the cause of those motions to the Sun, in whose vicinity he says the <term>eccentric circles</term> <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit whose center is not the Earth or Sun, but a point offset from them.</note> of all five planets are connected as if by a certain knot (not a bodily one, but a mathematical one), and that this knot, together with the body of the Sun, revolves around the immobile Earth.

Among these three opinions about the world, each one has certain unique features by which they are distinguished. But those specific details can be so easily corrected and changed that these three principal opinions (as far as astronomy or the appearances of the heavens are concerned) are in effect perfectly equivalent and yield the same results.

<margin>The twofold purpose of the work.</margin>
**MY PURPOSE NOW** in this work is primarily to reform astronomical doctrine (especially regarding the motion of **MARS**) in all three forms; doing so in such a way that what we calculate from the tables corresponds to the appearances of the heavens, which until now has not been possible with enough certainty. Indeed, in the month of **August** in the year of Christ **1608**, the star of **MARS** was nearly four degrees ahead of the position predicted by the **PRVTENIC** calculus <note>The Prutenic Tables (1551) were the standard astronomical tables of the time, based on Copernicus’s work, but they had become increasingly inaccurate.</note>. In **August** and **September** of the year **1593**, the error was nearly five degrees; this error has now been entirely removed in my new calculation.

<margin>On the physical causes of motion.</margin>
Meanwhile, as I perform this and achieve it successfully, I even digress into the Metaphysics of **ARISTOTELIS**, or rather I investigate celestial physics and the natural causes of motions. From this consideration, clear arguments finally emerge by which only the opinion of **COPERNICVS** regarding the world (with a few things changed) is proved true, while the other two are proved false, etc.

Indeed, all things are so connected, intertwined, and mixed together that although I tried many paths—partly those worn by the ancients, partly those built in imitation of them—to reach a corrected method of astronomical calculation, no other path succeeded except for the one that relies on the very physical causes of motions which I establish in this work.

<margin>First step toward them. The planes of all six eccentrics meet in the single center of the solar body.</margin>
**TOWARD INVESTIGATING** the physical causes of motions, the first step was to demonstrate that the meeting point of those eccentrics does not happen at any other place (near the Sun) except in the very center of the solar body, contrary to what **COPERNICVS** and **BRAHEVS** believed.

If this correction of mine were introduced into the **PTOLEMAIC** opinion, it would require **PTOLEMÆVS** to investigate the motion not of the center of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in old models to explain complex planetary paths.</note> (around which the epicycle moves uniformly), but of some other point, which is at the same distance from that center as the center of the Sun's orbit is from the Earth in **PTOLEMY’s** model, and indeed on the same line or parallel ones.

**I COULD BE REPROACHED** by the followers of **BRAHE**, who might call me a rash innovator. They would say that since they followed the accepted opinion of the ancients and placed the meeting point of the eccentrics near the Sun rather than in it, they still managed to build a calculation that matches the heavens. And in the translation of Brahean numbers into the Ptolemaic form, **PTOLEMÆVS** could say to me that, as long as he holds and expresses the observations, no other eccentric is considered by him than that which is described by the center of the epicycle, around which the epicycle moves uniformly. Therefore, I must look again and again at what I am doing, lest by using a new method, I fail to provide what has already been provided by them in the old method.

Therefore, to meet this objection, it was demonstrated in the first part of the work that through this new method, the very same things can be accomplished or provided that were provided through the method of those ancients.

**IN THE SECOND** part of the work, I have addressed the matter itself, and I have expressed the positions of **MARS** in <term>apparent opposition</term> to the **SVN** no less—indeed, much more correctly—through my method than they had expressed the positions of **MARS** in <term>mean opposition</term> to the **SVN** through the old method.
<note>Mean opposition refers to when a planet is opposite the Sun's average position, while apparent opposition is when it is opposite the Sun's actual seen position. Kepler realized the latter was the true physical center of the system.</note>

Meanwhile, throughout the entire second part (as far as geometric demonstrations from observations are concerned), I left it in suspense as to who was doing it more correctly, they or I; since we both attained several observations (which act as the rule set for our mechanical models). However, I showed in the first part, especially in Chapter **6**, that my method is consistent with physical causes, while their old method is inconsistent.

But finally, in the **Fourth** part of the work, **Chapter 52**, through certain other observations no less infallible than the previous ones—which their old method could not reach, but mine reached most beautifully—I demonstrated most solidly that the eccentric of **MARS** is situated so that the center of the solar body itself falls on the line of its <term>apsides</term> <note>Apsides are the points in an orbit where the planet is closest to or farthest from the center.</note>, and not some point nearby; therefore, all the eccentrics meet in the **SVN** itself.

To show that this holds true not only regarding Longitude but also regarding Latitude, I demonstrated the same thing in the **Fifth** part from observed latitudes in **Chapter 67**.

He details how his corrections drastically improve the accuracy of Mars's predicted positions compared to older tables.</summary>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

These things could not have been demonstrated earlier in the work, because these astronomical demonstrations require an exact knowledge of the causes of the **second inequality** <note>The "second inequality" refers to the apparent backward (retrograde) motion of planets, which we now know is caused by the Earth passing them in its orbit.</note> in the motion of the planets. Similarly, in the third part, something new and unknown to my predecessors had to be uncovered first, etc.

<margin>The second step toward the physical causes of motions. Even in the theory of the Sun or Earth, the Equant <note>An "equant" is a mathematical point used by ancient astronomers to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down; Kepler found that even the Earth's orbit required a similar adjustment.</note> rules; therefore the Sun's eccentricity must be bisected.</margin>
**FOR INDEED**, I demonstrated in the third part that whether the old method using the Sun’s "mean" (average) motion is valid, or my new method using the "apparent" (actual observed) motion, either way, something of the causes of the **first inequality** <note>The "first inequality" describes the actual variations in a planet's speed as it moves through its own elliptical orbit.</note> is mixed into the second inequality, which affects all planets. Thus, I demonstrated to **PTOLEMY** that his <term>epicycles</term> <note>Smaller circles centered on the circumference of a larger circle, used to explain planetary paths.</note> do not have their physical centers at those points around which their motions are uniform. Likewise, I demonstrated to **COPERNICUS** that the circle in which the Earth moves around the **SUN** does not have its physical center at that point around which its motion is regular and uniform. So too, I demonstrated to **TYCHO BRAHE** that the circle in which the "intersection" or "node" of the aforementioned <term>eccentrics</term> <note>Off-center circular orbits.</note> travels does not have its physical center at that point around which its motion is regular and uniform. For if I grant to **BRAHE** that the intersection of the eccentrics differs from the center of the **SUN**, he must then say that the circuit of that intersection—which matches the Sun's circuit exactly in size and time—is eccentric and shifts toward Capricorn, while the Sun's eccentric circuit shifts toward Cancer. Yet the same thing happens to the epicycles of **PTOLEMY**.

But if I place this intersection or "node" of the eccentrics in the very center of the Solar body, then this circuit—common to both the node and the Sun—is indeed eccentric from the Earth and shifts toward Cancer, but only by *half* the eccentricity <note>Kepler is arguing for "bisecting the eccentricity," a key discovery where the center of the orbit is halfway between the Sun and the point of uniform motion.</note> belonging to the point around which the Sun’s motion is regular and uniform.

And in **COPERNICUS**: the Earth’s eccentric circle indeed shifts toward Capricorn, but only by half of that eccentricity by which the point of uniform motion for the Earth is distant in that same direction of Capricorn.

So in **PTOLEMY**: in those diameters of the epicycles extending from Capricorn to Cancer, there are three points at equal intervals—the two ends distant from the middle—separated by distances which, in proportion to the diameters, equal the total eccentricity of the Sun compared to the diameter of its circuit. Of these three points, those in the middle are the centers of his epicycles; those toward Cancer are the points around which the epicycles' motions are uniform; and finally, those toward Capricorn are the points whose eccentrics we seek *if we follow the apparent motion instead of the mean motion of the Sun*, as if the epicycles were attached to the eccentric at those points. Thus, in every planet's epicycle, the total theory of the **SUN** would be contained, along with all properties of its motions and orbits.

<margin>The Earth moves, the Sun stands still. Physical astronomical arguments.</margin>
With these things demonstrated by an infallible method, the first step toward **Physical causes** has been confirmed, and a new step toward them constructed—most clearly in the opinions of **COPERNICUS** and **BRAHE**, and more obscurely (though probably) in the **PTOLEMAIC** system.

For whether the Earth moves or the Sun moves, it is certainly demonstrated that the body that moves does so in an unequal manner: slowly when it is farther from the resting body, and quickly when it has approached the resting body most closely.

Now, therefore, the difference between the three opinions in Physics appears immediately: through conjectures, certainly, but conjectures no less certain than those of Physicians regarding the use of body parts, or any other physical matters.

First, **PTOLEMY** is dismissed. For who would believe that there are as many "theories of the Sun" (identical to one another, and indeed equal) as there are planets? Especially when one sees in **BRAHE** that a single theory of the Sun suffices for the same tasks? It is, after all, a most accepted axiom in Physics that Nature uses the fewest means possible.

<margin>* Of whom it is most just to make most honorable and grateful mention and memory; since I build this entire edifice upon his foundation, having borrowed all my material from him.</margin>
That **COPERNICUS** is better than **BRAHE** * in celestial physics is proven by many things.

First, **BRAHE** removed those five solar theories from the theories of the planets and traced them back to the centers of the eccentrics, hid them, and forged them into one; but the actual effect produced by those theories he left in the world. For any planet, besides its own proper motion, still moves in reality with the motion of the Sun (according to **BRAHE** no less than **PTOLEMY**), mixing both into one, which results in spiral paths. This happens because **BRAHE** most solidly demonstrated that there are no "solid orbs" <note>Ancient astronomers believed planets were carried on physical, transparent crystal spheres. Tycho Brahe proved these did not exist by observing comets passing through them.</note> in the heavens. **COPERNICUS**, however, entirely stripped the five planets of this external motion, showing it to be a deception caused by the conditions of our sight. Thus, in **BRAHE**, motions are still multiplied in vain, just as they were in **PTOLEMY**.

<margin>II.</margin>
Second, if there are no solid orbs, the condition of the "Intelligences" <note>original: "Intelligentiarum"; many believed that since there were no physical spheres, divine spirits or "souls" must be consciously guiding each planet through its complex path.</note> and "moving souls" would become very difficult; for they would be ordered to look to so many things at once to carry a planet through two mixed motions. At the very least, they would be forced to look simultaneously at the principles, centers, and periods of both motions. But if the Earth moves, I demonstrate that most of these things can be achieved not by "animate" <note>soul-driven</note> faculties, but by physical and magnetic ones. But these are common points. Others follow which arise specifically from the demonstrations on which we now insist.

<summary>Kepler argues that Copernicus’s model is physically superior to Ptolemy’s and Brahe’s because it adheres to the principle of simplicity (parsimony). He demonstrates that all planetary orbits share the Sun's eccentricity and suggests that planetary motion is caused by physical magnetic forces rather than "moving souls."</summary>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

### III.
For if the Earth moves, it has been demonstrated that it receives the laws of its speed and slowness from the measure of its approach to and retreat from the Sun. And yet, the same thing happens to the rest of the planets: they are sped up or slowed down by this approach to and retreat from the Sun. Up to this point, the demonstration of these things is Geometrical.

From this most certain demonstration, it is now gathered by physical conjecture that the source of motion for the five planets is in the **SUN** itself. It is therefore very likely that the source of the Earth's motion is in the same place as the source of the motion of the other five planets: namely, likewise in the **SUN**. It is therefore likely that the Earth moves, since a likely cause for its motion is apparent.

### IV.
On the contrary, it is most likely that the **SUN** stands still in its place at the center of the world—both for other reasons and especially because the source of motion for at least five planets is in it. For whether you follow **COPERNICUS** or **TYCHO BRAHE**, in both systems the source of motion for five planets is in the **SUN**; in **COPERNICUS** it is even the sixth, namely the Earth. It is more likely that the source of all motion remains in its own place rather than being moved.

### V.
But if we follow **BRAHE’S** opinion and say that the **SUN** moves: first, this remains demonstrated—that the **SUN** moves slowly when it goes far away from the Earth and fast when it approaches, and this is not just in appearance, but in reality. For this is the effect of the *Equant* <note>A mathematical tool used to account for the observed speed changes of planets; Kepler proved even the Sun/Earth relationship required one.</note> circle, which I had introduced into the theory of the **SUN** through necessary demonstration.

Upon this most certain conclusion, using the physical conjecture mentioned above, we would have to build this physical philosophy: that the **SUN**, together with that whole massive burden of the five eccentric orbits (to speak crudely), is moved by the Earth—or that the source of motion for the Sun and the five orbits attached to it lies within the Earth.

But let both bodies, the Sun and the Earth, be inspected, and let a judgment be made about both: which one is better suited to be the source of motion for the other? Would the Sun move the Earth, he who moves the rest of the planets? Or would the Earth move the Sun—the mover of all the others and many times larger than itself? Therefore, lest we be forced to concede that the Sun is moved by the Earth (which is absurd), we must grant immobility to the Sun and motion to the Earth.

### VI.
What shall I say about the periodic time of **365 days**? Since this is intermediate in length between the period of **MARS** (687 days) and **VENUS** (225 days), does not the Nature of things cry out with a loud voice that the circuit in which those **365 days** are spent is also located in the middle between the circuits of Mars and Venus around the Sun? And thus, this circuit belongs to the Earth around the Sun, not the Sun around the Earth. But these things belong more properly to my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>Kepler's first book, *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), which attempted to explain the spacing of the planets.</note>; nor should other arguments be mentioned here than those treated in this work.

### VII.
Therefore, for the other metaphysical arguments—drawn from the "dignity" of the star or from Light itself—which favor the Sun's place in the center of the world, see my said booklet and the work of **COPERNICUS**; and there is something in **ARISTOTLE**, Book II of *On the Heavens*, under the name of the Pythagoreans, who understood the Sun by the name "**FIRE**." I touched on some points in the *Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>Kepler’s 1604 work on optics.</note>, Chapter 1, page 7. See also Chapter VI, especially page 225.

<margin>Objections against the motion of the Earth.</margin>
### VIII.
Indeed, concerning why it is fitting for the Earth to orbit outside the center of the world, you will find a metaphysical argument in Chapter IX, page 322 of that book.

I hope for **PARDON** from the reader, however, if I point out certain remedies here against several objections that occupy people's minds and thus steal the light from these arguments. For these are not very far removed from what I dispute in this work concerning the physical causes of planetary motion, especially in the third and fourth parts.

<margin>1. On the motion of heavy things.</margin>
The "motion of heavy things" <note>Kepler is addressing the contemporary understanding of gravity.</note> prevents many from being able to believe that the Earth is moved by an animate or, rather, a magnetic motion. Let them consider the following propositions:

<margin>The doctrine of Gravity is erroneous.</margin>
A mathematical point, whether it is the center of the world or not, cannot move heavy things either effectively or objectively so that they approach it. Let physicists prove that there is such power in a point, which is neither a body nor understood in any way except by relation alone.

It is impossible that the "form" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, the internal essence or soul-like quality of an object.</note> of a stone, by moving its body, should seek out a mathematical point or the center of the world, without regard for the body in which that point is located. Let physicists prove that natural things have a "sympathy" for that which is nothing.

But heavy things do not tend toward the center of the world in this way—as if they were fleeing the edges of a round world. For the proportion by which they are distant from the center of the world is invisible and accomplishes nothing compared to the distance from the edge of the world. And what would be the cause of this hatred? With what power, what wisdom would heavy things need to be endowed so they could accurately flee from an enemy surrounding them on all sides? Or what cleverness would the edges of the world need to pursue such a tiny enemy?

Nor are heavy things driven into the center by the rapid whirling of the "prime mover" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere in the old geocentric system.</note>, as in swirled water. For that motion, if we suppose it exists, is not continued down to these lower regions; otherwise we would feel it and be carried away with it, even the Earth itself. Indeed, we would be snatched away first and the Earth would follow—all of which are absurdities to my opponent. It appears, therefore, that the common doctrine of gravity is erroneous.

<summary>Kepler argues that the Sun must be the center of the solar system because it acts as the physical source of motion for the planets, and he begins to debunk the Aristotelian view of gravity as a tendency toward a mathematical center.</summary>
