-># INTRODUCTION.<-

<sig>(***) 4</sig>

<margin>The true doctrine of gravity.</margin>
The true doctrine of gravity, therefore, rests upon these axioms:

Every material substance, insofar as it is material, is naturally inclined to rest in any place in which it is set alone, outside the sphere of influence <note>original: "extra orbem virtutis" — literally "outside the orb of power," referring to the range of a body's gravitational pull.</note> of a related body.

Gravity is a mutual material tendency between related bodies toward union or conjunction (of the same order of things as the magnetic faculty), such that the Earth attracts a stone much more than the stone seeks the Earth. <term>Magnetic faculty: Kepler viewed gravity as a form of magnetism, a radical step toward seeing the universe as a machine rather than a living being.</term>

Heavy bodies (even if we were to place the Earth at the center of the world) are not carried toward the center of the world because it is the center, but as the center of a rounded related body—namely, the Earth. Therefore, wherever the Earth is located or wherever it is transported by its "vital faculty," <note>Kepler uses "facultate sua animali" (animal or vital faculty), reflecting his early belief that planets possessed a sort of "soul" that guided their movements.</note> heavy bodies are always carried toward it.

If the Earth were not round, heavy bodies would not be carried from all sides in a straight line toward the midpoint of the Earth, but would be carried toward different points from different sides.

If two stones were placed in some location in the world near each other, outside the sphere of influence of a third related body, those stones would come together at an intermediate place, much like two magnetic bodies; each would approach the other by a distance proportional to the other's mass. <note>This is a remarkable precursor to Newton’s law of universal gravitation and the concept of a center of mass.</note>

If the Moon and the Earth were not held back in their circuits by a "vital force" or some other equivalent force, the Earth would ascend toward the Moon by a fifty-fourth part of the distance between them, and the Moon would descend toward the Earth by about fifty-three parts of that distance; there they would be joined—assuming, however, that the substance of each is of one and the same density.

If the Earth ceased to attract its own waters to itself, all the waters of the sea would be lifted up and would flow into the body of the Moon.

<margin>The reason for the ebb and flow of the sea.</margin>
The sphere of the "pulling power" that is in the Moon extends all the way to the Earth, and it lures the waters toward the Torrid Zone <note>The Tropics.</note>, specifically meeting the Moon wherever it is directly overhead. This is imperceptible in enclosed seas, but perceptible where the channels of the Ocean are widest and the waters have a spacious freedom to move back and forth. When this happens, the shores of the lateral zones and climates are left bare, as are any bays that create retreats for the nearby Ocean even under the torrid zone. Thus, as the waters rise in the wider bed of the Ocean, it can happen that in its narrower bays—provided they are not too tightly enclosed—the waters may even seem to flee from the Moon while it is present, because they sink as the supply of water is drawn away to the outside.

But as the Moon swiftly flies across the zenith, since the waters cannot follow so quickly, a tide of the Ocean toward the West occurs under the Torrid Zone until it strikes against the opposite shores and is bent back by them. When the Moon departs, the assembly of waters (or the "army" that is on its way toward the Torrid Zone) is dissolved, being abandoned by the pull that had summoned it. Having gained momentum—as happens in water vessels—it returns and surges back to its own shores, covering them. This momentum created by the Moon's absence then generates another momentum, until the Moon, returning, catches the reins of this momentum, moderates it, and drives it around together with its own motion. Thus, all shores that are equally open are filled at the same hours, while more recessed shores are filled later; some in different ways due to the various entrances of the Ocean.

<margin>The effects of the marine tides.</margin>
From this—to digress briefly—the *Syrtes* <note>Classical name for dangerous quicksands and sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.</note> and heaps of sand are accumulated. Innumerable islands are born or erased in whirlpool-like bends (as in the Gulf of Mexico). It seems that the soft, blessed, and crumbly Earth of the Indies was finally broken through and pierced by this eternal tide and flood, aided by some universal earthquake. For it is reported that in ancient times there was a continuous landmass from the Golden Chersonese <note>The Malay Peninsula.</note> toward the east and south. Now, with the Ocean poured out—the one that was behind, between China and America—those shores of the Moluccas and other neighboring islands, stretched out into the deep as the surface of the sea subsided, suppress the belief in this former continuity.

<margin>The Taprobane of the ancients is lost today.</margin>
Indeed, *Taprobane* <note>A name used by ancient Greeks for a large island in the Indian Ocean, usually identified as Sri Lanka.</note> also seems to have been submerged by this (as is consistent with the reports of the people of Calicut, that some places there were submerged long ago). The Chinese Ocean poured into the Indian Ocean through broken gates, so that today nothing remains of Taprobane except the peaks of mountains, which present the appearance of innumerable islands under the name of the **Maldives**. For that Taprobane was once situated in that location—opposite the mouths of the Indus and the Cape of Kori toward the south—is easy to prove from the Cosmographers and Diodorus Siculus. This is also supported by the fact that in Ecclesiastical History, a certain man is said to have been the common Bishop of Arabia and Taprobane; they were certainly neighbors, not separated by five hundred German miles (indeed, more than a thousand by the routes used in that age) to the East. As for the island today thought to be Taprobane—Sumatra—I believe it was formerly the Golden Chersonese, joined to the Isthmus of India at the city of Malacca. For the Chersonese <note>A peninsula.</note> which we believe today to be the "Golden" one seems no more deserving of the name Chersonese than Italy does.

Although these matters belonged to another place, I wanted to explain them in one context to give greater credit to the sea tides and, through them, to the pulling power of the Moon.

For it follows that if the pulling power of the Moon extends to the Earth, much more does the pulling power of the Earth extend to the Moon and much higher; therefore, nothing that consists of earthly matter in any way, even if carried up on high, can ever escape this strongest embrace of pulling power.

<summary>Kepler defines gravity as a mutual physical attraction between related bodies like the Earth and Moon, using this principle to provide the first correct physical explanation of tides as being caused by the Moon's gravitational pull.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s introduction to the Astronomia Nova. Having previously defined gravity as a mutual attraction between bodies, he now addresses the concept of "lightness" and tackles common physical and theological objections to the motion of the Earth, specifically how objects fall back to their starting point and how to interpret Biblical passages that seem to contradict a sun-centered system.</meta>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

<margin>The true doctrine of lightness.</margin>
In truth, nothing is absolutely light if it consists of corporeal matter; rather, a thing is comparatively lighter if it is rarer <term>Rare: In early physics, "rare" refers to low density—having less matter within the same amount of space.</term> either by its own nature or due to accidental heat. By "rare," I do not mean only that which is porous and full of many cavities, but generally that which contains a smaller quantity of corporeal matter within the same volume of space occupied by something heavier.

The definition of light things is followed by their motion. One must not think that they flee toward the very surface of the world while being carried upward, or that they are not attracted by the Earth: for they are simply attracted less than heavy things, and thus are displaced by the heavy things. Once this occurs, they come to rest and are held by the Earth in their own place.

<margin>Regarding the objection that projectiles thrown straight up fall back to their place.</margin>
Even though the Earth's drawing power <note>original: "virtus tractoria" — the attractive force Kepler identifies as a precursor to the modern concept of gravity.</note>, as stated, extends very far upward; nevertheless, if a stone were separated from the Earth by so great a distance that it became significant compared to the Earth's diameter, it is true that if the Earth moved, such a stone would not follow it perfectly. Instead, it would mix its own powers of resistance with the Earth's drawing powers, and thus would untangle itself somewhat from that "snatching" of the Earth. This is not unlike how "violent motion" <term>Violent motion: An Aristotelian term for motion caused by an external force (like a throw), as opposed to "natural motion" (like falling).</term> untangles projectiles somewhat from the Earth’s grip, so that they either rush ahead if thrown toward the east, or fall behind if thrown toward the west. In this way, they might leave the place from which they were thrown, being compelled by force; nor could the "snatching" of the Earth entirely prevent this violence as long as the violent motion is in its full vigor.

But because no projectile is separated from the surface of the earth by even a hundred-thousandth part of the Earth's diameter—and even the clouds and smoke themselves, which contain the smallest amount of terrestrial matter, do not fly even a thousandth part of the diameter into the air—the resistance and natural inclination to rest of these clouds, smokes, and objects thrown straight up can do nothing to hinder this "snatching" of themselves. This is because their resistance is as nothing compared to the force. Therefore, that which is thrown perpendicularly upward will fall back to its own place, entirely unhindered by the motion of the Earth; for the Earth cannot be pulled away from underneath it, but snatches up those things flying in the air, having them linked to itself by magnetic force no less than if those bodies were actually touching it.

Once these propositions are understood and carefully weighed in the mind, not only will the absurdity and the falsely imagined physical impossibility of the Earth's motion vanish, but it will also be clear how one should respond to physical objections, however they are framed.

<margin>The opinion of Copernicus.</margin>
Although it pleases Copernicus more to think that the Earth and all earthly things, even those torn away from it, are animated by one and the same "motive soul" <note>original: "anima motrice" — early astronomers often debated whether planets were moved by physical forces or internal "souls."</note> which, by rotating the Earth as its body, also rotates those small parts torn from its body; so that through violent motions a force is applied to this soul diffused through all parts, just as I say a force is applied to the corporeal faculty (which we call gravity, or the Magnetic faculty) likewise through violent motions.

Nevertheless, for those things detached from the Earth, that corporeal faculty is sufficient; the "animal" soul is superfluous.

<margin>II. Regarding objections about the speed of the Earth's motion.
III. Regarding objections about the immensity of the heavens.</margin>
As for the fact that many fear the worst for themselves and for things born of the earth because of the speed of this motion, they have no cause for fear. See regarding this matter Chapters 15 and 16 of my book *On the New Star in the Foot of the Serpent* <note>original: "de Stella serpentarii" — Kepler's 1606 work on a supernova.</note>, pages 82 and 84.

There you will also find a full-sailed defense of the immensity of the world-sphere, which is usually objected to as "monstrous" in Copernicus. For it is demonstrated there that the proportions are quite sound; on the contrary, it is the speed of the heavens that would be disproportionate and monstrous if the Earth were ordered to stand entirely immobile in its place and position.

<margin>IV. Regarding objections from the disagreement and authority of the Holy Scriptures.</margin>
However, there are far more people moved by piety to withhold their assent from Copernicus, fearing that a lie might be charged against the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures if we say the Earth moves and the Sun stands still.

Let them consider this: since we learn most and the most important things through the sense of sight, it is impossible for us to detach our speech from this sense of the eyes. Therefore, many things occur daily where we speak according to the sense of the eyes, even though we know for certain that the thing itself is otherwise.

An example is found in that verse of Virgil: *We are carried out from the port, and the lands and cities recede.* <note>original: "Provehimur portu, Terraeque urbesque recedunt" — from Virgil's Aeneid, III.72. Kepler argues that just as the shore seems to move to a sailor, the Sun seems to move to an observer on Earth.</note>
Likewise, when we emerge from a narrow valley, we say a great field "opens itself up" to us.

So Christ said to Peter: *Lead out into the deep* <note>Luke 5:4.</note>—as if the sea were higher than the shores. For so it appears to the eyes, and students of Optics demonstrate the causes of this fallacy. Christ, however, uses the most accepted manner of speaking, which nevertheless arose from this fallacy of the eyes.

Thus we imagine the rising and setting of the stars—that is, an ascent and descent—even though at the same time some say the Sun is "descending" while we say it is "ascending." See my *Optical Part of Astronomy*, Chapter 10, page 327.

So also even now the followers of Ptolemy <term>Ptolemaic: Refers to the ancient system where the Earth is stationary at the center of the universe.</term> say that the planets "stand still" when they appear to linger near the same fixed stars for several continuous days; even though they believe the planets are actually moving then, either downward in a straight line or upward away from the Earths.

So every class of writers says "Solstice" <note>original: "Solstitium" — literally "sun-standing."</note>, even though they deny that the Sun truly stands still.

So also no one will ever be so devoted to Copernicus that they will not say the Sun "enters" Cancer or Leo, even though they mean to imply the Earth enters Capricorn or Aquarius. And other things similarly.

<summary>Kepler explains that gravity (a magnetic-like attraction) keeps objects on the rotating Earth, making them fall back to their starting point. He also argues that the Bible uses the language of human perception rather than scientific description, meaning phrases like "the sun rises" do not contradict a moving Earth.</summary>
<keywords>gravity, lightness, density, Earth's rotation, Copernicus, magnetic faculty, Biblical interpretation, perception vs reality, Virgil, projectiles</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s introduction to the Astronomia Nova. Having previously argued that "lightness" is merely a relative lack of density and that the Earth exerts a drawing force (an early concept of gravity) on objects, Kepler now turns to the theological and sensory objections to the Earth's motion. He focuses on how the Bible uses human-centered, sensory language rather than scientific precision when describing the natural world.</meta>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

Now, in truth, the sacred scriptures also speak with men in a human manner concerning common things (in which it is not their purpose to instruct men), so that they may be understood by men. They use things that are common knowledge among men to suggest other more sublime and divine truths.

Is it any wonder, then, if Scripture also speaks according to human senses at times when the truth of things differs from those senses, whether men are aware of it or not? For who does not know that there is a poetic allusion in Psalm 19? There, while the course of the Gospel—and thus the pilgrimage of Christ our Lord undertaken for our sake into this world—is sung under the image of the Sun, the Sun is said to emerge from the "tent of the horizon" like a bridegroom from his chamber, and "rejoice like a giant to run his course." Virgil imitates this: <note>original: "Tithono croceum linquens aurora cubile."</note> *Aurora, leaving the saffron-colored bed of Tithonus.* Indeed, poetry existed first among the Hebrews.

The Psalmist knew that the Sun does not literally emerge from the horizon as if from a tent (even though it appears so to the eyes); however, he believed the Sun moved because it appears so to the eyes. And yet he says both, because both appear that way to the eyes. He should not be judged to speak falsely in either case; for the comprehension of the eyes has its own truth, suitable for the Psalmist's more hidden purpose of foreshadowing the course of the Gospel and thus the Son of God. Joshua also mentions the valleys against which the Sun and Moon moved, obviously because it appeared this way to him at the Jordan. And yet both achieve their intent: David, by revealing the magnificence of God (and with him Sirach <note>Referring to the Book of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, in the Apocrypha.</note>), which caused these things to be represented to the eyes in this way, or even expressed these visible things with a mystical meaning; Joshua, however, so that the Sun would be held <term>FOR HIMSELF</term> in the middle of the sky for an entire day, according to the perception of his eyes—even if, during that same span of time, it remained "under the earth" for other people.

But unthinking people look only at the contradiction of words—"the Sun stood still," which means "the Earth stood still"—not considering that this contradiction arises only within the limits of <term>Optics</term> <gloss>The science of how we see light and motion</gloss> and <term>Astronomy</term>. It does not, therefore, carry over into common human usage. Nor do they want to see that Joshua had only one wish: that the mountains themselves would not snatch the Sun away from him. He explained this wish in words conforming to the perception of the eyes, since it would have been quite inappropriate at that time to think about Astronomy or about "living errors" <note>An "error" in this context refers to a wandering motion or a scientific misconception.</note> of the senses. For if someone had warned him that the Sun does not truly move against the valley of Ajalon, but only appears to, would Joshua not have cried out that he was asking for the day to be lengthened for him, by whatever means it might happen? He would have responded in the same way if someone had started a legal dispute with him about the Sun’s eternal rest and the motion of the Earth.

Furthermore, God easily understood from Joshua’s words what he wanted; and He provided it by inhibiting the motion of the Earth, so that the Sun seemed to him to stand still. For the sum of Joshua's petition came down to this: that it might *appear* thus to him, whatever it <term>MIGHT ACTUALLY BE</term> in the meantime. Indeed, this appearance was not vain or useless, but was joined with the desired effect.

But see Chapter 10 of the Optical part of Astronomy; <note>Kepler refers here to his 1604 work, *Ad Vitellionem paralipomena*, where he explains the physics of sight.</note> you will find the reasons why the Sun appears to move to all men, but the Earth does not. Specifically, since the Sun appears small and the Earth appears large; and the Sun’s motion is not grasped by sight because of its apparent slowness, but only by reasoning, due to its changed proximity to the mountains after some time. It is impossible, therefore, for a mind that has not been previously warned to imagine anything other than that the Earth, with the vault of heaven placed over it, is like a great house in which the Sun, with such a small appearance—like a bird wandering in the air—passes from one region to another while the house remains immobile.

This very imagination of all men provided the "first line" in the sacred page. *In the beginning,* says Moses, *God created the Heaven and the Earth*; because, obviously, these two parts are the most prominent to the sense of the eyes. It is as if Moses said to Man: "God created this entire worldly building which you see—bright above, dark and most widely stretched out below, upon which you stand and by which you are covered."

Elsewhere, man is asked if he knows how to investigate the height of heaven above and the depth of the earth below; because, to the common man, both seem to extend through equally infinite spaces. And yet no one has emerged who, being of sound mind, would hear this and think the diligence of Astronomers—whether in showing the contemptible smallness of the Earth compared to heaven, or in investigating astronomical distances—should be limited by these words. For these verses do not speak of a dimension reached by reasoning, but of a real one, which is utterly impossible for a human body fixed to the land and breathing the open air. Read all of Job chapter 38 and compare it with those things discussed in <term>Astronomy</term> and <term>Physics</term>.

If someone cites from Psalm 24 that "the Earth is prepared upon the floods" to establish some new philosophy—absurd to hear—that the Earth floats on rivers, should it not rightly be said to him: "Let the Holy Spirit be, and do not drag Him into the schools of Physics to be mocked"? For the Psalmist intends to hint at nothing else there but what men already know and daily experience: that the lands (raised high after the separation of the waters) have great rivers flowing through them and seas flowing around them. Surely it is the same way of speaking as elsewhere, when the Israelites sing that they "sat upon the rivers of Babylon," meaning "next to" the rivers, or "at the banks" of the Euphrates and Tigris.

If one willingly accepts this, why not also accept that in other places, which are usually opposed to the motion of the Earth, we should similarly turn our eyes from Physics to the purpose of Scripture?

<summary>Kepler argues that the Bible uses poetic and sensory language (accommodated to human perception) rather than scientific terminology, explaining that passages about the Sun "standing still" or the Earth being "unmoved" describe how things appear to the observer, not their physical reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s theological defense of his astronomical findings. Having argued that the Bible uses poetic and human-centered language to describe the Sun's movement (as in Psalm 19 and the story of Joshua), he now addresses specific passages in Ecclesiastes and Psalm 104 that seem to claim the Earth is physically stationary. Kepler argues these are moral lessons or hymns of praise based on sensory experience, not scientific treatises meant to contradict the Earth's motion.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

"One generation passes away," (says Ecclesiastes) "and another generation comes, but the Earth stands forever." <note>original: "Generatio præteriit... & generatio advenit, Terra autem in æternum stat."</note> Does Solomon here dispute with Astronomers? Certainly not; rather, he reminds men of their own mutability, while the Earth, the home of the human race, always remains the same. The motion of the Sun perpetually returns to itself; the Wind is driven in a circle and returns to where it began; rivers flow from their springs into the sea and return from the sea to the springs. Finally, as these people perish, others are born; the play of life is always the same; there is nothing new under the Sun.

You hear no physical dogma here. The "novelty" mentioned is moral, regarding a matter that is evident in itself and observed by the eyes of all, but little considered. Therefore, Solomon emphasizes it. For who does not know that the earth is always the same? Who does not see the Sun rise daily from the east, the rivers flow continuously into the sea, the fixed successions of the winds return, and one generation of men succeed another? But who considers that the same play of life is perpetually acted out, with only the characters changed, and that there is nothing truly new in human affairs? Therefore, by mentioning those things which everyone sees, Solomon warns of that which is wrongly neglected by most.

Indeed, some think that a physical discussion is entirely contained in Psalm 104, since it is concerned with physical things throughout. And there, God is said to have "founded the earth upon its stability," and that "it shall not be tilted for age upon age." Yet the <term>Psalmist<gloss>The author of the Psalms, traditionally King David.</gloss></term> is very far from the speculation of physical causes. He rests entirely in the greatness of God, who made all these things, and composes a Hymn to God the creator, in which he surveys the world in the order it appears to the eyes.

If you consider it well, this is a commentary on the <term>Hexaemeron<gloss>A theological term for the "Six Days" of creation described in the Book of Genesis.</gloss></term> of Genesis. For just as in that account the first three days were given to the separation of the regions—the first of Light from the outer darkness, the second of the Waters from the waters by the interposition of the expanse, and the third of the Lands from the seas, where the earth is clothed with plants and shrubs—so the three later days are for the filling of those regions: the fourth of the Heavens, the fifth of the Seas and the Air, and the sixth of the Lands. Thus in this psalm there are just as many distinct parts, analogous to the works of the six days.

For in the second verse, the author surrounds the Creator with Light—the first of creatures and the work of the first day—as if it were a garment.

The second part begins in the third verse and deals with the "waters above the heavens," the extension of the sky, and with weather phenomena, which the Psalmist seems to count among the upper waters—namely, the Clouds, Winds, <term>Whirlwinds<gloss>Latin: *presteribus*, often referring to fiery storms or waterspouts.</gloss></term>, and Lightning.

The third part begins from the sixth verse and celebrates the earth as the foundation of the things he considers here. For he refers all things to the earth and the animals inhabiting it: namely because, by the judgment of the eyes, there are two primary parts of the World: Heaven and Earth. Here, therefore, he considers that the Earth has not subsided for so many ages, has not cracked open, and has not collapsed; although no one has discovered upon what it is founded.

He does not wish to teach what men are ignorant of, but to recall to mind what they themselves neglect: namely, the greatness and power of God in the creation of so great a mass, so firm and stable. If an Astronomer teaches that the earth is carried through the stars, he does not overturn what the Psalmist says here, nor does he tear away the experience of men. For it is nonetheless true that the lands do not collapse—being the work of God the architect—as our buildings are accustomed to collapse, consumed by age and decay. They do not tilt to the sides, the dwellings of living creatures are not disturbed, and mountains and shores remain fixed and unmoved against the onslaughts of Winds and waves, just as they were from the beginning. Moreover, the Psalmist adds a most beautiful <term>hypotyposis<gloss>A rhetorical term for a vivid, lifelike description of a scene.</gloss></term> of the separation of the waves from the continents: and he adorns it with the addition of springs, and the benefits which the springs and rocks provide to birds and quadrupeds. Nor does he omit the decoration of the surface of the Earth mentioned by Moses among the works of the third day; but he traces it deeper from its cause, namely from celestial watering: and he adorns it with the mention of the benefits that return from that decoration for the food and joy of man and the habitats of beasts.

The fourth part begins in verse 20, celebrating the work of the fourth day, the Sun and Moon, but especially the benefit that returns from the distinction of times to living creatures and Man, who is already the subject matter here: so that it clearly appears that he is not acting as an Astronomer here.

For if he were, he would not have omitted mention of the five Planets; nothing in nature is more admirable or more beautiful than their motion, and nothing testifies more clearly to the wisdom of the Creator among those who can understand it.

The fifth part is in verse 26 concerning the work of the fifth day, and it fills the seas with fish and adorns them with Navigations.

The sixth part is more obscurely attached from verse 28 and deals with the Animals inhabiting the lands, created on the sixth day. And finally, in general, he adds the goodness of God sustaining all things and creating new ones. Therefore, everything he had said about the world he refers to living creatures. He mentions nothing that is not common knowledge, because his intention is to extol what is known, not to inquire into the unknown, but to invite men to consider the benefits that return to them from these individual Works of the days.

Advice for Astronomers.
</margin>
And I also implore my reader, not forgetting the divine goodness bestowed upon men, to the consideration of which the Psalmist especially invites him; where, having returned from the temple, into the scho-

He explains that these texts are poetic hymns celebrating God's providence and the stability of the human environment, not physical proofs against the Earth's motion.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the transition in Kepler's introduction from theological arguments back to the scientific and physical foundations of his work. He moves from defending the Copernican system against biblical literalism to outlining the specific "steps" of his discovery process, including his breakthrough regarding elliptical orbits.</meta>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

Now that he has entered the study of Astronomy, let him join me in praising and celebrating the wisdom and greatness of the Creator. I reveal these to him through a more skillful explanation of the world's form, the investigation of causes, and the detection of visual errors. In this way, he may not only embrace the "steadfastness" and stability of the Earth as a gift from God for the safety of all living nature, but also recognize the Creator’s wisdom in the Earth's motion, which is so hidden and so admirable.

<margin>Advice for the Uninformed:</margin>
However, if someone is too dull-witted to grasp the science of Astronomy, or too weak in faith to believe Copernicus without offending his piety, I advise him to leave the School of Astronomy behind. Let him condemn the opinions of philosophers as much as he likes and, ceasing this worldly wandering, return home to cultivate his own little field. There, lifting his eyes—the only ones he sees with—to this visible sky, let him pour himself out with his whole heart in thanksgiving and praise to God the Creator. He should be certain that he offers no less worship to God than the Astronomer, to whom God has granted the ability to see more clearly with the eye of the mind, and who is both able and willing to celebrate his God for the things he has discovered.

<margin>Commendation of the Brahean Hypothesis:</margin>
For this reason, the opinion of <term>Brahe</term><note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the preeminent observational astronomer whose data Kepler used. Brahe proposed a "Tychonic" system where the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun.</note> regarding the form of the World should be moderately—indeed, significantly—commended to the learned. By treading a middle path, as it were, it frees astronomers (as much as possible) from the useless equipment of so many <term>epicycles</term><note>Smaller circles moving along the circumference of larger circles, used in older astronomy to explain planetary backtracking.</note>; it embraces the causes of motions that were unknown to Ptolemy, just as Copernicus did; and it grants a place for physical speculation by accepting the Sun as the center of the planetary system. On the other hand, it serves the common crowd of the literate by eliminating the motion of the Earth, which is so difficult to believe. This is despite the fact that, in Brahe’s theory, the planetary demonstrations are entangled in many difficulties and "celestial physics" is considerably disturbed.

<margin>V. Regarding objections about the authority of the Saints.</margin>
And so much for the authority of Holy Scripture. As for the opinions of the Saints <note>Referring to the Church Fathers.</note> regarding these natural matters, I respond in a single word: in Theology, the weight of authority is to be considered, but in Philosophy <note>In this period, "Philosophy" included what we now call science.</note>, it is the weight of reason. Thus, Saint Lactantius denied that the Earth was round; Saint Augustine, while conceding its roundness, nonetheless denied the existence of the <term>Antipodes</term><note>The idea that people lived on the "other side" of the Earth.</note>; and the Holy Office of today, while conceding the smallness of the Earth, nonetheless denies its motion. But Truth is more sacred to me: I demonstrate through philosophy, with all due respect for the Doctors of the Church, that the Earth is round, inhabited all around by Antipodes, of a most contemptible smallness, and finally, that it is carried through the stars.

But enough about the truth of the Copernican hypothesis. I must return to the purpose from which I began this introduction.

I began by saying that in this work, I would present the whole of Astronomy not through "fictitious hypotheses," but through physical causes. I have reached this summit by two steps: first, by discovering that the <term>eccentrics</term><note>The off-center circular paths of the planets.</note> of the planets meet in the body of the Sun; and second, by realizing that an <term>equant circle</term><note>A mathematical tool used to explain the varying speeds of planets; Kepler discovered it applied to the Earth's orbit as well.</note> exists in the theory of the Earth, and its eccentricity must be bisected.

<margin>Third step toward physical hypotheses of motion. That the eccentricity of Mars's equant must be precisely bisected.</margin>
Therefore, let this be the third step: by comparing Part Two with Part Four, it was most certainly demonstrated that even the eccentricity of Mars's equant must be precisely bisected—a point that Brahe and Copernicus kept in doubt for a long time.

Therefore, by an induction made from all the planets, it was demonstrated in advance in Part Three: since there are no "solid orbs" (as Brahe demonstrated from the paths of comets), the body of the Sun is the source of the <term>Virtue</term><note>In this context, "virtue" refers to a physical power or force.</note> that drives all the planets around. I also defined the manner of this by arguments: while the Sun remains in its place, it nevertheless rotates as if on a lathe. It emits from itself into the vastness of the world an <term>immaterial species</term><note>original: "speciem immateriatam"; a non-physical influence or "likeness" through which the Sun's power acts on the planets.</note> of its own body, analogous to the immaterial species of its light. This "species" rotates along with the rotation of the Solar body like a very rapid vortex throughout the whole extent of the world; it carries the bodies of the planets along with it in a circuit, with a grip that is strong or weak depending on whether it is denser or thinner, according to the law of its outflow.

Having explained this shared power by which all the planets are carried around the Sun, each in its own circle, the next step in my arguments was to assign individual "movers" to each planet, residing within the planetary globes themselves—for I had already rejected solid orbs following Brahe's opinion. This is exactly what I dealt with in Part Three.

By this line of reasoning, these established "movers"—it is incredible to say how much labor they caused me in Part Four! When I ordered them to produce the distances of the planet from the Sun and the "equations of the eccentric," they produced faulty ones that disagreed with observations. This was not because they were wrongly introduced, but because I had bound them to the "treadmills" of circles, fascinated by common opinion. Bound by these shackles, they were unable to do their work.

<margin>Fourth step toward physical hypotheses. That the path of a planet described in the sky is an oval path.</margin>
Nor was there an end to my weariness until I built the fourth step toward physical hypotheses. Through most laborious demonstrations and the handling of many observations, I discovered that the path of a planet in the Heavens is not a circle, but an **Oval** path—perfectly **Elliptical**.

Geometry then stepped in and taught me that such a path is produced if the planet's own movers...

<meta>This page continues Kepler's introductory defense of his new astronomy. Having previously addressed theological concerns, he now transitions into the physical mechanisms of his system, specifically the "magnetic" forces that govern planetary motion and the structure of the book itself.</meta>

<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

# INTRODUCTION

...let us assign this task to the planet: that of balancing its body in a straight line extended toward the Sun. Not only this, but the equations of the <term>Eccentric</term><note>In older astronomy, an "eccentric" was a circular orbit where the center was not the Earth; Kepler is refining how these calculations are made consistent with physical reality.</note> were made correct and consistent with observations through such a <term>libration</term><note>original: "librationem." Kepler uses this to describe a back-and-forth oscillation or "balancing" movement of a planet along the radius of its orbit.</note>.

Finally, therefore, the crowning touch was placed upon this building, and it was demonstrated geometrically that a balancing of this kind is usually produced by a **magnetic physical power**. Thus, these "movers" specific to the planets were shown with high probability to be nothing other than qualities of the planetary bodies themselves, similar to how a magnet seeks the pole and attracts iron. In this way, the entire system of celestial motions is managed by purely physical—that is, magnetic—powers, with the sole exception of the rotation of the Sun’s body as it remains in its own space, which seems to require a <term>vital power</term><note>original: "vitali facultate." Kepler suggests the Sun might have a "soul" or living force to keep it spinning, while the planets respond to its magnetic influence.</note>.

For in the fifth part, it was demonstrated that our physical hypotheses, which have now been introduced, also satisfy the calculations for latitudes.

However, in parts III and IV, something was also granted to the "Mind," so that the planet's own mover might join Reason with the animate power of moving its own globe—should anyone, terrified by certain seemingly strong external objections, wish to distrust the physical nature of bodies. This is provided that such a person accepts that this "Mind" uses the apparent diameter of the Sun as a measure for its balancing, and possesses a sense for the angles that astronomers seek out.

<margin>Synoptic Table.</margin>
Let this much be said, then, for the sake of the physicists. Astronomers and geometers will find everything else in its proper order from the following arguments of the individual chapters. I wanted these to be somewhat more detailed, both to serve in place of an **INDEX**, and so that a reader who finds themselves stuck in the obscurity of either the subject matter or the style might seek some light from these arguments, guided by the Synoptic Table. Thus, they may more clearly perceive the logic of the order and the coherence of matters gathered into the same chapter—even if it is perhaps less conspicuous in the text itself—among the arguments divided into their paragraphs. Therefore, I ask that the reader view this favorably.

<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction into the "Summaries of Each Chapter," where Kepler justifies his unique "historical" method of presentation. He explains why he chose to narrate his path to discovery rather than simply presenting the final results.</meta>

# SUMMARIES
# OF EACH
## CHAPTER.

<margin>S</margin>INCE there is one *Method* taught by the nature of the subject and another required by our own understanding—and both are artificial—the sincere reader should expect neither of them from me in their pure form. For my primary aim here is not merely to explain the motions of the heavens (which is done in textbooks on the *Sphere* and the *Theories of the Planets*), nor is it only to teach the reader and lead them from first principles and self-evident facts to final conclusions (the path Ptolemy mostly followed). Instead, a third element is added, which I share with *Orators*: because I am delivering many new things, I must make it clear that I have been compelled to do so. In this way, I may earn and retain the reader's assent and remove any suspicion that I am simply fond of making innovations.

It is no wonder, then, if I mix into the previous methods a third one familiar to *Orators*, which is the *historical* account of my discoveries. Here, the concern is not only the shortest path by which the reader may be led to knowledge of what is being taught, but primarily the arguments, the long-winded detours, and even the chance occasions by which I, the author, first arrived at these results. We do not merely forgive Christopher Columbus, Magellan, or the Portuguese when they recount their errors—by which the first opened *America*, the second the *Chinese Ocean*, and the others the *Circumnavigation of Africa*—we would actually be unwilling to have those errors omitted, as we would lose the great pleasure of reading them. Therefore, I should not be faulted for pursuing the same path for the reader's benefit throughout this work. For although we do not become participants in those *Argonautic* labors just by reading about them, and though the difficulties and "thorns" of my discoveries may infest the reading itself, this is the common fate of all *Mathematical* books. Nevertheless, as we are human beings delighted by different things, there exist those who, having overcome the difficulties of perception, will be flooded with great pleasure upon seeing this entire series of discoveries placed before their eyes.

That the entire work has been composed using this Method will now be clear from the summaries of each Chapter. I have, moreover, taken care that whenever the text requires a *Geometric* demonstration, a diagram, or a preparation, it should be printed in *italic type* <note>original: "literâ cursoriâ," literally "running letter." Kepler uses this to distinguish technical proofs from his narrative prose.</note> (as the print shops call it). If this is not maintained everywhere, attribute it either to the subject matter, which mixes *Physics* with Geometry, or to the *Typesetters*, who did not always grasp my signals.

### CHAPTER I.

*Explains the reasoning by which Astronomers detected that the first motion differs from the secondary motions (or the Planets' own motions); also, how two inequalities, called the First and the Second, were found in the Planet's own motion.*

The occasion for this chapter, and indeed for the entire first part, is this: when I first came to Brahe, I found that he, along with Ptolemy and Copernicus, judged the <term>second inequality</term><note>The "second inequality" refers to the apparent irregular motion of a planet caused by the Earth's own movement (retrograde motion).</note> of the Planet to be based on the <term>mean motion</term><note>The "mean" motion is the average, idealized circular speed, as opposed to the "apparent" or actual observed speed.</note> of the Sun. However, four years earlier, for physical reasons, it seemed to me that it should begin from the Apparent motion of the Sun, as you have in the *Cosmographic Mystery*. A dispute having arisen between us, Brahe countered that since he had used the Mean Sun, he had accounted for all Observations of the <term>First Inequality</term><note>The "first inequality" refers to the planet's actual variation in speed along its own orbit.</note>. I replied that this did not prevent me from accounting for the same First Inequality using the Apparent motion of the Sun; therefore, it must be seen in the Second inequality which of us acts more correctly.
What I replied, then, had to be demonstrated in the first part of the Work.

### CHAPTER II.

*Therefore, since the task concerning the equivalence of hypotheses was complex, I began with the first and simplest case: when a Concentric with an Epicycle is exchanged for an Eccentric.*

Lest the Geometry be dry, I disputed the physical, rational, or mental causes by which it is agreeable for both equivalent hypotheses to be managed and the motions completed; this is done differently if solid spheres are granted, and differently if they are denied. Indeed, Brahe demonstrated from the passage of Comets that there are no solid spheres.

### CHAPTER III.

*Maintaining this simple Eccentric (or that which is equivalent to a concentric with a single Epicycle), it is taught what changes occur—either to the perception of the eyes or in the natural causes of the motions—if the mean motion of the Sun is exchanged for the apparent motion; that is, if the sight (or rather the source of power) is mentally transposed to another place.*

### CHAPTER IV.

1. Having finished the simple Eccentric, we move to the Eccentric with an <term>Equant</term><note>An "Equant" is a mathematical point used by Ptolemy to explain why planets seem to move at different speeds at different points in their orbits.</note> (that is, with double eccentricity), which Ptolemy had assigned to the first inequality of the five Planets. 2. Assuming the solidity of the spheres, its absurdity is demonstrated; but if denied, its physical harmony and probability are shown. 3. It is then shown how Copernicus transformed this Eccentric with an Equant into a Concentric with two Epicycles. 4. This Copernican hypothesis is shown to be physically mediocre if solid spheres are assumed, but absurd if they are denied. 5. It is also proved that it fails in geometric beauty regarding the path of the Planet. 6. Nor is it equivalent in all things to the Ptolemaic Eccentric: there is a small difference in the first inequality, but a larger one in the second. 7. Included there is a demonstration of a shorthand method for computing the equation from both forms of the Hypothesis. 8. A way to erase the difference between both Hypotheses. 9. Finally, another form of this Copernican hypothesis through a <term>Concentrepi-cycle</term><note>A combined term for a concentric and epicycle model.</note>.

### CHAPTER V.

This fifth chapter relates to the fourth just as the third did to the second. For the business is handled more seriously. 1. Regarding those things that change in the hypothesis if the sight (or source of power) is transposed from its former place to another by the use of the Sun's Apparent motion instead of the mean. 2. Also, what things in the physical causes of motions are changed by that same hypothesis. 3. This transposition is outlined and arranged in the form of the first Ptolemaic inequality. 4. It is demonstrated that by admitting two fixed <term>apsides</term><note>The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or farthest from the body it orbits.</note>—one the ancient one, the other arising from the transposition—the form of the...

However, once a single line of apsides <note>The line connecting the points where a planet is nearest to and farthest from the center of its orbit.</note> is established and passed through the old center of the **Eccentric**, it is demonstrated that the necessary original appearances do not follow (even if the path remains the same), nor is the form of the hypothesis fully retained. 6. ### C H A P T E R VI.

Here, the things demonstrated in Chapter V—especially in numbers 6, 7, and 8—are in a sense put into practice. Up until now, we were dealing with those hypotheses that concerned the <term>first inequality</term> <note>The variation in a planet's speed as it moves around the zodiac, caused by the elliptical shape of its orbit.</note>, which varies among different authors. Now, we also add those attributed to the <term>second inequality</term> <note>The apparent "looping" or retrograde motion of a planet, which we now know is caused by the Earth's own motion around the Sun.</note>; these are named after their authors—Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Tycho Brahe—as the primary versions (compared to those discussed so far). Indeed, by common usage, when we name the "Copernican Hypothesis," we imply the one dealing with the second inequality. 1. Therefore, I compare these at the beginning.

2. In the Copernican system, I show how the hypothesis of the first inequality was derived from the mean motion of the Sun, and how the **Eccentricity** arises from a <term>vicarious Sun</term> <note>original: "puncto Solis vicario." This refers to the "mean Sun," a mathematical point used in calculations rather than the actual physical body of the Sun.</note>. 3. I argue physically that this is not done correctly; rather, the **Eccentricity** ought to be calculated from the actual center of the body of the Sun. 4. Whether we should consider the second inequality to be caused by the apparent motion of the Sun, which is what physical reasoning demands here. 5. It is demonstrated in this way that the positions of longitude in the first inequality vary little, but the distances of the planet's body from the body of the Sun differ greatly. 6. The location in the "great orbit" of the Earth <note>The Earth's path around the Sun.</note> is demonstrated geometrically, in which the maximum difference in distances presents the greatest error to the observer. 7. The magnitude of the error is gathered by arithmetic operations and can reach up to one degree and about 20 minutes.

8. In the Ptolemaic hypothesis, I show how the hypothesis of the first inequality was derived from the mean motion of the Sun. 9. Generally, many things are disputed from physical or metaphysical contemplation, both against the mean motion of the Sun and against this hypothesis itself. 10. Specifically, some things are brought as objections against the mean motion of the Sun in particular. 11. Whether the physical objections are satisfied if we consider the second inequality to be caused by the apparent motion of the Sun. 12. The position, size, and form of the new hypothesis are demonstrated by the transposition of the **Equator** point. 13. The discrepancy in the appearances of the first inequality, the location on the **Epicycle** where the greatest error in the appearances of the second inequality occurs, and the magnitude of this error are applied from the preceding sections.

14. In the Brahean hypothesis, I show how the hypothesis of the first inequality was derived from the mean motion of the Sun; therefore, the center of the **Concentric** of Mars is attached to the Sun’s orbit, not in the center of the Sun’s body, but near it. 15. I dispute a few things against the Brahean hypothesis in general, but specifically more things against this form of attachment based on Physics, contending that the attachment—to speak plainly—ought to occur in the very center of the Sun’s body. 16. The position, size, and form of the new hypothesis are declared through the transposition of the point of attachment, and from the preceding sections are applied the locations of both the **Eccentric** and the "great orbit" carrying the eccentric (or the Concentric with epicycles), in which the greatest error occurs.

## P A R T II.

### C H A P T E R VII.

I explain the specific occasions: how I happened upon the theory of Mars, what moved me to follow the apparent motion of the Sun, and why I prefixed the first part, now completed, in this manner. You have the summary of the argument in Chapter I.

### C H A P T E R VIII.

This presents the hypothesis of the first inequality of Mars as it was established by Brahe; it includes a Table containing the foundations—namely, the <term>acronychal observations</term> <note>Observations made when a planet is in opposition to the Sun (rising as the sun sets), which are crucial for determining its true orbit.</note>—and the result, namely the calculated positions according to the observations and their examination, directed toward seeing whether this hypothesis agreed with the observations down to the smallest detail.

### C H A P T E R IX.

Deals with the corrected assumption of the observed positions. 1. The necessity is shown for establishing a position in the **Ecliptic** <note>The Sun's apparent path among the stars.</note> corresponding to the planet's position in its own proper circle. 2. The equality of the arcs reaching from the **Node** <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> to the observed position of the planet and the position on the Ecliptic (which the table follows) is refuted. 3. That equality is also refuted if the other arc is terminated not in the observed position but in the true position of the orbit. 4. The method of reducing the angle via observed latitudes is also refuted, and a method of reducing via the angle of inclination of the planes is established.

### C H A P T E R X.

This pertains to the same subject: having examined the accepted positions in the Table, whether they were correctly and safely deduced from neighboring observations to the opposition of the "mean Sun"; a small warning about other subtleties is added, especially concerning **parallaxes**. And thus far the examination of the Table.

### C H A P T E R XI.

Being about to begin my own adaptation to the apparent Sun through legitimate reduction and deduction (so that I might not err in any way), I first investigate the diurnal **parallaxes** of Mars. 1. I relate what Brahe thought of them. 2. I prove from Brahe’s observations, via hourly and diurnal motions, that they are almost imperceptible and smaller than we think the Sun’s parallaxes to be. 3. For the sake of the exercise, I also apply my own observations looking at the same thing: by which I explain a peculiar method of investigating diurnal parallax through <term>stationary latitude</term>.

### C H A P T E R XII.

1. A method for investigating the **Nodes** of Mars: Brahe’s particular method from a nearby observation, and a critique. 2. Another method, which presupposes the known equations of the **Eccentric** from the *Prutenic Tables* <note>Planetary tables based on the Copernican model, published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551.</note>, Ptolemy, or Brahe. By which it is simultaneously demon-

## SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

### C H A P T E R XIII.

*1. It is shown that the reasoning regarding the inclination of the planes is somewhat more complex across all three forms of hypotheses. 2. One method, assuming the equations of the **Eccentric** <note>An orbital circle where the center is not the Sun/Earth.</note> are known, for when Mars is at its evening setting or morning rising through the first inequality at the limits: for then the observed latitude equals the true inclination of the limits to the Ecliptic. 3. It is shown at what arc of elongation from the Sun this is true, both in the Copernican and Ptolemaic hypotheses; and this is completed by several observations near both limits. 4. A second method, requiring nothing but selected and rare observations in which the Sun is in the nodes and Mars is in quadrature <note>A 90-degree angle from the Sun.</note> with the Sun; and this is completed through several observations. 5. This is expanded so that Mars, other conditions remaining the same, can be in a place other than the Sun's quadrature, and thus the certain inclination of a specific place—other than the limit—is gathered. 6. This method is also applied to the Ptolemaic hypothesis, which has some difficulty. 7. A third method proceeds through latitudes observed in opposition to the Sun, adding the previously known proportion of the orbits; it is carried through all three forms of hypotheses.*

### C H A P T E R XIV.

*Based on the demonstrations in Chapter XIII, the opinion of the Ancients—as if the planes of the eccentrics are oscillatory—is further refuted. For it is demonstrated that the inclination, at least within the span of one or two centuries, is constant.* <term>oscillatory<note>original: "libratilia." This refers to the ancient belief that orbital planes wobbled back and forth like a balance scale.</note></term>

### C H A P T E R XV.

*The positions held by Mars at the moments of opposition with the Sun's apparent motion are investigated arithmetically from neighboring observations; these are corrected by the precautions handled thus far. Finally, a table of these is presented as the foundation for a new operation.*

### C H A P T E R XVI.

*Therefore, in imitation of the ancients, while setting aside physical causes, it is assumed that the path of the planet is a circle. It is also assumed that within its compass there is some point around which the planet completes equal angles in equal times <note>This is the "Equant" point, a mathematical tool to explain why planets seem to speed up and slow down.</note>; and between that point and the center of the Sun, the center of the planetary circle resides at an unknown distance. These things being established, and using four acronychal <note>When a planet is directly opposite the Sun in the sky.</note> observations with their positions in the Zodiac and time intervals, the location of both centers in the Zodiac, the distance from the center of the Sun, and the proportion of each eccentricity (both to each other and to the radius of the circle) are investigated by a most laborious method.*

### C H A P T E R XVII.

*By comparing the positions of the **Aphelion** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> and the **Nodes** <note>The points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> from the time of Ptolemy with the findings of our own time, their motion is calculated, which is necessary for the following chapter.*

### C H A P T E R XVIII.

*Finally, it is shown that if this hypothesis (which relies on the apparent motion of the Sun) is discovered, all observed motion in longitude near the Sun's opposition is **saved**—and this much more certainly than before, when the Brahean hypothesis relied on the Sun's mean motion.* <term>saved<note>In astronomy, to "save the appearances" means to create a mathematical model that matches the observed data perfectly.</note></term>

### C H A P T E R XIX.

*1. Even though the discovered hypothesis has so far performed its duty regarding the motion in longitude near the Sun's opposition, it is demonstrated that it does not perform its duty regarding the motion in latitude near the Sun's opposition. 2. It is demonstrated that neither does the Brahean hypothesis perform its duty here, both being in the Copernican form. 3. The same applies to the Ptolemaic and Brahean forms of the hypotheses. 4. It is shown that the error regarding latitudes lies in the fact that the eccentricity was not bisected. 5. But if the eccentricity is bisected, then the hypothesis deviates in the motion of longitude. From these things, the reason is revealed that drove me to desert the ancients and investigate these matters more diligently.*

### C H A P T E R XX.

*1. Just as this hypothesis of mine was proven erroneous by the motion in latitude near the Sun's opposition in the previous chapter, it is now proven so by the motion in longitude away from the Sun's opposition. 2. The same is true for the Brahean hypothesis, which relies on the Sun's mean motion. 3. The demonstration is also applied to the Ptolemaic and Brahean forms of motion. 4. A finger is pointed toward the sources of the errors and the method of correction. 5. A preliminary theorem is inserted regarding what lines in the plane of the Ecliptic should be substituted for the lines of the planet's distance from the Sun in the plane of the planet's **Eccentric**, when the planet has some latitude.*

### C H A P T E R XXI.

*Causes are sought from geometry which result in a false hypothesis producing the truth; and it is shown to what extent this can happen. And here is the end of the second part, in which I have imitated the Ancients.*

I demonstrate in three forms of hypotheses that, if the Equant is assumed (which pleased me), the Great Orb (or the **Epicycles** for Ptolemy) appears to increase and decrease, as Brahe asserted. 3. # SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

## CHAPTER XXIII.
*Having found in the previous chapter the distances of the Sun from the Earth at two places in the Zodiac, and having added the location of the Sun’s **Apogee** <note>The point where the Sun or a planet is farthest from the Earth.</note> or the Earth’s **Aphelion** <note>The point where the Earth is farthest from the Sun.</note>; the **eccentricity** <note>The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the circle of the Sun or Earth is sought through geometric demonstration: which is presupposed to be a perfect circle.*

## CHAPTER XXIV.
*The same thing is demonstrated as in Chapter XXII, but using four observations offered more at random, which nonetheless have Mars in the same place on the **Eccentric** <note>The circular path of a planet when its center is not the Earth.</note>: namely, that some part of the Sun’s or Earth’s eccentricity must be given to the **Equant** circle: and this is also compared across the three forms of hypotheses <note>The Ptolemaic (Earth-centered), Copernican (Sun-centered), and Tychonic (Geo-heliocentric) systems.</note>; and also assuming Brahe's restoration of the motions of Mars, which relies on the mean motion of the Sun.*

## CHAPTER XXV.
*Having found in the previous chapter three sets of distances of the Sun from the Earth at three places in the Zodiac; through geometric demonstration, which assumes nothing further except a perfectly circular path, we investigate not only the eccentricity of the Sun’s or Earth’s circle (as in Chapter 23), but also the location of the Sun’s Apogee or the Earth’s Aphelion. This is found to be nearly the same as what was found by Brahe from the Sun’s own observations, even though only observations of Mars are used here.*

## CHAPTER XXVI.
*These four observations from the fourth chapter are transferred from the mean motion of the Sun to the true motion, and from Brahe's restoration to my own; and the same conclusion is gathered as in Chapter XXV. The demonstration is proposed in all three forms of the hypotheses.*

## CHAPTER XXVII.
*By an even bolder method, I presuppose no restoration of Mars at all; and by taking other observations of Mars—no fewer than four, compared as above—I demonstrate not only the eccentricity of the Sun or Earth and the Aphelion together as before, and the proportion of the Orbits at this place on the Eccentric, but also the very place of Mars on the Eccentric relative to the **Fixed Stars**, which was previously assumed to be known from the restoration.*

## CHAPTER XXVIII.
*Nearly the same form of demonstration: but assuming the eccentricity and Aphelion of the Sun or Earth, which have now been proven so many times; and having joined several observations—here five, compared with one another as before—it is shown that the same eccentric position for Mars always results, nearly as in Chapter XXVII. You must remember, however, that in all the preceding chapters of Part III, the path of the Earth is presupposed to be a perfect circle; as it indeed appears to the senses. For on account of the small eccentricity of the **Ellipse** <note>Kepler is hinting at his great discovery: orbits are actually ovals (ellipses), not circles.</note>, it can take very little away from it.*

## CHAPTER XXIX.
*The Eccentric is set as a perfect circle, with a known eccentricity, and a doubled eccentricity for the Equant point. Then, from these settings, the distances are sought geometrically: first of the Apogee and Perigee, second the distances at an **equated anomaly** <note>The angle of a planet from its farthest point, adjusted for its speed.</note> of 90 degrees, and third the remaining distances. In the same place, a shortcut is demonstrated for seeking four distances in a single operation. Furthermore, the point on the circle that is one semi-diameter distant from the center of the Sun is demonstrated. Finally, another point on the circle is demonstrated, in which one part of the **equation** <note>The correction needed to find the true position of a planet from its average motion.</note> is at its absolute maximum.*

## CHAPTER XXX.
*The distances of the Sun and Earth are set out in a Table: and a method for extracting them is taught which, although it is shown to exceed the limits of the starting principles and makes the path of the star **oval** <note>This is a pivotal moment in the book where Kepler realizes the orbit cannot be a circle.</note>, and therefore rightly calls for the following Chapters XXXI, XL, XLIV, and LV, where this difficulty is removed; it is nevertheless shown not to depart perceptibly from those things that had been demonstrated thus far.*

## CHAPTER XXXI.
*Brahe feared that by bisecting the eccentricity of the Sun, I would disturb his own solar equations. Therefore, this fear is removed here by demonstrating that—whether through the whole eccentricity, or through the bisected one, or through the doubling of that which is built from the half-eccentricity—the same equation always results for the Sun. Thus, the difficulty in Chapter XXX is one thing, and here in Chapter XXXI is another. There, the concern was for the distances; here, the concern is for Brahe’s equations. There, the cause of fear was the shape of the path; here, it is the ratio of eccentricity. There, the consideration was anticipated; here, it is proper to this place.*

## CHAPTER XXXII.
*First, an induction is made: that all planets without exception use an Equant circle, or a bisection of the eccentricity of the Equant point. Upon this principle, this universal rule is built by geometric demonstration: that the **delays** <note>The amount of time a planet spends in a specific part of its orbit.</note> of a planet in equal arcs of the Eccentric are proportional to the planet's distance from the point from which the eccentricity arises. **Listen closely, physicists!** <note>Kepler is addressing "natural philosophers" because he is moving from pure math into the physical causes of motion.</note> For here, a deliberation is undertaken concerning an incursion into your territory.*

## CHAPTER XXXIII.
*Now, from the conclusion of the preceding demonstration, and by adding other purely physical and admitted axioms, it is proven that the distances of the planet from the center from which the eccentricity is computed are the **dispensing causes** of the planet’s delays in equal arcs of the eccentric.*

*Second, it is taught that these dispensing causes of the delays reside in the other limit of the distances, which is common to all distances: namely, in the center of the Planetary System.*

*Third, it is added to these things thus demonstrated—partly from **PART ONE**, as demonstrated with probability; partly from **PARTS FOUR AND FIVE**, as demonstrated by necessity and geometry; and partly also in this very place and in **PART TWO** it is made probable—that the body of the Sun itself is in the center of the Planetary System.*

*Fourth, from this it is now made agreeable that the **motive power** <note>The physical force that actually moves the planets.</note> or the dispenser of delays is in the body of the Sun: Physical arguments are added.*

# SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

(***) 3

*Then it is inferred in passing that the Sun rests in the center of the world, while the Earth moves around the center of the world. Here the Physicist should take note: these physical speculations rest upon the motion of the Earth, but they are derived from other sources and remain valid in the systems of both Tycho Brahe and Copernicus. Indeed, on the contrary, the motion of the Earth and the stillness of the Sun are justified by these very speculations.*

*Fifthly, it is demonstrated that the **Moving Power** <term>Virtus motrix: Kepler’s hypothesized physical force that pushes the planets in their orbits.</term> behaves exactly like Light: it occupies space, is weakened over a larger area, and is concentrated in a smaller one.*

*Sixthly, it is demonstrated from this that the thing which moves the planets from place to place is an **immaterial species** <note>original: "speciem immateriata"; an influence or force that acts without physical contact, similar to the way light travels.</note> of that power which exists in the body of the Sun, similar to the immaterial influence of Light.*

### CHAPTER XXXIV.

*Physical speculation is woven throughout, and it is demonstrated from the preceding points that the influence of the power which carries the planets travels through the vastness of the world, rotating like a river or a **vortex** <note>A swirling flow; Kepler imagines the Sun’s power "sweeping" the planets along.</note>, moving faster than the planets themselves.*

*Secondly, it is demonstrated from this that the body of the Sun also rotates around its own axis: here the periodic time of this rotation is investigated through probability, while at the same time it is debated what moves the Earth and what moves the Moon.*

*Thirdly, the body of the Sun is proven to be quasi-magnetic. And by the example of the Earth, it is shown that there are **Magnets** in the heavens.*

### CHAPTER XXXV.

*An objection is resolved: whether the motion of the stars, if it comes from the Sun, is hindered by the interposition of other bodies as Light is. At the same time, many points from the previous chapter are clarified: namely, how the Moving Power and Light are related, one being the companion of the other.*

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

*Other objections are resolved. The first is framed geometrically, arguing from a point in the body of the Sun to a line, and from there to its flat surface as it appears to us, and finally to its spherical shape. This aims to prove that light is spread in a different proportion of density than the moving power. But it is answered using the principles of **Optics**, showing that the starting point of the argument cannot be a point or a line, but the surface itself. Then it is denied that the apparent size of the Sun's disk should be considered in a physical effect—a point that could have been explained at greater length. For it cannot even be a sign of this physical effect, since it uses a different proportion, even if it becomes a sign of something else later. Thus, a method of spreading is asserted for Light that is perfectly measured to the distribution of planetary motions.*

*Another objection argues the opposite: that Light is unsuitable for aiding motion because it is also spread toward the poles. This is solved using the established physical principles through pure geometry, so that from the solution, the natural cause of the **Zodiac** <note>The narrow band of the sky where the planets are always found.</note> becomes clear, and why the planets never leave the Zodiac.*

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

*From the established physical principles, the causes are sought for that inequality in the Moon's motion which Tycho Brahe called the **Variation** <note>A change in the Moon's speed discovered by Brahe; it moves fastest at New and Full Moon.</note>, which makes the New and Full Moon faster than at other times. Here, two false opinions on this matter are removed. Next, the causes are sought for why the **Equation** <note>A mathematical correction used to find the true position of a celestial body.</note> of the Moon is greater during its quarters than when it is in conjunction or opposition with the Sun. Other matters are added to explain the peculiar power by which the Moon is moved.*

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

*Besides the common moving force from the Sun, it is proven by two arguments that individual planets manage their own motions through other individual moving causes: one argument is drawn from the motion in longitude, the other from the motion in latitude.*

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

*In the beginning, six physical axioms are presented which are necessary for investigating the power specifically attributed to individual planets.*

*Throughout this entire chapter, two preconceived opinions reign: First, that the planet's path is arranged in a perfect circle; Second, that this journey is managed by a **Mind** <note>Kepler explores the old idea that planets might be guided by "intelligences" or souls, though he is moving toward purely physical explanations.</note>. It is therefore debated how this Mind could create a circle from the planet’s journey. First, it is demonstrated that this could happen if the planet's own power strives to carry its body in a perfect **Epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note>, while meanwhile the body is also swept along by the Solar power. Five physical absurdities are opposed to this. Second, it is demonstrated that it could happen if the planet observes a certain point outside the Sun, staying at an equal distance from it throughout its circuit around the Sun. However, this observation of a certain "incorporeal point" is refuted by three absurdities.*

*Third, it is demonstrated that a perfect circle could be formed if the planet's own power balanced the planet on the diameter of an Epicycle stretched toward the Sun, according to a prescribed law as if descending from the circumference of an Epicycle. But it is simultaneously shown that correct **librations** <term>Libration: A back-and-forth oscillating motion.</term> cannot be described by a planet if it stays on the diameter of an Epicycle; nor do they correspond to the arcs of the **Eccentric** produced, nor to the time, nor to the adjusted **anomaly** <note>The angular distance of a planet from its starting point.</note>. This is based on the position that a perfect circle must result from the planet's composite journey.*

*Fourth, it is also denied that the planet's own power "conceives" in its Mind an imaginary Eccentric or Epicycle and, following its rule, arranges the distances required for a perfectly circular path.*

*As long as we think the planet’s path is perfectly circular, it remains in doubt by what standard the planet's own Mind weighs these librations of its body.*

*Having thus examined the standard of this libration, I proceed to the means by which the planet's Mind might grasp this standard. Whether an Epicycle is the standard, or its diameter, or the center of the Eccentric—all these are rejected as unfit to be grasped, and they require a proportional medium, suitable for being understood, through which they are grasped by the Mind. Here it is asserted that the Mind of the planet looks to the increasing and decreasing diameter of the Sun, using that as an indicator of its body’s distance from the Sun, a likelihood drawn from the latitudes. Objections regarding the Sun's smallness and the lack of senses in planets are also answered. Finally, it is suggested that the opinion regarding governance by a Mind is not entirely <note>original: "ἀντικεῖσθαι" (antikeisthai); to be opposed or contradictory.</note>.*

*Lastly, a difficulty is opened regarding the motion of the planetary body from place to place by an inherent animal force. Thus, with many difficulties raised on all sides, the sole purpose is to call into doubt, by physical reasons, the previously held opinion of the planet's journey being perfectly circular (and partly the idea of a governing Mind for this libration). Shortly hereafter, in Chapter 44, this will be completely overturned by Geometry.*

### CHAPTER XL.

1. *The method by which the physical part of the equation, or the **delay** <note>original: "mora"; the time spent by a planet in a certain part of its orbit.</note> of a planet in any arc of the Eccentric, is found from the distances.*

[Chapter 40 continued] ...by the distances of the points of its arc from the Sun. 2. Here is a geometric demonstration showing how the distances of infinite points of an arc from the Sun are contained, as nearly as possible, in the area located between the arc and the lines connecting the Sun to the ends of that arc. It also shows how a single triangle between the Sun, the center of the eccentric, and the end of the arc represents both parts of the **equation** <term>Equation: In Renaissance astronomy, an "equation" is the correction added to a planet's average motion to find its true position.</term>; the **Optical part** <note>The part of the planet's apparent motion caused by our perspective from Earth.</note> is shown by the angle at the end of the arc, and the **Physical part** <note>The part caused by the planet's actual change in speed.</note> by the area. 3.
