Here, geometers are challenged to find the area (to "square") of this space. 8. The space between two Conchoids is demonstrated not to have the same width in places equidistant from the middle. More on this in Chapter 43.

-> CHAPTER XLI. <-

Given that the planet's path is a perfect circle, and taking the distances of Mars from the body of the Sun at three positions of the eccentric (which were most certainly demonstrated in the third part), it is elicited by geometric demonstration that the resulting position of the **Apogee** <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> is false, the eccentricity is false, and the proportion is false.

-> CHAPTER XLII. <-

By a new method, the distances of two positions of the eccentric are investigated: near the **Aphelion** <note>The point farthest from the Sun.</note> using five observations, and near the **Perihelion** <note>The point closest to the Sun.</note> using three. Then, by halving the periodic time and the circle of the Zodiac, the position of the Aphelion is most certainly investigated and found to be the same as in the first and second parts. From this, the mean longitude of Mars is corrected. Indeed, by comparing both distances, the true eccentricity and the proportion of the orbits of Mars and the Earth are elicited. Since the eccentricity of the eccentric is most certainly established (though not with total refinement) from observations of the Sun, it simultaneously becomes clear that it is half of the eccentricity of the **Equant** <note>An imaginary mathematical point used by previous astronomers to keep planetary speeds appearing uniform.</note> found elsewhere. Thus, the speculations introduced from Chapter 32 also hold true for Mars.

-> CHAPTER XLIII. <-

It is taken as a foundational fact, as demonstrated in Chapter 42, that the eccentricities are in a double proportion to each other. Secondly, it is assumed that the planet's orbit is arranged in a perfect circle. Thirdly, it is assumed (as demonstrated in Chapter 33) that the delays of the planet in equal arcs of the orbit are in proportion to the distances of those arcs from the Sun. These things being granted, the resulting equations are found to be faulty, disagreeing with experience. Then a warning is given as to where that falsehood lies hidden. 2. For this matter, it is necessary to measure the space between the two Conchoids from Chapter 40; since this involves some **lack of technical method** <note>original: "atechnian"</note>, geometers are challenged. Thus it is established that since the conclusion is false, one of the premises must be entirely false.

-> CHAPTER XLIV. <-

It is demonstrated by two arguments that the planet's orbit is not a circle, but an **Oval figure**.
In the first argument, the demonstrations of Chapters 40, 41, and 42 are presupposed. For a perfect circle, whose diameter was found in Chapter 42, produces certain distances, while the observations repeated in Chapter 41 require different and indeed shorter distances at the sides. But an oval figure allows for such distances. Therefore, the orbit is oval.
In the second argument, the same points from Chapter 43 are presupposed. The delays to which experience testifies are not allowed by a circular figure, but are allowed by an Oval one. Therefore, the orbit of the planet is Oval.

-> CHAPTER XLV. <-

In what follows, the reader will recognize my gullibility, as I judge everyone by my own character. Indeed, the occasions by which men arrive at the knowledge of celestial things seem to me no less admirable than the nature of the celestial things themselves. I therefore explain these occasions diligently—no doubt with some tedium to the reader. Yet the victory is more pleasant when won through danger, and the Sun emerges brighter from the clouds. Attend then, reader, to our dangers and beginnings; contemplate the clouds, horrific in their blackness; contemplate them, I say, for behind these clouds the Sun of truth certainly lies hidden and will shortly emerge. I explain the occasions that invited me to assume something false once again: that the planet, by an innate power, strives for a perfect **Epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> and traces equal parts of it in equal times; but that this same planet is snatched away by the external power of the Sun, moving unequally in equal times, as described so far. From this, it is demonstrated that the orbit or path formed by both causes results in an Oval figure.

-> CHAPTER XLVI. <-

1. First, this physical hypothesis, which belongs to an Epicycle, is exchanged for an eccentric. 2. Then, one method of describing the line of the planet's motion according to this view is taught. 3. Four **difficulties** <note>original: "amechaniai"</note> are reviewed which occur regarding this method. Here it is shown that the mean between the sums of the terms is not the same as the mean between the terms themselves. 4. A second method of describing this line is proposed, and the difficulty of this method is also shown. Both methods are nonetheless useful for operations using numbers. 5. A third method of describing the planet's orbit is proposed by joining two hypotheses. 6. A fourth method, which someone might suggest, is rejected. 7. It is demonstrated that the line thus created is truly an Oval, not an Ellipse.

-> CHAPTER XLVII. <-

Assuming, however, that the line of the planet's path is a perfect Ellipse, it is demonstrated that the area of the ellipse is smaller than the area of the circle by almost the small area of the Epicycle (or the circle described by the eccentricity of the eccentric). 2. The area of that circle is investigated, and thus also the area of the egg-shaped plane. 3. It is shown that a geometric section of that egg-shaped area in a given ratio is also necessary; here geometers are challenged. 4. The **lunule** <note>original: "meniscus"; the crescent-shaped area.</note> by which the Oval area differs from the circle is stretched out into a straight line geometrically, as much as possible. 5. It is proposed for geometers to consider whether, when thus extended, it is double the true lunule. 6. Since there is no ready method for dividing an Ellipse or an Oval on its own, it is demonstrated that an Ellipse can be conveniently divided with the help of a circle. 7. With the Ellipse and circle thus divided, the method for computing both the distance and the equation is shown. 8. The equation is computed at an anomaly of 90 degrees, where the area is expressed in numbers of the diametric square. 9. A method for correcting the eccentricity based on the physical reason for the equation. 10. The equation is computed at the **octants** <note>The 45-degree points of the orbit.</note>.

...octants of the anomaly, where the area of the Equatory triangle is expressed in numbers signifying seconds. 11. Once these false **equations** <term>Equation: In Kepler’s time, this referred to the "correction" needed to turn a planet's average motion into its observed, variable motion.</term> were detected, the causes of the error were investigated no less thoroughly than before in Chapter 47.

-> # SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS <-

## CHAPTER 48.

I have attempted to eliminate all the inconveniences or imperfections of geometry from Chapter 46 by turning away from areas and toward the numerical sections of the circumference of an **Oval**. <note>Kepler spent several years trying to model the orbit as an egg-shaped "oval" before realizing it was a perfect ellipse.</note>

1. It is taught how, by this path and based on the distances found at equal intervals of time, one may geometrically seek the corresponding portion of the Oval path, following the demonstrations in Chapter 33 and assuming the total length of the Oval is known.
2. A geometric reason is given for the <term>atexia</term> <note>From the Greek 'ataxia,' meaning "disorder" or "irregularity"; here Kepler refers to the geometrical inaccuracy of using a single midpoint distance to represent an entire arc.</note> which uses a single distance from a midpoint instead of the two distances at the beginning and end of an arc.
3. Regarding another *atexia*, which nonetheless proceeds by a geometric path, it is demonstrated how the endpoints of the portions of the Oval approach the center of the **eccentric** <note>The center of the circular path used as a reference, which is not the same as the Sun's position.</note>, and thus the angle at that center which the portion of the Oval subtends; finally, from this, the angle which the same portion of the Oval subtends at the center of the Sun is found.
4. Another *atexia* is used to seek the length of the oval path, but one which accompanies other geometric speculations. For two circles are given, along with two means between them—one Arithmetic and one Geometric—the former of which produces a larger circle and the latter a smaller one. Therefore, by two arguments, the **Ellipse** <note>Kepler is beginning to see the Ellipse as a mathematical "middle ground" between other shapes.</note> is proven equal to the Arithmetic mean: one more common argument based on the narrowing of the extremes, and another purely geometric one, which demonstrates that the Ellipse certainly exceeds the lesser mean; thus, it is probable that it equals the greater mean.
5. A single process for seeking the equations is described, which neglects what was said in numbers 3 and 4, as if they compensate for one another in the parts just as they do in the sum.
6. It is demonstrated geometrically that the visual amplification caused by nearness (mentioned in number 3) and the opposite shortening of the Elliptic arcs (mentioned in number 4) are not equal in their parts.
7. The genuine process is reviewed, consistent with all the demonstrations of this chapter: and the equations found here are still shown to be in error.

## CHAPTER 49.

1. The previous method is shown to "beg the question" <note>A logical fallacy where the starting premises assume the conclusion is true.</note> and to fail in the very thing it proposed to do.
2. Therefore, setting aside not only the areas of Chapters 46 and 47 but also the Oval circumferences of Chapter 48, we return to the causes by which the Oval is produced. And because the **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> had previously been transposed onto the eccentric, where the planet’s own power was confused with the power from the Sun, the epicycle is now resumed along with the **concentric** <note>A circle sharing the same center as the Earth or Sun.</note>. The physical causes from Chapter 45 are applied so that the foundation for seeking equations by this path may be correctly established.
3. The method itself for the constructed equations is reviewed, and these equations are shown by experience to suffer from the same error as those in Chapter 47.
4. Suspicions of calculation errors that arose in Chapter 47 are cleared away, and it is concluded that the hypothesis of Chapter 45 itself is at fault.

## CHAPTER 50.

This chapter contains six attempts to find the equation through the distances themselves—that is, the "delay" of the planet in a certain arc of the eccentric—which I used before I knew that the sum of the distances was contained within the plane. Indeed, it is most certain from Chapter 33 that the delays must be taken from the distances. However, since there are three **anomalies** <note>Angles used to describe a planet's position: 1. Mean (time), 2. Eccentric (the arc), 3. True (as seen from the Sun).</note>—the first being the measure of time, the second the arc of the eccentric, and the third the angle the arc subtends at the Sun—I assigned individual distances to each of the 360 equal parts of all three anomalies. Thus, a threefold consideration of the distances was made. Furthermore, since it is clear from Chapter 33 that the planet’s daily path at **aphelion** <note>The point furthest from the Sun.</note> compared to its path at **perihelion** <note>The point closest to the Sun.</note>, as seen from the center of the Sun, is in the inverse double ratio of the distances of the planet from the Sun at aphelion and perihelion, I squared all the distances and divided by the mean distance of 100,000. This was so the result, compared to the 100,000 mean, would represent that double ratio that governs the apparent daily motions from the center of the Sun. To the three types of distances, three types of "third proportionals" were added. By investigating these, I hoped nothing would be overlooked concerning the effect of natural causes (which teach us to seek the planet’s eccentric position via distances). Thus, six methods were created.

In the first and second methods, which use the distances of the eccentric anomaly (the second type), something geometrically worthy of consideration occurs: the sum of the 360 "third" lines equaled the sum of the 360 radii (the "first" lines). This is proposed for geometers to demonstrate.

Furthermore, here is a comparison of these six methods: two (the fourth and fifth) lead to an absurdity and double the errors of the equations. The remaining four coincide with the methods of the preceding chapters. Two of these (the second and third) assume the planet's path is a circle, while two (the first and sixth) transfer the distances and produce an oval path according to the theory in Chapter 45. And just as the former err by excess, the latter err by deficiency; they hold the truth in the middle.

## CHAPTER 51.

Having detected that the equations become faulty through the Oval of Chapter 45, it is now also explored whether it errs regarding the distances.

Therefore, in this chapter, we first take the observations, and secondly, the distances of the Sun from the Earth as they were most certainly demonstrated in the Third Part; beyond this, nothing is assumed among the principles of the demonstration. From these, the distances of Mars from the Sun are demonstrated in many places of the eccentric throughout its entire circuit. Indeed, they are in places so selected that individual points from the ascending and descending semicircles are removed equally from the place of the aphelion (which was found previously by more than one way). From this, the aphelion is confirmed, and the reliability of the **Vicarious Hypothesis** <note>Kepler's own highly accurate but physically "incorrect" early model that used an equant point to predict longitudes.</note> is tested.

## CHAPTER 52.

From the things demonstrated in the previous chapter, it is further demonstrated that parts equally distant from the discovered aphelion, though equally distant from the Sun, are unequally distant from any other point outside the line through the Sun and aphelion. Therefore, the line of the **apsides** <note>The line connecting the points of greatest and least distance in an orbit.</note> of Mars passes through the body of the Sun itself, since the eccentric of Mars would be divided into two unequal segments by any other line. An anticipation of an objection is added: if anyone wished to build that eccentric upon another point so that it would be cut into two equal parts by a line other than the one passing through the Sun, he would be refuted by the observations. In the same way, it is demonstrated that since the Sun is on the longer diameter of the Oval eccentric, the "vicarious" point of the Sun (upon which Copernicus builds his eccentric) is outside that longer diameter. But it is not at all likely that the line of apsides of the Oval eccentric would be any line other than the longer diameter of the Oval. Therefore, the line of apsides does not pass wide of the Sun; and thus, the lines of apsides of all the planets meet in the very center of the Sun, not in some point of the "mean" position of the Sun.

## CHAPTER 53.

A specific method for seeking the distances of Mars from the Sun near its opposition with the Sun; and at the same time a demonstration...

<summary>Kepler summarizes his transition from circular to oval orbits, detailing his struggle to match physical causes (distances from the Sun) with geometric results. He concludes that the line of a planet's furthest and nearest points must pass directly through the physical body of the Sun.</summary>

...demonstration of a point on the Earth's orbit, from which the error committed in distance appears the greatest of all. This presupposes the difference between the positions of two **eccentrics** and that the distances of both from the Sun are moderately well known. By this reasoning, the reliability of the **Hypothesis Vicaria** <note>Kepler’s earlier "representative hypothesis" which, while mathematically accurate for predicting positions, was physically impossible because it did not account for varying distances correctly.</note> is explored at the same time as before in Chapter 51.

# SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS

## CHAPTER 54.

By collecting those things demonstrated throughout the work, the proportion of the **Eccentricity** of the **Orbs** is established and adjusted with great caution.

## CHAPTER 55.

At last, we return to the path from which we deviated in Chapter 45. For by an investigation of all cases, it is demonstrated that, just as the circle in Chapter 44 was too wide at the sides, so the **Oval** of Chapter 45 is too narrow. There are two arguments. The first is drawn from the distances: where the observations produced in Chapters 51 and 53 are compared with distances computed from the Hypothesis, based on the proportion of the orbs from Chapter 54 and the form of motions from Chapters 45, 46, and 49. And it is shown that the observed distances are longer. The second argument is taken from the **equations**. <note>The "correction" needed to convert a planet's mean motion into its true observed position.</note> For the equations computed from the circle in Chapter 43 erred in one direction; but those computed for the Oval of Chapter 45 via chapters 46 through 50 erred by just as much in the other direction.

## CHAPTER 56.

From here it is now demonstrated that distances are not to be taken from the circumference of the **Epicycle**—whether the **Planeta** moves uniformly in it (as in Chapter 45) or retains the proportion of the eccentric motion (as in Chapter 41)—but are instead to be taken from the diameter of the Epicycle. The premises are the same as in the former chapter.

## CHAPTER 57.

Since the physical reasons in Chapter 45 must necessarily have something false mixed in (because they produced a false effect), and now that the genuine effect is revealed, those physical reasons are restored, and the speculation of Chapter 39 is continued.

1. First, it is shown that the **libration** <term>Libration: A back-and-forth oscillation along a straight line. Kepler uses this to describe how a planet moves closer to and further from the sun.</term> on the diameter of the Epicycle (which yields distances consistent with observations) follows the natural laws of bodies.
2. Since libration is a movement from place to place, it is shown that this movement of the Planet's body is performed and completed by the Sun, no less than the circulation described in Part 3; yet in such a way that the "reins" of this libration are in the power of the Planet itself. This is declared by two examples: one of oars (which is imperfect), and the other of the perfection of a **magnet**.
3. In applying the magnetic example, two faculties are established on both sides—in both the Magnet and the Planet: one of direction, the other of "appetite" <note>original: *appetentiæ*. In this context, it refers to a natural attraction or physical tendency, similar to gravity or magnetic pull.</note>. A magnet is directed toward the pole, but iron "desires" it. Thus the globe of the Planet is directed toward the Fixed Stars, but "desires" the Sun. Therefore, I leave the work of **Direction** (on which the motion and position of the **Aphelius** depends) in doubt for now as to whether it belongs to a **Mind** or to **Nature**. The work of **Appetite** (on which the Eccentricity depends), I assign to Nature, and I show with "plainer logic" <note>original: *crassiori Minerva*, a Latin idiom for a rough or common-sense explanation</note> that the measure of libration found by observation is consistent with the physical cause, part by part.
4. After treating these things more accurately, starting from the work of Direction, and granting that the deviation arising from the "appetite" for the Sun detracts somewhat from it—just as a magnet directed to the pole still deviates slightly because of nearby iron and mountains—I demonstrate that by a natural and bodily faculty, even without the ministry of a "Mind," the position and the very slow forward movement of the Aphelion can be preserved.
5. Regarding the measure of Appetite, I demonstrate that it follows the ratio of a balance-scale: and specifically, the right sine of the **equated anomaly** <term>Equated Anomaly: The angular distance of a planet from its aphelion, as seen from the sun, adjusted for its varying speed.</term> measures the strength of the appetite at any point in time.
6. Regarding the libration completed at any time, reader, pay attention to what I demonstrate. Its measure is clear from Chapter 56: namely, the **versed sine** <term>Versed Sine: A trigonometric value (1 minus the cosine of an angle) that Kepler used to determine the distance a planet had moved inward or outward along its orbital radius.</term> of the **eccentric anomaly**, not the equated anomaly. That measure relies on observations. Here, then, I had to work so that from the said measure of strength at any place (which was the right sine of the equated anomaly), I might also demonstrate this measure of the line made by libration, namely the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly. To obtain this, it had to be shown that, with a quadrant divided into several equal parts, the versed sine of some arc has an insensibly smaller proportion to the versed sine of the whole quadrant than the sum of the sines in the arc has to the sum of the sines in the quadrant.
7. Here, two things seemed to stand in the way of connecting this premise with that conclusion. First, that the eccentric anomaly, which shows the measure of libration, was larger in the upper semicircle and showed more "sines" than the equated anomaly which shows the measure of strength. My answer is that this happens correctly; because in that equated anomaly, the Planet also spends more time, and therefore pours out more forces.
8. The second obstacle: the sines of the equated anomaly are shorter than the sines of the eccentric anomaly in the upper semicircle. It was shown, therefore, that the versed sine itself also falls short somewhat from the sum of the sines of its arc, and thus is equivalent to the sum of the shorter sines.
9. What can be objected to this is partly dissolved by the example of the Magnet; partly it provides the occasion, once "Nature" is brought into doubt, of passing to the concept of a **Mind**, to see whether and in what way a Mind could effect Eccentricity by the process of libration.
10. Therefore, having established what was most certainly demonstrated in Chapter 56—that the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly measures the libration—it is now demonstrated that the versed sine of the equated anomaly measures the increase of the Sun’s apparent diameter. That is, the Sun’s apparent diameter not only begins to increase when the versed sine of the equated anomaly begins, and becomes greatest when this is at its maximum, but also that it is at its midpoint when the versed sine of the equated anomaly is the semi-diameter (even though the eccentric anomaly’s versed sine is larger at that time).
11. Conversely, when the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly is the semi-diameter, it is demonstrated that the Sun's apparent diameter is still smaller, since it is between the extremes.
12. To show that this measure is suitable and comprehensible to the "Mind" of the Planet, a comparison is first established between the eccentric anomaly and the equated anomaly. I deny that the angle of the eccentric anomaly, if offered as a measure, could have been comprehended by the Planet's Mind.
13. But it is made probable that the angle of the equated anomaly, whose versed sine is proportioned to the increase of the Sun's diameter, *is* comprehended by the Planet's Mind.
14. Since, however, not this angle, but its versed sine measures the increase of the Sun's diameter, it is shown to be probable by physical reasons and examples of natural things that the Planet's Mind can comprehend the "sine" (that is, the physical strength) of this angle.
15. A comparison is made of the two modes handed down so far by which the proper motions of the planetary bodies (the librations) are performed: Nature was put in charge of one, Mind in charge of the other. Finally, I conclude in favor of **Nature**, rejecting the need for a **Mind**.
16. Among the arguments for this, the chief is the geometric uncertainty admitted in this form of motion if it were through the ministry of a Mind; this is explained.
17. It is shown that from that uncertainty, an occasion for the progress of the **Aphelia** can exist. But because in Chapter 35 another cause for the progress of the Aphelia was suggested, a comparison of both is made here; and it is shown that even if some efficacy is left to the Sun's power, it does not cause the progress of the Aphelia, whether Nature or Mind moves it.
18. Thus the physical positions are limited, lest the Sun's intervention harm anything else.
19. To show how there can be a progress of the Aphelion from this, it is associated...

<summary>This page summarizes Kepler's realization that planetary orbits are neither perfect circles nor specific ovals, but are governed by physical "librations" (oscillations). He introduces magnetic force and the "appetite" of planets to explain why they move closer to or further from the Sun, ultimately favoring physical "Nature" over an governing "Mind."</summary>

# SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

<margin>...that a peculiar work of the mind <note>The "work of the mind" refers to the idea that an intelligent soul might guide the planet, an idea Kepler often contrasts with physical, "natural" forces.</note> must be associated through its intervention: which in Number 17 was rejected as absurd. By this, a conclusion is more freely reached in favor of that opinion which, in Number 4, assigned the motion of the **Aphelion** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> to Nature.</margin>

## CHAPTER 58.

1. Having found the true account of the **libration** <note>The back-and-forth oscillation of a planet along the radius of its orbit.</note> of a planet, it is shown how, while that libration stands, the orbit of the planet (composed of both motions: the circulation and the libration) can be made even in a **cheek-like** <note>original: "buccosa." Kepler uses this term to describe an oval that is "puffy" or wider than a perfect ellipse.</note> shape; and how I fell into this cheek-like shape through a plausible error.
2. That orbit is proved to be in error through the **equations**, while the distances remain true; in contrast to what happened previously, when errors were always made in the distances and the equations simultaneously.
3. I show how, as if doing something else and having recalled the **Ellipse**, I unknowingly corrected the error.
4. It is demonstrated that a cheek-like orbit is produced from the erroneous hypothesis I commonly used.
5. But because the Elliptical orbit exhibited the correct equations, it is shown that the libration into the distorted cheek-like orbit has come into doubt.

## CHAPTER 59.

1. By ten propositions of the Geometry of the Ellipse, it is demonstrated in the eleventh proposition—no less than in the cheek-like orbit introduced in Chapter 58 and convicted of falsehood—that even in a perfect Ellipse there exist the distances established by librations and supported by observations. Therefore, since the Ellipse provides both the distances and the equations, the orbit of the Planet is Elliptical.
3. In the same place, it is demonstrated by the twelfth proposition that the **area of the Ellipse** is the most perfect measure of the distances of the unequal arcs of the Ellipse corresponding to equal arcs of the circle.
4. By the solution of an objection concerning the unequal arcs of the ellipse, it is shown by the thirteenth proportion that this Ellipse agrees exactly with the physical principles of the third part.
5. It is demonstrated by the fourteenth proposition that the arcs of the Ellipse are to be determined by lines drawn perpendicular to the degrees of the circle: concerning the beginning and the end of the quadrant by two perfect demonstrations; but concerning the intermediate progress, somewhat more imperfectly, yet by a sufficiently clear **indication** <note>original Greek: "ἔνδειξιν" (endeixin). A term for a proof that points toward a truth even if not a formal geometric deduction.</note>: here, Geometers are challenged.
6. These things having been concluded, especially those said in Number 3, and applying what was said in Number 1, it is further demonstrated by the fifteenth proposition that the Area of the circle itself is the most perfect measure of the distances assigned to the unequal arcs of the Ellipse (established by the perpendiculars of the equal arcs of the circle): as attested by the operation of numbers. In both ways, the observations are satisfied.

## CHAPTER 60.

1. From the things demonstrated in Chapter 59, a method for the equations is established.
2. A demonstration of the rule: how from a given **Eccentric anomaly**, the **mean anomaly** and the **equated anomaly** <note>Terms describing the planet's position relative to its "average" timing (mean), its position on the eccentric circle, and its "true" observed position (equated).</note> are elicited.
3. Given the equated anomaly and the **Eccentricity**, how the Eccentric anomaly is elicited; one method, which rests on a most beautiful and clearly Geometric speculation regarding the small lines of the Planet's entry from the circumference of the circle to the line of **apsides** <note>The line connecting the points of minimum and maximum distance from the Sun.</note>, and contains five problems: it is completed through the Rectangles of the quadrant.
4. Another method for this problem through analytical rules.
5. A **disordered** <note>original Greek: "ἄταχος" (atachos). Kepler refers to his iterative, non-direct method for solving what is now known as the "Kepler Equation."</note> method, as if by the Rule of False Position, for finding the Eccentric anomaly and the equated anomaly when the mean anomaly or time is given: and the reason why a Geometric method cannot be provided.

->PART V.<-

## CHAPTER 61.

The hypothesis of longitude having been found, both locations of the **Nodes** <note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note> are now more accurately investigated from observations.

## CHAPTER 62.

The distances having been found, the **Inclination** of the planes is now more accurately investigated from **acronychal** <note>Observations made when a planet is at "opposition," or directly opposite the Sun in the sky.</note> observation; and this in both semicircles. 2. The proportion of the visible latitude to the Inclination of each place is demonstrated, based on the distances of the Sun and Earth from the Planet. 3. A table of visible latitudes at the opposition of the Sun, compared with those computed from our Hypothesis.

## CHAPTER 63.

1. The physical cause of the excursion into latitude <note>The planet's movement above or below the plane of the ecliptic.</note> is provided. 2. It is demonstrated Geometrically that a plane is circumnavigated from this excursion. 3. It is disputed whether this is a **bodily Nature** or a **work of the Mind**, and a conclusion is reached in favor of Nature. 4. It is disputed whether the axis of latitudes is the same as, or different from, the axis that causes Eccentricity: and it is shown what shape the body must necessarily be if its Nature alone performs everything. 5. Having posited solid orbs, a plain and ready hypothesis of latitude is provided.

## CHAPTER 64.

The doctrine of latitudes having been delivered, the **diurnal parallax** <note>The apparent shift in a planet's position when viewed from different points on the Earth's surface.</note> is more accurately examined, and by two arguments—one through the location of the nodes, the other through the inclination of the planes—it is proved to be almost imperceptible.

## CHAPTER 65.

The quantity of the maximum latitudes, both in oppositions and in conjunctions, is determined, allowing for all motions through all **revolutions** <note>original Greek: "ἐξελιγμοὺς" (exeligmous). Large cycles of planetary motion.</note> and a proper span of centuries. 2. The same quantity is determined for our own century.

## CHAPTER 66.

The quantity of the maximum latitudes outside of the **syzygies** <note>The alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth, and a planet.</note> is investigated, and the locations are determined. 2. The cause is provided...

# SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

<margin>...that a peculiar work of the mind <note>The "work of the mind" refers to the idea that an intelligent soul might guide the planet, an idea Kepler often contrasts with physical, "natural" forces.</note> must be associated through its intervention: which in Number 17 was rejected as absurd. By this, a conclusion is more freely reached in favor of that opinion which, in Number 4, assigned the motion of the **Aphelion** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> to Nature.</margin>

*...the cause of the paradox concerning the latitude in opposition to the Sun. 3. An accurate method of calculating the latitude outside the **acronychal** <note>A planet is at its "acronychal" position when it is in opposition to the Sun, rising exactly at sunset.</note> position.*

## CHAPTER LXVII.

*The same thing is demonstrated as in Chapter 70: That the eccentricities arise from the very Center of the Sun, and not from a **vicarious point** <note>A "vicarious point" refers to the center of an equant or a point offset from the true physical center, used in older astronomy to make the math work.</note> of the Sun; and this is done by two arguments, the first from the positions of the **nodes** <note>The two points where a planet's tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note>, the other from the inclination of the planes.*

## CHAPTER LXVIII.

*1. The changed theory of the latitude of the Fixed Stars, proposed through physical causes and the **mean Ecliptic** <note>The Ecliptic is the Sun's apparent path; the "mean" version is a smoothed-out, theoretical reference plane.</note>, or rather the **Royal circle** (as we say "the Royal Road") introduced. 2. It is shown that the Northern limit of the Ecliptic is in the 5 1/2 degree of Aries; thus it is made probable that this mean or constant path passes through the positions of the planetary **apsides** <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is either closest to or farthest from the Sun.</note>. 3. The mean Ecliptic, or rather the Royal circle, is established from the change in the **Obliquity** <note>The angle of tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit.</note> of the common or true Ecliptic: where in the margin is the Theory of the **precession of the equinoxes** <note>The slow, 26,000-year wobbling cycle of the Earth's axis that changes the positions of the stars over time.</note>; through an annual cylindrical translation of the Earth’s axis and poles, and a very slow inclination which deflects the cone. 4. From this it is proved that the Inclination of the planes of Mars and the Ecliptic does not remain the same in all ages. 5. The same is concluded, though more obscurely, from a comparison of Ptolemaic observations with our own.*

## CHAPTER LXIX.

*1. What the ancients observed regarding Mars and left in writing. 2. Concerning the inequality of the precession of the equinoxes, for and against. 3. Concerning the useless number of spheres according to more recent authors. 4. Whether the eccentricity of the Sun was once greater? Or, concerning the length of summer and winter in the age of Ptolemy. 5. That the **Apogee** <note>The point where the Sun is farthest from the Earth.</note> of the Sun at the time of Hipparchus is uncertain; and his usual method of investigation. 6. The positions of the Fixed Stars at the time of Ptolemy are somewhat uncertain, and the method of investigation. 7. What error in the positions of the Fixed Stars flows back into the theory of Mars. 8. From three of Ptolemy's acronychal observations adjusted to modern **Equations** <note>Mathematical corrections used to find a planet's true position from its average motion.</note>, a correction of the motions for the time of Ptolemy is constructed, and this in eight rounds, according as one thing or another from Ptolemy's previously examined knowns was changed. 9. Therefore, to settle this uncertainty, it is shown that—by the neglect of refraction and the defect of the Sun's eccentricity canceling each other out—those positions remain for the Fixed Stars which Ptolemy assigned to them in the **Zodiac**. 10. On this foundation, the **Epoch** <note>A reference date used as a starting point for astronomical calculations.</note> of the mean motion of Mars is established for the times of Ptolemy and Christ. 11. The Epoch of the mean motion of the Sun from the Fixed Stars is also added for the times of Ptolemy and Christ.*

## CHAPTER LXX.

*The proportion of the orbits of Mars and the Sun, the latitude of Mars, and the eccentricity of the Sun are examined for ancient times through two ancient and unreliable observations.*

## FOR THE MOST PART, AS WELL AS OF THE AUTHORS,
### WHO ARE MENTIONED.

It transitions from general observations about the perfection of circular motion to the specific irregularities observed in the movement of Mars.</meta>

->IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.<-

## COMMENTARIES
### ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANET
# M A R S
#### PART ONE
### ON THE
## COMPARISON
### OF HYPOTHESES.

#### CHAPTER I.

#### On the difference between the first motion and the second or "proper" motions, and within the proper motions, the first and second inequality.

**E**ternity testifies that the motions of the planets are circular. Reason, having borrowed from experience, immediately presumes that their revolutions are perfect circles. For among shapes, the circle—and among bodies, the heavens—are considered the most perfect. But when, paying close attention, experience seems to teach otherwise; namely, that the Planets stray from the simple path of a circle; great wonderment arises, which finally impelled men to inquire into the causes.

From this very beginning, Astronomy was born among men. Its goal is understood to be to teach the causes why the motions of the stars <note>In the 17th century, planets were often called "wandering stars."</note> appear irregular from Earth when they are most orderly in the heavens, and to investigate by which circles the stars are moved, so that by their benefit, the locations and appearances of those stars can be predicted for any given time.

<margin>
Definitions:
1. <term>First motion</term> <note>Also known as diurnal motion.</note> is that of the whole sky and of all the stars in it, from the east through the south to the west, and from the west through the bottom of the sky to the east, in a period of 24 hours; in the present diagram, ABCD.
2. <term>Second motion</term> <note>The orbital motion of the planet itself.</note> is that of the individual Planets from the west toward the east, from A into E, from F into G, in longer periods of time.
4. A <term>Great circle</term> of a sphere is one which is equally distant from both of its poles.
3. <term>Lesser circles</term> are those which are closer to one of the poles; just as HLK is closer to pole Q than to pole R.
</margin>

When the distinction between the <gloss>1</gloss> first motion and the <gloss>2</gloss> second motions was not yet established, men looking at the Sun, Moon, and stars noted their daily journeys, which were perceived by the senses to be nearly equal to circles. However, they were joined one to another in the manner of a ball of yarn, and these circles were for the most part <gloss>3</gloss> lesser circles in the sphere, and very rarely <gloss>4</gloss> great circles (*as now ABCE, FMNG, cutting the equator AB at CN*). Part of them were in the South, part in the Nor- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page with "North."</note>

<meta>catchword: in North-</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the first chapter of Kepler's masterpiece, establishing the fundamental definitions of planetary motion and the historical motivations for the study of astronomy. Kepler acknowledges the ancient belief in "perfect circular motion" while setting the stage for his investigation into the irregularities of the orbit of Mars.</summary>

<keywords>Astronomia Nova, Mars, first motion, second motion, great circle, planetary motion, Johannes Kepler, celestial mechanics, celestial sphere</keywords>

--- Page 46 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Chapter I. Kepler is transitioning from a general discussion of circular motion to the specific way astronomers distinguish between the "first motion" (the daily rotation of the whole sky) and the "proper motions" (the individual paths of the sun, moon, and planets). He begins to address the apparent speeds of these bodies and critiques contemporary philosophers who reject mathematical astronomy.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

in the North.

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>

They also saw that the stars are distinguished by their speed in this daily and apparent motion. The **Fixed Stars** are the swiftest of all; because if they were joined to any of the Planets yesterday [as <term>H</term> was to <term>A</term> and <term>F</term>], they are the first to arrive at the setting [as <term>H</term> travels through <term>LK</term> and back to <term>I</term>]. The **Sun** is slower [in <term>ABE</term>], because on the following day, being located at <term>E</term>, it follows the Fixed Stars <term>I</term> to the setting, to which it had been joined the day before at <term>HA</term>. Slower still than this, and the slowest of all the heavenly bodies, is the **Moon**; because although today it set with the Sun [the Sun at <term>A</term> and the Moon at <term>F</term>], on the next day [after the whole sky and the Moon itself have rotated through <term>F M N O G</term> around the earth], it follows the setting Sun [at <term>E</term>] by a quite large interval [<term>EG</term>]. 

Hence the Pythagoreans <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophers who believed the universe was governed by mathematical and musical ratios.</note>, when they distributed musical sounds among the stars, attributed the deepest [lowest] pitch to the Moon, and the <term>hypate</term> <note>The lowest-sounding string on a Greek lyre.</note> among the strings of the lyre, for the reason that the motion of both was the slowest. From this arose the terms **to precede** <note>original: προηγέσθαι (proegesthai)</note> and **to be left behind** <note>original: ὑπολείπεσθαι (hypoleipesthai)</note>. The former term originally suited that star which, on the following day, arrived first at the setting [as the Sun <term>E</term> was said **to precede** the Moon <term>G</term>]. The latter term, however, applied to a star that was slower in the first motion [like the Moon here], as if it were being abandoned and **left behind** [at <term>G</term>] by the swifter ones [<term>E</term> and <term>I</term>]. On these matters, see more in chapter 10 of my *Optics*.

This first sketch of Astronomy—which consists of no explanation of causes, but only the truest and slowest experience of the eyes, and which can be explained neither by diagrams nor by numbers, nor be brought forth for future times, since it is perpetually at odds with itself, so much so that no single spiral is equal to another in its duration of time, and no curve of the same size passes into its neighbor—this sketch, I say, some today nevertheless attempt to restore. They trample upon the labor, diligence, erudition, and science of two thousand years, generally forcing an admiration of themselves upon the unlearned with their vain efforts. Those more skilled judge such people to be either talking nonsense or—if they wish to be heard as Philosophers, like that fellow **Patrizi** <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a philosopher who criticized traditional Aristotelian and mathematical astronomy.</note>—to be "insane with reason," and quite rightly so.

For it was the success of Astronomers to understand that two simple motions are confused: the **first** and the **second**, the **common** and the **proper**. From this confusion necessarily follows that tangled series of bundled motions. Thus, once that common and externally-driven daily rotation <note>The apparent rotation of the sky caused by the Earth's spinning.</note> is separated out, it is no longer the Fixed Stars that are the swiftest and the Moon the slowest. On the contrary, the Moon is swift in itself and by its own motion <term>FG</term>, while the Fixed Stars are clearly either the slowest or entirely unmoved. 

And when any Planet, such as the Moon <term>G</term>, is **left behind** <note>original: ὑπολείπεσθαι</note> by the Sun <term>E</term> or the Fixed Stars <term>I</term>, it is actually being carried **forward** <note>original: in consequentia; meaning "in the order of the signs," or West to East.</note> through <term>FG</term> faster than the Sun through <term>AE</term> or the Fixed Stars through <term>HI</term>. But if it should appear **to precede** <note>original: προηγέσθαι</note> among the Fixed Stars, it is proceeding in **retrograde** <note>Apparent backward motion, from East to West.</note> motion: *as if the Sun <term>A</term>, released from the same starting gates <term>AH</term> yesterday with the Fixed Star <term>H</term>,*

<margin>
☉ [Sun] ☾ [Moon] ♃ [Jupiter].
* **Forward** <note>In consequentia</note> is according to the series of the signs from Aries into Taurus, etc. This series moves from the setting [West] through the south into the eastern region, and from there toward the bottom of the sky, and back again to the west: from <term>F</term> to <term>G</term>, and from <term>A</term> to <term>E</term>.

This was a great advancement in Astronomy for learning the simplicity of motions. For instead of infinite spirals, always joined with a new one from the end of the previous *E* or *G*, there were left almost single circles *FG* or *AE*, and one common motion—either of all the Planets and even the whole world in a direction contrary to their proper motions, or, according to <term>Aristarchus</term> <note>Aristarchus of Samos (3rd century BCE) was an ancient Greek astronomer who first proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis and revolves around the Sun.</note>, while the world stands still, the globe of the earth *τ* rotates around its axis *QR* in the same direction as the proper motions.

NOW THAT THE FIRST AND DIURNAL MOTION HAS BEEN SEPARATED, and only those motions are considered which are detected by comparing several days and which belong to each Planet individually, a much greater confusion appeared in these themselves than before, when the daily and common motion was still entwined with them. For even if this remaining confusion existed before, it was observed less, and met the eyes less, because the daily motion was very swift. And thus this remaining confusion, then sliced into tiny parts, was spread over many days and many daily spirals. But now that this minute cutting and distribution of the star's proper motions over so many days has been removed—the daily motion having been taken away—the whole proper motions of the stars, however great they were, and the total confusion of several motions shone forth more clearly.

First, it appeared that the three <term>superior planets</term> <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note>—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—adjust their motions to the proximity of the Sun. For if the Sun approached them, they moved forward and faster than usual. When the Sun came to the signs opposite the Planets, they retraced the path already measured with a <term>crab-like step</term> <note>A description of retrograde motion, where a planet appears to move backward in the sky from our perspective.</note>. In the intervening times, they became stationary. And this happened perpetually, in whatever signs of the zodiac the Planets were found. At the same time, it was obvious to the eye that the Planets appeared large when they were moving backward, and small when they were moving forward and swiftly, awaiting the arrival of the Sun. From which it was easily apparent that they are lifted on high and recede from the earth when the Sun approaches, and when the Sun departs into the opposite signs, they descend again toward the earth. Finally, it was observed that these aforementioned spectacles of retrogressions and increased brightness are transposed through the signs of the zodiac in an order that tends from the western region through the south toward the east; so that what had just happened in Pisces would soon happen similarly in Aries, then in Taurus, and so on.

If anyone should bundle all these things together, and at the same time believe that the Sun truly moves through the zodiac in a year’s space—which <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century CE), whose Earth-centered model dominated astronomy for 1,400 years.</note> and <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>Kepler's mentor (1546–1601), who proposed a model where the Sun orbits Earth while other planets orbit the Sun.</note> believed—then it is necessary to admit that the circuits of the three superior Planets through the ethereal space, since they are composed of several motions, are in fact spiral; not as before, in the manner of a ball of yarn, with spirals arranged next to each other; but more truly in the shape of a **Lenten bread** <note>original: *panis quadragesimalis*. This refers to a pretzel, which was a traditional bread consumed during Lent; Kepler is describing the "loops" planets seem to make in the sky.</note>, in roughly this manner..

## Chapter I.

<margin>This is an accurate drawing of the motions of the star Mars, which it traverses through the ethereal air from the year 1580 to the year 1596, if it is true that the earth stands still, as Ptolemy and Brahe claim. To continue these motions further would have been a complicated task; for the connection is infinite, never returning into itself. And note that while such a vastness of the Martian orbit is required, the spheres of the Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Fire, Air, Water, and Earth are included in the narrowest little circle around Earth A, and its small space B; and from this very small space, a most significant little portion yields to Venus alone—surely much greater in proportion than was granted here to Mars out of the whole space of this diagram. We are forced to assign similar spirals to the four remaining planets, and indeed much more complex ones to Venus, if the earth stands still. Ptolemy and Brahe explain the causes, order, constancy, and regularity of these spirals: the former <note>Ptolemy (2nd century CE), whose geocentric model used "circles upon circles."</note> by single epicycles <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> rotated on the eccentrics of each planet, which would imitate the motion of the Sun; the latter <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), who proposed that the planets orbit the Sun while the Sun orbits the Earth.</note> by all the eccentrics rotated in the single orbit of the Sun. However, both leave the spirals themselves in the sky in reality. Copernicus, by attributing a single annual motion to the earth, strips all the planets entirely of these most complicated spirals, leading each individual planet into individual, very bare, almost circular orbits. Mars traverses this one and the same orbit as many times in the said period of time as you see "garlands" here twisted toward the center, plus one—say, nine times—while in the meantime the earth returns through its circle sixteen times.</margin>

AGAIN, however, it was noticed that these segments of the spirals of each planet are unequal in different signs of the zodiac; so that in some places a planet would move backward through a longer arc of the zodiac, in others through a shorter one, sometimes in a longer and sometimes in a shorter space of time. Nor was the increase of light for a **retrograde** <note>Appearing to move backward across the sky; this happens when Earth passes a planet or a planet passes Earth.</note> planet always the same. But if the times and locations of the intermediate segments of the retreats were computed, neither were times equal to times nor arcs to arcs, nor did any times correspond to their arcs in the same proportion. There was, however, for each planet a certain sign of the zodiac from which sign to the opposite, through each semicircle, all these things were successively increased.

From these observations it was understood that two <term>inequalities</term> <note>Historical term for "anomalies" or variations where a planet's speed or path deviates from a perfect, uniform circle.</note> were confused into one in each planet: the first of which was restored with the return of the planet to the same sign of the zodiac, and the other with the return of the Sun to the planet.

<margin>The Sun has only one single inequality with respect to the time within which it is completed. For as far as the causes of this inequality are concerned, those two concur, both in the Sun and in the remaining planets, as will be discussed below.</margin>
Therefore, the causes and measures of these inequalities could not be investigated in any other way unless the confused inequalities were separated and each inspected individually. They decided, therefore, that they must begin with the first inequality, because it was more constant and more easily handled; for they saw an example of it in the motion of the Sun, which was not subject to the second inequality. To separate the second from this first inequality, they could do so only by considering the planets on those nights on which they rise at sunset; which they therefore called <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: "ἀκρονυχías" (akronychias). This refers to "opposition," when a planet is exactly opposite the Sun in the sky, rising just as the Sun sets.</note>. For because presence and...

...tance and the conjunction of the Sun accelerates them beyond their usual pace, while the opposition of the Sun pulls them in the opposite direction; certainly before and after these points they are moved far from their positions, which they would have represented through the <term>first inequality</term> <note>The variation in a planet's speed caused by its elliptical orbit (though Kepler is still working through circular models here).</note>. <margin>Definition. <note>original Greek: Oρος</note> * The **apparent position** of the Sun is that which the Sun is seen to occupy through its inequality. The **mean position** is that which it would occupy if it lacked its inequality.</margin>
SINCE, HOWEVER, there is one <gloss>*</gloss> **mean motion** of the Sun and another **apparent motion**, because the Sun is also subject to a first inequality; the question is, which of these strips the planets of their **second inequality** <note>The "looping" or retrograde motion that occurs because the Earth is also moving.</note>, and whether the planets should be observed in opposition with the apparent or the mean position of the Sun. Ptolemy chose the mean motion; because he judged that the difference, if any occurred between using the mean or apparent motion of the Sun, could not be detected by observations; indeed, the form of calculation and demonstrations would be made easier by using the mean motion of the Sun. Copernicus and Tycho followed Ptolemy in their versions. I, as you have in my *Mysterium Cosmographicum* <note>Kepler's first major work, "The Secret of the Universe" (1596).</note> chapter 15, establish the **apparent position** and the very body of the Sun as the target: and I will prove this with demonstrations in the fourth and fifth parts of the work following.

First, however, in this first part I will demonstrate that whoever uses the apparent motion of the Sun instead of the mean, establishes an entirely different planetary orbit in the ether, whichever of the more famous opinions about the world <note>Referring to the systems of Ptolemy, Copernicus, or Tycho Brahe.</note> they follow. Since this demonstration relies on the **equivalence of hypotheses**, we shall begin with this.

***

### C H A P T E R  II.

#### Concerning the first and simple equivalence of the eccentric and the concentric-epicycle, and their physical causes.

AND AT THE START, I here embrace that **equivalence of hypotheses** demonstrated by Ptolemy in Book III and Copernicus in Book III, chapter 15, which were adopted to account for the first inequality; where an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center is slightly off-set from the Earth.</note> performs the same as an <term>epicycle on a concentric</term> <note>A small circle (epicycle) carrying the planet, while the center of that small circle moves along a larger circle centered on the Earth.</note>: provided that the line of apsides <note>The line connecting the points where the planet is closest to and farthest from the center.</note> in the eccentric, and the line through the center of the epicycle and the planet in the concentric, remain perpetually parallel; and here the radius of the epicycle equals the eccentricity there, while the radii of the eccentric there and the concentric here are equal; and the planet moves uniformly in the eccentric there, such that it covers equal arcs in equal times.

*LET* a *first be the location of the eye, and the center of the concentric* B B, *in which is the epicycle* B C, B E: *and let the arcs between the two* B’s, *or the angles* B a B, *be equal: and let the Planet be first at* C, *then at* E *and* G: *and let the lines* B E *and* B G *be parallel to* B C. *Then, let* β <note>The Greek letter beta, representing a second center.</note> *be the center of the eccentric* γ ζ: *and let* β γ *and* β ε *be equal to* A B: *and let* α *be the point where the eye is, and* β α <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance between the true center of a circle and the observer's position.</note> *be equal to the semi-diameter of* B C *and* B E, *and parallel to them: and let the arcs* γ ε *and* γ ζ, *that is, the angles* γ β ε *and* γ β ζ, *be equal both to each other and to the previous angles* B A B. *I say that the distances* A C *and* α γ *are equal; and so also are* A E *and* α ε; A G *and* α η; A D *and* α δ; A H *and* α ϑ; A F *and* α ζ. *Likewise, the angles* E A C *and* ε α γ *are equal: and the Planet, although its motion is uniform, will nevertheless be seen from both sides to be slow from* A a *when it is at* C γ, *and fast when it is at* D δ. *This, I say, Ptolemy demonstrated in Book III <note>Referring to Ptolemy's Almagest, the foundational text of ancient astronomy.</note>. There is no need for more words. The diagram speaks for the Geometer; let others consult Ptolemy.*

AS FOR THE PHYSICAL explanation of these diagrams, one differs from the other more than it might seem. To make this clear, we must look a little deeper and explain it in two ways: one according to <term>Purbach</term> <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), an astronomer whose textbook updated Ptolemaic theory for the Renaissance.</note> based on Aristotelian principles, and the other according to <term>Tycho</term> <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), Kepler’s predecessor, who provided the precise data Kepler used.</note>.

PTOLEMY described these bare circles for us just as geometry, applied to observations, indicates them. PURBACH established the manner in which they would be traversed, following Aristotle, who attempted the same regarding the geometric suppositions of <term>Eudoxus and Callippus</term> <note>Fourth-century BCE Greek astronomers who proposed a system of nested spheres.</note>, by which they had handed down the science of astronomy.

For while those authors employed 25 spheres to demonstrate all the <term>inequality</term> <note>The variation in a planet's speed or position compared to a perfectly circular, uniform motion.</note> of the planets, ARISTOTLE, believing the heaven to be filled with solid spheres, judged that another 24 "revolving" <note>Also known as "unrolling" or "counter-rotating" spheres.</note> spheres should be interspersed; specifically so that each lower sphere might be freed from the "snatching" motion it would suffer from the sphere above it due to the contact of their surfaces. Therefore, when he had accumulated 49 spheres in total (or 54 or 55 according to Callippus), he added individual motors to each one. Any one of these motors would provide its own sphere—and all the lower ones it enclosed—with a very uniform motion within the higher sphere that closely surrounded it, as if in a certain place. From this, a constant ratio would proceed, both for the direction in which the motion ought to be carried and for the speed with which the sphere was to be restored to its starting point. And since it pleased that Philosopher that the motion...

->PART ONE.<-

<margin>Chapter II.</margin>

Since he [Aristotle] established that the world is eternal, he also established that the movers are eternal. Since these move through infinite time, and since he knew that no material thing is capable of infinity, he wanted them to be immaterial as well, and "separate principles," and for that reason, immobile. But when he had constructed an eternal world from the eternity of motion, and since this duration of essence was the goodness and perfection of the whole world—opposed to destruction, which would be evil—he attributed the highest perfection to those principles, along with the understanding of it, and from that good intellect, a will to pursue it, lest a good thing should not act well. In this way, he introduced to us separate minds—finally, gods—as the ministers of the perennial motion of the heavens. They <note>The followers of Aristotle or later scholastic commentators.</note> also added a <term>motive soul</term> <note>original: "anima motrix"</note>, bound more closely to the spheres and giving them form, while the Mind only stood by—either because it seemed necessary for the mover and the thing moved to meet in some respect, or because the power, by reason of the space to be traversed, was not infinite (just as no motion is infinite, but occurs in a measured time through a measured space). Therefore, they assigned this power of moving to the soul, and for that reason allowed it to be material to a certain extent, so that it might inhabit the spheres of the heavens.

And this coupling of mind and soul is indeed very consistent with the specific observations of astronomers, although the argumentation of the philosophers is rather Metaphysical. For just as in man, one thing is the moving faculty and another is the Will which uses that moving faculty according to the information of the senses—which differ from the moving faculty both in their instruments and in the excellence of their construction (which is more admirable in the organs of the senses than in the vehicles of the motive faculty)—likewise, if we set these very Aristotelian spheres before us for contemplation, two things occur to us: <gloss>I</gloss> *Motive force* <note>original: "Vis motrix"</note>, sufficient for a round sphere, from whose vigor and constant strength the time of revolution arises; <gloss>II</gloss> *And the direction* <note>original: "plaga", referring to the specific quarter or region of the heavens.</note> in which it must go. Of these, the former is more correctly assigned to the animal faculty, but the latter to an intelligent or remembering nature. For even if, through this solidity of the spheres, all celestial motions or appearances were so provided for that nothing is left to the providence of the presiding movers, and every variety of motion arises from the arrangement and plurality of the spheres—and nothing else is required than for the motive souls to receive and retain their vigor, and from the first beginning of creation be urged into their respective directions, and released as if from the starting gates <note>original: "carceribus", the stalls used in Roman chariot racing.</note> into the open spaces—nevertheless, one must consider that it is the work of that supreme Mind itself to send each planet into its own direction, as if into a certain and peculiar province. This duty Aristotle, who knew or believed nothing regarding the beginning of the world, necessarily assigned to the authors of the motions themselves. And the followers of Aristotle, and even **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a prominent scholar who wrote on the "subtlety" of nature.</note>, a Christian by profession, openly argue that this motion of the spheres is voluntary, and that the principle of will for them is understanding and desire.

To return, then, to **Purbach** <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), whose "Theoricae Novae Planetarum" attempted to give physical reality to Ptolemaic models.</note>, with him certain others (especially the writers of small books on the spheres) explain the first diagram in such a way that they imagine for yourself one solid concentric sphere with the thickness of the entire epicycle, and within it an epicycle, and within the epicycle, the Planet.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin> Therefore, to these two spheres they attributed two <term>motive souls</term> <note>original: "animas motrices"; the guiding intelligences or spirits thought to inhabit and move the celestial bodies</note> (if they carry through the physical consideration), giving each the same proportion of power, so that they complete their periods in the same amount of time, though in opposite directions.

The second diagram requires two <term>deferents</term> <note>Circles along which the center of another circle (an epicycle) or a planet moves.</note> (which are still immobile for now, as long as we remain in this simplicity of motions and remove the progression of the apogees from our minds), and one sphere with the thickness of the planetary body. In that sphere, they placed a soul which, by steady effort, drives it around in the direction it was pushed from the beginning. Thus, if we grant this solidity of the spheres and the other assumptions, in the first diagram <term>BC</term> and <term>BE</term> will remain parallel; in the second, the sphere <term>γ ε</term> will travel around the center <term>β</term>, even if the movers do not look toward <term>AC</term> in the former case, nor toward <term>β</term> in the latter. For they are guided by material necessity, or rather by the arrangement and contiguity of the spheres.

But **BECAUSE TYCHO BRAHE** has destroyed the solidity of the spheres by most certain arguments <note>Tycho Brahe observed that comets passed through the regions where the "solid spheres" were supposed to be, proving the heavens were not composed of hard, crystalline shells.</note>—which until now could serve those motive souls (even blind ones) as a staff to find the required force—and because the planets consequently complete their courses in the pure <term>ether</term> <note>The subtle substance believed to fill all space beyond the Earth's atmosphere.</note>, just like birds in the air, we must therefore philosophize differently about these diagrams.

Let it be established among our starting principles that all the force by which motions of this kind are administered dwells in the body of the planet itself, and is not to be sought outside of it.

Since, therefore, the planet must complete a perfect circle by its innate force in the pure ether—an epicycle in the first diagram, an eccentric in the second—it is manifest that there will be two duties for this mover: one, that it must have the power to transport the body; the other, that it must be endowed with the knowledge to find the circular boundary through that pure ethereal breeze, which is distinguished by no such physical markers. This is a work of the mind. Do not tell me that the motive faculty itself, the offspring of a simple and brute soul, is naturally suited for circular motion, just as it is the nature of a stone to descend in a straight line. For I deny that any perennial motion that is not straight was ever established by God without a mental guardian. Indeed, within the human body, all muscles are moved by the principles of rectilinear motions: namely, they either swell by contracting into themselves, or are thinned by the separation of their ends; in the first case so that a limb approaches the muscle, and in the second so that it recedes: which

<summary>Kepler rejects the ancient idea of solid celestial spheres, citing Tycho Brahe's observations, and argues that since planets move through "pure ether," their circular motion must be guided by an internal "mind" or "soul" rather than physical tracks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s argument against the idea of "intellectual" movers that can create circular motion without physical references. He transitions from discussing the geometry of the spheres to the physical mechanics of how motion is actually produced in nature.</meta>

### PART ONE.

The same principle applies in its own way to circular muscles, which,
<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
assigned as guardians to the body's passages, loosen the passage when they are stretched by their circular filaments, but constrict it when those same filaments return to the shape of a narrower circle. There is no limb that can be rotated evenly and easily on its own. Indeed, the bending of the head, feet, arms, and tongue are achieved by certain mechanical devices through many straight muscles moved or stretched here and there. By this method, the <term>motive faculty</term> <note>original: "facultas motrix"; the power or soul responsible for movement</note>, though by its nature it pulls in a straight line, can twist a limb into a circle. In the same way, water is driven upward by certain machines—not because the nature of the body that causes the motion tends upward, but because the arrangement of the channels ensures that, as a greater weight pulls downward, the water must necessarily yield upward. Even if the motion of certain limbs were perfectly circular, it would not be perpetual. This should not be surprising, since the mind presides over the animal faculty in the human body. Certainly, if there had been any way of instructing a motive faculty so that it could rotate a body on its own, it would not have been overlooked in the human body.

Furthermore, it is entirely impossible for a mind to show a circular path without a fixed goal—either a center or some body—that would appear at a greater or smaller angle as one approaches or recedes. For a circle is both defined and completed by one thing: the equality of distance from the middle. No matter how much you exalt these motive faculties, a circle is nothing else—even to God—than what has just been said. Geometers do teach that a circle can be completed if three points on the circumference are given; but this very act presupposes that some part of the circumference (going through those three points) has already been made. Who, then, will show the Planet this starting point from which it may shape the rest of its journey? Therefore, it is impossible for the planet’s mover—following the opinion of *Avicenna* <note>A famous Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose works on philosophy and medicine were central to medieval and Renaissance science</note>—not to either imagine the center of its orbit and its distance from it, or be aided by some other property of the circle that must be provided to form the circle itself.

**NOW, THEREFORE**, the physical hypothesis of these two diagrams will be shaped differently for us. In the latter case, which is simpler—if what we have proposed is true, that the mover which drives the Planet through the path $\gamma$ $\epsilon$ $\delta$ exists within the Planet itself—it would be necessary for the Planet's mover to perceive the apparent size of the body at $\alpha$, as seen (or as if seen) from $\gamma$, $\epsilon$, $\eta$, and $\delta$. Because of this, the Planet would strive to move both uniformly (which the powers of a complete and unhindered motive soul achieve) and to represent all the distances $\alpha \gamma$, $\alpha \epsilon$, $\alpha \eta$, $\alpha \delta$ in such an order that they follow from the <term>eccentric</term> <note>original: "eccentricus"; an orbital circle where the center of motion is not the center of the world</note> $\beta$ $\gamma$ according to geometric law. To reach this goal, the mover must also know how much longer $\alpha \gamma$ is than $\alpha \delta$—that is, how great the eccentricity of the path is that it is about to travel, relative to the body at $\alpha$ around which it will go. In this way, the planet's mover would be occupied with many things at once. If anyone rejects this, they must necessarily say that the Planet looks toward point $\beta$—a point which lacks any body or real mark—and maintains equal distances from it.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
But the previous diagram is explained physically in this way: one might conceive of some **motive power** <note>original: "virtus motrix"; the physical or spiritual force Kepler is investigating as the cause of motion</note> which, being itself without a body, revolves in a concentric circle at B with an equal exertion of strength around a body at A, maintaining equal distances from it. Let there be another power in the body of the Planet C itself, which is able to perceive the incorporeal power at B, estimate its own proximity to it, maintain that distance, and finally revolve around it uniformly. Thus, this power would again be occupied with several tasks at once. But it is also inherently incredible that some immaterial power should reside in something that is not a body, moving in place and time, yet having no subject—moving itself, I say, from place to place. And I bring up these absurd assumptions for this purpose: to finally establish that it is impossible for every cause of motion to reside either in the body of the Planet or elsewhere in its orb; and to pave the way for persuading others of different, easier forms of motion.

I have explained these things <term>hypothetically</term> <note>original: "ὑποθετικῶς" (hypothetically)</note>, provided that Astronomy testifies regarding these diagrams that the path of the Planet is such a perfect eccentric circle; if it finds anything else, the physical speculations will also change.

In this equivalence of hypotheses, therefore, not only are the apparent angles at A and α the same, but the very truest paths of the Planets through the **ethereal air** <note>the subtle medium Kepler believed filled space</note> remain the same on both sides. For whatever kind and size of arc the Planet completes from C to E around the angle CAE, it also completes a similar arc of the same size from γ to ε around the equal angle γαε.

Thus, while the path of the star remains the same, but with the eye moved from $\beta$ to $\alpha$, different appearances will follow, and at the same moments of time. For the same locations $\delta$ $\zeta$ are viewed differently from $\beta$ and from $\alpha$. Conversely, with the eye remaining at A, and the quantity of the star’s path E G, I H remaining, but its position being changed, the star will again appear in different places, even if it stands in the same place on its journey; because the entire journey has been shifted. Therefore, since the Planet—whether viewed from $\alpha$ or from $\beta$—is at point $\delta$ or $\zeta$ at the same moment in both cases, and indeed the hypotheses are equivalent; for this reason, it must be said that the locations I and E of the different epicycles are occupied by the Planet at the same moment, and likewise G and H. There is only this difference: in the first diagram, while the eye remains fixed, the path of the Planet is moved from its position by the variation of the epicycle; but in the second diagram, the position of the Planet’s path also remains the same, while the position of the eye is changed by the same amount in the opposite direction. Nevertheless, if it is necessary, the path can remain fixed in the former and the eye in the latter, by transposing what now remains fixed, through the demonstrations of the previous chapter.

For this hypothesis (though **PTOLEMY** was unaware of it) establishes two moving powers by which any planet is carried. One of these it places in body **A** (which in the reformation of Astronomy will be the Sun itself), and it says that this power strives to drive the planet around itself, but that it has infinite degrees for the infinite points of distance from **A**: so that, just as **AD** is the longest distance and **AF** is the shortest, so the planet is also slowest at **D** and fastest at **F**. It would therefore be necessary for an understanding and a desire for a circle to exist within the planet, and for the proportion of its own slowness and speed to differ from the degrees of the external power. But if astronomical demonstrations supported by observations testify that the path of the planet is not entirely circular—contrary to what this hypothesis holds—then this physical consideration will also be set up differently, and the power of the planet will be freed from these such laborious requirements.
