Furthermore, when $\gamma$ <note>Greek letters refer to labels in the accompanying astronomical diagrams.</note> is on the line $\alpha \beta$, let the Planet be at $\epsilon$, the point nearest to $\beta$. But when $\beta$ is at a right angle to $\delta$, let the Planet be at point $\eta$, the point furthest from $\delta$, the center of the larger epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used in ancient astronomy to explain retrograde motion</term>. And Tycho Brahe follows this particular hypothesis of Copernicus religiously in its specific details.

This hypothesis, when considered physically, might hold up if one grants the existence of solid spheres; but if you remove the solid spheres—as Brahe rightly does—it describes something nearly impossible. For besides the fact that it assigns three guiding minds <note>Kepler refers to the traditional idea that celestial bodies were moved by "intelligences" or "minds" rather than physical forces like gravity</note> to a single Planet, these minds would be confused by the motion and approach of one another toward the body at $\alpha$. For it is impossible even to imagine how any of them could keep track of its own center when that center is no fixed body and is itself in motion. Furthermore, while Copernicus strives to surpass Ptolemy in the uniformity of motions, he is in turn surpassed by Ptolemy in the perfection of the planetary path. For in Ptolemy’s model, the Planet traces a perfect circle with its body through the ethereal air. Copernicus, however, confesses in Book V, Chapter 4, that for him the path of the Planet is not circular, but bulges out at the sides, as is easily demonstrated in this figure.

*For if from $\epsilon$, the position of the Planet at apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion</term>, you extend the interval $\alpha \beta$ (the semi-diameter of the orbit) to $\vartheta$, and from $\vartheta$ you draw $\vartheta \kappa$ parallel to $\alpha \delta$, the circle $\epsilon \kappa$ described from $\vartheta$ will indeed pass through $\epsilon$ and its opposite position at perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion</term>. But since it touches the straight line $\delta \eta$ only at $\kappa$, and the Planet passes through $\eta$, it does not remain on the circle $\epsilon \kappa$, but departs from this path. Ptolemy might rightly object to Copernicus regarding this "exorbitance" of the planetary path from a perfect circle; I, however, do not object. For it will be demonstrated below in the fourth part that when two physical powers, each simple in their capacity for moving the Planet, concur, it is necessary that the Planet deflect slightly from a circle—not by bulging outward, as in this Copernican hypothesis, but by moving in the opposite direction, toward the center.*

If, moreover, Copernicus were to retain that freedom of his to establish the proportions of the epicycles, it could happen that the path of the Planet would turn out to be twisted—higher before and after the apogee than at the apogee itself, and lower before and after the perigee than at the perigee itself. This very thing happened to Tycho in his lunar models, insofar as he imitated Copernicus here.

But I shall demonstrate with numbers that these two forms of hypotheses are not even simply equivalent.

Indeed, the Ptolemaic form can be computed more concisely than by Ptolemy himself in the following manner. *First, in the triangle CBE, the mean anomaly <term>Mean Anomaly: An angle used to track a planet's progress as if it moved at a constant speed</term> ECB or DCE is given; the side CB (the eccentricity of the equant) and BE (the radius of the orbit) are also given. Therefore, as the radius of the orbit is to the sine of ECB, so CB is to the sine of CEB: and since ECD equals the interior and opposite angles CEB and CBE...*

<margin>
**Definitions:**
**Mean anomaly** is the time elapsed since the Planet was at apogee, expressed as an angle. For the total time in which the Planet returns from apogee to apogee is divided into 360 degrees, like a circle.
**True anomaly** is the arc of the zodiac between the position of the apogee and the apparent position of the star (as seen from the center of the zodiac).
**Equation** is the difference between the two anomalies.

In a certain equivalence attempted in the hypothesis of **TYCHO’S** lunar tables, I transposed those two Copernican epicycles into such a Ptolemaic eccentric with an equant point: nonetheless, I also added an epicycle because of another and peculiar inequality of the Moon.

**FINALLY**, since through the second chapter, in this Copernican form, the larger epicycle with its concentric can be transposed with perfect equivalence into an eccentric whose eccentricity is equal to the semi-diameter of the larger epicycle, therefore, by adding the smaller epicycle to this very Copernican eccentric, an eccentrepicycle <note>A hybrid model combining an eccentric circle with an epicycle.</note> will be born, matching exactly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for perfect precision.</note> the double epicycle in the concentric, and no more different from the Ptolemaic eccentric with an equant because of this.

**I**T OCCURS IN TWO ways: one, in which the Ptolemaic and Copernican forms are equivalent; the other, which is unique to the Copernican form; which, as it is more foreign to our purpose, we shall explain first. For it remains closer to itself than the other.

<margin>Theorem. <note>original: "$\Theta \epsilon \gamma$." likely an abbreviation for Theorema. </note>
The word "eccentric" here has a unique meaning.</margin>
With center $\gamma$ and distance $\gamma \delta$, let an eccentric circle be drawn, in which $\alpha \gamma$ is first the line of apsides <term>line of apsides: The line passing through the points in an orbit where a planet is closest to and farthest from its center of motion.</term> and $\alpha$ is the point of sight <note>The observer's position.</note>: let this be continued to $\epsilon$. Let $\gamma \alpha$ be the amount of eccentricity or the radius of the larger Copernican epicycle. For the equivalence of both was discussed at the end of the preceding Chapter IV. Therefore, with center $\epsilon$ and distance $\epsilon \eta$, let a smaller epicycle be drawn; and, when its center is at $\epsilon$, let the Planet be at $\eta$ falling on the line $\epsilon \gamma$, so that it is not the star itself, but the center of the epicycle carrying the star, that traverses the eccentric $\epsilon \delta$. Through Chapter IV, the Copernican form is expressed here. For this, through Chapter III, we shall establish another equivalent in truth—that is, in the indication of the actual planetary path—though with a different appearance; and we shall achieve this by moving the point of sight from $\alpha$. We could do the same through the end of Chapter III even while the sight remains at $\alpha$, by moving the eccentric and keeping the lines parallel, so that only the position is varied while the size of the eccentric remains the same. However, what we have now undertaken we shall complete as follows. Taking a point of sight outside the previous line of apsides, which we shall call $\beta$, so that $\beta \gamma$ is a different quantity from $\alpha \gamma$ (that is, of a new eccentricity or a new semi-diameter of the larger epicycle), we shall draw a new line of apsides $\beta \delta$ through $\beta \gamma$, and in $\delta$ we shall draw an epicycle equal to the previous one. Although the center of the epicycle is here in the apsis <note>The highest or lowest point of the orbit.</note> $\delta$, we shall not now place the Planet in the point nearest to $\gamma$ itself as before, but having considered the angle $\epsilon \gamma \delta$, we shall set for it a double angle $\vartheta \delta \gamma$ toward $\epsilon$, and we shall place the Planet at $\vartheta$ when the epicycle is in the apsis $\delta$. For in this way the Planet would be placed even if the sight were at $\alpha$ and the epicycle at $\delta$. In this manner, therefore, the same truth of the composite planetary path remains perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a common Latin idiom for precision.</note> preserved, but the appearance is changed. For when the lines of sight are inclined, as here $\beta \vartheta$, $\alpha \vartheta$ or $\beta \eta, \alpha \eta$, then they also fall upon different places against the Fixed Stars.

YOU MAY OBJECT: Even when the lines of sight are parallel, they fall upon different places against the Fixed Stars; therefore, it is not necessary for this that they be inclined toward each other. I ANSWER: This is indeed true; but then the space of the Fixed Stars intercepted between both lines is not perceptible to the sight, unless the distance between the parallels is perceptible relative to the radius of the Fixed Stars.

In Physical consideration, besides those things said in Chapter III, this also must be established to obtain this identity of the path despite the varied appearance: that the mind <note>Kepler often refers to a "mind" or "intelligence" (anima motrix) as the guiding force that moves a planet along its path.</note> to which the smaller epicycle is entrusted looks to a different point of the circuit than the mind of the larger epicycle. For the larger epicycle or the eccentricity in the second position is restored to the line $\beta \delta$, but the smaller one to the line $\alpha \epsilon$, not passing through the sight; because the sight in the second position is placed at $\beta$, whereas in the first position (with the sight established at $\alpha$) both epicycles would be restored to the same $\epsilon \alpha$.

Thus, the same form of the hypothesis does not simply remain physically the same, even if the same path for the planet is obtained. And **MÄSTLIN** <note>Michael Mästlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s university professor and a key supporter of the Copernican system.</note> used this form of transposition when he constructed that table for Chapter 15 in my *Mysterium Cosmographicum* <note>Kepler's first book (1596), which attempted to explain the structure of the universe using the five Platonic solids.</note>. For Copernicus, while translating Ptolemaic ideas into his own general form of hypotheses, imagines the observer to be located at some nearly immobile point very near the Sun, which is distant from the center of the actual solar body by the entire eccentricity of the solar orbit. But I, while adapting Copernicus to the subject matter of that book of mine, had need of a different fiction. For the point of sight had to be transferred by imagination from that point into the actual center of the solar body, and from there (namely, from the body of the Sun) the departures of the planetary bodies had to be calculated, following the same path that Copernicus's suppositions formed. But (as has now become clear) not exactly the same path was produced for me for the sake of specific times through this translation of the line of apsides; the difference was, however, very small, and in that little book it was clearly of no importance. For there it was only a matter of the location of the path, which remained the same in this way.

<margin>CHAPTER V</margin>
I now come to the first method of establishing the proposed equivalence, which is common to the specific hypotheses of various authors. I will first demonstrate this in the Ptolemaic form.

-><note>Geometric diagram: An eccentric circle with center $\beta$. The line of apsides <note>The line connecting the points where a planet is closest to and farthest from its center of motion.</note> runs through $\iota$ and $\beta$. Points $\alpha$ (sight/power), $\gamma$ (equant), and $\delta$ (a second observation point) are marked along this line. A point $\eta$ on the circumference represents the planet's position.</note><-

With center $\beta$, let the Ptolemaic eccentric $\iota \zeta \eta$ be drawn. Let the line of apsides be $\iota \beta$. Let the point of sight be at $\alpha$, and the equant point <term>equant: an imaginary mathematical point used to account for the observed speed changes of planets; Kepler is beginning to challenge its purely mathematical nature here</term> be at $\gamma$.

When I say the sight is at $\alpha$, I mean this either as a mathematical fiction or in truth. Physically speaking, the sight should not be placed at $\alpha$ so much as the very moving power <term>power: Kepler's 'virtus,' a physical force he believed emanated from the Sun to drive the planets</term> itself, which provides the planet with its circuit around it, making it slow or fast in proportion to its proximity to $\alpha$, as was stated above. Let some point on the circumference outside the line of apsides (say $\eta$) be connected with $\gamma, \beta,$ and $\alpha$. Let it be such that, through this hypothesis, the angles $\iota \alpha \eta$ through the whole circuit can be computed to be nearly as large as those observed from $\alpha$; and after certain times, let these be measured uniformly by the angle $\eta \gamma \iota$.

*It will be shown later, in the second part, how it is discovered through astronomical observations what angle $\eta \alpha \iota$ is owed to any given angle $\eta \gamma \iota$. Again, let the sight or the moving power be at a point outside the line $\iota \alpha$, which we call $\delta$. Let it be given to us that at $\delta$ also, through astronomical observations at certain times, certain visual angles were detected—that is, how much the planet is seen to move under the Fixed Stars at any time when viewed from $\delta$. Let it also be given that these appearances at $\delta$ fit into a hypothesis conforming to the previous one, changed only by the amount of eccentricity <note>The distance the center of the orbit is "off-center" from the observer.</note>. Since, however, it is certain that at one and the same time the planet completes one and the same path in the heavens, and not one path for an observer at $\delta$ and another for one at $\alpha$; it is therefore also certain that the planet cannot appear to both observers (both the one at $\alpha$ and the one at $\delta$) to have equal motion at the same time.* 

*For let a portion of the planet's true path be $\iota \eta$, and let the planet complete that in a certain time, say twenty days. Since therefore $\alpha$ is closer to $\iota \eta$ than $\delta$ is, that portion $\iota \eta$ will therefore appear larger from $\alpha$ than from $\delta$ through the principles of Optics. Therefore, in those same twenty days, the planet will be seen to have moved more by the one watching from $\alpha$ than by the one at $\delta$. And since every planet perpetually maintains a certain and same number of days in which it returns to the same point of the Fixed Stars, any slowness must be compensated by an opposite speed. Since therefore the planet appears slower to the observer at $\delta$ in the portion $\iota \eta$, it will therefore appear faster to that same observer at $\delta$ than to the one at $\alpha$ in another portion of the orbit. From this it follows that the planet appears slowest in one place to the observer at $\delta$, and in another place to the observer at $\alpha$. Yet the planet itself, in truth, cannot be slowest except in one specific place in its orbit.*

With these things thus prepared, the question is whether one and the same true path in the heaven...

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

The Planet (as is presupposed) should be able to represent both appearances—both to the observer at $\delta$ and to the one at $\alpha$—each with their own specifics, and such as the forms of Ptolemaic calculation on both sides allow and admit.

But if the Planet were of equal speed in all parts of its orbit, the answer would be as given in the third chapter, that it is so. However, because the Planet is slowest at one place of the eccentric by a true and real delay <note>Kepler distinguishes here between "real" physical slowing and "apparent" optical slowing</note>, and fastest at the opposite, the answer must be: not clearly.

The reason is this: two slowings-down are mixed together. One is real and physical at one place on the eccentric; the other is optical and apparent in a place that is not just one, but is that which is furthest from whichever position of sight is chosen. *Therefore, when the sight $\alpha$ falls on the line drawn through center $\beta$ of the eccentric and center $\gamma$ of the equant <term>equant: a mathematical point used in ancient astronomy to account for the speed variations of planets</term>, standing on the part of the line opposite to that which has the equant center $\gamma$, then both slowings-down converge toward the same point of the fixed stars toward $\iota$. But when the sight moves away from this line, as at $\delta$, then a straight line projected from $\delta$ through the center of the circle $\beta$ shows the location of the optical slowness at $\eta$, while the true and physical slowness is at $\iota$. And of these inequalities or slowings-down, one dilutes the other, and they accumulate in an intermediate place between $\iota$ and $\eta$, as if a line were projected from $\delta$ through $\gamma$ to point $\zeta$. Thus, if someone used such a calculation in which $\delta \beta$ was the line of apsides <term>apsides: the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center of motion</term> of the eccentric, and $\beta \gamma$ was the line of the equant's eccentricity, then indeed, while the planet's true path $\iota \eta$ remained the same, it would be represented differently from $\delta$ than from $\alpha$. For to the one at $\delta$, the Planet would be slowest at $\zeta$, while to the one at $\alpha$, it would be slowest at $\iota$. Yet no such thing would be represented at $\delta$ that we required above to be represented by a hypothesis conforming to the previous one. For the forms of the hypotheses differ in this: there, $\beta$ is in the middle between $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ (which physical reasoning also requires, if the moving power <term>moving power: Kepler's "virtus motrix," a physical force he believed the Sun exerted on planets</term> is at $\alpha$), but here, center $\beta$ would not be in the middle between $\delta$ and $\gamma$, nor would the line of the equant's eccentricity pass through the sight $\delta$ (as it did there). Even if it did pass through $\delta$ as $\delta \gamma$, it would still not cut the eccentric into two equal parts, because it does not pass through the center $\beta$, nor would it allow the Planet to be seen from here as slowest in opposite places and fastest in the other.*

SINCE THEREFORE it is established that, while the path of the Planet in the heavens remains exactly the same, the form of the hypothesis cannot remain exactly the same, the question is further asked: If the same form of hypothesis is established at $\delta$, how much would the Planet's path be changed from the previous one, and how much would this new establishment of the hypothesis from $\delta$ vary the previous appearances at $\alpha$? First, if the *center of the equant is moved from $\gamma$ to the line $\delta \beta$, and $\beta \mu$ is made equal to $\beta \gamma$, the position of the planetary path clearly remains the same, but the Planet is slowest with physical slowness not at $\iota$ but at $\eta$. Therefore, something is changed in the Planet's path that cannot be changed;*

because *Physical* slowness does not follow the observer's vision in the same way as *Optical* slowness does. And <margin>Chapter V.</margin>
even if the same Planet completed the path $\iota \eta$ in twenty days, which would appear larger at $\alpha$ and smaller at $\delta$: nevertheless, if you consider the parts of this time, the ratio of applying them to the parts of this path will be greatly disturbed, and much more so in other parts that are not interposed between the lines $\iota \eta$. Especially, the quantity of its equations <term>equation: in early astronomy, this refers to the "correction" added or subtracted to a planet's average position to find its actual position</term> will change noticeably for the vision at $\alpha$, if you take away from the observer at $\delta$ the fact that the Planet is not slowest at $\iota$; that is, if you transfer the point of the equant from $\gamma$ to $\mu$. For when a straight line is drawn through $\gamma \mu$ to point $\nu$ on the circumference, and $\alpha \nu$ is connected, only this equation $\alpha \nu \mu$ will be equal to the previous one $\alpha \nu \gamma$; but above $\nu$, the equations from $\mu$ will be smaller, and below $\nu$ they will be larger: just as at $\eta$, the angle $\mu \eta \alpha$ is much smaller than $\gamma \eta \alpha$. Furthermore, even then, what we had intended was not accomplished; that is, the previous form of the hypothesis is not yet clearly established. *For it is not as $\alpha \beta$ is to $\beta \gamma$, so $\delta \beta$ is to $\beta \mu$: for $\beta \mu$ is equal to $\beta \gamma$ itself, but $\delta \beta$ is greater than $\alpha \beta$. But if you make it so that $\alpha \beta$ is to $\beta \gamma$ as $\delta \beta$ is to $\beta \mu$, then $\beta \mu$ will become greater than $\beta \gamma$.* From which it follows that the equation seen at $\alpha$ will be much more corrupted, and indeed even the maximum equation, because of the increased eccentricity <term>eccentricity: the distance between the center of the planet's circular orbit and the center of the system (like the Sun or Earth)</term>.

Therefore, the Planet will not only be slowest in a different place than before, but also with a different and indeed greater measure of true slowness. It appears, therefore, that the equivalence we sought cannot be established by drawing the line of apsides <term>line of apsides: the line passing through the points where a planet is closest to and farthest from the center of its orbit</term> from $\delta$ through $\beta$, the center of the eccentric. And since it has simultaneously become clear how much it matters that the same point $\gamma$ of the equant be retained, we must therefore either break through here or nowhere.

What will happen then, if a new line of apsides is drawn from $\delta$ through $\gamma$, the old point of the equant, and the new hypothesis is made to conform to the old one? That is, if the center of the eccentric is moved from $\beta$ to the line $\delta \gamma$, and it is made so that $\alpha \beta$ is to $\beta \gamma$ as $\delta \zeta$ is to $\zeta \gamma$, and $\zeta$ becomes the center of the eccentric? Naturally, this will happen: the path of the Planet in the sky will not remain exactly the same. *For let an eccentric equal to the previous one, $\epsilon \kappa \lambda$, be drawn from $\zeta$. And through $\zeta \beta$, let a straight line be continued to the circumferences, on this side to $\xi$ and $o$, and on the other side to $\rho$ and $\pi$. Therefore, as great as $\zeta \beta$ is, so great are $o \xi$ and $\rho \pi$; and the Planet becomes that much closer to $\beta$ at $o$ and that much more remote at $\xi$ than if it had run along the previous eccentric. But at $\zeta$, the Planet becomes slowest in another region; for previously the apsis <note>The point of slowest motion</note> was at $\iota$, now it is at $\kappa$.* And from this adjustment it results that for the previous sight located at $\alpha$, its views are left as nearly as possible as they were. This, indeed, is the only thing sought here. We will now prove this with numbers familiar to the motion of Mars, even if Tycho Brahe <note>original: "Braheus"</note> provided slightly different ones; which will not hinder us, as we are only performing preliminary exercises <note>original: "προγυμναζόμεθα," a Greek term for preparatory training</note> here.

*Let these values be assumed in $\delta \gamma \alpha$. Let $\delta \alpha$ be 3584, the quantity of the Sun's eccentricity, of which the eccentricity of Mars $\delta \gamma$ is 30138: and let the angle $\alpha \delta \gamma$ be 47 degrees 59 minutes 1/4, the difference between the apogees <note>Apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of the Sun and Mars. Therefore, from the three given points $\delta \gamma \alpha$, the new eccentricity of Mars will be given, and it will be 27971, and the angle $\delta \gamma \alpha$ will be 5 degrees 27 minutes 47 seconds. But if the previous apogee of Mars, $\delta \gamma$, is placed at 23 degrees 32 minutes 16 seconds of Leo, the new apogee of Mars, $\alpha \gamma$, will fall at 29 degrees 0 minutes 3 seconds of Leo.*

Let $\beta \xi$ be 100,000, and $\alpha \gamma$ be 18,034 in such units—which was previously 27,971 in units where $\delta \gamma$ was 30,138. Therefore, in this dimension, $\delta \gamma$ will be 19,763. Then $\delta \vartheta$ will be 12,352 and $\vartheta \gamma$ will be 7,411; and $\alpha \beta$ will be 11,271 and $\beta \gamma$ will be 6,763. Thus, the first hypothesis of the **Ptolemaic inequality** <note>original: "inæqualitatis Ptolemaica"; in older astronomy, an "inequality" refers to a variation or irregularity in a planet's motion that requires a geometric correction</note> is constructed upon both $\delta \xi$ and $\alpha$. Then, in the former dimension where $\delta \alpha$ is 3,584, $\vartheta \beta$ or $o \xi$ will be 1,344. But in units where $\beta \xi$ is 100,000, $\vartheta \beta$ or $o \xi$ will be 880. Let these values be saved.

To find the starting point of the calculation by which we investigate how much the appearances change for the vision at $\delta$ through the transposition of the **eccentric** <term>eccentric: an off-center circular orbit, used by ancient and Renaissance astronomers to explain why planets seem to speed up and slow down</term> from $\rho \vartheta o$ into $\pi \beta \xi$, we must proceed as follows. Since $\gamma$ is the common center in whose circle the times are marked, let $\gamma \epsilon \iota$ denote the same moment in both hypotheses. Therefore, if the planet runs along the eccentric $\epsilon o$, it will then be at $\epsilon$ with the **equation** <term>equation: a correction or "equalizing" value added to or subtracted from a planet's mean position to find its true position</term> $\delta \epsilon \gamma$. But if it runs along the eccentric $\iota \xi$, it will be at $\iota$ with no equation, as the lines $\alpha \iota$ of the apparent motion and $\gamma \iota$ of the **mean motion** <note>The "mean motion" is the theoretical position of a planet if it moved at a perfectly constant speed in a perfect circle</note> coincide. Again, after a certain time—the measure of which is $\iota \gamma \zeta$ or $\epsilon \gamma \kappa$ (at the vertex of which is positioned $\delta \gamma \alpha$, which has already been found to be 5 degrees, 27 minutes, 47 seconds)—let there be some common moment designated by $\gamma \kappa \zeta$. Then the planet, moving along the eccentric $\epsilon o$, will be at $\kappa$ and lack an equation; but moving along $\iota \xi$, it will be at $\zeta$ with the equation $\gamma \zeta \alpha$. Thus, the planet is always on the line projected from $\gamma$ on both sides, at the point where it intersects either eccentric.

If the eye were at $\gamma$, no difference in appearances would occur, whether the planet were at $\kappa$ or $\zeta$. But because the vision is placed by the craftsmen <note>Kepler likely refers to traditional astronomers like Ptolemy here</note> at $\delta$, and by me at $\alpha$, the question is: At what place on the circumference is the distance of the eccentrics on this line projected from $\gamma$ most perceptible to the vision at $\delta$? For that distance to become perceptible, three things must coincide. First, the distance itself must be large, which is why it is greatest around $o \xi$ and $\epsilon \pi$. Second, it must be presented as directly as possible to the vision at $\delta$; otherwise, as at $\zeta \kappa$ and the opposite location, it disappears according to the principles of **Optics**. Therefore, it appears greatest in the intermediate places below $\xi$ and above $\rho$. Third, it must be near $\delta$ itself; for this reason, it becomes closer above $\epsilon$ than below $\xi$, because the center of the other eccentric, $\beta$, deviates to the right side of $\delta$. If we establish a right angle at point $\gamma$ on the line $\gamma \delta$, with a perpendicular projected from $\gamma$ to the circumferences, we will come as close as possible to the place where this appearance is greatest. Let the perpendicular to $\delta \gamma$ pass through $\gamma$, which shall be $\sigma \phi$ intersecting the eccentric $\vartheta$ at $\sigma$ and the other at $\tau$; and let the perpendicular $\beta \chi$ be dropped. At moment $\gamma \sigma$, the planet will be at $\sigma$ and $\tau$, and at moment $\gamma \phi$ it will be at $\upsilon$ and $\phi$. First, the quantity $\upsilon \phi$ must be sought. Let $\vartheta$ be connected with $\upsilon$ and $\beta$ with $\phi$. Therefore, in the triangle $\vartheta \upsilon \gamma$, $\vartheta \upsilon$ is given as 100,000 (since $\vartheta$ is the center of the eccentric $\upsilon$), $\vartheta \gamma$ is 7,411, and the angle $\vartheta \gamma \upsilon$ is a right angle.

## PART ONE.

<margin>Chapter VI.</margin>
**S**O FAR WE HAVE SPOKEN about the hypotheses <note>hypotheses: in this context, the mathematical models or geometric arrangements used to predict planetary positions</note> of the first inequality <note>first inequality: the variation in a planet's speed caused by its own elliptical path (or eccentric circle in older models) as it moves through the zodiac</note> of the Planets, which is completed whenever the Planet returns to the same sign of the zodiac. Now we pass to the second inequality, which is completed not in some constant and single sign of the zodiac, but in the conjunction or opposition of the Sun with the Planet. Men have therefore marveled greatly at this: and one person has brought forward one cause, and another another, for how it happens that a Planet joined to the Sun is rendered swift, direct, high and small, but on the opposite side of the Sun <term>retrograde</term> <gloss>retrograde: appearing to move backward against the stars</gloss>, low and large, and in the intermediate times <term>stationary</term> <gloss>stationary: appearing to stand still before changing direction</gloss> and of middling size.

LATIN authors <note>original: "Latini authores" — referring to medieval and Renaissance scholars of the Latin West</note> judged that a power resided in the aspects <note>aspects: the specific angular distances between celestial bodies, such as 90 or 120 degrees</note> and rays of the Sun, by which the other Planets were in truth attracted. Their opinion cannot be demonstrated by numbers, and for that reason, it is not Astronomical; but it is also not likely, once the true causes are found: and it is manifestly false, since Saturn begins to <term>retrocede</term> <gloss>retrocede: to move backward</gloss> in the square <note>square: an aspect of 90 degrees</note> of the Sun or beyond, Jupiter in the trine <note>trine: an aspect of 120 degrees</note>, Mars in the biquintile <note>biquintile: an aspect of 144 degrees</note> or before the sesquadrate <note>sesquadrate: an aspect of 135 degrees</note>, all at an inconsistent interval.

PTOLEMY said that in a certain place of the Planetary circle—which suffices for the first inequality—it is not the Planet itself that is fixed, but the center of an <term>epicycle</term> <gloss>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one</gloss> carrying the Planet fixed on its own circumference, which in turn is carried by that principal Planetary circle. He claimed the form of the motion was such that if the center of the <term>epicycle</term> were with the Sun, the Planet would also be at the top of the <term>epicycle</term>, and would move with the Sun toward the same region. As the Sun recedes from the center of this <term>epicycle</term> (for the Sun is swifter than it), the Planet simultaneously descends in the <term>epicycle</term>. However, since the motion of the <term>epicycle</term> around its own center becomes swifter than the motion of the center around the earth, it happens that when the Planet traverses the lower parts of the <term>epicycle</term> while the center of the <term>epicycle</term> is turning in opposition to the Sun, by the composition of motions it becomes truly <term>retrograde</term>. Thus Ptolemy adapted his opinion to numbers and <term>Geometry</term>, but he did not remove the wonder of it. For the cause is still sought that connects all the <term>epicycles</term> of the Planets to the Sun, so that they always complete their period in the meeting of their center with the Sun.

COPERNICUS, along with the most ancient Pythagoreans and Aristarchus, and together with them I, deny that this second inequality is inherent in the Planet’s own motion itself, but only that it appears so; it actually happens by the annual gyration of the earth around the immobile Sun. Therefore, just as in Chapter 1 the daily motion <note>daily motion: the apparent rotation of the heavens every 24 hours</note> was separated from the proper motions of the Planets, so now the second inequality of the Planets is likewise separated from the first by Copernicus, and indeed in the same way. For other practitioners recognize the first motion as something foreign to the Planets, but they nevertheless believe that it truly exists in the Planets and is applied to them so that the Planets are carried by it. Copernicus concedes that it neither exists in them by itself, nor is it applied from the outside, but is only attributed to them by a deception of vision. For while the earth is turned upon its axis from west to east, it appears to our vision that the rest of the world is turned from east to west. In the same way, I say, Copernicus asserts that the Planets do not truly become <term>stationary</term> and <term>retrograde</term>, but only appear so. For the earth, in addition to its other motion, also [moves] by an annual...

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANET MARS

<margin>Chapter VI.</margin>
...moved in a very great circle (which he calls the **Great Orb** <note>Great Orb: in Copernicus's system, this refers to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note>), those who believe the earth stands still think that the Planets and Sun are moved in the opposite direction. They believe that when the Sun is placed between the earth and the Planet, the motions of the earth and Planet are combined in our vision, which makes the Planet appear swift. However, when the earth is placed between the Sun and the Planet, the Planet appears to be left behind and thus moves backward <gloss>retrograde</gloss>, because the earth is moving faster than the Planet.

**TYCHO BRAHE** holds a view similar to the Latin authors: it is not that the Sun attracts the Planets through its <term>aspect</term> <gloss>aspect: the angular relationship between celestial bodies</gloss>, but rather that the Planets "pay court" <note>original: "adulari"; Kepler uses this colorful term to describe how the planets seem to follow the Sun's lead</note> to the Sun. They strive to keep the Sun (even though he is moving) nearly in the center of their revolutions, while they arrange their own true paths around the Sun (as if he were immobile). By this reasoning, every Planet in the heavens completes the Sun's own path in addition to its own particular path. The result of these combined motions is exactly <note>original: "ad unguem" — literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for perfect precision</note> the same as that found in **PTOLEMY** (namely, a spiral), as was stated in Chapter 1. In astronomical terms, **PTOLEMY** established <term>epicycles</term> <gloss>epicycles: small circles whose centers move along the circumference of larger circles</gloss> on <term>eccentrics</term> <gloss>eccentrics: circular orbits whose center is offset from the central body</gloss>, while **BRAHE** established eccentrics on a single epicycle, which is the Sun's orbit itself.

In the following demonstrations, I shall join the models of all three authors together. For **TYCHO**, when I suggested this to him at times, replied that he would have done so of his own accord even if I had remained silent (and he would have done it, had he survived). As he was dying, he asked me—knowing I supported the **COPERNICAN** opinion—to demonstrate everything using his own hypothesis.

Furthermore, we will demonstrate the most perfect geometric equivalence of these three forms, both right now and throughout the whole book, even while we are doing other things. For the present, our plan must be pursued: we must demonstrate that a very great error is made regarding the <term>second inequality</term> <gloss>second inequality: the appearance of retrograde motion</gloss> if the Sun's <term>mean motion</term> <gloss>mean motion: the average speed of a body, ignoring its periodic speed changes</gloss> is used instead of its apparent motion, at the moment when the Planet is in <term>opposition</term> <gloss>opposition: when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun</gloss> at the start of this second inequality.

*I shall begin with the **COPERNICAN** opinion. With center β, let the earth's eccentric [orbit] γ υ be drawn, just as **COPERNICUS**, trusting in **PTOLEMY**, imagined it; let γ β be the <term>line of apsides</term> <gloss>line of apsides: the line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit</gloss>, κ the fixed position of the Sun, and β the point of the earth's uniform motion.*

*Let υ σ be drawn through β perpendicular to β γ, cutting the circumference at points υ and σ, and let υ and σ be connected to κ.*

***COPERNICUS**, therefore, intending to transfer the **PTOLEMAIC** numbers into his own form of hypothesis, computed the planets' eccentricities not from κ (the Sun) but from β, the center he estimated for the earth's uniform motion. For when lines are drawn from β—namely β γ, β υ, and β σ—whenever the Planet and the earth fall upon these lines, the Planet was supposed to have shed the second inequality, which occurred because of the earth's motion; for example, if the earth were at υ, the Planet would be found on the extension of the line β υ.*

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

Furthermore, by this reasoning, Copernicus placed the point of vision, by way of a fiction, at point $\beta$ <note>$\beta$ (beta) represents a simplified center for observations in Copernicus's geometric model.</note>. For as long as the Planet is on the line $\beta \upsilon$, it makes no difference for designating its position among the <term>Fixed Stars</term> <gloss>the distant background stars that appear not to move relative to one another</gloss>, whether it is viewed from $\sigma$ (sigma) or from $\beta$. The same can truly be said of the lines $\beta \gamma$, $\beta \sigma$, and infinite others meeting at $\beta$. Therefore, point $\beta$ is the meeting point of all <term>lines of sight</term> <gloss>linea visoria: the straight line from the observer's eye to the object</gloss>, and thus serves as a common fictional point for all observations. In reality, however, the point of vision—that is, the Earth, our home—is found at various different points on the circle $\sigma \gamma \upsilon$ at different times.

Since Copernicus believed, therefore, that the Planet is freed from the <term>second inequality</term> <gloss>the apparent variation in a planet's speed and direction caused by the Earth's own motion</gloss> whenever the Earth and the Planet are found on any single line extending from $\beta$, he sought out the observed positions of the Planets among the Fixed Stars at those moments of the Planet's **opposition** with the <term>mean place of the Sun</term> <note>mean place of the Sun: a mathematical average of the Sun's position, used by astronomers before they realized orbits were elliptical and varied in speed</note> using mathematical instruments. For once the Planet's position was found on some night near the Planet's opposition with the Sun, if the mean position of the Sun was found by calculation to be at the precisely opposite point at that time, that was the exact moment <note>original: "articulus temporis"</note>. If they were still somewhat distant on that night, he tracked down <note>original: "venatus est" — literally "hunted down"</note> this very moment, and the point or location the Planet would hold at that moment, by comparing two or more nights and the intervening daily motions of **MARS** and the Earth. When this was done as many times, and in as many places in the zodiac, as he thought necessary (as if it had been done at $\beta \gamma$, $\beta \upsilon$, $\beta \sigma$), then through...

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

Once these found locations of the Planet—$\beta \gamma, \beta \upsilon, \beta \sigma$—were established among the Fixed Stars or in the zodiac, the <term>craftsman</term> <gloss>artifex: referring to the astronomer, likely Copernicus</gloss> began to investigate the hypothesis of the <term>first inequality</term> <gloss>the variation in a planet's speed as it moves along its own orbit, independent of the Earth's motion</gloss>. He sought to determine how great the <term>eccentricity</term> <gloss>the distance by which the center of the orbit is offset from the center of the observer's world</gloss> of the Planetary circle was from the assumed point $\beta$, and toward which parts of the zodiac the <term>apogee</term> <gloss>the point in the orbit where the planet is farthest from the center</gloss> leaned, by comparing the angles formed by these observed locations at the center of sight $\beta$ with the time intervals that passed between them. I shall reveal the method for this business in its proper place below.

Now, let the calculation be completed, and let the <term>line of apsides</term> <gloss>the line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit</gloss> of the eccentric $\beta \delta$ emerge, as well as the eccentricity of the <term>equant point</term> <gloss>puncti æquatorii: a mathematical point used to explain how a planet appears to move at different speeds</gloss> $\beta \delta$, and the center of the eccentric on this line at point $\lambda$. This hypothesis should correspond to all the locations observed during the planet's **oppositions** with the <term>mean place of the Sun</term> <note>As established on the previous page, "mean place" refers to the Sun's average position rather than its actual appearance.</note>.

What is it then, **KEPLER**, that you find lacking here in Copernicus? Do you deny that this hypothesis corresponds in every way to the observations or the experiments of astronomers? That is not the issue right now. Nor was I led to a different opinion by the observations when I first undertook this labor. But this is what I found lacking: *Let $\beta \delta$ be extended so that it cuts the eccentric at $\chi$ and $\xi$ <note>chi and xi</note>. Around $\chi$, let a point on the eccentric be taken, called $\tau$ <note>tau</note>, and let it be connected with $\delta$ and $\lambda$. Since the arc $\chi \tau$ measures the angle $\chi \lambda \tau$, but the angle $\chi \delta \tau$ is larger than the angle $\chi \lambda \tau$ by the amount of the angle $\delta \tau \lambda$, and since $\delta$ is the point of uniform time; therefore, the time designated by the angle $\chi \delta \tau$ is greater—in respect to the whole period of time marked by four right angles <note>a full 360-degree circle</note>—than the arc $\chi \tau$ is in respect to the entire circumference.*

of the whole: *thus the Planet is truly slow (no longer merely through an illusion of sight) through the arc $\tau\chi$, and fast in the opposite arc $\epsilon\zeta$; it is slowest at $\chi$ and fastest at $\epsilon$. However, it is not farthest from the Sun $\varkappa$ at $\chi$, nor is it closest to it at $\epsilon$.* But by all reasoning, and indeed by the testimony of this very hypothesis regarding point $\beta$ which I am refuting, it is made consistent that this real slowing down of the Planet arises from its departure from the body of the Sun, and its acceleration from its approach to the Sun itself located at $\varkappa$. On the contrary, it cannot even be grasped by thought that there would be a force in point $\beta$ (which lacks a body) rather than in $\varkappa$, which is right next to it (in which sits the Sun, the heart of the world), such that this force would drive the Planet around slowly or quickly in proportion to its departure and return.

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
And even if someone does not yet grant that slowdowns and accelerations of this kind arise *physically* from the inner complexity of the <term>eccentrics</term> <gloss>circular orbits whose center is shifted away from the center of motion</gloss>, and instead stipulates that these variations of motion belong naturally to the <term>moving souls</term> <gloss>mentes motrices: a common Renaissance concept that celestial bodies were guided by intelligent spirits or "motive faculties"</gloss> residing in the body of the Planet, we shall again obtain the same probability. For what would be the cause for those minds, passing by point $\varkappa$ (which has a geometric affinity to the motion, for it is clothed in a body of no small magnitude), to look instead toward point $\beta$, which is removed from the Sun itself by only four semidiameters (or according to some authors, diameters) of the Solar body, and is vacant of any body and supported by nothing but a mere imagination? Add to this that Copernicus himself, in Book 5, Chapter 16, acknowledges that the Sun is plainly fixed at $\varkappa$, and therefore the <term>eccentricity</term> $\varkappa\delta$ is constant, while he claims that point $\beta$, which he treats as the center of the annual orbit, has been displaced by the passing of the ages, and thus $\beta\delta$ has been made shorter. In this way, $\beta$ either is no longer at the center of the world today, or it was not there in the past. But it is consistent that either the origin of motion is at the center of the world, or the moving souls look toward the center of the world; therefore, they look not toward $\beta$, but toward $\varkappa$, which Copernicus claims is fixed. This is what befits the center of the world.

Led by these probabilities, I concluded that the <term>line of apsides</term> <gloss>the line connecting the closest and farthest points of an orbit</gloss>, which is used to produce the <term>first inequality</term> <gloss>the planet's own change in speed as it orbits the sun</gloss> of the Planet, ought not to pass through $\beta$ but through the very same $\varkappa$ <note>original: "ipsissimum $\varkappa$" — Kepler emphasizes the physical Sun as the center</note>. Furthermore, we shall achieve this when we apply those locations of the Planet among the Fixed Stars which the Planet possesses at the moment of its opposition to the Sun’s apparent position.

*And indeed, when points $\varkappa, \beta$ and the Earth at $\gamma$ are on the same line, and the Planet itself coincides with them, such as if it were at $\tau$, then at that same moment the Planet is opposite to both the mean and the apparent position of the Sun, and its location remains the same whether it is designated by the line $\beta\tau$ or $\varkappa\tau$ running out among the Fixed Stars; it is truly stripped of its <term>second inequality</term>* <gloss>the apparent retrograde motion caused by Earth's own movement</gloss>*, whether that depends on the apparent or the mean motion of the earth.* But *when the earth comes to the side of its eccentric or its middle lengths, a sufficiently large difference intervenes. For let the earth have gone from $\gamma$ to $\upsilon$ (namely, the Sun having moved from the opposite region, from the <term>perigee</term> and Capricorn into Aries) and let the line of the mean motion of the Sun $\upsilon\beta$ be found in Aries, while the line of sight of the Planet in Libra is precisely opposite to it, namely $\upsilon\omega$. Since, therefore, $\upsilon\varkappa$ is beyond $\upsilon\beta$, further in the <term>order of the signs</term>* <gloss>consequentia: the standard eastward direction of the zodiac</gloss>*, the apparent position of the Sun is thus beyond the opposite of the Planet. And since $\upsilon$ is the seat of the earth's vision and $\omega$ is the Planet, and both descend toward $\epsilon$, the earth $\upsilon$ nevertheless moves faster; therefore the line $\upsilon\omega$ [is left] behind...*

*at that time it is still more inclined toward the line υ κ of the visible position of the Sun. Therefore, the apparent opposition preceded the mean one. Consequently, at the time preceding the moment marked by β υ, which we may call β ϑ, the Planet will fall upon the line drawn from κ through ϑ, namely at ζ. And then the line of sight of the Planet ϑ ζ (which a less experienced reader should carefully note) inclines more toward the "following" signs <note>original: "in consequentia"; meaning the direction of the zodiac signs (Aries to Taurus, etc.)</note> under the Fixed Stars than the line υ ω of the later time. This is because, even though ϑ ζ precedes the line υ ω in the "preceding" direction <note>original: "in antecedentia"; meaning the reverse order of the zodiac</note>, it is just as if ϑ, υ, and absolutely all points along the Earth’s circuit were a single point and the center of the sphere of the Fixed Stars. Therefore, it is not the distance between the terms ϑ and υ, but the inclination of the lines ϑ ζ and υ ω that causes the lines to fall upon different places in the zodiac—though they would coincide in sense if they had been parallel. Moreover, it is clear that ζ ϑ is inclined toward ω from the fact that the same time is assumed in which the Planet moves from ζ to ω and the Earth moves from ϑ to υ. However, the Earth is faster than the Planet. Therefore, the Earth covers a greater space ϑ υ than the space ζ ω of the Planet.*

*But it can also be taught more easily that the Planet is further along in the "following" signs at the preceding time, since it is retrograde during opposition, as is well known to everyone. It is apparent, therefore, what is changed in this reduction from the mean to the apparent motion of the Sun in those locations stripped of the <term>second inequality</term> <gloss>the apparent change in a planet's speed caused by the Earth's own motion</gloss>.*

*For in the opposite location τ E, the original locations remain at ζ or ω. Something is added to the seen location, because ϑ ζ (as was said) inclines more toward the "following" signs than υ ω; and something is taken away from the elapsed time, because ϑ is the sight at an earlier time than υ ω. In the opposite location, the reverse happens: namely, time is added, and location is subtracted. And thus these locations of the Planet differ greatly from the original ones. Consequently, in a newly established operation, much different effects result. For when we have transferred the sight to the Sun κ by a fiction (because we had looked at the Planet positioned at τ and ζ while the Earth was occupying the lines κ τ and κ ζ, namely at points γ and ϑ), the <term>eccentricity</term> <gloss>the distance the center of the orbit is shifted from the center of motion</gloss> will now arise from κ. But it was shown above in Chapter 5 that when the sight is transferred from β to κ, and a line is cast from η through the original point of equality δ, a new eccentric is indeed constructed by this new hypothesis; but one which leaves all its sightings undisturbed and as close as possible to the sight at β. Therefore, having connected δ κ, and the line E being divided at μ, such that δ λ is to δ μ as δ β is to δ κ, and a new eccentric η ε being designated from μ (which is equal to the prior one ξ χ), and a new line of apsides being drawn through η δ, a new hypothesis will arise whose <term>apsis</term> <gloss>the highest or lowest point in an orbit</gloss> is at η. Previously, we had abusively called χ the <term>apogee</term> <gloss>the point furthest from the Earth</gloss>, because in the line χ β, the Copernican center β had succeeded the Ptolemaic location of the Earth. Now, therefore, we shall call η by its proper name (since we are using the Copernican hypothesis) the <term>aphelium</term> <gloss>the point furthest from the Sun</gloss>, and its opposite point the <term>perihelium</term> <gloss>the point closest to the Sun</gloss>, because the Sun κ recedes furthest from η.*

IT HAS BEEN STATED how these twin opinions—mine and those of the other authors—differ physically. It has also been shown how both are geometrically delineated in the Copernican form. Thirdly, it has been emphasized that, astronomically, they do not differ in any way that should be considered significant regarding the points of conjunctions and oppositions. Therefore, a line is drawn through λ <note>lambda</note> and μ <note>mu</note>, the centers of the eccentrics <note>original: "eccentricorum"; these are circular orbits whose centers are shifted away from the Sun</note>, parallel to the line β κ. If this line is extended so that it cuts both eccentrics at two points, one below and one above, it will establish the maximum interval <note>original: "intercapedinem"</note> ε ς <note>epsilon-sigma</note> below, which is equal to λ μ. But because it is not the line from λ, but rather the line from δ <note>delta; representing the center of the world or the Sun</note> that designates certain identical moments of time (which we require here), let δ ς be drawn, cutting the eccentrics at ε and ς. This ensures that at one and the same moment, the Planet <term>Planet|While Kepler's work is titled for Mars, he often uses 'the Planet' to describe the general geometric behavior of any planet being modeled</term> certainly falls at ε in one model and at ς in the other. Therefore, if the Earth is located on the line δ ς—specifically at π <note>pi</note>—the Planet will be seen in the same place in the zodiac whether it is at ε or ς. For, based on the principles of optics, the line ε ς appears as a single point when viewed head-on. However, as the Earth moves out to either side of this line, the length of the line ε ς appears larger and larger, because it is being viewed at an angle <note>original: "ex obliquo"</note>.

We must find the point on the Earth's orbit <note>original: "orbis telluris"</note> from which the lines of sight passing through ε and ς diverge the most and form the greatest angle to the eye. This would be where the error is greatest if the Planet were placed at ς when it should have been at ε.

First, this angle will be greater below at ε than above near τ <note>tau</note>, because the Earth's orbit (described from β) brings the eye closer to ε ς than to τ. Furthermore, since δ ε lies beyond τ β, the interval ε ς is viewed more obliquely from the left side than from the right. It will therefore appear smaller from that side than from this, even if the Earth is at an equal distance from the line δ ς. Therefore, our point must be sought on the right side.

*I say that the line segment ε ρ <note>epsilon rho; representing the distance between two theoretical positions of the planet</note> subtends the maximum angle of vision when the observer's eye is positioned at that point where the circle of the Earth is touched by a circle drawn through ε and ρ. For let such a circle be described through ε ρ, which touches the circle υ σ <note>upsilon sigma; representing the Earth's orbit</note> on the side toward σ: let the contact occur at point υ. Now, let lines go out from ε and ρ both to the point of contact υ and to many other points on the circle υ σ before and after that contact. Since a circle touches another circle at only one single point, all the "legs" of the angles originating from ε and ρ and meeting at points on the Earth's circle υ σ will be cut by the circle passing through ε ρ—except for those lines which terminate at the specific contact point υ. According to Proposition 21 of the first book of Euclid's **Elements** <note>A fundamental geometric theorem stating that if two lines are drawn from the ends of a side to a point inside a triangle, they contain a larger angle than the lines forming the triangle's sides</note>, if those legs from ε and ρ were cut by the circle ε ρ before they met, they would meet at a larger angle if they coincided at the points of intersection. Furthermore, all angles established on the circumference of a circle over the same segment ε ρ are equal, according to Proposition 21 of Euclid's third book. Therefore, the angle at υ (the point of contact) is larger than all the others. Which was to be demonstrated.*

*In order to investigate this quantity using familiar numbers, we need to know the length of ε ρ itself, and the length of the perpendicular line falling from β <note>beta</note> onto the line δ ε <note>delta epsilon</note>.*

*We shall learn both of these by solving the triangles δ λ ε <note>delta lambda epsilon</note> and δ μ ε <note>delta mu epsilon</note>. In triangle δ λ ε, we previously established that δ λ is 7,411 <note>Kepler uses a scale where the radius is 100,000</note> in units where λ ε is 100,000, and the angle ε λ β is 47 degrees, 59 minutes, and 16 seconds. From this, the angle ε δ λ is found to be 44 degrees, 59 minutes, 10 seconds, and the side δ ε is 105,123. Therefore, in triangle ε δ μ, since angle ε δ λ is 44 degrees, 59 minutes, 10 seconds, and the angle λ δ μ was previously found to be 5 degrees, 27 minutes, 47 seconds, the entire angle ε δ μ is 50 degrees, 26 minutes, 57 seconds. Additionally, the side δ μ was previously given as 6,763 units where μ ε is 100,000.*

->PART ONE.<-

...serves the <term>inequality: the observed variation in a planet's speed or position compared to a uniform circular path</term>; here, just as before, the Planet itself is carried slowly or quickly according to its approach to or retreat from the Earth **k** in the circle **xz**. <margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

Indeed, this hypothesis can be attacked from Physics in another way. For the solidity of the spheres is, in a sense, characteristic of this form, which—through **Tycho Brahe’s** observations of comets <note>Brahe observed that comets passed through the regions where solid "crystalline spheres" were supposed to exist, proving the heavens were not solid.</note>—having been destroyed, this hypothesis seems to fall apart by itself. For it would be established that a moving force resides in the center of the epicycle (in a mathematical point, not a body), and drives itself by passing from place to place, and that in equal times it does so unequally; while at the same time and with itself it would attract the Planet to the proximity of the diameter of the epicycle, and simultaneously rotate it around itself in equal times equally. Such a great variety of tasks cannot fall upon a single moving mind, unless it be **GOD**, with the support of **ARISTOTLE** in Book 1 of his *Metaphysics*, Chapter VIII, who is pleased that individual minds preside over individual motions that are most equal and simply circular. Furthermore, how will some power sit in a non-body, or flow out from a non-body into the Planet?

But if you even divide the duties and place one moving intelligence in the center of the epicycle and another in the body of the Planet: the one in the center would regard the earth (a body, surely) and go around the earth in a circle unequally; whereas the one in a point of the circumference (namely, in the body of the Planet) would go around an incorporeal center, and do so equally. It will then be asked, as above: by what supports does it circle that incorporeal point? For it is not through a geometric imagination, as that which does not admit a geometric imagination of itself; nor can a mobile point in a non-body exist even by imagining it. And we humans, when imagining such points, use the supports of tables or paper, which we handle with our hands or remember having handled once. But neither is it through a physical outflow of power (which is in the center of the epicycle) out to the circumference and the body of the Planet. For we have already removed this outflow of power by dividing the duties of the composite motion between two minds.

Moreover, in the first and <term>eccentric: a circle whose center is not the Earth</term> motion, it is doubted whether any natural power prepared for inducing motion can exist in some point that lacks any body of its own? Much more, whether an incorporeal power of this kind can drive itself around the earth and pass from place to place? and most of all, whether it can communicate or induce motion in another through an outflow from itself, while leaning on no body as if on a "nest"? For what sublime things some will want to oppose to me concerning the essence, motion, place, and operations of the blessed angels and separated minds, are irrelevant. For we are disputing about natural things of a far lower dignity—about powers that use no choice to vary their action, and about minds that are certainly not "separated" <note>Kepler argues that planetary "minds" are not independent spirits like angels, but are physically bound to the planets they move.</note> since they are joined and tied to the celestial bodies they must carry. And these things can be objected against **Ptolemy** in general.

one. <margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin> Since **Ptolemy** determined that the Planet $\Omega$ <note>Kepler uses the symbol $\Omega$ to denote the planet's position</note> in this observation had shed its <term>second inequality: the variation in a planet's apparent motion caused by the Earth's own movement</term>, he therefore places $z$, the center of the <term>epicycle: a small circle on which the planet moves, while the circle's center itself moves along a larger orbit</term>, on the line $\kappa \Omega$. However, since $\kappa \epsilon$ <note>the line to the apparent Sun</note> has surpassed $\kappa \gamma$ <note>the line to the mean Sun</note>, the apparent position of the Sun is beyond the point of opposition with the Planet. Nor does the line $\kappa \Omega$ descend at a later time to be opposite $\kappa \epsilon$ itself; rather, it ascends toward $\kappa \psi$, because the lower parts of the epicycle $\Omega$ move in <term>retrograde: appearing to move backward against the stars</term> and are faster than the center $z$ itself, and the Planet is there as if in opposition with the Sun. Therefore, this apparent opposition preceded the mean opposition.

In the time, therefore, that precedes the moment designated by $\kappa \gamma$ (let this be $\kappa \odot$), when the Sun is seen on the line $\kappa \epsilon$, the Planet will be seen at its opposite, say at $i$ along the line $\kappa I$, which is in a straight line with $\kappa \epsilon$. And because it is now assumed that the planet sheds its second inequality at this true opposition, the center of the <term>epicycle</term> will also be seen on this line $\epsilon \kappa$, say at $o$. And since the Planet is retrograde, at the time $\kappa \odot$ (which is earlier than $\kappa \gamma$) the Planet is on the line $\kappa I$, which is later than $\kappa \Omega$. But $\kappa I$ and $\kappa \Omega$ are parts of the lines $\kappa o$ and $\kappa z$. Therefore, $\kappa o$ is also further along in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia," referring to the direction of the zodiac</note> than $\kappa z$.

Thus, it is apparent what changes in this reduction from the mean motion of the Sun to its apparent motion on the line of the center of the <term>epicycle</term>. For at $\tau$ and the opposite point of the original line, the motions of the center of the <term>epicycle</term> remain the same. At $z$, the center of the <term>epicycle</term> is moved forward along this line, but the time elapsed is reduced. In the opposite location, the contrary happens: that is, time is added, and the line of the center of the <term>epicycle</term> is pulled back in the order of the signs <note>original: "in antecedentia"</note>. And so these lines of the center of the epicycle differ greatly from the original ones. For this reason, when we investigate the causes and measure of the <term>first inequality: the planet's actual variation in speed due to its elliptical or eccentric orbit</term> by a new and repeated operation using these observed positions of the epicycle's center (specifically, from the observed positions of the Planet, behind which we assume the center of the epicycle lies hidden on the same line of sight), the result of the operation differs greatly from the previous one. Specifically, since in the semicircle containing the <term>apogee: the point furthest from Earth</term>, the time was shortened so that the Planet thus becomes faster, the resulting <term>eccentricity: the distance between the center of the circular orbit and the center of motion</term> of the equant will be smaller. And since in the larger quadrant $bz$ of that semicircle, which contains the apogee, the time was decreased equally as in the remaining smaller part, the Planet is rendered much faster in proportion in that remaining part of the semicircle. Therefore, the <term>perigee: the point closest to Earth</term> has approached that part, and the <term>apogee</term> has descended from $x$ toward $z$.

The magnitude of the new <term>hypothesis: a mathematical model or theory used to explain celestial motions</term> will thus become clear. Since the Planet $\Omega$ is assumed to fall on the line drawn from $z$, the center of the <term>epicycle</term>, through the Earth $\kappa$ only when this $\kappa z$ is in a single continuous line with $\kappa \epsilon$, the apparent position of the Sun, then $\kappa \epsilon$ and the lines drawn from $z$ through the body of the Planet always move parallel to each other. And since we have now accepted from **Ptolemy** that at the time the line of the Sun's mean motion was $\kappa \gamma$ (drawn through $\Omega$), the Planet was seen on the line $\kappa \Omega$, but we deny that the center of its <term>epicycle</term> $z$ was simultaneously on $\kappa \Omega$, let there be drawn (according to our position) a line parallel to $\kappa \epsilon$ from the Planet's position $\Omega$, which shall be $\Omega o$. The center of the <term>epicycle</term> is placed by us at this moment on the line $\Omega o$ or some line parallel and very close to it, depending on whether $\Omega$ (the marker of the Planet) on the line $\kappa z$ was closer to or farther from $\kappa$ itself. Let $\Omega o$ be equal to $\Omega z$ from whatever point of the line $\kappa z$ (which is now $\Omega$). And from $o$, let a line $oz$ be drawn parallel to $\kappa \gamma$ toward $z \kappa$. <margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

But as was shown at the end of Chapter 5, if a line $\Delta\Delta$ is drawn through $\Delta$ parallel to $\kappa\psi$, and $\kappa\psi$ is equal to $\Delta\Delta$, and this new $\Delta$ is connected with $\kappa$, and the new line $\kappa\Delta$ is divided at $m$ in the same proportion as the previous $\kappa\Delta$ was divided at $\Delta$: then by this new hypothesis a new <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is shifted away from the central reference point (like the Earth or Sun)</term> is constructed. This new eccentric differs in position from the previous one, but when applied to the vantage point at $\kappa$, it leaves almost all of its observations undisturbed. *Therefore, having described a new eccentric from $m$ that is equal to the previous one, and with the line $\kappa m$ extended in both directions, $H$ will be the new <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the observer</term>, the center of the <term>epicycle: a small circle carrying the planet, which itself moves along a larger circle</term> will be at points $B$ and $o$ of the new eccentric, and the Planet at $A$ will be closer and at $I$ further away than before.*

However, in those locations involved in the second inequality <note>Kepler refers to the "second inequality" as the variation in a planet's motion caused by the Earth's own annual orbit—what we now call retrograde motion</note> (provided that the Planet is assigned an epicycle equal to the eccentric of the Sun, which we must do if we wish to fully translate the power of what **COPERNICUS** and **TYCHO BRAHE** discovered into a **PTOLEMAIC** form), the previous observations are entirely and violently disturbed by introducing this new eccentric into their hypothesis. *This happens not because the <term>point of equality: also called the equant point, the center of uniform motion</term> $\Delta$ does not remain the same, but because around the locations of the Sun's <term>apsides: the two points—apogee and perigee—where a planet is at its maximum and minimum distance</term>, the centers of the Ptolemaic eccentric and our own are distant by the interval $\Delta m$. An equal distance between the centers follows, and thus an equal distance between the locations of the planetary body.* Furthermore, this discrepancy is not at its greatest when the center of the epicycle is moving around the Sun's middle longitudes. *For it has been said that in those locations, the position of the center of the epicycle is almost the same in both eccentrics, even though they are distant by the parallels from $\Delta\Delta$.*

Therefore, the discrepancy is greatest around the apsides of the Sun, and even larger around the <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the observer</term> in Capricorn, where the line $m\Delta$ is extended so that it intersects the eccentrics at $p$ and $E$. *For $pE$ is as large as $m\Delta$. But because the same moment of time is not designated by this single line $m\Delta$—since $m$ is not the point of equality, but $\Delta$ is—parallels should therefore come from $\Delta\Delta$ toward $pE$, which will mark the same moment. Let these be $ap$ and $aE$, and let $N$ and $\Pi$ be written for the positions on the epicycle.*

The question is: where does this discrepancy appear greatest in relation to the circumference of the epicycle? It is certain that it is not in the parts of the epicycle closest to the Earth at $\kappa$, because they would be on the same side as $\kappa$; nor in the highest parts, because they would be too remote. Therefore, it is in the parts nearest to the perigee of the epicycle. Thus, when the Sun and the Planet along with it are not quite in their perigee but very close to it—to put it briefly—at those points $N$ and $\Pi$ meeting at the same moment of time, through which a very small circle $\kappa$ is also drawn. Moreover, the center of that small circle is on a line drawn through $\kappa$, which, when extended upward and meeting the line $p A$ (also extended), encompasses an angle of $7\frac{1}{2}$ degrees.

Let anyone who is not satisfied with this adapt the demonstration from the previous sections to this case. The numbers indeed remain the same, except that in **PTOLEMY'S** model $m\Delta$ is larger than the $\mu \lambda$ used in the numbers above; for this reason, the difference in vision, namely $N \kappa \Pi$, is also larger.

<summary>Kepler demonstrates how shifting the solar reference point creates a physical displacement between his model and Ptolemy's, which is most noticeable when the planet is near its closest point to Earth (perigee).</summary>

The planetary system is conceived as being fixed to the orbit of the Sun; this point, I say, always moves along the line of the Sun’s <term>mean motion: the theoretical average position of a celestial body if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle</term>, staying at a distance from the Earth equal to the line $B S$, and describing a circle $V$ centered on the Earth that is equal to the eccentric circle $G S$. For this was the opinion of **TYCHO BRAHE**, except that he denied the existence of <term>solid orbs: the ancient belief that planets were carried on physical, crystalline spheres</term>. Therefore, what we said regarding the attachment of the whole planetary system to the orbit of the Sun was said for the sake of those who believe in solid orbs.

*Let the line $V C$ be extended, and let the planet be on this line beyond $C$. In this case, Brahe will place the point where the planetary system is attached at $V$. The sighting of the planet therefore occurs along the line $V C$. And even though the observer is at $C$ (the Earth), it is just as if they were at point $V$, upon which the <term>first inequality: the component of a planet's movement caused by its own eccentric path, rather than the Earth's motion</term> depends. Therefore, the position of the planet among the fixed stars is measured with instruments whenever the line of sight $C V$ passes through some point in the region of $V$ beyond $C$ (let this be on the lines $C V$ and $C G$, and their opposites). In this arrangement, the center of the planetary system would be on the circle $V P$, the Sun at $s$ and $G$, and the body of the planet in the region at $O$ and $F$. However, in the theory of **MARS**, the planet's eccentric orbit is in a smaller proportion to the Sun's eccentric orbit, so much so that the eccentric of Mars and the points $O$ and $F$ actually become closer to the Earth $C$ than the Sun $S$ is. This was one of the primary reasons why **BRAHE** denied the solidity of the celestial spheres.* <note>If the spheres were solid, the orbits of Mars and the Sun would collide; Brahe’s data showed they must pass through the same space.</note>

Therefore, from many such observations—indeed, from as many as could be obtained—**TYCHO BRAHE** was accustomed to investigating the hypothesis of the first inequality. He did this by setting aside the overall size of the orbit $V P$ and treating it as a single point, as if $V P$ were the center of the sy-

Now let the <term>pragmatia: a technical geometric construction or procedure</term> be completed, and let the line of apsides of the <term>eccentric: the off-center circular path of a planet</term> come forth as $v l d$ or $p l d$, where $d$ is the <term>equant: a mathematical point used to explain the varying speed of a planet</term> point, and $l$ is the center of the eccentric on this line, and the eccentric is $h o$ and $f h$. And let this hypothesis correspond to all observed positions of the planet at the moments of the planet's opposition with the Sun's <term>mean motion: the theoretical average position of the Sun if it moved at a constant speed</term>.

I omit for the present a more diligent examination of whether this hypothesis is generally consistent with physical principles—namely, one in which the Sun orbits the Earth, looking back at it with its own "moving mind" <note>Kepler refers to the traditional idea that celestial bodies might be guided by an inherent intelligence</note> and (since it lacks its own orb) urging itself forward unequally according to its approach to or departure from the Earth (unless you wish to make the Earth more excellent than the Sun and transfer the Sun's moving power to it); while the same Sun (as in Copernicus) emits a moving power to all the planets, rotating them around itself at a degree of speed corresponding to their degree of proximity to the Sun. Meanwhile, the planets strive to complete their approaches and departures to the Sun in a small <term>epicycle: a small circular path whose center moves along a larger circle</term>, and simultaneously follow the Sun (wherever it yields to the Earth) along the same tracks in an extraordinary manner. And thus, any planet (especially the Sun) looks toward several things at once, and the paths of the planets through the ethereal air truly become spirals (as in Ptolemy), just as they were depicted in Chapter 1. Whether these things are consistent, I say, we shall weigh elsewhere as the occasion arises. 

Now let this true form of the hypothesis be assumed in general terms. It is further asked whether it is specifically consistent for the planets to follow the body of the Sun itself (marked $s. g.$), or rather a point $v. p.$ empty of body, distant from the center of the Sun by four solar semidiameters (no more), which is now above the Sun, now below, now before, now behind. And further, whether it is more consistent that the force which drives the planets in a circle around the Sun resides in the very body of the Sun ($s. g.$), or in some such point ($v. p.$) empty of body. Briefly: if the axis of the planetary system (to derive the notion of the word crudely from a wagon), by which the orbits of the planets are attached as if by a nail to the orbit of the Sun—if this axis, I say, is very near the Sun, why is it not in the Sun itself? If this axis or point of attachment orbits the Earth both very near the Sun and at plainly the same time, why does it describe its own path? Why does it not follow plainly the same journey as the Sun?

<margin>
$\odot G \odot$.
The axis or center of the planetary system. Elsewhere the point was the center of attachment.
</margin>

Therefore, I conclude entirely that if **Tycho Brahe's** opinion concerning the system of the world is universally true, it must be understood in such a way that the center of the planetary system is situated not at $v p$ but at $s g$ in the very path of the Sun—indeed, that it resides in the Sun itself. Finally, to free the first (or eccentric) inequality from the second, one must use the oppositions of the planet with the <term>apparent position: the actual observed location of a celestial body in the sky</term> of the Sun, not with the mean position. This reasoning **Brahe** himself embraced without reluctance in his final days.

*Planet F will be opposite the Sun G itself. Therefore, the same location of the planet will appear among the fixed stars along the line GF—whether that line is continuous with line CP or with line CG, because both have become a single line. For either reason, therefore, the planet is truly stripped of the <term>second inequality: the apparent "looping" or backward motion of a planet caused by the Earth’s own movement</term>.
