Therefore, the vision of the planet along the line CO is still entangled in the second inequality.*

*Nor will CO incline <term>forward: in the direction of the zodiac signs (direct motion)</term> at a later time so as to be opposite CS itself; instead, it will ascend toward CF. This is because the motion of the Sun—and along with it the center of the planetary system and all its parts (and thus the planet o itself and L, the center of the eccentric)—moves from the line CO toward F in an upward direction, and much faster than the motion of the eccentric or the planet at o around L from point H toward the lower parts. Thus, the planet o is pulled back somewhat <term>retrograde: moving backward against the order of the zodiac signs</term>, not by its own proper motion on the eccentric, but by an external motion; for it is a self-evident fact that planets are retrograde when in opposition to the Sun. Therefore, at a time preceding the moment marked by CV (let this be CT), when the Sun is seen on line CQ, the planet will be seen at I, at the opposite of its apparent position.*

And because it is now assumed in this case that the <term>second inequality: the apparent backward "looping" of a planet caused by Earth's motion</term> is being cast off, therefore *Q C I* will be a single line—that is, the point from which the <term>eccentricity: the off-center nature of the orbit</term> arises will be on the line *C Q*. Therefore, because the vision of the retrograde planet *C I* occurs earlier in time than the later vision *C O*, and thus turns more toward the <term>preceding signs: the western direction in the zodiac</term>, the line *C Q* will be beyond *C V*, and *Q* (the new center of the system) will be beyond *V* (the old center). And since from *O V* a new line *I Q* is made, which is further along in the <term>following signs: the eastern direction</term> by the angle *O C I*, while the <term>line of apsides: the line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit</term> *V D* or *P D* (from which the motion begins) remains parallel to itself in every circuit; it appears, therefore, that in a shorter interval of time, the planet is found to have traveled further around the system's center *Q* than it did previously over a longer interval of time around the system's center *V*.

It is clear, then, what is changed in this reduction from the <term>mean motion: the theoretical constant speed</term> to the apparent motion of the Sun within the apparent eccentric motion. For when the center of the system stays at *G* or its opposite point, the line of the apparent eccentric motion remains the same; at *Q*, it is moved forward; at the opposite point, it is drawn back, since in the former case time is decreased and in the latter it is increased. And so these lines will differ greatly from the original ones. For this reason, when we investigate the causes and the measure of the <term>first inequality: the planet's actual varying speed in its own orbit</term> using several of these observed locations of the planet (in whose region we suppose the center of the system to be found, namely in the Sun itself) through a new and repeated operation, the result of the operation differs greatly from the previous one.

For since we are now transferring the point of attachment from the circle *V P*, in which <term>Brahe: Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used</term> moved it around, into the circle *G S*—that is, into the very body of the Sun—which always stands at a distance of *C B* above the old <note>original: "Braheanvm"</note> point, namely above *V P* in *S G* along a line parallel to *C B*; therefore, so that the point of equality *D* <note>The equant point, where the planet's motion appears uniform</note> remains the same (with the same moments of time marked through *C V*) and the planet can be at *O* while the point of attachment is at *S*, it is necessary to draw a new line of apsides through points *D* and *S* or *G*. Therefore, based on what was demonstrated in Chapter 5 (which I cited above in the explanation of the <term>Copernican form: the Sun-centered model</term>), once *D S* or *D G* is drawn and divided in the same proportion as *D P* or *D V* was divided by *L*, so that the point of division is *M*, a new eccentric circle should be described with this point *M* as the center and with the same interval as before. This will not only yield these later observations from which it was constructed, but when applied to the previous hypothesis, it will also preserve the observations used earlier within a precision of five <term>scruples: arc-minutes, or 1/60th of a degree</term>.

However, when computations are performed outside of the <term>acronychal position: the point where a planet is directly opposite the Sun in the sky</term> using both the old and this new eccentric, they may differ in some places (namely around the Sun’s <term>perigee: the point where the Sun is closest to Earth</term>) by more than one degree, if we follow the familiar numbers assigned to the star **MARS** published by **BRAHE**.

### CHAPTER VII.

# On the occasion by which I happened upon the theory of MARS.

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
**I**T IS TRUE that the divine voice, which commands men to learn Astronomy, is expressed in the world itself—not in words or syllables, but in the reality of the thing and the alignment of the human intellect and senses with the sequence of celestial bodies and their behaviors. Yet, nevertheless, some hidden fate also drives different men to different arts, making them certain that just as they are a part of the created work, so too are they a part of divine providence.

When I first became old enough to taste the sweetness of Philosophy, I embraced the whole of it with immense desire, being not at all concerned with Astronomy in particular. I certainly had the talent for it; nor did I have difficulty grasping the Geometrical and Astronomical subjects which the school curriculum provided, relying on figures, numbers, and proportions. But those were necessary studies, and there was nothing to suggest a primary inclination toward Astronomy. Since I was being supported by the expenses of the **DUKE OF WURTTEMBERG**, and I saw my fellow students (whom the Prince, when asked, would send to foreign nations) hesitating for various reasons out of love for their homeland, I had quite early and firmly decided that I would most promptly follow wherever I might be destined.

The first position to offer itself was an Astronomical function, to which (to tell the truth) I was pushed <note>original: "extrusus," literally "thrust out" or "expelled"; Kepler felt he was forced into the role by his teachers.</note> by the authority of my Teachers. I was not deterred by the distance of the place—a fear I had condemned in others (as I have already said)—but rather by the unexpected and lowly nature of the position, and by the thinness of my learning in this branch of Philosophy. I therefore approached this instruction more by talent than by knowledge, protesting many times that I was by no means giving up my right to another kind of life that seemed more splendid. What the successes of these studies were in the first two years is apparent from my *Mysterium Cosmographicum* <note>Kepler's first major work, "The Secret of the Universe" (1596), in which he proposed that the orbits of the planets were determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>. Furthermore, what stimulants my Teacher *Maestlin* applied to me to embrace the rest of Astronomy, you may read in that same booklet and in the letter from that man which is prefixed to *Rheticus's Narrative* <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus was the first disciple of Copernicus; his "Narratio Prima" was the first published account of the Copernican system.</note>.

I valued that **DISCOVERY** <note>Referring to his theory of the Platonic solids nesting between planetary spheres.</note> of mine very highly indeed, and all the more because I saw that *Maestlin* also approved of it so greatly. Nor did he spur me on so much by the untimely promise he made to readers regarding my entire **URANIC WORK** <term>Uranic work: literally "heavenly work," referring to Kepler's ambitious plan for a comprehensive astronomical system</term> (as he called it), as much as I myself burned to inquire, through the restoration of Astronomy, whether that discovery of mine could withstand the full precision of observations. For it had already been demonstrated in the book itself that it stood within the precision of common Astronomy.

From 그hat time on, I began to think seriously about gathering observations. When I wrote to **TYCHO BRAHE** in the year 1597, asking him to give his opinion on my little book <note>original: "libello"; referring to his first major work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (The Cosmographic Mystery).</note>, he replied mentioning, among other things, his own observations. This inflamed me with a great desire to see them. Indeed, **TYCHO BRAHE** himself was also a large part of my destiny; from then on, he did not stop urging me of his own accord to come to him. Since the great distance of the place might have deterred me, I attribute it again to divine providence that he came to Bohemia <note>Tycho had left Denmark after a falling out with the King and settled near Prague, which was much closer to Kepler in Austria.</note>. I arrived there at the beginning of the year 1600, with the hope of learning the correct eccentricities <note>term: eccentricity; the measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Planets. However, when I learned during the first eight days that he, like **PTOLEMY** and **COPERNICUS**, used the mean motion of the Sun <note>The "mean Sun" is a mathematical fiction used to simplify calculations; Kepler suspected that using the "apparent" or actual position of the Sun would be more accurate.</note>, whereas the apparent motion was more suited to my book (as is evident from that book itself), I obtained permission from the author to use the observations in my own way. At that time, his assistant **CHRISTIAN SEVERINI** <note>Christian Sørensen Longomontanus (1562–1647), Tycho's long-time Danish assistant.</note> had the theory of **MARS** in his hands. Time itself placed it there, because they were then engaged in the observation of the acronychal position <note>term: acronychal; refers to a planet being in "opposition," or directly opposite the Sun in the sky as seen from Earth.</note> or opposition of **MARS** with the Sun at 9 degrees of Leo. If **CHRISTIAN** had been working on another Planet, I would have fallen into studying that same one.

I believe, therefore, that it happened again by divine arrangement that I arrived at the very time when he was intent upon **MARS**. It is from the motions of Mars that we must either arrive at a knowledge of the secrets of Astronomy or remain forever ignorant of them.

**A TABLE** of mean oppositions from the year 1580 was being recalculated. A hypothesis had been devised which was said to represent all of them within a proximity of two minutes of longitude; I used those numbers (or ones differing only slightly) in chapter 5. At the beginning of the year 1580, the apogee <note>term: apogee; the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> was placed at 23 degrees 45 minutes of Leo. The maximum eccentricity, which is composed of the radius of both small circles, was 20,160, where the radius of the larger epicycle <note>term: epicycle; a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain complex planetary movements.</note> would be 16,380. Therefore, in the Ptolemaic form of the first inequality, the eccentricity of the equant point <note>term: equant; a mathematical point used to explain the observed speed changes in planetary orbits.</note> was 20,160 or slightly less.

From this hypothesis, a table of equations for the eccentric orbit was built for each degree, as well as a table for the corrected mean motion, made by adding one and three-quarters minutes to the mean motion of the Prutenic Tables <note>The *Tabulae Prutenicae* or Prutenic Tables (1551) were astronomical tables based on Copernicus's work.</note>. These mean motions, the apogee, and the nodes <note>term: node; the point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> were calculated for four hundred years, just as was done for the Solar and Lunar motions in the first volume of the *Preliminary Exercises* <note>original: *Progymnasmata*; Tycho Brahe's massive work on astronomy.</note>. **CHRISTIAN** was stuck only on the latitude during the acronychal positions and on the parallaxes of the annual orbit. There was indeed a hypothesis and a small table for latitudes, but the observed latitude could not be derived from it. This was an obstacle for him, as he was about to set to work on the Lunar motions.

**SINCE**, therefore, I suspected what was actually the case—that the hypothesis was not quite right—I prepared myself for the work according to the opinions I had previously conceived and expressed in my *Cosmographic Mystery*. At the beginning, there was much dispute between us as to whether a different method of hypothesis could be established, which...

You see here that the mean location of the Sun is sometimes distant from the opposition of the observed location of Mars on the ecliptic by 13 ½ minutes, which is almost triple that which could be erred by the translation of the hypothesis <note>The "translation of the hypothesis" refers to shifting the mathematical model or framework to better fit the data; Kepler is saying the error is too large to be a simple modeling mistake.</note>. Therefore, the certainty of their own hypothesis did not constrain me from seeking another.

But they admitted this discrepancy by design, as appears from this: because since the nodes <note>The "nodes" are the two points where a planet's orbit intersects the ecliptic.</note> are around 17 degrees of Taurus and Scorpio, and the limits <note>The "limits" are the points where the planet reaches its maximum distance (latitude) north or south of the ecliptic.</note> are around 17 degrees of Leo and Aquarius, as will be said below, the additions and subtractions were made chiefly at 17 degrees of Cancer, 25 degrees of Virgo, 4 degrees of Scorpio, 27 degrees of Sagittarius, and 13 degrees of Pisces—intermediate places: none at 21 degrees of Leo or 18 degrees of Scorpio, at the nodes and limit. Therefore, the cause for them was that they thought the Planet is not stripped of its second inequality <note>The "second inequality" is the apparent back-and-forth (retrograde) motion of a planet caused by the Earth's own movement around the Sun.</note>, unless the Sun had departed as much from the node as the Planet in its own orbit. Yet even this plan was not consistent. For at 3 degrees of Sagittarius, there ought to have been the greatest variation according to this mind of theirs, because Sagittarius is very close to the 45th degree, where this variation is usually greatest. But at 17 degrees of Cancer they subtracted 5 minutes; at 3 degrees of Sagittarius only 1 minute. ## Concerning the reduction of the ecliptic position to the circle of MARS.

But it is TIME that we discuss accurately this reduction to the ecliptic or the orbit of the Planet, which serves as the foundation.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin> ...at 3 degrees of Scorpio <note>♏</note> it was still indeed 1 ½ degrees [of latitude], but immediately at 27 degrees of Sagittarius <note>♐</note> it is southern and very large, at 4 degrees; even larger at 14 degrees of Sagittarius. From this it is gathered, roughly speaking <note>original: "crassiori Minerva," literally "with a coarser Minerva," an idiom for a rough estimate or common-sense calculation.</note>, that the ascending node is a little before 18 degrees of Taurus <note>♉</note>, and the descending node much after 3 degrees of Scorpio. Therefore, the nodes <note>The two points where a planet's tilted orbit intersects the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note> will be around 17 degrees of Taurus and 17 degrees of Scorpio; the limits <note>The "limits" are the points of maximum latitude, 90 degrees from the nodes, where the planet reaches its furthest point north or south of the ecliptic.</note> will be around 17 degrees of Leo <note>♌</note> and Aquarius <note>♒</note>. 

Therefore, since the plane of the eccentric orbit of MARS is inclined to the plane of the ecliptic, nearly the same thing happens as occurs with the right ascensions of the parts of the ecliptic: that for the observed arcs of one circle, the same observed arcs of the other circle do not correspond, except for those that, beginning from the nodes, end at the limits. I say "observed arcs" because here it is necessary to mentally separate the planet's eccentricity and proceed just as if the journey of MARS were in the sphere of the Fixed Stars just like the ecliptic and truly intersected it. 

And indeed, when it is asked what the <margin>☉ ♃ ♁ What is the ecliptic position of a planet? Opposed to it is the orbital position, or the position considered in relation to the orbit.</margin> ecliptic position of a planet is, astronomers define it thus: it is namely the point of the ecliptic where the circle of latitude (perpendicular to the ecliptic) passing through the position of the planet's body among the Fixed Stars intersects the ecliptic.

It is clear, therefore, through the demonstrations of Theodosius <note>Theodosius of Bithynia, a Greek astronomer and mathematician known for his work "Sphaerica" on the geometry of the sphere.</note> on the Sphere, that unless this circle passes through the poles of both circles (the ecliptic and the planetary path), it will always intercept unequal arcs measured from the common intersection of the circles. And since this circle of latitude is perpendicular to the ecliptic, if it does not pass through the poles of the planetary orbit, it will be oblique to the orbit. Therefore, the arc between the position of the planet in its own orbit and the nearer node is always greater than the arc between its ecliptic position and that same node.

<margin>What does it mean to refer a planet to the ecliptic?</margin> When we observe the planets, we do not convince ourselves that we have defined their certain positions until we have referred them to the ecliptic; indicating at which point on the ecliptic the circle of latitude passing through the body of the planet is found. Thus, the ecliptic position exists for the sake of our memory and understanding. On the other hand, when we calculate a planet according to its own model, we are dealing not with the ecliptic but with the planet's path itself, which is inclined to the ecliptic. 

So that the observed position can be compared with the calculated one, it is necessary either to lengthen the arc between the ecliptic position and the nearer node, or to shorten the arc between the body of the planet and that same node, so that from the former comes the orbital position, and from the latter the ecliptic position. This is done by either adding or subtracting, depending on whether the node preceded or followed the planet's position.

PTOLEMY did not judge this care regarding the planets to be necessary; COPERNICUS did not neglect it in the case of the Moon; TYCHO BRAHE diligently embraced it for the sake of precision.

HOWEVER, in this <term>reduction</term> <note>The mathematical adjustment used to map a position from an inclined orbit onto the flat plane of the ecliptic.</note> now applied, I have two things I find lacking, both of which I will refute with the same list and diagram.

-># PART TWO.<-

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
Let ***A*** be the location of a node among the **Fixed Stars** <note>The distant stars that form the unchanging background of the sky.</note>, and ***AB*** be an arc of the ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky, which represents the plane of Earth's orbit.</note>. Let an equal arc ***AC*** be established, and let the **Planet** be seen at ***C***. Also, let a perpendicular arc ***CE*** be drawn from ***C*** to the ecliptic.

First, therefore, the ancients thought that since ***E*** is the location on the ecliptic and ***C*** is the location on the **Planet's** own orbit, the **Planet** would then be in opposition to the **Sun** when the **Sun** is at ***E*** and the **Planet** is observed at ***C***. But the makers of the astronomical tables <note>Specifically referring to the creators of the Prutenic or Alfonsine Tables, which astronomers used to predict planetary positions.</note> thought, as was said above, that the **Planet** is not accurately in opposition to the **Sun** unless the arc ***AB*** (the distance of the Sun's opposite point from the node) is made equal to ***AC*** (the visible distance of the **Planet** from the node).

But the matter stands otherwise. The **Planet** is indeed viewed as being exactly opposite the **Sun** at that time, but it is not: and the convenience we seek from the opposition of the **Planet** with the **Sun** is more corrupted by this equality of ***AC*** and ***AB*** than they hoped it would be improved. For why are **Planets** observed when in opposition to the **Sun**? Surely it is for this reason: so that they might then lack the **second inequality of longitude** <note term="second inequality">This is the apparent "looping" or retrograde motion of a planet caused by the Earth passing it in orbit, rather than the planet's own movement.</note>. Yet, with the **Sun's** opposite at ***B*** and the **Planet** residing at ***C*** between the nodes and the limits <note>The "limits" are the points where the planet reaches its maximum distance north or south of the ecliptic.</note>, the **Planet** is more entangled in the second inequality of longitude than if the **Sun's** opposite were at ***E*** while the **Planet** remained at ***C***. 

For let ***G*** be the **Sun**, the center of the **Planetary** system in which all the orbits intersect the ecliptic, whether in the **Copernican** or **Braheana** <note>Referring to the systems of Nicolaus Copernicus (Sun-centered) or Tycho Brahe (Earth-centered, but with planets orbiting the Sun).</note> form. Let ***G*** be connected with points ***A*** and ***E*** on the ecliptic; and let the Earth be on the line ***EG***, specifically at point ***H***. Let ***H*** be connected with ***C***: and from point ***H***, let the **Sun**, ***G***, be viewed as being at the opposite of ***E***; but let the **Planet** be viewed from that same ***H*** at its location ***C*** among the **Fixed Stars** on the line ***HC***. Therefore, in this view, the **Planet** is certainly on the line ***HC***. It is, however, much lower than the **Fixed Stars**. Let it be at point ***I*** on the line ***HC***: and from ***G***, through ***I***, let a straight line be drawn, which will fall upon the arc ***CE***. For the entire plane ***CEHG*** is beneath the arc ***EC***. Let the point of incidence be ***F***, and from ***A*** through ***F*** onto ***BC***, let a third arc ***AF*** be drawn, intersecting ***BC*** at ***D***. 

It is clear that the plane of the **Planet’s** eccentric orbit, as seen from ***H*** at ***C***, is not arranged under ***AC*** but under ***AF***; and with the **Sun's** opposite residing at ***E***, the **Planet** would truly be under ***F***; but with the Sun placed at ***B***, the planet would be under ***D***, provided it appears under ***C*** from both sides. However, ***AD*** is shorter than the legs of the isosceles triangle ***BAC***. Therefore, ***B*** (the Sun's opposite) is removed further from ***A*** than the location ***D*** where the **Planet** is at the moment they assumed. The **Sun**, therefore, truly stands beyond the opposite of the **Planet's** true location. But this is contrary to their purpose.

Furthermore, even if the **Planet's** orbit were under ***AC***, it does not follow that ***AB*** should be taken as equal to ***AC***. Nor, because this orbit is truly under ***AD***, should ***AB*** be taken as equal to ***AD***. For because the **Planet** is observed in opposition to the **Sun** specifically to strip away the second inequality of longitude, and that longitude must be judged in the **Planet's** own genuine orbit (or the arc ***AD*** standing above it); certainly, unless the **Sun's** opposite falls on an arc drawn through the **Planet's** location at a right angle to that orbit—that is, unless angle ***ADB*** is a right angle—***B*** (the Sun's opposite) will not be joined to ***D*** according to longitude. But if ***ADB*** is a right angle, then ***AB*** is longer than ***AD***. Therefore, they are not equal. Thus, that equality of arcs ***AC*** and ***AB***, so sought after in the tables, is plainly torn down.

Just as the entire latitude <term>e c</term> makes <term>a c</term> longer than <term>a e</term> by the arc <term>e b</term>: and the part of this visible latitude <term>f g</term> or <term>h i g</term>, which is from the second inequality, makes that same <term>a c</term> longer than <term>a f</term>. In STADIUS <note>Johannes Stadius, author of popular astronomical ephemerides or position tables.</note>, it is 1 degree 52 minutes. At the hour of 9:40 (which TYCHO sets as the moment of observation), it would be further forward by 1 minute 4 seconds: namely, either at 6 degrees 42 minutes 54 seconds or at 6 degrees 45 minutes 54 seconds. They place it at 6 degrees 46 minutes 10 seconds of Gemini.

You see that this opposition (as far as precision is concerned) is a little more uncertain, because it uses a daily motion that was not observed but borrowed from elsewhere, which itself differs by three minutes between different authors over these five days.

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>

**III.** In the year 1585, on January 31, at 12 hours 0 minutes, Mars was placed at 21 degrees 18 minutes 11 seconds of Leo. By comparing observations, the daily motion was found to be 24 minutes 15 seconds. The moment of opposition followed at 19 hours 35 minutes—a difference of 7 hours 35 minutes, during which a daily motion of 7 minutes 41 seconds in retrograde <note>original: "in antecedentia," referring to the planet appearing to move backward against the stars.</note> is appropriate. Therefore, at the designated moment, it would have been at 21 degrees 10 minutes 30 seconds of Leo, which is what was adopted. There is no mention of parallax. No mention of refraction was necessary, because Mars was high and in the midheaven. Thus, I find that a brief warning about refraction in the table was (rightly) neglected.

**IV.** In the year 1587, on March 7 at 19 hours 10 minutes, they derived the position of Mars from observations as 25 degrees 10 minutes 20 seconds of Virgo. They retained this in the table, but changed the time to 17 hours 22 minutes. The difference is 1 hour 48 minutes. Given a daily motion of 24 minutes, this produces exactly the same number of minutes <note>Kepler is noting a calculation where the time difference and the arc of motion happen to align numerically in his units.</note> (namely 1 minute 48 seconds), and no more. It ought, therefore, to have been 25 degrees 8 minutes 32 seconds of Virgo, which also comes closer to the point opposite the Sun. The difference is of almost no significance.

**V.** In the year 1589, on April 15 at 12 hours 5 minutes, they established the position of Mars with great diligence at 3 degrees 58 minutes 21 seconds of Scorpio, and corrected it for the parallax of longitude so that it was 3 degrees 57 minutes 11 seconds. There remain 1 hour 30 minutes until the assigned moment of opposition; over this time, a daily motion of 22 minutes moves the planet back by 1 minute 22 seconds, placing it at 3 degrees 55 minutes 49 seconds. They assumed 3 degrees 58 minutes 10 seconds. That value is closer to the mean motion of the Sun.

**VI.** In the year 1591, on June 6 at 12 hours 20 minutes, Mars is placed at 27 degrees 15 minutes of Sagittarius. There remain 2 days 4 hours 5 minutes until the assigned moment. Over four days, it was found to advance by 1 degree 12 minutes 47 seconds. Therefore, for the 2 days 4 hours 5 minutes, 39 minutes 29 seconds are appropriate. Thus, at the moment of opposition, Mars was at 26 degrees 35 minutes 31 seconds of Sagittarius. There is no need for horizontal variations <note>A term for diurnal parallax.</note> in longitude, because Mars was in the midheaven and at the beginning of Capricorn. The table has 26 degrees 32 minutes of Sagittarius.

**VII.** In the year 1593, on August 24 at 10 hours 30 minutes, they report Mars at 12 degrees 38 minutes of Pisces with an observed daily motion of 16 minutes 45 seconds; this was near the nonagesimal <note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon, where longitudinal parallax is zero.</note> where there is no parallax of longitude. The assigned moment of opposition had preceded this by 8 hours 17 minutes (for it was at 2 hours 13 minutes), to which a motion of 5 minutes 48 seconds in the direction of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia," or forward motion.</note> corresponds. Thus, the planet falls at 12 degrees 43 minutes 48 seconds of Pisces. The table has 12 degrees 43 minutes 45 seconds.

**IIX.** In the year 1595, on October 30 at 8 hours 20 minutes, they found Mars at 17 degrees 48 minutes of Taurus, with a daily motion of 22 minutes 54 seconds. The assigned moment preceded this by 11 hours 48 minutes, to which a motion of Mars of 11 minutes 7 seconds in the direction of the signs is due, so that it would have been at 17 degrees 59 minutes 7 seconds of Taurus. But it had been displaced in the east due to parallax. Thus, perhaps from another meridian observation, they put 17 degrees 56 minutes 15 seconds of Taurus in the table.

**IX.** In the year 1597, on December 10 at 8 hours 30 minutes, they once place Mars at 3 degrees 30 minutes of Cancer, and again at 4 degrees 1 minute of Cancer; the mean of these is 3 degrees 45 ½ minutes of Cancer. The moment of opposition followed after 3 days 5 hours 5 minutes, to which, according to Magini <note>Giovanni Paolo Magini (1555–1617), an Italian astronomer.</note>, 1 degree 15 minutes in retrograde motion corresponds. Therefore, Mars would have been at 2 degrees 30 ½ minutes of Cancer; it is placed at 2 degrees 28 minutes of Cancer in the table. The cause of the coarse observation made with a radius <term>cross-staff</term> <note>A handheld navigation and astronomical instrument, less accurate than the large fixed instruments Tycho used previously.</note> is evident from the time. Tycho had departed from the island <note>Tycho Brahe left his observatory on the island of Hven in 1597 after a falling out with the Danish king.</note>, leaving his instruments behind.

<margin>Chapter XI.</margin>
The nodes <note>the two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit</note> cannot be known without diurnal parallax <term>diurnal parallax: the tiny shift in a planet's apparent position caused by the observer's movement as the Earth rotates</term>, provided that this shift is somewhat large. Therefore, we must begin with parallax, for the investigation of which I shall propose two methods.

**THE FIRST METHOD** (used by others as well) will be examined using the Brahean observations.
In the year **1582**, when **MARS** was in opposition to the **Sun** in Cancer, I found incredible diligence in observing, under **Tycho's** own manuscript title: **"FOR INQUIRING INTO THE PARALLAXES OF MARS,"** but from which you could elicit either no parallax at all, or only a very tiny one for **MARS**. I say nothing of the fact that (in their usual manner) they compared the star **MARS** to stars near the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent annual path, used as a reference line in the sky</term> which were often quite far away. Since, therefore, the parallax of a moving star is usually sought by comparing morning and evening observations (**MARS**, when opposite the **Sun**, moves with retrograde <term>retrograde: the apparent backward motion of a planet across the sky</term> motion), it happened that Mars was observed in the morning against one set of stars and in the evening against another. For if a fixed star were available in the morning (one higher than ♂ <note>original: ♂, the symbol for Mars</note>) and it were near the ecliptic, by the evening (with **MARS** now turning toward the western region) that star either sets or is unsuitable for this delicate business due to refraction <term>refraction: the bending of light by the Earth's atmosphere, which makes objects near the horizon appear higher than they actually are</term>. Another star, therefore, had to be substituted. But if one fixed star is swapped for another, there is always less certainty in the business than if the same star were retained. 

However, since **BRAHE** frequently affirmed to learned men that from the observations of this year, a parallax of **Mars** was found to be significantly greater than that of the **Sun**, I—in order to more deeply inspect this operation or calculation—searched through the entire book with the greatest diligence. And I did indeed find the title that claimed to show the method for seeking the parallax of **Mars** from that year's observations. But behold, an unexpected thing! They had fitted the position of **Mars** found by observation to a **Copernican model** that had been most laboriously and diligently drawn. In that diagram, they took up the immense labor of solving, with the most long-winded numbers, all the triangles that arose from the double epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circular orbit used in older astronomy to explain planetary loops</term> in the concentric circle. At last, this was the end of the calculation: they pronounced that the parallax of **Mars** truly becomes greater than that of the **Sun**. Thus, **Brahe** had proposed one thing, but his calculating assistants performed another. He wanted them to seek the parallax of **Mars** from morning and evening observations compared with one another; they, however, sought how much parallax the **Copernican model** would produce. Whether **Brahe** pronounced his findings on parallaxes based solely on this faith in his assistants is unknown to me.

Let us consult the observations themselves (as far as concerns our business).
In the year **1582**, on the night between the 23rd and 24th of **November**, the distances from the fixed stars remained the same at different hours. This was, therefore, the point of its station <note>the time when a planet appears to stand still before changing direction</note>.
The motion of the following two days was 11 and 15 minutes.
On the night of **December 26**, it passed between the second and seventh [stars] of ♊ <note>original: ♊, the symbol for Gemini</note>, being distant <gloss>by</gloss> the radius from the head of the lower of the **Gemini** (or from the second) by 2 degrees 25 minutes or 2 degrees 26 minutes; but from the seventh, by 1 degree 6 minutes or 1 degree 7 minutes, so that the latitude was

...approximately 4 degrees 9 minutes. Therefore, at 8:28 <margin>Chapter XI.</margin> the planet was 44 degrees 41 minutes distant from the eye of the Bull <note>original: "oculo Tauri," the star Aldebaran</note>, whose latitude was 5 degrees 31 minutes South and longitude 4 degrees 12 ½ minutes in Gemini <note>original: ♊</note> in the year <term>1600</term>. From this, the longitude of **MARS** for the year <term>1600</term> was nearly 17 degrees 53 ⅓ minutes of Cancer <note>original: ♋</note>; that is, at the completion of <term>1582</term>, it was 17 degrees 38 minutes of Cancer, at an altitude of 40 degrees 50 minutes. It was, therefore, outside the effects of refraction <term>refraction: the bending of light by Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects look higher than they really are</term>.

Conversely, at 7:15 on the morning of <term>December 27</term>, it was 36 degrees 43 minutes distant from the heart of the Lion <note>original: "corde Leo," the star Regulus</note>, whose latitude is 0 degrees 26 ½ minutes; hence its longitude at the completion of <term>1582</term> was 17 degrees 28 ¼ minutes of Cancer, at an altitude of 14 degrees 4 minutes—therefore, within the range of refraction. Thus, from 8:24 ½ in the evening until 7:15 the next morning (a period of 10 hours 46 ½ minutes), it was seen to move retrograde <term>retrograde: the apparent backward motion of a planet relative to the stars</term> by 9 ⅔ minutes.

To find the daily motion, on <term>December 29</term> at 7:47, the distance of **MARS** from the southern foot of Erichthonius <note>original: "pede Erichthonii," likely referring to a star in the constellation Auriga (the Charioteer), often identified with the mythical Erichthonius</note> was recorded as 29 degrees 38 ½ minutes. On the <term>30th</term> at 8:08, the distance from the same star was 29 degrees 13 ½ minutes. Therefore, in 24 hours 21 minutes, the position changed by 25 minutes. This daily rate also held for the <term>27th</term>. Therefore, in 10 hours 46 ½ minutes, a movement of 11 ½ minutes was expected; yet we saw only 9 ⅔ minutes. Let us consider this.

Evening <term>parallax</term> <term>parallax: the apparent shift of an object's position when viewed from different locations</term> throws a rising, more easterly **MARS** (because it is in retrograde) toward the east; in the morning, it throws a setting, more westerly Mars toward the west. Just as the parallax of the Moon slows down its observed daily motion, so conversely this same parallax of **MARS** accelerates its retrograde motion. If, therefore, parallax is felt, it is felt as an excessive increase in retrograde motion. But here, the motion was diminished. Therefore, there is no parallax. Conversely, however, <term>refraction</term> (the opposite of parallax) is felt. Now, the refraction at an altitude of 13 degrees is 4 minutes according to the table of Fixed Stars, or 8 minutes according to the table of the Sun; the smallest part of this affects the longitude, because <term>Cancer</term> descends very obliquely. Thus, at most, 3 minutes of refraction in longitude occurred, which, when added to the 9 ⅔ minutes, makes 12 ⅔ minutes of motion in 10 ¾ hours free from refraction. If this had also been free of parallax, it should have been 11 ½ minutes. Therefore, the excess of 1 ⅙ minutes is the parallax in longitude for both observations combined—which is clearly a tiny, unreliable, and negligible amount.

On the evening of <term>January 16, 1583</term>, at 7:30, **MARS** was 23 degrees 29 minutes distant from the bright star in the foot of Erichthonius. On the following morning at 5:00, its distance from the heart of the Lion <note>Regulus</note> was 43 degrees 58 minutes, at an altitude of 15 degrees. And **MARS** appeared, by the ruler, exactly on the same straight line as both stars. Since the motion of **MARS** occurs along this line, **Brahe** noted that a parallax of longitude could be derived from this, using the daily motion of **MARS**. This is calculated as follows: On <term>January 16</term> at 10:30, it was 23 degrees 27 minutes from the bright star in the foot of Erichthonius. On <term>January 17</term> at 10:45, it was 23 degrees 12 ½ minutes from the same. The daily motion would therefore be 14 ½ minutes. To follow **Brahe's** advice, we must establish the distance between the foot of Erichthonius and the heart of the Lion, which is found to be 67 degrees 21 minutes. Subtracting the distance of **MARS** from the foot of Erichthonius (23 degrees 29 minutes) leaves the distance of **MARS** from the heart of the Lion as 43 degrees 52 minutes at 7:30 in the evening; by 5:00 the next morning, it was 43 degrees 58 minutes, an increase of 6 minutes. There are 9 ½ hours between them, for which 5 ⅚ minutes of the daily motion are due. Here...

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

Therefore, the sum of both parallaxes is no more than 0 ½, except for what is added to it by as much as **MARS'S** refraction of longitude at an altitude of <margin>Chapter XI.</margin> 15 degrees. This is actually very little, for *Cancer* and *Leo* descend quite obliquely, and the great Northern latitude of **MARS** caused **MARS** and the Heart of the *Lion* <note>original: "cor Leonis," the star Regulus</note> to be at almost the same altitude.

On the 17th day of January, in the evening at 5:20, **MARS** was 23 degrees 16 minutes from the foot of *Erichthonius* <note>original: "pede Erichthonii," the star Beta Tauri in the constellation Auriga</note>. On the following day, the 18th, in the morning at 3:00, this distance was 23 degrees 9 minutes. In the evening at 5:05, it was 23 degrees 1 ½ minutes. Thus, the motion over 23 hours and 45 minutes is 14 ½ minutes; however, the motion over 9 hours and 40 minutes is 7 minutes—it ought to have been 6 minutes. We retain no more than 1 minute for the parallax of longitude. Refraction disturbs nothing, for on both sides, the altitude of *Mars* was about 30 degrees.

Similarly, from the seventh star $\pi$ <note>a star in the constellation Auriga</note> at 7:34, it was 7 degrees 51 minutes away. At 4:52 in the morning, it was 7 degrees 59 minutes away from the same star. Therefore, in 9 hours and 18 minutes, it moved 8 minutes. We are one minute better informed than before. Regarding this star (in the armpit, $\pi$), *Brahe* wrote as follows: *Note, I take the distance of $\mars$ <note>Mars</note> from this star for this reason: because its course shows, as it were, the parallax of $\mars$. I wanted to transcribe this so that the reader may be certain that Brahe did not lack a plan.*

On January 18, in the evening at 8:52, the distance between $\mars$ and the Heart <note>Regulus</note> was 44 degrees 32 minutes. In the morning at 4:30, the same distance was 44 degrees 27 ½ minutes. Therefore, the motion over 7 hours and 53 minutes was 15 ¼ minutes. On the following day, January 19, at 7:03, this distance was 44 degrees 32 ½ minutes. Thus, the motion over 22 hours and 11 minutes is 10 ½ minutes. And for 8 hours, fewer than 4 minutes are owed. We gain about 1 ½ minutes for the parallax.

But come, let us compute for the 17th day of January how much the increase in hourly motion ought to have been, based on a parallax larger than is commonly believed for the *Sun*. For since we think the parallax of the *Sun* is three minutes, let **MARS** have four.

-># SECOND PART<-

It follows that the hourly motion of <term>Mars (♂)</term><note>The planet Mars, represented by its traditional symbol</note> should have appeared four minutes greater than that which proportionally follows from its daily motion. Since the observations <margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin> reject this, the <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions; used by astronomers to determine distance</note> of Mars is therefore not that large.

Similar observations exist from the years 1585, 1595, and elsewhere, from which the parallax is found to be very tiny, often zero. Sometimes it was even noted by **Brahe’s** own hand that the result fell into the contrary <note>This implies a "negative parallax," an impossibility in the physical model, suggesting observational error</note>. Let this, therefore, be the first method of investigating the parallax of Mars.

**Now I shall add a second** method for the sake of its beauty, in which I cannot use **Brahe’s** observations. While I use **my own**, I will present you with a ridiculous spectacle, and I will teach by example why **Brahe** had need of such great diligence, precision of instruments, assistants, and all the rest of his apparatus.

I have two instruments, which I use through the generosity of the Distinguished Lord **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann**, Baron: an iron **Sextant** and a brass Azimuth **Quadrant**; the former is two and a half feet in diameter, the latter three and a half, and both are marked to individual minutes.

Therefore, at this very time in 1604, when I am thinking about parallaxes (whether more of the Sun or of Mars, I cannot say; for my *Hipparchus* <note>Refers to Kepler’s own work, *Astronomiae Pars Optica* (1604), which he nicknamed his "Hipparchus"</note> also requires help from Mars for its lunar eclipses), a most convenient opportunity for observing presented itself—if only it had been in another climate and Mars had walked a little higher in the sky. For Mars remained stationary in both longitude and latitude around February 19/29 of this year 1604, and that in <term>Libra (♎)</term>. For this reason, from the rising of Mars until the rising of the Sun itself, the angle of the Horizon with the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere</note> continuously decreases. Therefore, according to Chapter 9 of my *Optical Astronomy*, if there is any parallax of latitude, it continuously increases. From the increase found through the "parallactic columns," from the region of the initial and final angle of the ecliptic with the Horizon, the total horizontal parallax is recognized at the head of the column.

## A series of my observations follows.

On the night between Thursday and Friday, which were February 17/27, while <term>Corvus</term><note>The constellation of the Crow</note> was crossing the meridian, the distance between Mars and <term>Spica</term><note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> was 9 degrees 44 minutes; between Mars and the <term>Northern Claw</term><note>original: "Lancem Boream," the star Beta Librae</note> it was 17 degrees 41 minutes; and between Mars and **Arcturus** it was 29 degrees 13 minutes. To test the **sextant**, we also measured the distance between **Arcturus** and **Spica**, which was 32 degrees 57 minutes; however, this ought to have been 33 degrees 1 minute 45 seconds. This is clear if the calculation is consulted using either the right ascensions and declinations, or the longitudes and latitudes, which **Tycho** assigned to these stars in Book 1 of his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s "Introductory Exercises" to his astronomical restoration</note>. Therefore, **my** distances were smaller than they should have been by 4¾ minutes, by which I corrected the distances of Mars from the fixed stars, so that it was 9 degrees 48 minutes 45 seconds from Spica; 17 degrees 45 minutes 45 seconds from the Claw; and 29 degrees 17 minutes 43 seconds from Arcturus.

I also took the meridian altitude of Mars with the **Quadrant** as 32 degrees 4 minutes, and that of Spica as 30 degrees 50 minutes. Since Spica has a declination of 9 degrees 2 minutes, a declination of 7 degrees 48 minutes is left for Mars. However, the altitude of Spica showed that my plumb-line was not positioned well enough.

<margin>CHAPTER 11.</margin>
...toward Arcturus, then lowered it as **Mars** (♂) was gaining some altitude. But the cause of such variation in observing in a single moment was the cold and the most piercing winds. For the iron could not be handled with bare hands, the pulley could not be closed, and the <term>ruler</term><note>The sighting arm or "regula" of the astronomical instrument</note> was not securely fixed until the minute was noted. **Vindemiatrix**<note>The "Grape-gatherer," a bright star in the constellation Virgo</note> showed an altitude of 53 deg. 5 min. on the meridian, a little higher than it should be. From this, the distance between **Mars** and **Arcturus** was gathered by calculation as 29 deg. 18 1/3 min. Since **Mars** was stationary at this time according to longitude—with both the <term>Prutenic</term><note>Astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551, based on Copernicus's work</note> calculations and my own in agreement—nothing could have changed in the meridian altitude by reason of its wandering along the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit</note>. Therefore, since the meridian altitude remained exactly the same (for my instrument leaves us in doubt regarding only a single minute), no change in latitude occurred in the meantime.

On the 22nd of February (or the 3rd of March), we tested the **SEXTANT** as we had used it above, and we found the distance between the <term>Lesser Dog</term><note>Procyon, the brightest star in Canis Minor</note> and the upper shoulder of Orion to be 26 deg. 2 min.; the calculation shows it as 26 deg. 2 min. 15 sec. Likewise, between the same Lesser Dog and **Palilicium**<note>An older name for the star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus</note>, 46 deg. 22 1/2 min. were found; **TYCHO BRAHE** indicates in his letters that this is 46 deg. 22 min. Therefore, when the star in the heart of **Leo** the Lion was culminating, and the ruler of the instrument was fixed at 29 deg. 17 min., Arcturus and **Mars** were less distant; but at 29 deg. 13 1/2 min. they were already more distant; finally, at 29 deg. 15 min., nothing could be faulted. Unexpected clouds then followed across the whole sky. However, clarity returned on the morning of March 4th, and when **Antares** had already culminated, the ruler was placed at 29 deg. 19 min., and the stars were seen equally on both sides. Yet it seemed something should be added; but at 29 deg. 20 min., too much had already been added. Once the observation was finished, **Saturn** preceded the meridian by less than the distance between **Jupiter** and **Saturn**.

On the night that followed, the 29th of February (or the 10th of March), the instrument having been knocked out of alignment in the meantime, this distance was first between 29 deg. 9 min. and 29 deg. 10 min., half an hour before the <term>Heart of Hydra</term><note>The star Alphard</note> culminated. Upon investigating again, it appeared between 29 deg. 12 min. and 29 deg. 13 min. because it was now higher and free from <term>refractions</term><note>The bending of light by the atmosphere, which is stronger near the horizon</note>. For when this observation was completed, it had an altitude of 19 1/6 deg. But a little later (I know not whether the <term>sighting vane</term><note>original: "pinnacidio"; the small plate with a hole or slit used for sighting stars</note> was moved), such a large measurement could not be tolerated. For it seemed to be 29 deg. 9 1/2 min. The **Tail of the Dragon** (☋)<note>The descending lunar node, where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note> was about half a degree away from the <term>midheaven</term><note>The point where the meridian meets the ecliptic</note>. At that time, the altitude of **Mars** was 24 3/4 deg. The **Tail of the Dragon** culminating had an altitude of 56 deg. 44 min., accurate to within a minute. When a third part of the distance between **Mars** and **Spica** had passed the meridian, it first seemed to us to be 29 deg. 9 1/2 min., as the <term>Cylinder</term><note>A part of the sextant's sighting mechanism</note>—which was very long—was not very well applied. Therefore, a little later, this could not be tolerated, but 29 deg. 10 1/4 min. (or a little less) seemed to be required. Moreover, **Mars** was seen from both sides of the Cylinder.

At that time, the distance between **Mars** and **Spica** was 9 deg. 26 min., and less than 9 deg. 27 min.
**Mars** culminated at an altitude of 30 deg. 19 1/2 min.

Then, the distance between **Mars** and the **Northern Scale**<note>The star Zubeneschamali in the constellation Libra</note> was 18 deg. 25 min.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS
<margin>CHAPTER 11.</margin>

To test the **SEXTANT** <term>sextant</term><note>An instrument used to measure the angular distance between two objects, such as stars</note>, the distance between **Spica** and the **Scale** <note>original: "Lancem"; referring to Alpha Librae in the constellation Libra</note> was taken as 27 degrees 39 minutes; however, it ought to have been 27 degrees 34 minutes. Likewise, the distance between **Spica** and the **Northern star of the forehead of Scorpio** <note>original: "Boream frontis Scorpio"; likely Beta Scorpii</note> was 39 degrees 32.5 minutes, when it ought to have been 39 degrees 26.5 minutes. Thus, the **sextant** was excessive by five minutes. The calculation of the position of **Mars** (♂) also confirms this. For unless you subtract five minutes from the distances of **Mars** from the Fixed Stars, the **right ascension** <term>right ascension</term><note>The celestial equivalent of longitude</note> determined through **Spica** and the **Scale** will disagree by ten minutes. But once subtracted (as the test requires), it will coincide most exactly: the right ascension will be 205 degrees 27 minutes 10 seconds, the **declination** <term>declination</term><note>The celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> 7 degrees 35.5 minutes; therefore the position is 26 degrees 18 minutes 48 seconds of **Libra** (♎), with a latitude of 2 degrees 47 minutes 20 seconds. You clearly see the latitude, while in the meantime the Planet has moved backward in longitude by 38 minutes. If you seek its distance from **Arcturus** using this found position of **Mars**, it will come out to 29 degrees 9.33 minutes—whereas on the faulty instrument, it was 29 degrees 14 minutes.

When the **Heart of the Scorpion** <note>Antares</note> had already reached its highest point in the sky, our measured distance (with the instrument having been bumped and then immediately restored) was 29 degrees 13.5 minutes. We therefore tested the **sextant** again, which showed 44 degrees 45 minutes between the **Pole Star** and the **Tail of the Swan** <note>Deneb</note>, though it ought to have been 44 degrees 39.5 minutes. Therefore, the instrument was in its original condition. Since **Saturn** (♄) had already passed the meridian by one degree, the measurement of 29 degrees 13.5 minutes could not be tolerated; yet it was more than 29 degrees 12.5 minutes, very nearly 29 degrees 13 minutes.

This, then, is the series of observations. I would be a madman if I tried to construct a highly refined system from these. Therefore, I offer these not as proofs, but as examples for someone more diligent and fortunate. I even hope that readers, through their disgust with these uncertainties, will all the more seek out the most certain observations of **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe, whose precise data Kepler would eventually use to solve the orbit of Mars</note>. But to the matter at hand.

> *The first and second days only concur to prove the station of the motion in latitude. On both sides, **Mars** stood at a distance of 29 degrees 18 minutes from **Arcturus**; on both sides its altitude at noon was 32 degrees 7 minutes or 6 minutes. Indeed, those days trained me to perform the following ones more correctly, had the necessary instruments been available.*

> *But on the 3rd of March, when the **Mouth of the Lion** <note>likely the star Rasalas or Al Jabhah in Leo</note> reached the meridian, the distance was 29 degrees 15 minutes; when the **Heart of the Scorpion** reached it, the distance was more than 29 degrees 19 minutes. Therefore, in the intervening time, the distance changed by about 4.25 minutes. And since **Arcturus** and **Mars** occupy nearly the same longitude, this change in distance argues for a variation in the **parallax** <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different locations; here, Kepler is looking for the difference caused by viewing Mars from the Earth's surface versus its center</note> of latitude. I am aware that 29 degrees 19 minutes is not far from 29 degrees 18 minutes, and that by analogy with the previous day, this should be the distance even at a similar hour, since **Mars** is stationary. I also know that when the **Mouth of the Lion** is at the **Midheaven** <term>M.C.</term><note>Medium Coeli; the highest point on the ecliptic at a given time</note>, **Mars** is at an altitude of 12.5 degrees, still subject to **refractions** <term>refractions</term><note>The bending of light by Earth's atmosphere, which makes objects near the horizon appear higher than they actually are</note>. However, we shall speak of this later. For now, let these things be ignored, so our example is not disturbed. Therefore, since the altitude of the **nonagesimal** <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note> was about 57.33 degrees when the **Mouth of the Lion** was culminating, and finally 28.5 degrees after the **Heart of the Scorpion** had culminated, the area in the parallactic table (where the column changes from a distance from the zenith of 32.66 degrees to a distance of 69.66 degrees) changes by 4.25 degrees. I find that this occurs under the column whose heading is 9 minutes. Thus, the maximum parallax of **Mars** would be 9 minutes. And since the distance between **Mars** and the Earth on this day was to the distance between **Mars** and the **Sun** (☉) as 28 to 60 (which is held by a **rough estimation** <note>original: "crassiori Minerva"; a Latin idiom meaning a plain or unrefined approach</note> from prior knowledge of the hypotheses of **Tycho** and **Copernicus**), the ratio of the parallaxes will be changed, and the maximum parallax of the **Sun** will be about 4 minutes 24 seconds, whereas it is usually set at 3 minutes 0 seconds.*

# SECOND PART,

<margin>Chapter 11.</margin>
Now, however, let us weigh the fact that **Mars** was at an altitude of 12 1/2 degrees. If the table for the refraction <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear higher in the sky than they actually are</note> of the **Fixed Stars** constructed at **Hven** <note>original: "Huenna"; Tycho Brahe's island observatory</note> is valid in **Prague** <note>original: "Praga"</note>, the refraction at this altitude was 4 minutes and 20 seconds. Of this, 2 minutes and 18 seconds are attributed to latitude, by which **Mars** was made closer to **Arcturus**. But if we also apply the **Solar** refractions to **Mars** (which often seems to be the case), the refraction at this altitude is 8 minutes and 45 seconds—twice as much. Therefore, the parallax <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations; here, the shift caused by viewing Mars from the Earth's surface instead of its center</note> of latitude would also be twice as large, namely 4 minutes and 36 seconds. In this way, all the variation shown by the observation at these two different moments would be due to refraction alone. In the first case, 2 minutes would be left for the parallax of latitude, which is the amount of variation under the column whose front is 5 minutes, so that in this way only 2 minutes and 25 seconds would fall to the **Sun** as the maximum minutes of parallax. Thus, refraction has made our third day of observation suspect and doubtful, and finally quite useless. I know that since **Arcturus** and **Mars** are 9 degrees apart—which is a third part of the latitude of **Arcturus** above the latitude of **Mars**—it happens then that not all the refraction of latitude is subtracted from the distance from **Mars**, and that parallax varies the latitude of **Mars** more than this distance from **Arcturus**. However, as that is very small, I thought it should be disregarded in the face of greater fears. Let him who is equipped with more subtle instruments observe it.

Now, on the fourth day, nothing else seems to be achieved but the destruction of all parallax for **Mars**. The distance at the meridian ought to have been 29 degrees 9 1/2 minutes with a corrected instrument, and therefore 29 degrees 14 minutes with the faulty one. Yet it was found to be 29 degrees 13 1/2 minutes at the last, when the parallax of latitude (if there were any) ought to have been greater, and through this, the distance from **Arcturus** would be greater. From that time, therefore, when **Mars** reached an altitude of 19 degrees, the distance was found to be 29 degrees 12 1/2 minutes, increased by only a single minute <note>original: "scrupulo"</note> at the end. This would be a very small parallax. And what is the reason for this? When it was 9 degrees high (with **Hydra** culminating), the distance was 29 degrees 9 minutes with the faulty instrument, and yet later at an altitude of 25 degrees and near the midheaven <note>original: "m. c."; meridianum coeli</note> it was again 29 degrees 9 minutes, and that twice, at different moments. Was refraction unable to do anything here at the beginning, so that the arc remained constant? Or should it rather be said that I (though I seemed to myself most diligent) erred in observing? Especially on account of the length of the **Cylinder** <term>cylinder</term><note>A sighting component on the astronomical instrument</note>.

From these observations, such as they are, it is established with certainty that the parallaxes of **Mars's** latitude were certainly not greater than 4 minutes—the amount taken up by the uncertainty of the instrument. It is more credible that they are very small. You will find more arguments on this matter below in Chapter 64.

That the parallaxes of **Mars** are indeed greater than the parallaxes of the **Sun** is argued by the reasoning of the **Tychonic** and **Copernican** hypotheses, from which the parallaxes of **Mars** could easily be computed if we were certain about the parallax of the **Sun**. Is the method of investigating the **Sun's** altitude and parallaxes from eclipses therefore uncertain? Entirely so regarding the exact quantity, but most certain regarding the fact itself. The **Sun** is not closer than 230 earth-radii, yet it is not infinitely many radii away. But between 700 and 2000 radii (the former figure offered in my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>original: "Mysterio Cosmographico"; Kepler's 1596 book</note>, the latter in observations of eclipses as the nearest and farthest limits), no certain number seems to have been demonstrated yet, as I shall prove in my *Hipparchus* <note>Kepler’s work in progress concerning the distances and sizes of the sun and moon</note>.

## CHAPTER XII.
### Investigation of the nodes of MARS.

**T**HEREFORE, although there is no lack of means for investigating the planets' first <term>inequality</term><note>The "first inequality" refers to the planet's non-uniform motion in its own orbit, while the "second inequality" refers to its apparent motion caused by the Earth's movement.</note> through observations, even when they are entangled in the second inequality: nevertheless, in this second part, I shall follow in the footsteps of previous authors and use observations made <term>at opposition</term><note>original: "ἀκρονυχίας" (akronychias). This refers to observations made when a planet is opposite the Sun in the sky, rising at sunset and visible all night.</note> for the sake of establishing trust. I do this because I profess some views contrary to theirs, and I would not want anyone to cry out that I am hiding later behind the thickets of my own method.

And since it has already become clear that nothing of any significance is missing in the diurnal <term>parallaxes</term><note>The apparent shift in position of Mars when viewed from different points on Earth.</note> of MARS used by Tycho, I will gradually approach the <term>reduction</term><note>The mathematical process of converting observed positions into a standardized coordinate system.</note> of the seen positions of MARS to the apparent opposite position of the SUN.

First, we need knowledge of the <term>nodes</term><note>The two points where the orbit of Mars intersects the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>. TYCHO BRA-
<margin>HE</margin>he was accustomed to investigating them in this way:

*In the diagram of chapter nine, let <term>A</term> be the location of the node, <term>E</term> the location of the Planet in the ecliptic in the year 1595, <term>C</term> the seen location of the Planet among the Fixed Stars at 17 degrees 56 minutes 5 seconds of Taurus, and <term>EC</term> the seen latitude, 0 degrees 5 minutes 15 seconds North. Moreover, the angle <term>EAC</term> is presupposed to be as nearly as possible 4 degrees 34 1/2 minutes, which is the maximum Northern latitude likewise observed in the year 1585. Therefore, in the right triangle <term>CEA</term> (or the isosceles <term>CBA</term>, for the difference is of no importance in this business), from the side <term>CE</term> and the angle <term>EAC</term>, he sought the length <term>EA</term>, the distance of the ecliptic position from the node. This operation is not erroneous because <term>EC</term> is small and near the node. However, the <term>precision</term><note>original: "ἀκρίβεια" (akribeia).</note> of the proof recommends another way. For it was said in chapter 9 that the angle <term>EAC</term> is not constant: hence, through different latitudes of different oppositions, different locations for the node will also emerge. For <term>EAC</term> is not as great as the maximum seen latitude, because the arc <term>AC</term> is bent; nor is <term>AC</term> the path of the Planet, but some interior path (say, <term>AF</term>), such as would be seen from the center of the Sun. Therefore, <term>A</term> will not necessarily be the node in this particular operation.*

Therefore, **I** have investigated the nodes differently, and indeed from the observations themselves on the day when they were in the node. This method, although it already requires certain preconceived ideas and will be treated more accurately below in the fifth part, should nevertheless be sampled now if only for the sake of agreement.

I presupposed that when a Planet is truly in the node by its eccentric motion, no arrangement of the Earth or the Sun can make it appear outside the node. For in the COPERNICAN hypothesis, this is consistent with the nature of things in itself: that the <term>moving power</term><note>Kepler's "motrix facultas"—the physical force he believed pushed the planets.</note> of any star is not bound to observe a foreign star (among whose number is the Earth), but has its own laws for its circuit. In the PTOLEMAIC hypothesis, this would be the same as saying that the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in old astronomy to explain planetary loops.</note> does not look back toward the line from the Sun through the

In the <term>Tychonic system</term><note>The model proposed by Tycho Brahe where the Earth is at the center, the Sun orbits the Earth, and the other planets orbit the Sun.</note>, the same things will be said concerning the <term>eccentric</term><note>An off-center circular path used to explain the varying speeds of planets.</note>.

I. In the year 1590, on the 4th day of March, at 7:10 in the evening, the <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of Mars was 9° 26' North; its <term>right ascension</term><note>The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note> was 22° 35' 10''. From this, the position is calculated as 24° 22' 56'' of Aries; its southern latitude was 3° 12'. <term>Parallax</term><note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations.</note> and <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes objects appear higher than they are.</note> were nearly equal and opposite, and were therefore neglected.

II. In the year 1592, on the 23rd day of January, at 10:15 in the evening, Mars was at 11° 34' 30'' of Aries; its latitude was 0° 2' South. The altitude of Mars was 25°; therefore, refraction (according to the table of Fixed Stars) was zero. The parallax was nearly the same as the Sun's, because Mars and the Sun were at a <term>sextile</term><note>An aspect where two heavenly bodies are 60 degrees apart.</note> distance, and thus were nearly equally distant from the Earth. Almost all of this parallax affects the latitude. Therefore, Mars must be raised North by about two minutes to be cleared of parallax, and thus it will fall exactly on the ecliptic. For by February 6th, it was already about 7 minutes in North latitude.

III. In the year 1593, on the 10th day of December, in the evening, MARS was observed at the <term>ascending node</term><note>The point where a planet's orbit crosses from south to north of the ecliptic.</note>. For after correcting for horizontal variations, it retained no more than 0° 0' 45'' of Northern latitude.

<margin>
* This rough argumentation is sufficient for the present purpose. Below, in chapters 61 and 67, after everything has been weighed more diligently, it is found to have been in the node on the 29th day at the 15th hour.
</margin>

IV. In the year 1595, on the 27th day of October, at 12:20, the true latitude of Mars after removing parallax was 0 degrees, 2 minutes, 20 seconds South. On the 28th, likewise with parallax removed, the latitude was 0° 0' 25'' North. Therefore, in the intervening time, it was in the ascending node.

Now, count back the 687 days of Mars's <term>eccentric revolution</term><note>The sidereal period: the time it takes Mars to complete one full orbit and return to the same spot relative to the stars.</note> from the noon of October 28th; the end of that period falls on December 10th, 1593, when Mars had been observed very near the node the previous night. Count back another 687 days; these end on January 23rd, 1592, when it was observed in the node itself. If you do the same a third time, you will land on March 7th, 1590, whereas on the fourth day preceding, it had some southern latitude, which it completed within the remaining four days, so that it fell into the node around the 7th.

From this, it is understood: it does not matter where the Earth is, whether under the Fixed Stars or in respect to Mars; it matters not in the <term>Ptolemaic system</term><note>The ancient Earth-centered model where planets move on epicycles.</note> where the Sun is in respect to the center of Mars's epicycle and Mars in the epicycle; it matters not in the <term>Tychonic system</term> where the center of the eccentric (or the Sun) is located in respect to the line from Mars through the Earth, for Mars to fall into the plane of the ecliptic. For the diameter of the nodes is always the same in Copernicus and Ptolemy, or always parallel to itself in Tycho; except that over the course of centuries, the nodes are shifted slightly. This motion was not detectable within these six years.

<margin>CHAPTER XII.</margin>
II. In the year 1589, on the night of April 15, the observed Northern latitude of Mars was 1 degree 7 minutes, greatly increased by the <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent shift in position due to the observer's location on Earth or the Earth's location in its orbit.</note> of the annual orbit because of the proximity of Mars and the Earth. After 21 days, the latitude decreased to a tiny 6 2/3 minutes North. Therefore, even if it decreased a little more slowly on May 6 as the planet moved away from the Earth, we will still err very little if we proceed proportionally: just as 60 minutes of decrease are to the remaining 6 2/3 minutes, so we make 21 days to the number of days after which Mars falls into the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun; when a planet's latitude is zero, it is "in the ecliptic."</note>. For the rule shows two and a third days, so that it would have been in the <term>node</term><note>The point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> on May 9.

By counting forward from there three times 687 days <note>687 days is the approximate orbital period of Mars.</note>, we arrive at the morning of December 30 in the year 1594, on which day Mars ought to have been in the node, and from there it would have slipped into the south by the morning of January 4, after 5 days. And indeed, from the observation of it on the said 4th of January, we assigned it a southern latitude of several minutes. It has not been observed in this location of the <term>eccentric</term><note>The off-center circular path of the planet.</note> more often. It is enough for us that the observation of the year 1595 is held, so that it does not disagree with us; regarding the year 1589, there is nothing to doubt. Nor should it move you that in the year 1589 we gave a motion in latitude of 6 2/3 minutes for 2 1/3 days, while in the year 1595, around January 4, we do not give as much for 5 days. For as will appear in this work, the latitude is greatly thinned out by the parallaxes of the annual orbit during <term>conjunction</term><note>When Mars is on the opposite side of the Sun from the Earth.</note> with the Sun (as in 1595), and increased during <term>opposition</term><note>When Earth is between the Sun and Mars, making Mars appear much closer.</note> (as in 1589). It is therefore fitting that the daily motion in latitude seems smaller in the year 1595 and larger in the year 1589.

How are the locations of both nodes now held among the Fixed Stars? Certainly, if a <note>original: "crassa Minerva" — a Latin idiom for a rough or "coarse" calculation.</note> rough calculation is elicited from the tables of Mars (which we therefore presuppose) for the <term>mean motion</term><note>The average speed of the planet, as if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant rate.</note> of Mars on both sides. Whether you perform this through the <term>Prutenic</term><note>Tables based on the Copernican system.</note> or the <term>Tychonic</term><note>Tables based on Tycho Brahe's observations.</note> tables, using the true <term>precession of the equinox</term>, you will find:

| Date | Position |
| :--- | :--- |
| In the year 1594, morning of Dec 30 | Mean position of Mars in 17 deg. 14 1/2 min. **Scorpio** |
| In the year 1595, morning of Oct 28 | Mean position of Mars in 5 deg. 31 min. **Taurus** |

Thus it appears that the diameter of the nodes does not pass through the center of equality of motion <note>The equant point.</note> but far below it. For it is further from 5 deg. 31 min. of Taurus to 17 deg. 14 1/2 min. of Scorpio than from the latter to the former.

But if you use the Tychonic <term>equations</term><note>Corrections applied to the mean motion to find the true position.</note>, 11 degrees 17 minutes must be added here, and 11 degrees 30 minutes subtracted there, so that 16 deg. 48 min. of Taurus results there, and 15 deg. 44 1/2 min. of Libra <note>Note: Context suggests Scorpio is intended here to be opposite Taurus.</note> here—the <term>equated</term> eccentric positions of Mars.

The nodes (as you see) are opposite one another, nearly from the center of the planetary system, at approximately 16 1/3 degrees of **Taurus** and **Scorpio**; this is what Ptolemy called the "Earth," and Copernicus and Tycho Brahe called the point "nearest the Sun" <note>The perihelion.</note>.

However, how much we are going to change in these locations of the nodes, when the theory of the Sun is transposed from the mean to the apparent motion of the Sun and the equations are changed, will be revealed below in the fifth part.
