# CHAPTER XIII.
## Investigation of the inclination of the planes of the ecliptic and the orbit of MARS.

<margin>
Nodes.
Inclination and latitude should be understood differently.
Inclination refers to the angle at the Sun or the center of the planetary system, formed by a line drawn to the body of MARS and its ecliptic position.
Latitude is the angle by which any inclination is viewed from Earth.
In Ptolemy, inclination is the angle of straight lines drawn from the Earth through the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>In old astronomy, a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note> and through its position in the ecliptic.
Latitude is the angle made by straight lines from the center of the Earth, one through the body of the Planet, the other through the position corresponding to it in the ecliptic.
</margin>

**N**ow that the nodes and limits have been found as closely as possible in the previous chapter, according to both Brahe's opinion and my own, we must now also inquire how much the plane of the orbit of MARS is truly inclined toward the plane of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun, representing the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note>.

Deducing this from observations is not quite so straightforward. For the angle of this inclination is established at the center of the planetary system, which for COPERNICUS and TYCHO is the Sun.

But a view is never directed from the Sun so that this inclination can be seen and measured against the fixed stars from that vantage point. Instead, the maximum <term>digression</term><note>The distance or deviation of a planet from the ecliptic.</note> of the limit from the ecliptic will be viewed from another location (and thus at another angle). In the **P**TOLEMAIC model, a more efficient method might seem to appear, but it does not. For it will be demonstrated that the plane of the epicycle remains perpetually parallel to the plane of the ecliptic. Therefore, place the center of the epicycle's plane at either limit: the Planet is in the same line of longitude from the center of vision through the center of the epicycle. Either it will be farther from the viewer than the center of the epicycle (and thus its distance from the ecliptic will appear smaller than the distance of the epicycle's center from that same ecliptic), or it will be closer to the viewer, and thus it will appear greater than the value we are seeking.

In this difficulty, we are consoled by this one thing: that the reason for which we seek the inclination among the principles is not such as to require the highest level of subtlety. It will therefore be permitted for us to use those methods which provide evidence for the quantity of inclination from a distance; of which we shall propose three.

IT APPEARS, moreover, from what has already been said, that we would be most correctly assisted if we could obtain an observation of the star Mars at such a moment when Mars, being equally distant from both the Earth and the Sun, is referred by a line drawn from the Sun through itself to 16 or 17 degrees of ♌ <note>Leo</note> or ♒ <note>Aquarius</note> (the locations of the limits). In the **P**TOLEMAIC model, this is when the center of the epicycle is moving in 16 or 17 ♌ or ♒ and Mars is equally distant from the Earth as the center of the epicycle. This problem will not apply to Mercury alone.

*Let* **B** *be the Sun, **A** the Earth. Let an <term>isosceles</term><note>A triangle with two sides of equal length.</note> triangle* **ACB** *be constructed upon* **AB**, *and let* **E** *be the position of the Planet, and* **C** *be the point on the plane of the ecliptic. With a perpendicular line* **CE** *erected toward the orbit of Mars, let the body of Mars be at* **E**. *Therefore,* **EC** *will appear equal from both the Sun* **B** *and the Earth* **A**: *this is self-evident.*

*However, so that it may be known in what arrangement Mars is equally distant from the Sun and the Earth, note that when the lines falling from* **C** *Mars and* **A** *Earth to the Sun* **B** *form a right angle* **CBA**, *then* **CB** *is shorter than* **CA**. *Therefore, it is necessary that* **B**, *the position opposite the Sun, and* **BC**, *the eccentric position of Mars, be less than 90 degrees apart, so that* **CAB** *and* **CBA** *are made equal. Therefore, when* **BC** *is directed toward 17 ♌, the Sun must be beyond 17 ♉ <note>Taurus</note> and before 17 ♏ <note>Scorpio</note>. Conversely, if* **BC** *is in 17 ♒, the Sun must be beyond 17 ♏ and before 17 ♉.*

If you also wish to proceed a little more precisely, assume—from the restoration of **Copernicus** or the anticipated **Tychonic** restoration—the proportion of the orbits of Mars and the Earth [in Copernicus], or Mars and the Sun [in Tycho], or the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circle whose center is offset from the center of the Earth or Sun.</note> and the epicycle [in Ptolemy], <note>original: "crassâ Minerva"</note> roughly speaking as 1525 to 1000; and this at 16° or 17° of <term>Leo</term><note>Leo (♌), the fifth sign of the zodiac.</note> as 5 to 3, and at 16° or 17° of <term>Aquarius</term><note>Aquarius (♒), the eleventh sign of the zodiac.</note> as 11 to 8.

Similarly, at 16° or 17° Aquarius, where **ab** is 1000, **ac** is 1375; and where **ad** is 1000, **ac** is 2750, showing in the table of secants an angle of 68 degrees and 40 minutes.*

*Therefore, when **bc** is in or near 16° or 17° Leo, the observed position of Mars (**ac**) and the observed position of the Sun (**ab**) must be separated by 72 ½ degrees; or when that **bc** is in 16° or 17° Aquarius, they must diverge by 68 ⅔ degrees. And because the sum of the two angles (**cab** and **cba**) at 17° Leo is 145 degrees, the angle **acb** will be 35 degrees at 17° Leo. *Likewise, in 17° Aquarius, because the sum of the angles (**cab** and **cba**) is 137 ⅓ degrees, the angle **acb** will be 42 ⅔ degrees. For this reason, Mars must be seen through **ac** either in 24 ¼° Sagittarius (with the Sun through **ab** in 16° <term>Libra</term><note>Libra (♎), the seventh sign of the zodiac.</note>) or in 0° Aries (with the Sun being in 9° <term>Gemini</term><note>Gemini (♊), the third sign of the zodiac.</note>).*

The first case could have occurred most recently in the month of November in the year 1586 or 1588.
The second in April in the years 1581, 1583, 1596, or 1598.
The third in September or October 1587 or 1589.
The fourth in May or June 1580, 1582, 1595, or 1597.

But this was not the maximum departure either, since Mars was not yet at the limit by about 25 degrees. Thus, once again, the maximum departure of the limit is established from a distance as about 1 degree 50 minutes.

I have set forth one method in which a moderately well-known ratio of the <term>orbs</term><note>The relative sizes of the planetary orbits.</note> is presupposed; the observations followed this method without much calculation, readily indicating the maximum inclination of the planes.

**NOW I SHALL OFFER ANOTHER** method, which requires more select and rare observations. If these are available, the answer to our question is revealed without any preconceived notion of the ratio of the orbs, and without being entangled in the labor of calculation.

When two planes intersect each other, any two lines drawn to the same point on the line of intersection in each plane, perpendicular to that line of section, always enclose one and the same angle.

*Let the plane of the ecliptic be A C D B, the plane of the orbit of Mars A E F B, the mutual line of intersection <insert>the nodes</insert> A B, and the Sun at A, the Earth at B. From A and B, let lines A C and B D be established at right angles to A B in the ecliptic plane, and A E and B F in the orbit of Mars. Let the planet be at F. The inclination of the limit (E A C) will be equal to the apparent latitude of the planet at F, namely F B D. Look therefore for a time when the line B A—that is, the Sun being positioned at 16 or 17 degrees of Taurus or 16 or 17 degrees of Scorpio—happens to coincide with a perfect <term>quadrature</term><note>An alignment where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart as seen from Earth.</note> of the Sun and Mars. In this case, there are ninety degrees or a quarter-circle between line B A (extending from the Earth through the Sun, which in this case is also the line of intersection of the planes) and line B D (extending from the Earth through Mars). Whatever the observed latitude of Mars (F B D) is at that moment, the maximum inclination of the planes (E A C) will be the same, even though Mars at point F does not depart as far from the ecliptic as it does at point E.*

The first such day occurs on April 22 in the year 1583, which I have also just now employed. The Sun was at 11 degrees of Taurus, five or six degrees below the <term>node</term><note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>. The Earth was therefore above the line of intersection toward Mars. At which...

Therefore, nothing can be taken from this against a maximum inclination of 1 degree 50 minutes; rather, it is confirmed from a distance.

> *The demonstration can be extended further. Let BA be a line drawn from the Earth through the body of the Sun to the location of the node at 17 degrees of Scorpio or Taurus: and let the planet be viewed at any location in the zodiac. The latitude it then appears to have measures the inclination of a point on the plane that is truly as far from the limit as Mars appears to be from that limit. Let Mars be viewed at BG. Draw AH parallel to it. The latitude that appears at G from B is the same as the inclination of point H. And BG and AH point toward the same degree among the fixed stars because they are parallel.* As in the observation of April 26, 1585: because the Sun was in 16 degrees of Taurus and Mars was seen in 21 degrees 26 minutes of Leo with a latitude of 1 degree 49 3/4 minutes, the inclination at 21 degrees 26 minutes of Leo in the <term>eccentric motion</term><note>The actual path of the planet around its orbital center, which is slightly offset from the Sun.</note> is 1 degree 49 3/4 minutes. # ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>

In the Ptolemaic <term>hypothesis</term><note>The ancient geocentric model where Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note>, the demonstration of this matter proceeds from here.

Let **A** be the Earth, **AB** the line through the Sun and its opposite at 17 degrees of Taurus or Scorpio, **AD** the line of sight to Mars, **D** Mars, and **BAD** a right angle. Therefore, **AD** will be at 17 degrees of Leo or Aquarius. And since **DC**, which exits from **D** parallel to **BA** (because the motion of Mars on its <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary paths.</note> follows the motion of the Sun in its own orbit), it will pass through **C**, the center of the epicycle. Let there be a point **E** on **AD**, and let **AE** be equal to **AC**. Thus, because **AC** will not be at 17 Leo or Aquarius, it will also not be as far distant from the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</note> as the northern <term>limit</term> **E**<note>The 'limes Boreus' or the point where the orbit reaches its maximum northern distance from the ecliptic.</note>. Therefore, **D** will not be as far from the ecliptic as **E**, because **CD** and all points of the epicycle are equally distant from the ecliptic, since the plane of the epicycle is perpetually placed parallel to the plane of the ecliptic to achieve <note>original: "hypothesium æquipollentiam"</note> equivalence between the hypotheses. 

But as much as **D** or **C** is less distant from the ecliptic than **E**, so much closer is it to **A** than **E**, so that the distance **D** is that much greater, and both are viewed from **A** at the same angle. For as the distance of **C** from the ecliptic is to the distance of **E** from the same, so is the sine of arc **CB** (which is **AD**) to the total sine **AE** from the spherical doctrine of inclined circles, because the circle **ECB** is inclined over **AB**. But **C** and **D** are equally distant, as was just said. Therefore, as the distance **D** (or the perpendicular dropped from **D** onto the ecliptic) is to the perpendicular from **E**, so is **AD** to **AE**. Therefore, the triangles **ADδ** and **AEε** will be similar (since they are right-angled at points **δ** and **ε** on the ecliptic), with proportional sides, and with their sides (**AD**, **AE**) converging in the plane of the ecliptic, described from the same point (**A**) and tending toward the same point of longitude at 17 Leo or Aquarius. Therefore, **AD** and **AE** will also converge on a line in the orbit: that is, the line drawn from the Earth at **A** through Mars at **D** will, in this position, coincide with the location of the center of the epicycle **E**, when it is at the limit. And thus the angle of both the maximum inclination of the limit and the observed latitude of Mars in this position will be the same.

THE THIRD METHOD requires calculation and a preconceived proportion of the orbits: we shall only touch upon this for the sake of agreement. For the accurate and genuine treatment of it is reserved for Part Five and Chapter 63, nor is it necessary here.

In **TYCHO'S** table of <term>oppositions</term><note>The configuration where a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note>, the observed latitude at 21 degrees 16 minutes of Leo was 4 degrees 32 1/6 minutes.

Let **A** be the Sun, **B** the Earth, and **C** Mars in the <term>eccentric</term><note>The circular path of a planet which does not have the Earth exactly at its center.</note>. Therefore, the line **AE** running out through the Earth **B** among the fixed stars will fall upon the ecliptic, and **AC** upon the orbit of Mars. And since Mars is at 21 degrees of Leo, very near the limit, the angle **EAC** will be nearly at its maximum. I investigate it thus: Let **BA** be 1000, **AC** 1664, and **EBC** 4 degrees 32 1/6 minutes. Therefore, as **AC** is to **EBC**, so **BA** is to **BCA**, which is 2 degrees 43 minutes 27 seconds. When this is subtracted from **EBC**, it leaves the sought angle **BAC** as 1 degree 48 minutes 43 seconds. This angle at the limit itself would be about 1 degree 49 minutes, and it varies slightly if the proportion of **BA** to **AC** varies, which will be discussed below. In this way, from any <term>acronychal observation</term><note>An observation made at nightfall when the planet is rising and the sun is setting.</note> where the latitude is somewhat large, the inclination of that point of the orbit is first sought, and then the maximum inclination, by considering the distance from the node or the limit. As on August 24, 1593, the observed latitude during an opposition with the Sun is given as 6 degrees 7 minutes southern.

Mars is at 12 ½ degrees of <note>original: ♋︎ (Cancer)</note>. Therefore, let <term>B A</term> be 1000, and <term>A C</term> be 1389 from the previous calculation. Thus, as <term>C A</term> is to the <term>sine</term><note>A trigonometric function used to calculate angles and distances in triangles.</note> of angle <term>C B E</term>, so <term>B A</term> is to the <term>sine</term> of angle <term>B C A</term>, which is 4 degrees, 21 minutes, and 10 seconds. <margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin> When this is subtracted from <term>C B E</term>, it leaves the sought angle <term>B A C</term> as 1 degree, 42 minutes, and 10 seconds. This position is actually about 26 degrees from the <term>limit</term><note>The point of maximum latitude (distance) from the ecliptic.</note> and 64 degrees from the <term>node</term><note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>. We should not be concerned about the three extra minutes here; they arise from the assumed proportion, which will be discussed below in part four.

In the <term>PTOLEMAIC</term><note>The geocentric system where Earth is at the center.</note> form, **a** will be the Earth, **c** the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle.</note> of **Mars**, and **D** the lowest point of the epicycle, because **Mars** is considered to be in <term>opposition</term> to the **Sun**.

And because the line **E A** of the **Sun** is in the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The path of the Sun; the plane of Earth's orbit.</note>, and the plane of the epicycle is placed parallel to the plane of the ecliptic, **C D** will be parallel to **E A**. Therefore, **B A C** and **A C D** are equal—namely, the inclination of the <term>eccentric</term> and the epicycle. Moreover, **C D** is equal to **B A** due to the full <note>original: "æquipollentiam"</note> equivalence of the hypotheses; or certainly, as in **COPERNICUS** the ratio of **A C** [is determined], so is the ratio of the semi-diameter of the **PTOLEMAIC** epicycle **D C** to the line **C A** from the Earth to the center of the epicycle. Therefore, angles **C D A** and **C B A** are equal, and **E B C** and **B A D** are equal—namely, the apparent latitude.

# CHAPTER XIV.

## The planes of the eccentrics are <term>UNSWAYING</term><note>original Greek: ΑΤΑΛΑΝΤΑ (atalanta); meaning they remain at a fixed inclination rather than oscillating.</note>.

<margin>* See Michael Maestlin’s *Epitome of Astronomy* in the explanation of the theory of the superior planets, on the last leaf.</margin>
**T**HE complexity of his own hypothesis so deceived Ptolemy that he heaped many monsters into the doctrine of latitudes. For when he considered that the plane of the epicycle was twisted in all directions, and did not immediately see through those clouds of his hypothesis that the plane of the epicycle is actually parallel to the plane of the ecliptic, he devised a threefold latitude. To support these contradictions, he completely distorted his epicycle from its parallel position. He did not choose his values based on the reliability of observations (which he did not have in great number), nor from the measurement of those he did have (because he lacked certainty), but instead chose middle-ground values, leaving the extremes in error.

<margin>The cause of latitudes.</margin>
Hence you may see that in the common calculations (for instance, in the *Ephemerides* of **MAGINI**), no conjunction of Mars and the Sun ever occurs that is not, as they say, <note>original: "per corpus"</note> "through the body" (a physical overlap). If this were true, nature would have devised the arrangement of latitudes in vain, for the purpose of latitudes is to prevent too frequent physical conjunctions from causing excessive disturbances of the sublunary powers <note>The physical and astrological influences felt on Earth.</note>.

**COPERNICUS**, himself unaware of his own riches, took it upon himself to represent **PTOLEMY** rather than the nature of things, even though he had come closest of all to nature. On this matter, read **RHETICUS** in his *Narration*. For while Copernicus rejoiced that the types of latitudes were increased by the Earth’s approaches to the stars, he did not dare to reject the remaining Ptolemaic increases in latitude (which this approach of the Earth could not account for). Instead, to represent those as well, he devised <term>librations</term><note>Oscillations or swaying motions of the orbital planes.</note> of the planes of the eccentrics, by which the angle of inclination (which was constant and fixed in Ptolemy) would vary—

<summary>Kepler calculates the inclination of Mars's orbit to be 1 degree 53 minutes and begins a critique of Ptolemy and Copernicus, arguing that their complex models of oscillating orbital planes are incorrect. He introduces his own view that the planes of planetary orbits are fixed and "unswaying."</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>
...might be varied, and that (which seems like a monster) not according to the laws of its own <term>eccentric</term><note>An orbital path that is circular but whose center is shifted away from the central body (the Sun).</note> motions, but clearly according to those of the Earth's entirely foreign orbit. See **COPERNICUS**, Book VI, Chapter I.

Armed with my own disbelief, I have always fought against this irrelevant linking of different orbits as a cause of motion, even before I had seen the observations of **TYCHO**. I congratulate myself all the more that the observations have been found to stand with me, as has happened with many other of my preconceived opinions.

But lest anyone should distrust me for this very reason—that I might handle the observations with prejudice—behold, I have now most solidly demonstrated that there are no <term>librations</term><note>Oscillatory or "swinging" motions that would cause the tilt of an orbit to change over time.</note> of the eccentric inclinations. For having proposed three ways of investigating the maximum inclination: in the first, the Sun was near the <term>sextiles</term><note>An angular distance of 60 degrees.</note> and <term>quintiles</term><note>An angular distance of 72 degrees.</note> of Mars (that is, as close to the <term>conjunction</term><note>When the Sun and a planet appear in the same part of the sky.</note> of Mars as Mars can easily be seen and observed); in the second, it was in <term>quadrate</term><note>A 90-degree angle between two celestial bodies.</note> with Mars; in the third, it was clearly in <term>opposition</term> to it. Yet in all three positions of the Sun, with Mars remaining in the same place on its eccentric, it showed one and the same inclination of its <term>limit</term><note>The point of greatest latitude or distance from the ecliptic.</note> (about 1 degree 50 minutes) toward the North, and an equal amount toward the South in the opposite place. Thus in Chapter XII, with Mars moving in its eccentric and positioned at the <term>nodes</term><note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>, it appeared that no matter where the Sun was positioned in its own orbit (whether very near Mars or far from it), no visible latitude for Mars was ever seen. And below, in the fifth part, it will be proved by many more arguments that the declination from the ecliptic is constant for every location in the orbit of Mars.

Therefore, let us most firmly conclude that the inclination of the eccentric planes to the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun, representing the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> does not vary at all. (For why should I not conclude this in general, since there is no reason why it should apply to the Sun alone among the planets? Especially as I have demonstrated the same thing from observations for Venus and Mercury). And he who follows **PTOLEMY** should learn from this that the plane of the <term>epicycle</term><note>In the older geocentric system, a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> is perpetually parallel to the plane of the ecliptic. For this has now been demonstrated when the center is at the limits; and in Chapter XII it was proved that when the center is at the nodes, the epicycle coincides clearly in all its parts with the ecliptic.

<margin>Peter Apian's *Caesarean Work*.</margin>
Now, who will provide me with a fountain of tears so that I may, according to his merit, deplore the miserable industry of **APIANUS**? In his ***CAESAREAN WORK***, following the trust of **Ptolemy**, he spent so many good hours and wasted so many most ingenious meditations, so that with spirals and wreaths and helices and volutes and that whole labyrinth of most intricate curves, he might express the figments of men—which the nature of things clearly does not acknowledge as her own. Yet that man showed us that, with his divine gifts of a most sharp mind, he could easily have been a match for Nature herself. For the rest, he delighted his soul by most bravely overcoming these delusions (in which he had challenged Nature herself) and casting them into diagrams; and he obtained the palm of perennial fame thereby, regardless of what damage that fortune brought to the Works themselves. What shall we say of the <term>vain craftsmanship</term><note>original: κενοτεχνίᾳ (kenotechnia), meaning empty or useless skill.</note> of the automaton-makers, who manufacture six hundred or even twelve hundred little wheels, so that they might triumph over the latitudes (that is, over human figments) expressed in their Works and thereby increase their price?

He laments the wasted genius of Peter Apian, who created complex mechanical models for planetary motions that Kepler deems non-existent in nature.</summary>

## CHAPTER XV.

# Reduction of observed positions at the extremes of nights to the line of the Sun's apparent motion.

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>

**H**aving completed this inquiry, and having demonstrated the positions of the <term>nodes</term><note>The two points where a planet's tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>, the inclination of the planes, and its constancy (all of which were necessary for the upcoming <term>reduction</term><note>The process of adjusting raw observations to account for geometric effects, such as the tilt of an orbit, to find a planet's "true" position.</note>), we will now define what positions the Planet occupied in its own orbit when the Sun was diametrically opposite to it. The years 1580 and 1597 could have been omitted from this argument, as they provide no suitable evidence due to a lack of certainty in the observations.

I. Suppose, however, that in the year 1580, on the 12th day of November at 10 hours 50 minutes, Mars was seen at 8° 37' Gemini, and its motion over five days was 1° 55'. Since the Sun at that time stayed at 8° 45' 36" Sagittarius, and its motion over five days was 5° 5', the sum of both motions becomes 7° 0'. In truth, the Sun is distant from Mars by 7° 51' 24". Out of this, 7 full degrees are completed in 5 days or 120 hours. By the same proportion, the remaining 51' 24" will be completed in 14 hours 41 minutes. Therefore, the moment of <term>opposition</term><note>When Mars and the Sun are on exactly opposite sides of the Earth.</note> was on November 18 at 1:31 AM. The position was at 6° 28' Gemini on the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the reference plane for astronomical measurements.</note>. Here it is 20 degrees away from 16 1/2 degrees <note>Kepler is likely measuring distance from a node.</note>. I wish to know how much longer the arc of the orbit is, from the node to the arc of latitude continued through 6° 28' Gemini.

<margin>Landsberg’s doctrine of triangles.</margin>
Therefore, according to the doctrine of Triangles by **PHILIP LANDSBERG** (a man I name for the sake of honor and gratitude, who supplied me with the best and most fit axes for astronomical constructions in abundance, close at hand, and at a low price of time; without him, these would have had to be sought from afar with clumsy handles and great hindrance to the work), the tangent of the side 20, multiplied by the secant of the angle of inclination (1° 50'), after discarding the last 5 digits, increases by only 18 1/4 parts, to which about 35 seconds correspond. Therefore, while Mars stands opposite 6° 28' Gemini, it is further forward in its own orbit by 35". It should thus be placed at 6° 28' 35" Gemini—a very small correction, surely not necessary. The latitude is 1° 40' North.

II. In the year 1582, on the 28th day of December at 11:30 PM, Mars was seen at 16° 47' Cancer, while the Sun's true position was 17° 13' 45" Capricorn. The moment of opposition had therefore already passed. The Sun's daily motion was 61' 18", and Mars's was 24'; the sum is 85' 18". At this moment, the stars were distant from each other by 26' 45". Just as 1° 25' 18" relates to 24 hours, so 26' 45" relates to 7 hours 32 minutes. Subtracting these from 11:30 PM leaves the moment of true opposition on December 28 at 3:58 PM. The position was 16° 54' 32" Cancer on the ecliptic, and through reduction (which adds 5") it is at 16° 55 1/2' Cancer. The latitude is 4° 6' North, according to the reliability of the **BRAHEAN** table of oppositions. For among varying observations, I find these latitudes: on the night after December 26, 4° 6' or 4° 2'; on the night after December 29, 4° 8' or 4° 6 1/2'.

III. In the year **1585**, on January 31 at 12:00 midnight, <term>Mars</term> was seen at 21° 18' 11" Leo [♌]. The <term>Sun</term> was at 22° 21' 31" Aquarius [♒]. Thus, the true <term>opposition</term><note>The moment when the Earth is directly between the Sun and Mars, making the planet appear exactly opposite the Sun in the sky.</note> had already passed. The distance between them was 1° 3' 20". The daily motion of the Sun was 61' 16", and that of Mars was 24' 15", the sum being 85' 31". Now, as 1° 25' 31" is to 24 hours, so 1° 3' 20" is to 17 hours 46 minutes. For these hours, roughly 18' of motion corresponds to Mars. Therefore, the time of opposition was January 30 at 7:14 PM (19 hours 14 minutes). The position of Mars on the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</note> was 21° 36' 10" Leo. For the <term>reduction</term><note>Adjusting the position from the ecliptic to the planet's own tilted orbital path.</note>, a very small amount is subtracted because Mars is already beyond the limit. Thus, the extension of the arc of the orbit from the following node tends toward the preceding ones. But because Mars is only 4 or 5 degrees away from the <term>node</term><note>The point where Mars's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane.</note>, the subtraction is essentially imperceptible. The latitude, according to the *Tychonic* table, was 4° 32' 10" North. For the observation on January 31 at 12:00 gave 4° 31'. The *Tychonic* assistants added the remainder due to <term>diurnal parallax</term><note>The slight shift in a planet's apparent position caused by the observer's specific location on Earth's surface compared to the Earth's center.</note>.

IV. In the year **1587**, on the night following March 4 at 1:16 AM, the position of Mars was found, relative to the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "ex corde ♌"; the star Regulus</note> and the Ear of Grain of the Virgin <note>original: "spica Virginis"; the star Spica</note>, to be 26° 26' 17" Virgo [♍], with a visible latitude of 3° 38' 16" North. But because Mars was raised 37 1/2 degrees above the horizon, the diurnal parallax must be considered; it removes a small amount from the longitude, so on this account the planet is at 26° 26' Virgo with a slightly larger latitude. Since the Sun is nearly twice as far from the Earth as Mars is, the parallax of Mars will be nearly twice as large as that of the Sun. Given the Sun's parallax is 3', that of Mars becomes about 5'. With 9° Sagittarius [♐] rising, the <term>nonagesimal</term><note>The highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon.</note> is 55 degrees from the zenith; in that region, under the heading of 5' in our parallax table, a latitude parallax of 4' is shown. Thus, the latitude seen from the center of the Earth would have been 3° 42' 22" North. This will serve us below in the fifth part for examining the parallaxes of Mars more accurately, once the most precise inclination and the most certain distance of Mars from the Earth in this position are established. The true position of the Sun was at 23° 59' 11" Pisces [♓]. Therefore, the true opposition was following. The stars were distant by 2° 26' 49". The daily motion of the Sun was 59' 35", and Mars 24'; the sum is 1° 23' 35". As this is to 24 hours, so 2° 26' 49" is to 1 day, 18 hours, and 7 minutes. For this time, 42' 7" of motion belongs to Mars. Therefore, the time of true opposition was March 6 at 7:23 AM. The position of Mars was 25° 43' 53" Virgo on the ecliptic. However, 5" must be subtracted for the reduction to the orbit. It was therefore at 25° 43' Virgo in its orbit. The latitude was decreasing. It was therefore a little less than 3° 38' North, or 3° 42' as corrected by parallax.

V. In the year **1589**, on April 15 at 12:05 in the following night, the planet was found at 3° 58' 20" Scorpio [♏] with a decreasing North latitude of 1° 4' 20". The altitude of Mars was 22 1/2 degrees, where <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light by the atmosphere which makes stars appear higher than they are.</note> from the fixed stars is zero, and from the Sun's table is 3 1/2'. The parallax, however, is about twice as large as the Solar parallax, namely 6 minutes on the horizon. 24° Sagittarius [♐] was rising. Therefore, the distance of the nonagesimal from the zenith is 64°, showing a diurnal latitude parallax of 5' 24". Whether it was truly that much will appear below from an accurate consideration of latitudes. For the North latitude, freed from diurnal parallax (if it suffered no refraction), would then come out to 1° 9' 45" North. And because the altitude of the nonagesimal was 26°, the longitude parallax on the horizon is 2' 38". VI. In the year **1591**, on the night following June 6 at 12:20 AM, Mars was found at 17° 14' 42" <term>Sagittarius</term> [♐] with a southern latitude of 3° 55 1/2'. Here, care was taken regarding refraction from the table of fixed stars (which was great, since Mars at its highest point [the meridian] had an altitude no greater than 6 degrees); however, no mention was made of parallax. But Mars is now at a distance from the Earth of half the Solar distance. Therefore, the <term>horizontal parallax</term> is over 6 minutes (assuming the Sun's is 3 minutes). However, I omit this: partly because the refraction from the Solar table (which, as I said, is more probable) is provided as 4 1/2 [minutes] greater than what <term>Brahe</term><note>Tycho Brahe, the master astronomer whose data Kepler is using.</note> used here, by which the parallax is nearly canceled out; and partly because Mars, being on the meridian and near the <term>winter solstice point</term><note>original: "punctum brumale"; the point in the sky where the Sun is at its lowest noon altitude of the year.</note>, had no parallax in longitude. Regarding the latitude, however, we must see below in Part Five whether it might have been a few minutes less, specifically because parallax projects the planet too far to the South.

The Sun was at 24° 58' 10" <term>Gemini</term> [♊]. The difference between the stars was 2° 16' 10". The daily motion of the Sun was 57' 8"; of Mars (over four days) 1° 12' 24", because on June 10 at 11:50 PM it was at 26° 2' 18" Sagittarius. Therefore, for one day, it was 18 minutes 12 seconds. The sum of the daily motions is 1° 15' 20". This corresponds to 1 day, 19 hours, and 24 minutes, which, when added to June 6 at 12:20 AM (since the opposition follows), shows the date to be June 8 at 7:43 AM. The position of Mars was 26° 41' 48" Sagittarius; to this 52 seconds are added for the reduction to the orbit, so that it is approximately 26° 43' Sagittarius. The latitude is six minutes greater than on June 6, because according to the reliability of the observations, the latitude here increases until the fortieth day after opposition, and between June 6 and June 10 it increased by nearly thirteen minutes. Therefore, neglecting parallax and keeping the amount of refraction, it would be 4° 1 1/4'.

The position of Mars was 12° 16' **Pisces** [♓]. The latitude was nearly 6° 2' south, provided that the horizontal variations truly canceled each other out.

VIII. In the year 1595, on October 30 at 8:20 PM, the planet was found at 17° 47' 15" **Aries** [♈], not far from the <term>nonagesimal</term><note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon. Observing near here minimizes the errors caused by atmospheric refraction and parallax.</note>, so that we might be certain of the parallax, although that too was guarded against. The latitude was 0° 5' 10" North. The position of the Sun was 16° 50' 30" **Scorpio** [♏]. The celestial bodies were distant by 56° 45'. The daily motion of the Sun was 1° 0' 35"; of Mars, 22' 54", as appears from a comparison of surrounding observations. The sum of the daily motions is 1° 23' 29". If the distance of the stars is divided by this, the result is 40 hours and 47 minutes of a day, or 16 hours and 19 minutes. Therefore, the true opposition was October 31 at 12:39 PM. The position of Mars was 17° 31' 40" **Taurus** [♉], which does not require a <term>reduction to the orbit</term><note>An adjustment to account for the tilt of Mars's path relative to the Earth's path; it is unnecessary here because Mars is at its "node," the point where the two paths cross.</note>, since it is situated almost exactly at the node. The latitude was about 0° 8' North, but the analogy of the preceding and following days suggests a latitude of about 5' North.

IX. In the year 1597, on December 10 at 8:30 PM, let the position of Mars truly be (as above) 3° 45 1/2' **Capricorn** [♑]; the position of the Sun was 29° 4' 53" **Sagittarius** [♐]. The distance between the bodies was 4° 46' 27". The daily motion of the Sun was 61' 20"; of Mars, 23' 40" (for in the year 1580 in **Gemini** [♊] the daily motion was 23', and in 1582 in **Leo** [♌] it was 24'). Therefore, the sum of the daily motions is 1° 25' 0". By these elements, the time of true opposition is shown to follow after 3 days, 7 hours, and 14 minutes: on the morning of December 14 at 3:44 AM. The position of Mars was 2° 27 1/3' **Cancer** [♋]. The reduction to the orbit (truly absurd in this instance, since the observation itself has an uncertainty of several minutes) requires about 52 seconds to be added. Thus, the corrected position is 2° 28' **Cancer** [♋]. The latitude, according to the reliability of the table, was 3° 33' North.

On the same night (which follows the day of December 10) at 12:30 AM, <term>Fabricius</term><note>David Fabricius, a German astronomer and contemporary of Kepler.</note> in East Friesland found the position of Mars at 3° 46 1/4' **Cancer** [♋] <note>original: "3. 46 1/4 ♋"; likely a typo for Capricorn in his raw data or Cancer as the calculated opposition point</note> with a latitude of 3° 23' North. By this observation, the matter effectively comes to nearly the same result. For the motion of 3 hours and 40 minutes is 3 1/2 minutes; so that by <term>Tycho's</term><note>original: "Braheanam"; referring to the observations of Tycho Brahe.</note> observation at 12:30 AM, Mars could have been at 3° 42' **Cancer** [♋], two minutes beyond Fabricius's position.

X. In the year 1600, on January 13/23 <note>The double date indicates the difference between the Julian and Gregorian calendars.</note> at 11:40 PM, with the time adjusted for <term>Uraniborg</term><note>Tycho Brahe's famous observatory on the island of Hven.</note>, the planet was seen at 10° 38' 46" **Leo** [♌]. The position of the Sun was 3° 26' 30" **Aquarius** [♒]. The bodies were distant by 7° 12' 16". The daily motion of the Sun for several following days was 1° 1' 3"; of Mars, 23' 44"; the sum is 1° 24' 47". Therefore, the opposition followed after 5 days, 2 hours, and 22 minutes—namely, on the morning of January 19/29 at 2:02 AM before dawn. Mars was in 8° 38' **Leo** [♌]. There is no need for reduction, as it is very near the limit. The latitude, according to the table, was 4° 30' 50" North.

XI. In the year <term>1602</term> <gloss>February 18 / 28</gloss><note>Kepler provides both the Julian and Gregorian calendar dates; the 10-day difference was standard for the era.</note> in the evening at 10:30 PM, using <term>Tychonic</term> instruments (assisted by the student <term>Matthias Seiffard</term>, who had been left behind by <term>Tycho</term>), I took the distance of <term>Mars</term> from the middle star of the tail of the <term>Great Bear</term> <note>Ursa Major; the star is likely Alioth.</note>
<margin>Chapter XV.</margin> as 52° 22'. Since the distance between the Heart of Leo <note>Regulus</note> and <term>Procyon</term> was 37° 22' 20", when it ought to have been 37° 19' 50", it was understood from this that the <term>Sextant</term> was in excess by 2 1/2 minutes. Therefore, the corrected distance of <term>Mars</term> from the tail of the <term>Bear</term> was 52° 19 1/2'. And since the latitude of the <term>fixed star</term> is 56° 22', a subtraction leaves 4° 2 1/2', provided that <term>Mars</term> had been precisely at the same longitude as the <term>fixed star</term>. But because there was a difference of 3 1/4 degrees (as appears from the following observations), a small correction must be applied. For let AB be in the parallel of the ecliptic nearest to 4° 43' 30", B be <term>Mars</term>, C be the <term>fixed star</term>, and BC be 52° 19' 30". 
<margin>The explanation for the lack of precision is given in the book on the star of the Serpent-bearer <note>Kepler refers to his work *De Stella Nova*, concerning the supernova of 1604 in Ophiuchus.</note>.</margin> Dividing the secant of BC by the secant of AB produces the secant CA as 52° 14', which, when taken away from 56° 22' (the latitude of the <term>fixed star</term>), leaves 4° 8' <term>North</term> as the observed latitude of <term>Mars</term>. At the same time, we found the distance between <term>Mars</term> and the Heart of <term>Leo</term> <note>Regulus</note> to be 19° 23' (corrected to 19° 20 1/2'), and between <term>Mars</term> and the bright star in the wing of <term>Virgo</term> <note>likely Gamma Virginis</note> 21° 20' (corrected to 21° 17 1/2'). From these two distances (by means of the latitudes of the stars and <term>Mars</term>), the longitude of <term>Mars</term> was found in 13° 19' 6" **Virgo** [♍], the calculations agreeing.

<term>OTHERWISE</term> at 12:40 AM, the meridian altitude of <term>Mars</term> was found with two <term>Quadrants</term> to be 50° 19', while that of the tail of <term>Leo</term> <note>Denebola</note> was 56° 45'. From the declinations and right ascensions of the <term>fixed stars</term> and our distances, the position of <term>Mars</term> is constructed as 13° 19' 30" **Virgo** [♍], Latitude 4° 7' 55", and this in the <term>Tychonic</term> manner. I have added another method to this for the sake of showing agreement and so that it might appear that, although the demonstration is not the most exquisite, shorthand methods of either calculation or our understanding can nevertheless be applied in some places; for there is less labor in the former method than in words. It <note>the ecliptic</note> was rising at 5° **Virgo** [♍] in <term>PRAGUE</term>. Therefore, the <term>nonagesimal</term><note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon.</note> was distant from the zenith by about 32 1/2°. And because <term>Mars</term> was further away than half the distance the <term>Sun</term> is from the earth, the <term>parallax</term> therefore of about 5 minutes in the region of 32 1/2 degrees (in our <term>Parallactic</term> table) shows a latitude parallax of 2' 41": so that the <term>Northern</term> latitude, as viewed from the center of the earth, would be 4° 10 1/2'. And because the altitude of the nonagesimal was 57 1/2°, the <term>parallax</term> of longitude on the horizon is 4' 13". But because <term>Mars</term> is 38 degrees from the nonagesimal, the parallax of longitude for this place corresponds to 2' 36", by which <term>Mars</term>, being freed, would be placed at approximately 13° 18' **Virgo** [♍]. The position of the <term>Sun</term> at that moment was 10° 16' 42" **Pisces** [♓]. The distance of the stars was 3 degrees 1 minute 18 seconds. The daily motion of the <term>Sun</term> was 1° 0' 4": that of <term>Mars</term> was 24' 5". For in 21° **Leo** [Ω] in the year <term>1585</term> it was 24' 18": in 26° **Virgo** [♍] in the year <term>1587</term> it was 24'; the sum of the daily motions is 1° 24' 9". The true opposition therefore followed after 11 days, 3 hours, 43 minutes. That is, on the day <gloss>February 21 / March 3</gloss> at 2:13 AM, <term>Mars</term> was in 12° 27' 35" **Virgo** [♍]. For the reduction to the orbit, 40 seconds must be subtracted, so that <term>Mars</term> is in 12° 17' **Virgo** [♍] with a latitude slightly smaller than before; for the latitude was decreasing. Therefore, it was about 4° 10' or 4° 7 1/3' neglecting parallax.

Since these [observations] were not obtained on continuous days, for the sake of certainty I am pleased to consult
<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
also those observations which *David Fabricius*—a diligent student of astronomy in East Friesland—shared with me.

On the 16th day of February, <term>Old Style</term> <note>The Julian calendar, which remained in use in many Protestant regions like East Friesland at this time.</note>, at 5:00 in the morning, he began taking the distances of the planet from the Tail of Leo <note>The star Denebola.</note> on account of its latitude, and from the Neck of Leo and, conversely, from the bright star of the Southern Wing of Virgo <note>The star Vindemiatrix.</note> to verify its longitude with a twofold argument.

I could use the method of argument that *Tycho* was accustomed to using in the first volume of his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* (1602), a foundational work on the fixed stars and solar theory.</note>, when the <term>declination</term> of the planet (as in this case) was missing. But because that method is spread out over ten operations, I prefer for the sake of brevity to proceed as I did before with my own observations. For there is no underlying danger in doing so.

First, the Wing of Virgo at our time is at 4° 36' 30'' of Libra with a northern latitude of 2° 56'. From this, *Fabricius* found Mars to be at a distance of 20° 18' in <term>precedence</term> <note>Meaning the planet is located "before" the star in the order of the zodiac, or further West.</note>. Therefore, Mars is placed roughly <note>original: "crassa Minerva" - a Latin idiom for "roughly" or "using plain common sense."</note> at 14° 18' 30'' of Virgo. This longitude will be corrected shortly. Truly, the Tail of Leo is at 16° 4' of Virgo with a northern latitude of 12° 18'. And Mars was found to be at a distance of 8° 17' from the Tail. The distance of its parallel from the Tail is sought, since the difference in longitude is 1° 45'. Dividing the <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric function; Kepler uses it here to solve for the sides of a spherical triangle on the celestial sphere.</note> of 8° 17' by the secant of 1° 45', the secant of the sought arc comes out to 8° 6'. This [arc], when subtracted from the 12° 18' northern latitude of the <term>fixed star</term>, leaves a northern latitude for Mars of 4° 12'. I now assume this as certain and compare it with the latitudes of the fixed stars according to the laws of triangles. I find the longitude of Mars from the Wing of Virgo to be 14° 19' of Virgo; from the Neck of Leo, 14° 23' 36'' of Virgo. The mean of these is 14° 21' 18'' of Virgo. It appears the <term>sextant</term> produced distances somewhat larger than they should be, from which a latitude of 4° 14' North would also result.

On the following night of February 23 at 12:00 AM, he observed Mars from five fixed stars: from the Tail of Leo and Arcturus for latitude; from Spica of Virgo following it for longitude once; and from the Neck and Heart of Leo <note>The star Regulus.</note> preceding it, conversely.

By mechanical means or by estimation, I foresee Mars falling at 11 1/3° of Virgo. It was found to be at a distance of 9° 24' from the Tail of Leo. From this, its latitude comes out to 4° 6'. And now, using this and the latitudes of the fixed stars, with the distances added—17° 26' from Regulus, 17° 51' from the Neck of Leo, 37° 28' from Spica, and 44° 15' from Arcturus—the position of Mars comes out to: 11° 21' 23'' of Virgo from Regulus; 11° 20' 52'' from the Neck of Leo; and 11° 17' 40'' of Virgo from Spica. Again (as you see), the distances err by excess. For Mars is pushed less into <term>consequence</term> <note>Moving forward in the order of the zodiac signs (Eastward).</note> from the Heart and Neck, and more into precedence from Spica and Arcturus—and more so from Arcturus, because it has a great Northern latitude. The mean (neglecting Arcturus) of 11° 19' 20'' of Virgo is as nearly true as possible. And the latitude is also slightly increased, namely 4° 7' 40'' North. Therefore, from February 15 at 5:00 PM to February 23 at 12:00 AM, over 7 days and 19 hours, Mars moved 3 degrees and 0 minutes. In 187 hours, it moved 180 minutes. One hour is almost exactly one minute. If you also weigh this, on February 16 <term>parallax</term> (if there is any) would have decreased the longitude, while on February 23 it would have added something.

And because the final observation follows, the time of the opposition found by me was 11 days, 21 hours, and 47 minutes. Therefore, add the motion corresponding to this time, which is 1° 7', and the position comes out to 12° 26' Scorpio. Thus, there is a most beautiful agreement, and it could not be greater, considering that we were both alone and not equipped with those conveniences which **Tycho Brahe** possessed.

The latitude on the 16th day was also 4° 12', and on the 33rd day it was 4° 7' 40'' <note>original: "4. 7 2/3"</note>. It is therefore consistent that on the intermediate 21st day it should be 4° 9', and by subtracting the <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in the position of a celestial object when viewed from different locations, such as two points on Earth or from Earth and the Sun.</note>, it would be a little more. Indeed, I myself estimated it to be a little less than 4° 10' 30'', that is, 4° 10'.

**XII.** Finally, in the year 1604, when I had already published a written <term>ephemeris</term> <note>A table providing the calculated positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</note> in which the planet was placed on the night between the <gloss>29th & 30th of March \\ 8th & 9th of April</gloss> <note>Kepler provides both the Julian (Old Style) and Gregorian (New Style) dates, which were 10 days apart at this time.</note> on a line stretching from Arcturus to Spica, that alignment clearly appeared. For on the evening of April 8th, it inclined toward the east, and on April 9th, already toward the west. Then, using **Hofmann’s Sextant** <note>A precision instrument used for measuring the angular distance between stars, made by the craftsman Hans Hofmann.</note> (with my assistant **Johannes Schuler**), I found the distance between Arcturus and Spica to be 33° 4'; it ought to have been 33° 1' 15''. Therefore, there was an excess of 2' 45''. Immediately after, I found the distance between Arcturus and **Mars** to be 29° 43' 30''. Therefore, correctly, it was 29° 41'. Since the latitude of Arcturus is 31° 2' 30'' North, there remained 2° 21' 30'' for the latitude of **Mars**. Then, the distance between the Heart of Leo <note>The star Regulus.</note> and **Mars** was 54° 8' 30'', and immediately between the Heart of Leo and Spica it was the same amount, though it ought to have been 54° 2'. Thus, there would have been an excess of 6' 30'', whereas previously it was only 2' 45''. From where this ambiguity of 4 minutes arose could not be discerned due to obstacles thrown in our way, so that we could not proceed with observing. However, let the excess be (as before) 2' 45''; for which reason the distance between Mars and the Heart of Leo is 54° 6'. The error regarding Spica perhaps occurred because Mars was sighted again instead of Spica, as they were near each other. From this, the latitude of Mars comes out to 2° 21' 30'' and the longitude to 18° 25' Libra. The hour is obtained from the fact that the Back of Leo <note>The star Zosma (Delta Leonis).</note> was culminating, the <term>right ascension</term> <note>The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note> of which was 163° 13' at the time of observation. The position of the Sun at noon was 18° 56' 24" Aries, the right ascension of which was 17° 27' 55". Hence, the difference in right ascensions is 145° 45', which is resolved into 9 hours and 43 minutes. Scorpio 22° 30' was rising. Therefore, the distance of the <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>The point of the ecliptic that is 90 degrees from the horizon; it is the highest point of the ecliptic currently in the sky.</note> from the zenith was 39°. The distance between Mars and the Earth was slightly greater than half the distance between the Sun and the Earth. Therefore, the parallax was about 5' 30'', and for the latitude 3' 28''. Therefore, the cleared latitude is 2° 25', and whether it was correctly cleared we shall consider below. And because the altitude of the nonagesimal was 51°, and the distance of Mars from the nonagesimal was 56°, the parallax of longitude was 3' 32''. Thus Mars would be at 18° 21' 30'' Libra. The position of the Sun at our moment was 19° 26' 8" Aries. The distance between the stars was 58° 30'. The Sun's daily motion was 58' 38", and that of Mars 22' 36". For in the year 1587 it was 24' in Virgo, and in the year 1589 it was 22' 8" in Scorpio. The sum of the daily motions is 1° 21' 14". From these elements, it is concluded that the true opposition preceded [this time] by 17 hours and 20 minutes, namely on the day <gloss>29th of March \\ 8th of April</gloss> at 4:23 in the morning. The position of Mars was 18 degrees 37 minutes 50 seconds Libra. For the reduction to the orbit, subtract about 39 seconds, so that the position of Mars is 18 degrees 37 minutes 10 seconds Libra. The latitude is slightly greater than 2 degrees 25 minutes, but neglecting the parallax it is 2 degrees 22 minutes North.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## Method of investigating the hypothesis for satisfying the <term>first inequality</term>. <note>The variation in a planet's actual speed as it moves around the sun, which Kepler eventually discovered was due to elliptical orbits.</note>

<note>Large decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicts an astronomer working at a desk with celestial instruments.</note>
PTOLEMY, in Book IX of his *Great Work* <note>original: "Operis Magni", referring to the Almagest.</note>, Chapter IV, when about to attack the first inequality of the Planets, sets out a certain superficial explanation of the suppositions he wishes to use. The sum of which is this: We perceive that the Planet lingers unequally in opposite semicircles. For example, from $2\frac{1}{2}^{\circ}$ through Leo to $26\frac{3}{4}^{\circ}$ Sagittarius is less than a semicircle; from $26\frac{3}{4}$ Sagittarius through Aquarius to Cancer is more than a semicircle. And yet the Planet is found to linger longer in the former than in the latter, whereas by the law of equality, the opposite should have occurred. For from the mean longitude of 2 signs, $23^{\circ} . 18'$ to 9 signs, $5^{\circ} . 44'$ there are 6 signs, $12^{\circ} . 26'$, which is more than a semicircle—that is, more than half—

## PART TWO.

...half of the periodic time of the Planet. Thus, from 12° 16' Aries through Leo to 12° 27' Libra
<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
is nearly a semicircle plus 11 minutes. However, by subtracting the <term>mean longitude</term> <note>The position a planet would have if it moved at a constant speed.</note> of that first position (11 signs 9° 55') from the mean longitude of this second position (5 signs 14° 59'), the difference is found to be 6 signs 5° 5', which is indeed more than half [a full circle], by 5° 5'. The Planet therefore stays for a much shorter time while traveling from Libra through Aquarius to Aries. If you weigh the neighboring locations individually and compare the intervening arcs with the times or the arcs of mean longitude, you will find that the Planet is slowest in one specific place under the zodiac, fastest in the opposite place, and in the intervening parts (in proportion to its proximity to one or the other) it gradually increases or decreases its pace.

These things argue first that the motion of the Planet (though it appears unequal) is nevertheless governed by circulations, of which this is the ordered moderation and return to the same state. For if the Planet moved in straight lines forming angles (as if it traveled along the sides of a pentagon—<note>Kepler refers here to his early theories in *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), where he attempted to relate planetary orbits to the five Platonic solids.</note> thoughts I once entertained), according to the proportion of the lines, there would sometimes be a sudden change from a faster to a slower motion with a clear distinction, and this would happen in not just one but several places of the zodiac, depending on the number of sides. Since, however, such a great <term>inequality</term> <note>A term used by astronomers of this period to describe any departure from uniform circular motion.</note> remains in the motion of the Planet even after removing the inequality that depends on the Sun, it cannot be managed or demonstrated by the position of a simple circle (in whose center the observer is placed). It can, however, be done through a combination of several circles or something like it (as **PTOLEMY** set forth in Book III), and that in two ways, as simply as possible: either by the use of an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center is offset from the center of the Earth/observer.</note> circle or a concentric <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note>.

Accordingly, **PTOLEMY** chose the eccentric for the <term>first inequality</term> <note>The variation in a planet's speed relative to the stars, caused by the shape of its own orbit.</note>, for the sake of distinction and to aid understanding, because an epicycle would be necessary for the <term>second inequality</term> <note>The variation in a planet's appearance caused by the Earth's own motion (retrograde motion).</note>. Then, reflecting on this general statement, he denies that a bare eccentric is sufficient for the planets. For after he frequently weighed what was likely to happen—moving an epicycle for the second inequality and an eccentric for the first—and compared the observations, it appeared that the center of the epicycle comes much closer to the earth at <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> and goes further away at <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> than that simple eccentric (which provides the first inequality) would allow. From here, he slides directly into the measurement of this approach, and reports that he discovered that the center of the eccentric which carries the center of the epicycle is precisely halfway between the center of vision (or the Earth) and the center of equality (or the eccentric which accounts for the first inequality). Although no demonstration was provided, he nevertheless relies on this principle in his treatment of the three superior planets.

<margin>See the margin at Chapter XIX regarding this.</margin>
**COPERNICUS** (as often elsewhere) religiously follows his teacher here as well, adapting his own model to this same measure.
**ASTRONOMERS** wondered at this, and not without reason; and **I** also (from the mouth of **MAESTLIN** <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor.</note>), as you see in my *COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY*, Chapter XXII, page 79. However, what I thought in that cited booklet—that **PTOLEMY** had used blind guesswork to establish this—is actually otherwise. He was able...

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
...for I will show below how to prove this with the best demonstration from suitable observations. You might only wish this of the craftsman <note>Kepler likely refers to a predecessor like Copernicus or even Ptolemy</note>, that he had transmitted those observations to posterity along with his demonstration.

Since I then thought that this was a **very great postulate** <note>original Greek: *μέγα λίαν αἴτημα* (*mega lian aitema*). In geometry, a postulate is an assumption made without proof to serve as a starting point.</note>, and I saw that COPERNICUS also clearly doubted it while he discussed the changed <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of Mars (his numbers disagreeing with this bisection), I thought of a Method that would lead me to recognize the proportion of both eccentricities (because, as I said, it was not certain that it was doubled). Since PTOLEMY, using three <term>acronychal</term> <note>Observations made when a planet is in "opposition," meaning it is directly opposite the sun in the sky and visible all night.</note> observations and this preconceived opinion about the proportion of eccentricities, could determine the location of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note>, the correction of the mean longitude, and finally the quantity of the eccentricities; **I** saw that if this problem were weakened (by taking away the axiom about the proportion of eccentricities), it would become unstable and the solution would not be unique. Therefore, it had to be strengthened in turn by a fourth acronychal observation. 

Equipped with this skill, I came to TYCHO in the year 1600, and I learned with joy that he too had investigated this proportion rather than merely assuming it, as his numbers indicate. For he makes the center of the <margin>* The definition of which is at the beginning of Chapter V of this book.</margin> (*COPERNICAN) eccentric stand at a distance of 13,680 parts from the observer, while the <term>point of equality</term> <note>Often called the equant point, where the planet’s motion appears uniform.</note> stands at a distance of 3,780 of those same parts from the center. In the PTOLEMAIC form, this would be as if he made the distance between the observer and the center of the eccentric 9,900, and the remaining distance between the center of the eccentric and the point of equality 7,560.

<margin>Regarding the *Forerunner*, or the *Cosmographic Mystery*.</margin>
I myself could have used the bisection as a certainty, and with better right than PTOLEMY, because in Chapter XII of my *MYSTERY* <note>Kepler’s first book, *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596).</note> I had brought forward a physical cause for that bisection. But for that very reason I had come to TYCHO: so that I could inquire more certainly from his observations into my own opinions promulgated in that book. This I have done without prejudice, and I continue to do so. If I survive until Astronomy reaches its purity and perfection, so that a judgment can be pronounced in the case (which I have brought before its tribunal in that book), I promise the reader that I will retract that book; having confirmed what I found to be true, I will faithfully reveal the rest which I found to be otherwise.

But to the matter at hand. *With center **b**, let the <term>eccentric</term> <note>An off-center circular orbit.</note> **F G** be drawn: in it, let the diameter of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the points of the orbit closest to and farthest from the center.</note> **H I** remain as if immovable for several years. If this carried a risk of error, we would not lack the means to guard against it. On this line, let **A** be the observer below **b**; above **b**, let **c** be that center at which angles are proportional to the intervals of time <note>The equant point, which Kepler uses to measure time and speed.</note>, since they are not proportional around **A** (as was said a little above). Let **F**, **G**, **D**, and **E** be four observations arranged around the circumference of the circle, in such a way that the Planet, stripped of its <term>second inequality</term> <note>The apparent "looping" or retrograde motion caused by the Earth's own movement; by "stripping" it, Kepler treats the observations as if the observer were at the center of the system.</note>, appears as if the observer had been at **A**. For in* PTOLEMY'S *system indeed...*

## SECOND PART.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
Indeed, the observed location is the center of the earth, but for TYCHO and COPERNICUS the vision is along the lines FA, GA, DA, and EA, where A represents the Sun. As stated above, by either method <note>Whether one uses a geocentric or heliocentric model</note>, the Planet is equally stripped of its <term>second inequality</term> <note>The apparent backward or "retrograde" motion of a planet caused by the Earth's own movement.</note>. Now, let all the points be connected to one another: let AF be at 25° 43' of Scorpio ♏︎, AG at 26° 43' of Sagittarius ♐︎, AD at 12° 16' of Capricorn ♑︎, and AE at 17° 31 2/3' of Aries ♈︎. From this, four angles are given around point A: namely, FAG is 91° 0', GAD is 75° 33', DAE is 65° 15 1/3', and EAF is 128° 11 1/3'. These must be corrected slightly due to the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>The slow, continuous shift in the orientation of Earth's axis, which changes the perceived positions of the stars over centuries.</note>. For among the Fixed Stars, the Planet was not moved quite as far in E during the final observation as indicated by these numbers. Therefore, angle FAE is a little larger, and the others are smaller by the same amount. In the same way, the angles around point C are obtained by subtracting the <term>mean longitudes</term> <note>The theoretical position of a planet if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant speed.</note>.

**PROPOSITION.** It is now necessary to assume such sizes for angles FAH and FCH that, once they are established, points F, G, D, and E will stand on a single circle, and B (the center of that circle) will lie between points C and A on the line CA.

**THE SOLUTION** is not strictly Geometric, since Algebra is not Geometry; rather, it is achieved through a "double false position" <note>A method of trial and error where two initial guesses are made, and the results are used to calculate the correct value by interpolation.</note>. For even Algebra fails us here, because the terms of the art applied to straight lines are not derived into angles through those lines, unless one were to throw the entire doctrine of Sines into this single operation.

But look at what we are commanded to do. For if we assume the angle FAH, since the line AF has a fixed position among the Fixed Stars, the other leg AH will also be assumed to have a fixed position among the Fixed Stars. Let AH be the line of the <term>apogee</term> (or in the COPERNICAN and TYCHONIC sense, the line of the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note>). Therefore, we are commanded to assume and establish that which we were actually seeking. For we took this path specifically to learn the location of this aphelion. In the same way, since AH (which is CH) will have obtained its place among the Fixed Stars through this assumption of ours, and since it passes through C (the center of the <term>equant circle</term> <note>An imaginary point used to explain the observed speed changes of planets; the planet appears to move at a constant speed around this point.</note>, and thus also through the beginning from which its parts begin to be counted, namely from the <term>apsis</term> <note>The highest or lowest point in an orbit.</note> conceived above H), and we are commanded to assume the angle FCH, then the line CF will also obtain a place on the circumference of the equant. But this is the mean longitude, which corresponds to the observed place of the Planet at point F. And we were seeking knowledge of this mean longitude. We are therefore assuming, in addition to the apogee, another of the very things we were seeking.

**BUT INDEED**, it is not unusual for Geometers, Arithmeticians, or Logicians to use a form of argument that leads to the impossible <note>original: *ad impossibile ducentis*, often called "reductio ad absurdum."</note>. If they see that something absurd follows from their assumptions, they reject them as false; they continue this until, by cutting away the excesses and defects in this manner, the truth itself (which, in the Mathematical disciplines, lies hidden in the middle between the two) is uncovered. In the present case, it is done in the following way:

**LET** the line CA be given a name and be treated as a given value. Because FCH and FAH are assumed, and consequently the inclinations of the remaining lines to HCA are also known, and since AC is a common side to the four triangles (CFA, CGA, CDA, CEA) whose angles are given; therefore, in terms of the measurement of AC, the four lines AF, AG, AD, and AE will be given. And because in the four new triangles FAG, GAD, DAE, and EAF, the sides are now given along with the angles at A between each pair of sides; then the individual angles at the bases from each triangle—namely AFG, ADG, ADE,

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>

ADE; AFE. But AFG and AFE are parts of angle GDE. Now, in the quadrilateral DEFG (if indeed it is inscribed in a circle, as is the hypothesis here), it is required that two opposite angles (such as GFE and GDE) together equal the sum of two right angles <note>In a cyclic quadrilateral (a four-sided shape where all corners touch a circle), opposite angles always add up to 180 degrees.</note>. Therefore, having joined the four angles we have just found, if the sum differs from this measure of two right angles, we shall declare that the assumptions were false—whether the error lies in one of the two assumptions or in both.

Therefore, still retaining one angle, *FCH*, but changing the other, *FAH*, one must return to the beginning and investigate the sum of the four angles anew. If this sum deviates further from two right angles than the previous sum did, it is proof that the change to *FAH* was undertaken incorrectly. Therefore, the opposite must be done: for example, if you had perhaps increased it, now decrease it; or vice versa. But if you have come closer to the correct measure, you will know you are on the right path. Then, by comparing the error that existed at the start to that which now remains, you will proceed in the same proportion, either increasing or decreasing angle *FAH*.

Yet it is not certain for that reason that a single correction will immediately bring your four angles to the correct measure. For the proportion of circular increments <note>The way angles change as they move around a circle</note> is not the same as that of linear increments. You must repeat the labor again and again, until your sum of the sought angles is 180 degrees, or as close as possible; for you may safely neglect the smallest differences.

WHEN you have achieved this, so that the angles *F* and *D* (and therefore the remaining *G* and *E*) reside on the same circumference, you must then explore the other condition that follows: namely, whether *B*, the center of that circle, stands between *C* and *A* on the same line <note>This refers to the "line of apsides," the main axis of the orbit connecting the sun, the center of the orbit, and the point of uniform motion.</note>. For it was said above that PTOLEMY assumed this entirely, and physical reasons require that the slowest motion occurs where the star is at its greatest distance from the Sun *A*, as at *H*. This cannot happen unless *A*, *B*, and *C* are on the same line. To investigate this, let the known lines (*GAD*, *DAE*) be joined so that angle *GAE* is known; and in triangle *GAE*, from this angle and the sides (*GA*, *AE*), let side *GE* be sought. Therefore, in triangle *GFE*, angle *GFE* stands at the circumference. Thus, angle *GBE* at the center is double it. Previously, *GFE* was investigated through its parts *GFA* and *AFE*. Again, therefore, in the isosceles triangle *GBE*, the angle *GBE* and side *GE* are given. Consequently, the angles at the base and the radius of the circle *GB* will not be unknown, in proportion to the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance the center of the orbit is shifted away from the Sun.</note> *AC* assumed at the start. And because *BG* and *BGE* are now held, and previously *AG* and *AGE* were held, by subtracting *AGE* from *BGE* (or vice versa, if that is the case), *AGB* will remain. Therefore, in triangle *AGB*, *AG*, *BG*, and the intercepted angle *AGB* are given. If this differs from the *CAG* first assumed, it is proof that *B* falls outside the line *CA*, contrary to what is proper. Therefore, we shall again declare the assumptions *FCH* and *FAH* to be false.

## PART SECOND

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>

...now an absurdity is encountered, namely that the positions D, E, F, and G do not fit into a circle (as had already happened above, before we had finally established the quantity of angle FAH). It is therefore clear that the angle FCH must also be changed. Let it be changed, then—that is, let another quantity for FCH be assumed at will. Keeping that value, let FAH be varied through four, five, or six trials until the four angles joined at F and D once again make two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>. Then, through the triangles GAE, GFE, GBE, and BDA, one must strive toward a second inquiry into the angle BAD, comparing it with the CAD that was last established. There you will see again whether you have receded further from the truth or have come closer to it. According to the nature of the excesses or defects, and the proportion of the additions, you will return to the start again and again, until you find BAD to be as much as the CAD (or HAD) you had assumed for that trial. When you have reached that point, finally, in triangle BDA, you will give the line BD a "round" name (one hundred thousand units) <note>Kepler uses 100,000 as a base value for calculations, similar to how we use 100 for percentages today</note>. In that same proportion (using the angles as intermediaries), you will seek both BA, the <term>eccentricity of the eccentric</term> <note>The distance from the center of the orbit to the Sun</note>, and CA, the <term>eccentricity of the equant</term> <note>The distance from the center to the mathematical point where the planet's motion appears uniform</note>. Subtracting BA then leaves CB. Then you shall pronounce that both the position of the apogee and the correction of the mean motion (which you had assumed in the final operation) are correct, at least as far as this form of the hypothesis is concerned.

->**IF YOU** are weary of this laborious <term>METHOD</term>, you should rightly pity me, for I went through it at least seventy times with a great loss of time. You will cease to wonder that this is now the fifth year since I first attacked *Mars*, although almost the entire year 1604 was spent on *Optical* investigations.<-

**THERE WILL EXIST** sharp Geometers like *VIETA*, who will think it is a great thing to demonstrate the <term>lack of art</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀτεχνίαν* (*atechnian*), meaning a lack of formal geometric proof</note> of this <term>METHOD</term>. For *VIETA* objected to this very thing in *PTOLEMY*, *COPERNICUS*, and *REGIOMONTANUS*. Let them go, then, and solve the diagram themselves by Geometry, and they shall be great Apollos to me <note>A reference to the god of wisdom; Kepler is challenging critics to find a better way</note>. For <term>ME</term>, it is enough to have shown a <term>non-technical</term> <note>original Greek: *ἄτεχνον* (*atechnon*)</note> thread of light (by which one is nonetheless directed to the exit) for building four or five conclusions from a single argument—one containing four observations and two hypotheses—that is, for finding a way back out of the labyrinth. If the <term>METHOD</term> is difficult to grasp, the matter is much more difficult to investigate without a <term>METHOD</term>.

In that first instance, the observed longitude was 25° 43' in Virgo (♍), and the mean longitude was 6 signs, 0° 47' 40''. The annual motion of the Fixed Stars is 51 seconds, as *BRAHE* demonstrated in his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe's "Introductory Exercises," his major astronomical work</note>. Therefore, from the year 1587 on March 6th to the year 1591 on June 8th, there are 4 years and 3 months. This corresponds to a precessional motion of 3' 37''. Therefore, we must set the observed position in the year 1591 at 26° 39' 23'' in ♍, and the mean longitude at 9 signs, 5° 46' 18''. Likewise, from the year 1587 on March 6th to the year 1593 on August 25th, there are 6 years and 5 1/2 months. To this belongs a precessional motion of 5' 30''. Thus it must be set...

### For the angles at F and D.

The angles AFG, AFE, ADG, and ADE are nearly half the complements of the angles at A to a semicircle: <note>In a triangle, if you know one angle (A), the sum of the other two is the "complement to a semicircle" (180° - A). If the sides forming angle A were equal, the other two angles would be exactly half that complement.</note> however, those at F are smaller, because the lines AG (50703) and AE (52302) were found to be shorter than AF (59433); and those at D are larger, because the said lines AG and AE are longer than AD (48052). And since those four angles around A equal four right angles <note>360 degrees</note>, therefore their complements to a semicircle will also together equal four right angles: because four semicircles are eight right angles. <note>4 × 180° = 720°; 720° - 360° = 360°</note>. Therefore, half the sum of the complements is two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>, which is what we wish the sums of GFE and GDE to be together. <note>Kepler is checking if the opposite angles of the quadrilateral add up to 180°, which would prove the points F, G, D, and E lie on a single circle.</note> Therefore, by as much as the angles at F fall short of the halves of their complements, by that same amount must those at D exceed their complements. But the tangents of the differences of the angles in this kind of triangle are obtained if you divide the differences of the sides by the sums of the sides, and multiply the quotient by the tangents of the half-complements. <note>This is the "Law of Tangents" used to solve for unknown angles in a triangle.</note> Therefore, if the two differences of the angles at F equal the sum at D, angle F together with angle D will equal two right angles.

In such a small error, however, no disadvantage is incurred by one who, in the **CAG** triangle, seeks **BA** from known angles and sides, as if **B** were precisely on the line **CA**.

AND BY THIS METHOD, the hypothesis of the first inequality was investigated from four <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: ακρονυχίαις; an "acronychal" position refers to a planet being in "opposition," meaning it is directly opposite the Sun in the sky as seen from Earth.</note> positions of Mars.
