# PART THREE.

...smaller [distances] corresponding to the lowest $\lambda\zeta$. For $\gamma\kappa$ and $\mu\zeta$ are equal, and $\gamma\iota$ is smaller than $\gamma\kappa$, while $\lambda\zeta$ is larger than $\mu\zeta$.

<margin>Neither from time elapsed: Nor from the angle at the SUN, or the equated anomaly:</margin>
And this same cause prevents $\gamma\iota, \iota\lambda, \lambda\zeta,$ from being proportional either to the times of equal arcs $CD, DE, EF$ traversed, or to the angles at the **SUN** $CAD, DAE, EAF$. For the time or delay of the **PLANET** in equal parts of the eccentric, $CD, DE, EF$, decreases continuously from the highest point to the lowest; the angles at the **SUN** increase continuously; but the distances $\gamma\iota$ increase in the middle, as $\iota\lambda$.

Therefore, if the path of the **PLANET** is a perfect circle, the measure of the **PLANET'S** descent on the diameter $\gamma\zeta$ is neither time, nor the space of the eccentric traversed, nor the angle at the **SUN**.

And indeed, physical speculations also reject these measures.

<margin>Neither from an imaginary epicycle or eccentric.</margin>
What if we should say this then? Even if the motion of the **PLANET** does not occur in an epicycle <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circular orbit whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle; a standard tool in ancient astronomy that Kepler is trying to replace with physical causes.</note>, could this libration <term>libration</term> <note>A back-and-forth oscillation or swaying; here, the planet's movement toward and away from the sun along a radius.</note> still be managed so that the distances from the **SUN** are made to match those that exist when an epicycle is truly traversed?

First, this would attribute to the power proper to the **PLANET** a knowledge of an imaginary epicycle and its effects in arranging the distances from the **SUN**. It also attributes a knowledge of future speed and slowness which the common motion from the **SUN** is about to cause; because here there is necessarily assumed the same imaginary intensification and relaxation <note>original: "intensio & remissio". This refers to the planet speeding up and slowing down.</note> of the imaginary epicyclic motion as there is of the true eccentric motion. These things are more incredible than the previous ones, where the motion of the body was joined with a knowledge of an actual epicycle or eccentric. Therefore, let the arguments disputed there be understood as repeated here: for the opinions almost coincide.

<margin>The measure of this libration will be revealed below in Chapter 57.</margin>
And yet, in the lack of a better opinion, we must for now acquiesce to this one. The more absurdities it involves, the more gladly some Physicist will admit below in Chapter 52—as **OBSERVATIONS** will testify—that the path of the **PLANET** is not a circle.

<margin>
### II.
By what means or by what measure does the Planet grasp its distance from the SUN?
</margin>
We have spoken so far of the measure that concerns the form of this libration. It **REMAINS** that we also inquire into the measure of this measure—namely, the quantity or the motion through a place. For it is not enough to know how much the **PLANET** ought to stand away from the **SUN**; it is also required that it knows, by doing what, it may stand away at the correct interval.

<margin>To what extent should a sense of the size of the SOLAR body be attributed to Planets?</margin>
Whoever, then, has been driven by that supposition of a perfectly circular path to place a mind in the **PLANET** to preside over this libration, could say nothing else than this: the mind of the **PLANET** looks to the increasing and decreasing size <note>original: "amplitudinem". Kepler is wondering if the planet "sees" the Sun getting bigger as it gets closer.</note> of the **SUN'S** diameter, and by using this as a sign, it understands what distances of its own body it has produced from the **SUN** at any given time. This is because, just as sailors cannot understand from the sea itself how much space of waves they have traversed, because that path is distinguished by no boundaries; but rather they know it either from the duration of the voyage (if the wind and wave remained constant and the ship never rested), or from the quarter of the wind and different altitudes of the pole, or from a joined consideration of all or at least some of these; or, if the gods please, from a combination of some small wheels, driven with the help of fins lowered into the waves—the kind of instrument some vain mechanics claim to possess for the waves of the Ocean...

He uses a nautical analogy to show how difficult it would be for a planet to track its own distance from the Sun without a physical mechanism.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER 39.</margin>
...they transfer the rest of the path: In exactly the same way, the **PLANET’S** mind cannot itself measure the place or space traversed toward the **SUN**, since there is only pure etheric air <term>etheric air</term> <note>The "aura aetheria," believed by 17th-century astronomers to be the fluid-like substance filling space.</note> between them, marked by no landmarks; instead, it must either use time (and through that time, an equal exertion of forces, which was already denied in the preceding sections); or a physical machine, which is ridiculous (for we assume the stars are round, following the example of the **SUN** and **MOON**; indeed, it is likely that the entire field of etheric air moves along with the **PLANETS**); or finally, it must use some suitable signs that vary with the **PLANET’S** changing distance from the **SUN**, of which there is no other available except the single apparent diameter of the **SUN**.

<margin>In this way, the Planets would become <term>geometers</term> <note>original Greek: γεωμέτραι</note>, measuring their own distance from the Sun through a single observation: namely, from the apparent size of the Sun’s body.</margin>
*Thus we humans know the* **SUN** *is 229 of its own diameters away from us, when its diameter is 30 minutes, and 222 diameters away when it is 35.*

And indeed, if it were certain that this movement along the diameter of the epicycle <term>epicycle</term> <note>An auxiliary circle used in ancient astronomy; here Kepler refers to the back-and-forth "libration" of the planet toward and away from the Sun.</note> could not be achieved by some material and physical or magnetic power of the **PLANET**, nor by a simple animal force, but was governed by the **PLANET’S** mind, then nothing absurd would be established. For that the **SUN** is also observed by the **PLANETS** in other ways is testified by their latitudes <term>latitudes</term> <note>The vertical tilt or angle of a planet's orbit relative to the Earth's orbital plane (the ecliptic).</note>. For since the **PLANETS**, for the sake of these latitudes, withdraw to the sides away from the middle and "royal road" of this power from the **SUN** (as if from the very current of a river, as said in Chapter 38), they would describe circles that appeared smaller from the **EARTH** or the center of the **WORLD** if they did not meanwhile look back at the **SUN** and complete their approach and retreat in a line tending through the center of the **SUN**. But all the **PLANETS** describe great circles <term>great circles</term> <note>A circle on a sphere whose center is the same as the center of the sphere.</note> that intersect the ecliptic in places opposite the **SUN**, as was demonstrated above from observations in Chapters 12, 13, and 14 regarding **MARS**.

<margin>That there is something in the Planets like a mind, which looks back at the body of the Sun.</margin>

<margin>See the margin of Chapter 63.</margin>
Therefore, both the libratory diameter **$\gamma \zeta$** <note>The line of the planet's back-and-forth oscillation.</note> tends toward the **SUN** itself, and the latitudes respect the **SUN** entirely. Although I am going to transfer this matter of latitude as well, later in Part 5, from the realm of the **MIND** to the realm of **NATURE** and magnetic faculties.

<margin>What can be objected to the solar body's perception.</margin>

<margin>† Smallness.</margin>
**AND DO NOT** tell me that this diameter of the **SUN** is quite small, and its variation so slight that it could not serve as a rule. For it is certain that it does not vanish entirely for any of the **PLANETS**. While on **EARTH** it is thirty minutes, on **MARS** it will be twenty, on **JUPITER** seven, on **SATURN** three, but on **VENUS** forty, and on **MERCURY** clearly eighty, and up to one hundred and twenty. You should not complain about the smallness of this body, but rather about the unsuitable dullness of human senses, which do not follow such small things.

Behold, however small this body is, it is nonetheless fit—as I have demonstrated in the previous sections—for moving such distant bodies in a circle. Everyone knows about the illumination of the **WORLD** by such a small body. It is therefore credible that if those movers are endowed with any faculty for observing this diameter, it is as much sharper than our eyes as its work and perennial motion are more constant than our turbulent and confused affairs.

### PART THREE.

<margin>
**CHAPTER 39.**

2. The lack of sensory instruments.
</margin>

So, **KEPLER**, will you then assign two eyes to each of the **PLANETS**? Not at all. Nor is it necessary. For it is no more required that they be given feet and wings so that they can move. Indeed, **BRAHE** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), whose precise observations Kepler used to calculate planetary orbits.</note> has already eliminated the idea of solid spheres. Nor has our speculation exhausted all the treasures of nature, such that it should depend on our knowledge how many senses there ought to be. Yet we have admirable examples ready at hand. For tell me, from a physical perspective, with what eyes do the animal faculties <term>animal faculties</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "animal" refers to the "anima" or soul/vital force that governs movement and perception in living things.</note> of sublunary bodies <note>Objects or beings existing "below the moon," i.e., on Earth.</note> observe the locations of the stars in the zodiac? How do they perceive the harmonic arrangement between them (which we call an <term>aspect</term> <note>A specific angular relationship between planets, such as 90 or 120 degrees, believed to exert influence.</note>), so that they react and catch fire in their own work? Or did my Mother mark the locations of the stars with her own eyes, so that she knew she was born in the configuration of **SATURN**, **JUPITER**, **MARS**, **VENUS**, and **MERCURY**, through sextiles and trines <note>Sextiles (60°) and trines (120°) are considered "harmonious" or favorable angles in astrology.</note>? And because of this, did she strive to give birth to her children—especially me, her firstborn—on those specific days when many of those same aspects (especially of **SATURN** and **JUPITER**) recurred, or when many of the original positions were occupied by squares, oppositions, or the bodies themselves? These things have certainly been observed in every example that has occurred to this day. But why do I say these things, which are just as absurd as the others, except to those who have exercised themselves in the study of nature more diligently than is common today?

Therefore, that same person whom we suppose is saying that the **PLANET’S** path is a perfect circle, will say this: that the **PLANET** aims, through its <term>libration</term> <note>A back-and-forth oscillation or swaying motion along a line.</note>, to ensure that the apparent diameters of the **SUN**—after equal arcs of the eccentric have been completed—appear to it in nearly the same <margin>* For in Chapter 57, the proportion will be a bit different.</margin> \* inverse proportion as the lines $\delta\alpha, \varepsilon\alpha, \zeta\alpha$ (or those equal to them, $\iota\alpha, \kappa\alpha, \zeta\alpha$) are to the longest line $\gamma\alpha$. And by this consideration of the **SUN’S** diameters, the various proximities from $\gamma, \eta, \iota, \lambda, \zeta$ come about at the stated moments of time.

It must be known, however, that the increase of the **SUN’S** diameter and the arc of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; here used to model the planet's varying distance.</note> do not fit each other well. Therefore, this motive mind must have a very good memory to accommodate the unequal <term>versed sines</term> <note>A trigonometric function ($1 - \cos \theta$) used in early astronomy to measure distances along a radius.</note> of the epicycle arcs to the equal increases in the **SUN’S** diameter. On this matter, see Chapters **56** and **57** below.

<margin>
**III.**
By what animal faculty the mind obtains that distance from the Sun which it seeks for the body.
</margin>

**AND LET THESE THINGS** be said regarding the sign of the distance covered. It remains for me to advise in three words concerning the third point: the animal faculty for transporting the **PLANETARY** body. Anyone who says the body of the **PLANET** is transported by an innate force says something that is in no way probable. For we denied this at the beginning. But neither can this force be simply attributed to the **SUN**. For the same thing that attracts the **PLANET** would, in turn, also repel it: which conflicts with the simplicity of the **SOLAR** body. But he who, by some peculiar reasoning, refers this transport to a mutual consensus between the body of the **SUN** and the **PLANET**, shapes the entire subject of this chapter differently; for that reason, a specific chapter, **57**, is assigned to this matter below.

You see, considerate and ingenious reader, that this opinion concerning a perfect eccentric circle for the **PLANETARY** journey involves many incredible things in physical speculations; not indeed because it sets the **SUN’S** diameter as a sign for the **PLANETARY** mind—for perhaps even the truest opinion will do that—but because it assigns incredible things both to the mind and to the motive soul.

# C H A P T E R  XL.
## An imperfect method of calculating equations from a physical hypothesis, which nevertheless suffices for the theory of the SUN or the EARTH.

SO PROLIX a discussion was necessary to pave the way toward the natural form of equations <term>equations</term> <note>In historical astronomy, an "equation" is the difference or correction added to a planet's mean (average) position to find its true position.</note>, about which I shall have more to say in the fourth part. Now we must return to the equations of the **SUN’S** eccentric in particular, which is the primary subject of this third part, and for the sake of which these general matters were presented in the preceding eight chapters.

MY FIRST error was that the path of a **PLANET** is a perfect circle—a thief of time all the more harmful because it was supported by the authority of all philosophers, and was particularly fitting for metaphysics. Let the path of a **PLANET**, therefore, be a perfect eccentric circle <note>An eccentric circle is a circular orbit where the Sun is not at the exact center, but slightly off-set.</note>, for the amount that the oval shape detracts from it in the theory of the **SUN** is imperceptible. Those things which will be necessary in the future for the other **PLANETS** because of this deviation <note>Kepler is realizing that while the Sun/Earth orbit looks like a circle, the other planets like Mars will require an elliptical or "oval" path.</note> will follow below in Chapters 59 and 60.

<margin>To find the physical part of the equation through the distances of the Planet from the center of the Sun.</margin>
Therefore, since the delays of a **PLANET** in equal parts of the eccentric are in the same proportion to each other as the distances of those parts themselves, and yet every single point in the entire semicircle of the eccentric changes its distance, I took upon myself no small labor to investigate how the sums of the individual distances could be obtained. For unless we have the sum of all of them (which are, however, infinite in number), we cannot say how great any particular delay is; therefore, the equation will remain unknown. For just as the total sum of distances is to the total periodic time, so any part of the sum of distances is to its own time.

Thus, at the beginning, I divided the eccentric into 360 parts, as if these were the smallest possible particles, and I assumed that within one such part, the distance does not change at all. Therefore, I investigated the distances at the start of these parts or degrees using the method from Chapter 29, and I gathered them into one sum. Afterward, for the revolutionary time <note>The time taken for one full orbit.</note>, although it was defined as 365 days and 6 hours, I assigned another more rounded name, and said that it was worth 360 degrees, or a whole circle, which among astronomers is called the mean anomaly <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The position of a planet if it moved at a perfectly constant speed in a perfect circle.</note>. Thus, just as the total sum of distances is to the sum of the time, I made any individual distance relate to its own time. Finally, I accumulated the times for each individual degree; and having compared these times, or degrees...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 40, where Kepler moves from a "mechanical" method of calculating planetary positions to a geometric one. He describes his realization that the area of a sector of an eccentric circle can represent the sum of distances, laying the groundwork for what we now call his Second Law of Planetary Motion.</meta>

<page-num>193</page-num>

->PART THREE.<-

the <term>physical equation</term> <note>The "physical equation" is the correction needed to account for the planet's changing speed as it moves closer to or further from the Sun.</note> resulted from the degrees of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle of a planet's position measured from the center of its circular orbit.</note>, or from the number of parts up to which the distance was sought; <margin>CHAPTER 40.</margin> to this, the optical equation—found by the method in Chapter 29 using those same distances—had to be added, so that the whole equation could be obtained.

BUT since this method is mechanical and tedious, and since it was not possible to compute the equation for any single degree by itself while setting the others aside, <margin>To find the physical part of the equation through areas.</margin> I looked around for other means. Since I knew that there are infinite points on the eccentric and infinite distances to them, it occurred to me that all these distances are contained within the plane of the eccentric. For I remembered that long ago, **ARCHIMEDES**, when seeking the ratio of the circumference to the diameter, had likewise cut the circle into infinite triangles; for this is the hidden power of his <term>proof by contradiction</term> <note>original: "demonstrationis per impossibile" — a logical method where a statement is proven by showing that its negation leads to a contradiction.</note>. Therefore, instead of dividing the circumference into 360 parts as I did before, I now cut the plane of the eccentric circle into as many parts, by lines drawn from the point from which the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance the Sun is offset from the center of the orbit.</note> is calculated.

*Let AB be the line of apsides <note>The line passing through the points where the planet is closest to and furthest from the Sun.</note>; A the **SUN** (or the **EARTH** for **PTOLEMY**); B the center of the eccentric CD; let its semicircle CD be divided into any number of equal parts CG, GH, HE, EI, IK, KD; and let the points at A and B be connected to the points of these divisions. Therefore, AC will be the longest distance, AD the shortest, and the others in order will be AG, AH, AE, AI, AK. Since triangles are equal if their bases are equal, and since the sectors or triangles CBG, GBH, and the rest—resting upon the smallest parts of the circumference and thus not differing from straight lines—all have the same height (because the sides BC, BG, BH are equal), they will all be equal. But all these triangles are contained within the area CDE, and all the arcs or bases are contained within the semicircumference CED. Therefore, by composition, as the area CDE is to the arc CED, so is the area CBG to the arc CG. And by permutation, as the arc CED is to the arcs CG, CH, and each in order, so is the area CDE to the areas CBG, CBH, and each in order. Therefore, no error is committed if, instead of using arcs, the areas are treated in this manner, and instead of the angles of the eccentric anomaly CBG, CHB, the areas CGB, CHB are used.*

Furthermore, just as the lines extended from B to the infinite parts of the circumference are all contained within the area of the semicircle CDE, and the lines extended from B to the infinite parts of the arc CH are all contained within the area CBH: so also do the lines extended from A to those same infinite parts of the circumference or arc do the same. Finally, since both sets of lines—those from B and those from A—fill one and the same semicircle CDE; and since those drawn from A are the distances themselves, the sum of which is sought: I therefore concluded that by calculating the area CAH or CAE, the sum of the infinite distances in CH or CE is obtained. I did not think this because an infinite number can be traversed, but because I believed the measure of the power collected in the distances for accumulating <term>delays</term> <note>Kepler's term for the time a planet spends in a certain part of its orbit; slower speed means a longer "delay" or stay.</note> resides in this area, so that we might thus gain knowledge of the area without counting every tiny part.

He is now refining how this area-based calculation accounts for the various "equations" (corrections) used in astronomy.</meta>

<meta>Catchword: Known</meta>

# CHAPTER 40.

Therefore, from what was said above, just as the area $C D E$ relates to half of the period of return, which we may call 180 degrees, so the areas $C A G$ and $C A H$ relate to the duration of the delays in $C G$ and $C H$. Thus, the area $C G A$ shall become the measure of the time, or the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The mean anomaly is the position a planet would have if it moved at a constant speed. Kepler is using the area of the sector to represent this passage of time.</note>, which corresponds to the arc of the eccentric $C G$, since the mean anomaly measures time.

Previously, however, the part $C G B$ of this area $C A B$ was the measure of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle of the planet's position measured from the center of its circular orbit, rather than the Sun.</note>, whose <term>optical equation</term> <note>The "optical equation" is the correction needed for the planet's position due to the observer's perspective from a point (the Sun) that is not the center of the orbit.</note> is the angle $B G A$.

*Therefore, the remaining area, namely that of triangle* $B G A$, *is the excess (in this case) of the mean anomaly over the eccentric anomaly; and the angle* $B G A$ *of that same triangle is the excess of the eccentric anomaly* $C B G$ *over the equated anomaly* $C A G$. *Consequently, knowledge of this same triangle provides both parts of the equation corresponding to the equated anomaly* $G A C$.

<margin>The reason why, above in Chapter 31, in the third method, the part of the equation was merely doubled to represent the whole equation.</margin>
And from this, the reason is also clear why, in Chapters 30 and 31, I said that the parts of the equation in the theory of the **SUN** were very nearly equal. *For because any arc, and the angle standing upon it at the center (such as* $C G$ *and* $C B G$ *previously), is measured by its own area, which is called a sector (such as area* $C B G$); *therefore, by placing the foot of the compass at* $G$ *with the distance* $G B$, *let the circumference of an arc be drawn, cutting* $G A$ *at* $o$. *Thus, as the area* $G B C$ *is to the angle* $G B C$, *so the area* $B G O$ *is to the angle* $B G O$. *But the angle* $B G O$ *is the optical part of the equation. Therefore, the area* $G O B$, *by doubling the part of the equation, will measure the optical part of the equation, since in our previously explained calculation, the entire area* $G B A$ *itself must be consulted for the optical part of the equation.*

*Even if, therefore,* $A G B$, *the true measure of the <term>physical part of the equation</term> <note>The physical part of the equation accounts for the actual change in the planet's speed as it moves closer to or further from the Sun.</note>, exceeds* $O G B$, *the presented measure of the optical part, by a small space or area* $O A B$ (*and conversely, near the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center or Sun.</note> it is surpassed by it by some such small space): nevertheless, in a small eccentricity, such as that of the **SUN** or the **EARTH** (which we are dealing with in this third part), this is not perceptible. For the closer one comes to the line of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the closest and farthest points of an orbit.</note>, the more slender the whole triangle* $A G B$ *becomes, and therefore its small part* $A O B$ *as well, no matter how much its height* $A O$ *then increases. At the middle longitudes, however, the angle* $B E A$ *with its sector is in some places clearly measured by the area* $B E A$, *and the excesses and deficits begin to swap places.*

THEREFORE, the greatest difference that can occur is accumulated in the <term>octants</term> <note>The points halfway between the apsides (perihelion/aphelion) and the quadrants (90-degree points).</note>, or the places intermediate between the apsides and the quadrants; how great this is will now be made clear.

FOR SINCE in the theory of **MARS** I used the same form of computing by areas for some time, this difference could not be neglected because of the **PLANET'S** great eccentricity. Nor was the doubling of the optical part of the equation without perceptible error. Therefore, the surface of the "equating triangle" had to be investigated. This can be done by various means, but I will record the most shorthand method.

<summary>Kepler explains how the area of a triangle within the orbital circle represents the difference between a planet's mean motion (time) and its actual position, noting that while simple approximations worked for Earth's nearly circular orbit, the high eccentricity of Mars requires more precise geometric areas.</summary>

PART THREE

<margin>A brief inquiry into the area in the equatorial triangle.</margin>
<margin>CHAPTER 40.</margin>

## It is well known that triangles of equal height are in the proportion of their bases; I say that those with equal bases are also in the proportion of their heights.

Let $AGB$ and $AHB$ be triangles upon the same base $AB$, extended to $C$. From $G$, let a straight line $GN$ be drawn parallel to the common base $AB$, cutting $HB$ at $N$; let $N$ be connected with $A$; and from the vertices of the three triangles $G, H, N$, let perpendiculars $GM, HL, NP$ be drawn to the base, determining the heights of the triangles. Since $GN$ and $MP$ are parallel, and $GM, NP$ are perpendicular, $GM$ and $NP$ will be equal. But $GM$ is the height of triangle $AGB$, and $NP$ is the height of triangle $ANB$. Therefore, the triangles $ANB$ and $AGB$ have equal height; and because they are simultaneously upon the same base $AB$, they are equal. And since $ANB$ is a part of $AHB$, and they share the line of the bases $HB$ and the common vertex $A$, the triangles $NAB$ and $HAB$ have equal height. Therefore, as base $NB$ is to $BH$, so is triangle $NAB$ to $HAB$. But $NAB$ and $GAB$ were proven equal. Therefore, as $NB$ is to $BH$, so is $GAB$ to $HAB$. However, as $BN$ is to $BH$, so is $NP$ to $HL$, because $NBP$ and $HBL$ are similar triangles. Therefore also, as $NP$ is to $HL$, so is $GAB$ to $HAB$. But $NP$ and $GM$ are equal. Therefore, as $GM$ is to $HL$ (height to height), so is the area $GAB$ to the area $HAB$. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

<margin>The value of the triangle at 90 degrees of the eccentric anomaly.</margin>
Let $BE$ now be perpendicular to $CD$, and let triangle $BEA$ be right-angled at $B$. $BE$ will be the height and $BA$ the base. Therefore, multiplying 900—namely, half the base $BA$ (which for the Sun <note>original: "S O L E". Kepler refers to the solar theory or the observer's position at the Sun</note> is 1800)—by the height $BE$, namely 100,000, which is the radius of the circle, the area of triangle $BEA$ is produced according to Proposition 42 of the first book of <term>Euclid</term> <note>Euclid's Elements, Book I, Prop. 42 deals with constructing a parallelogram equal to a given triangle.</note>, specifically 90,000,000. But the area of a circle whose radius is 100,000 (according to the most recent calculation of <margin>Adrianus Romanus:</margin> <term>Adrianus Romanus</term> <note>Adriaan van Roomen (1561–1615), a Flemish mathematician famous for calculating $\pi$ to 16 decimal places.</note>, a most skillful Geometer) is 31,415,926,536, without an error of even one of these small parts. And just as this area of the circle relates to the 360 degrees of the <term>mean anomaly</term> or time—that is, to 21,600 <term>first minutes</term> <note>60 minutes per degree $\times$ 360 degrees = 21,600.</note> or 1,296,000 <term>seconds</term>—so in the same proportion, the area of the triangle 90,000,000 relates to 3,713 seconds, which is 1 degree, 1 minute, 53 seconds. Thus the area $BEA$ is worth 1° 1' 53". But the angle $BEA$ in Chapters 30 and 31 was also 1° 1' 53". Therefore, both parts of the equation are equal at this location, namely around 90 degrees.

In the other degrees of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term>, one must proceed as follows. Since the area $BEA$ is 3,713 [seconds], then as its height $EB$ is to the heights $HL$ or $GM$ of the others—which is to say, the <term>total sine</term> <note>The radius of the circle used in trigonometric calculations, here 100,000.</note> to the sines of $HBC, GBC$ (the eccentric anomaly)—so is 3,713 to the areas of the remaining triangles. Thus, 3,713 will be multiplied by the sines of the angles at $B$, and after discarding the last five zeros, the remaining values will be the seconds of the <term>physical equation</term> <note>The correction required to account for the planet's non-uniform speed according to the Area Law.</note> corresponding to that angle at $B$. For example, let $HBC$ be 45° 43' 46", as it was above in Chapter 31. The sine 71,605 multiplied by 3,713, with the last 5 digits discarded, results in 2,659 seconds, which is 44' 19". We assumed this part of the equation in the table above to be 43' 46", equal to the <term>optical part</term> <note>The correction for the planet's position due to the observer's perspective from the Sun, which is not at the center of the orbit.</note>.

Thus here the small area $ABO$, where it is greatest, does not exceed 33 seconds.

AND this is that fourth method of computing the equations of the eccentric, which I began to discuss above near the end of Chapter 34, which most closely expresses the nature of things itself and the observations prefaced in Chapters 32 and 33.

But nevertheless, there is a flawed reasoning <note>original: paralogismus</note> in my argument, though of no great importance; it arises from the fact that **ARCHIMEDES** divided the circle into infinitely many triangles, but with their bases on the circumference at right angles, such that their vertices were at the center of the circle, **B**. But for triangles with the vertex at **A** <note>the eccentric point, representing the Sun's position</note> standing upon the circumference, the ratio is not the same; because the circumference is cut obliquely everywhere by the lines drawn from **A**, except at points **C** and **D** <note>the aphelion and perihelion</note>.

And you could detect the error by experience, as I also did, by taking all the distances **AC, AG, AH**, for every single whole degree of the angles **CBG, GBH** (which distances, although they correspond to individual whole degrees of the angle at **A** in the table provided in Chapter <term>XXX</term> <note>Chapter 30</note>, and are thus divided into minutes of the angles at **B**: nevertheless, the distance from **A** can easily be proportionally assigned to any whole degree of the angle at **B**) and casting them into one sum. For the sum produced is greater than 36,000,000; yet the 360 distances from **B** produce a sum of no more than 36,000,000. And yet, if both sums were measured by the same area of the circle, these sums ought to have been equal.

<margin>
I say angles are divided into minutes when minutes are attached to the degrees.
</margin>
The error, however, is demonstrated in this manner.

> *Let any straight line besides **CD** be drawn through **B**, cutting the circumference, and let it be **EF**: and let the points of the sections **E, F** be connected with **A**. Since, therefore, the point **A** is not contained within the line **EF**, a figure or triangle **EAF** will be formed; therefore **EA** and **AF** joined together are longer than **EF**, according to the **22nd** proposition of the first book of **EUCLID**. But the area of the circle contains the sum of all lines **EF**. Therefore it contains a sum which is less than all the lines **EA, AF**, since between any opposite points of the eccentric and **A**, such a triangle is established, except between **CD** and **A**, where a straight line is formed instead of a triangle.*

Furthermore, by the same reasoning, it is also demonstrated (to add this in passing) that the distances from **A** corresponding to all 360 whole degrees of the angle at **A** (which are in the table of the previous Chapter <term>XXX</term>), collected into one sum, are less than 36,000,000. *For let any straight line besides **DC** be drawn through point **A**, which let be **EV**, and let **E** and **V** be connected with **B**. In the triangle **EBV**, the straight lines **EB** and **BV** joined together will be longer than **EA** and **AV**, the two opposite distances. But all 360 of **EB** and **BV** collected together make 36,000,000. Therefore, all 360 of **EA** and **AV** collected together will make less than 36,000,000.*

To repeat, then, what has already been said: this method of equations <note>mathematical corrections to find the planet's position</note> is indeed the most concise, and it rests upon the physical causes of the motions explained thus far, and in the theory of the **SUN** or the **EARTH** it satisfies the observations most scrupulously; but nevertheless it errs in two respects. First, because it assumes the <term>orbita</term> <note>the path or orbit</note> of the **PLANET** to be a perfect circle, which will be demonstrated to be untrue below in Chapter <term>XLIV</term> <note>Chapter 44</note>; second, because it uses a plane <note>the area of the sector</note> that does not exactly measure

<margin>
If an elliptical <note>original: "ecliptica," but in this context Kepler is referring to the non-circular, specifically elliptical path he is discovering</note> orbit of the Planet is assumed, this method fails in nothing. Take note of it, then.
</margin>

->**A Problem Proposed to Geometers, regarding the squaring of the space between conchoids.**<-

<margin>A problem proposed to Geometers, concerning the squaring of the space between conchoids.</margin>
**AND BECAUSE** this age possesses most excellent Geometers, who sometimes toil long and hard over matters of no obvious practical use, I appeal to each and every one of them to help me in finding a plane figure that is equal to the sum of all the distances combined. Geometrically, indeed (taking the word in a broad sense), I have found it myself: but let them teach me how to calculate <note>original: "numerare," meaning to find a numerical value</note> what I have geometrically drawn; indeed, let them teach me how to square <note>original: "quadrare," to find a square with an area equal to the figure</note> the figure I have found. 

Let the *semicircumference* **CED** *therefore be stretched out into a straight line, and let it be divided into as many parts as before by the points* **G, H, E, I, K**: and *from these points of division let perpendiculars be erected equal to the radius* **CB**: and *let the parallelogram be closed. This will be double the* **ARCHIMEDEAN** *triangle, by which he measures the area of a semicircle.* <note>Archimedes proved that the area of a circle is equal to a right triangle with one leg equal to the radius and the other equal to the circumference.</note> *If you create individual parallelograms from each sector in this manner, then the whole parallelogram, divided into parts, will be equal to the entire area of the semicircle: that is, a double ratio will prevail everywhere.*

<margin>* I call it a "conchoid" not that of Nicostratus <note>Original: Nicostrati. Kepler likely refers to the "conchoid of Nicomedes," a classic curve, but uses a different name here.</note>, which is infinite and named by him because it resembles a shell (concha): but rather that which is similar to a conchoid: just as we call a "Rhomboid" that which is similar to a Rhombus.</margin>

*In this same way, let the distances* **CA, GA,** *etc., also be extended, and let the points* **a** *be connected by a conchoid* **A. A. A. A. A.** *drawn through the individual points (of which there are infinitely many in potential); the figure* **AACD** *will then be equal to all the distances from* **A**. *For in a similar way, from the individual lines* **AG, AH,** *a single parallelogram is formed as closely as possible, except that the conchoid is not parallel to* **CD** *itself, but is inclined toward the radii* **GA, HA, EA,** *just as the distance is inclined toward the circumference in the circle itself: so that nothing hinders the fact that the conchoid* **AA** *is made longer than the semicircle* **CD.**

*However,* **EA** *is longer than* **EB.** *If one were to take* **CA, GQ, HR, EB, LS, KL, DA;** *as determined by the perpendiculars dropped from* **a** *onto the distances of the points from* **B** (*as if, in the circular diagram, a perpendicular* **AR** *descended onto the continuation of* **HB,** *defining* **HR** *as shorter than* **HA**), *then the figure between the conchoids* **AQRBSLA** *and* **CD** *would be clearly equal to the figure* **CBBD.** *For the conchoid would cut* **BD** *at the line* **EA**; *and because the highest and lowest* **BA** *are equal, and* **BQ** *is equal to* **LB,** *and* **BR** *to* **SB,** *and so on: therefore the figures* **BBRQA** *and* **BBALS** *would be congruent, one being the deficiency and the other the excess of the equal figures* **CBBE** *and* **EBBD**: *thus the whole figure between* **AQRBSLA** *and* **CD** *is equal to the whole between* **BB** *and* **CD.** *Therefore, the small space between the two conchoids* **AQRBSLA** *and* **AAAAAA** *measures the excess of the distances from* **A** *over the distances from* **B,** *in that measure in which the parallelogram is set equal to all the distances from* **B.**

<margin>The space between the conchoids is of unequal width in places equally distant from the middle.</margin>
And note that this space is not of the same width in places equally distant from the line **EA,** but is wider below. For in the circular diagram, let **HBR** be continued to **V,** so that **AH** and **AV** correspond to the angles **HBE** above and **FBV** below, which are equal and equally distant from the middle points **E** and **F.** And with center **A** and the interval **AV,** let an arc of a circle **XY** be drawn through **AH** and **BH.** If you then connect **AY,** the triangle **AYR** will be clearly congruent to the triangle **AVR,** for **AV** and **AY** and **AX** are equal...

<margin>CHAPTER 40.</margin>
I wished to present these preliminary remarks generally regarding the computation of the physical equation, so that—even though it is not yet sufficiently equipped with the necessary geometric aids, and not all the inequalities of the **PLANETS** have been revealed (especially since we have presupposed that the path of the **SUN** or the **EARTH** is a perfect eccentric circle, which will be denied later regarding Mars in Chapters 44 and 53)—this operation might not be too far removed from the speculation previously set forth. For as far as the theory of the **SUN** is concerned, in which we have been occupied until now, nothing hinders us: neither the neglect of the conchoid space, by which we take less than is right, nor the assumption of the perfect eccentric, by which we seem to have an excess; in so far as can be judged now, before everything has been explained. Indeed, let these things, rejected in this chapter under the mark of a paralogism <note term="paralogism">A piece of false reasoning or a logical fallacy</note>, be refuted below when we come to the truest method of equations, once that which gave occasion to the paralogism has been eliminated from the hypothesis.

**SINCE** I have therefore described to a hair <note>original: "ad unguem," a Latin idiom meaning "to the fingernail," implying perfect precision</note> the cause and measure of the **SECOND INEQUALITY**, which shows the **PLANETS** to the sight as stationary, direct, and retrograde, through the most certain observations and demonstrations; and since I have shown that this second inequality itself shares in the first inequality, and that the theory of the **SUN** or the **EARTH** (**COPERNICUS**) or of the epicycle (**PTOLEMY**) is similar to the theory of the other **PLANETS**, and having found the physical causes of this first inequality and adapted them to the calculation for the theory of the **SUN**: by right and merit I here finish the **THIRD PART**, as if it were a morning’s task; lunch being served, with my Master sounding a rest for my mind:

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

THE THINGS WHICH were demonstrated in the third part pertain to all the planets; wherefore they may not unjustly be called the **KEY TO A DEEPER ASTRONOMY**. <note>original: "CLAVIS ASTRONOMIÆ PENITIORIS"</note> We ought to rejoice all the more that this has been found, as it is certain that it could have been investigated by no other means except through the observations of the star **MARS**. For even though **PTOLEMY** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer whose Earth-centered model Kepler was refining.</note> detected this bisection of the eccentricity <note>The "bisection of eccentricity" refers to the discovery that the center of a planet's uniform motion (the equant) is a different point from the center of its circular orbit.</note> of the **SUN** in **VENUS** and **MERCURY** too—and for that reason introduced "eccentrics of eccentrics," or what is the same thing, the gyrations of the center of an epicycle (the demonstration of which is reserved for the specific treatises on these **PLANETS**) —yet the condition of the observations themselves, and the brief elongations of **VENUS** from the **SUN** (which do not allow her to be observed at night except when low in the sky), would have brought much hindrance to a methodical inquiry into this matter if it had stopped short of **MARS**. In the case of **MERCURY**, these things were attempted with even more absurdity; because he very rarely emerges from the rays of the **SUN**, and is further from the **EARTH** than **MARS** and **VENUS**, since these latter appear to be the nearest. Thus, truth would have had to be tracked down by us, along with **PTOLEMY**, in the most open fields, and felt out by hand, as it were, through thick shadows.

How much we owe to this common second <note>The Latin text reads "fecundæ" (fruitful), but in the context of astronomical theory, Kepler is referring to the "secundæ" (second) inequality—the component of a planet's motion caused by the Earth's movement.</note> inequality (found in the third part) concerning the **FIRST INEQUALITY** <note>The "first inequality" refers to a planet's actual speeding up and slowing down in its own orbit, distinct from the "second inequality" which is just an optical effect of our viewing position on Earth.</note>—which occurs by occasion of the eccentric and is proper to each **PLANET**—shall now be declared by the example of the star **MARS**.

<summary>Kepler identifies his discoveries regarding Mars as the "Key to a Deeper Astronomy," arguing that Mars was the only planet that allowed for such a precise breakthrough due to the observational difficulties associated with Venus and Mercury.</summary>

P A R T  F O U R.

## C H A P T E R  X L I.

### An investigation of the apsides, eccentricity, and the proportion of the orbits attempted from the observations already used, outside of opposition with the SUN, though under a false condition. <note>Kepler specifies a "false condition" because he is testing the assumption that the orbit of Mars is a perfect circle, an assumption he will eventually disprove.</note>

IN PART TWO, following the example of the ancients, I attempted to find the aphelion <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> and the eccentricity <note>The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> from acronychal observations <note>term: acronychal observations; observations made when a planet is exactly opposite the Sun in the sky, rising as the Sun sets.</note>, and together with these, the distances of the star MARS from the SUN throughout its entire circuit. And indeed, the equations of the eccentric <note>The mathematical corrections used to account for the non-uniform speed of a planet.</note> corresponded well enough with other observations made outside of the acronychal position. However, the eccentricity and the distances from the SUN were rejected by the annual parallaxes <note>The apparent shift in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own motion around the Sun.</note> of longitude and latitude. Therefore, so that the distances of the star from the center of the SUN could be investigated through the whole extent of the eccentric, the second inequality (the epicyclic one in PTOLEMY, or that of the ANNUAL ORBIT in TYCHO and COPERNICUS) had to be dealt with first in Part Three. Nay, if the path of the PLANET were a perfect circle, the first inequality of the PLANET (which is by reason of the eccentric) could have been investigated right away. For above in Chapter 25, we provided a method to investigate the position and size of a circle relative to a point inside it—its center, eccentricity, and apsides—from three distances of three points on the circumference from that point, and the angles at that point.

Now, in Chapter 26, the distance of MARS from the center of the SUN was found to be 147,750 <note>Kepler uses a scale where the Earth-Sun distance is roughly 100,000 units.</note> at 14° 21' Taurus [♉] near the node <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>, on October 25, 1595. In Chapter 25 again, the distance of MARS was found to be 163,100—slightly less—at 5° 25' 20" Libra [♎], on December 31, 1590. And because Mars is 41 degrees away from the node, the sine of 41° multiplied by the sine of the maximum inclination found in Chapter 13 yields a local inclination of 1° 12' 40". Its secant <note>A trigonometric function used here to calculate the diagonal distance from the Sun to Mars, rather than just the flat distance projected onto the ecliptic plane.</note> exceeds the radius by 22 parts out of 100,000, which in our measure is 34 parts. Thus the corrected distance of this position would be 163,134, slightly less. Let it remain 163,100. However, the secant of this inclination multiplied by the secant of 41 produces a secant of an arc longer by 50". Therefore, 50" must be subtracted from the position of MARS so that it is 5° 24' 30" Libra [♎].

Thirdly, in Chapter 28, the distance of MARS was found to be 166,180 at 8° 19' 20" Scorpio [♏] on October 31, 1590, being 68 degrees from the node. Thus the inclination of the place is 1° 42' 40", the secant of which exceeds by 45 parts, which in our measure is 75. Thus the corrected distance is 166,255. 16" are subtracted from the position of MARS for reduction to the ecliptic <note>Adjusting the planet's position on its tilted orbit to the standard coordinate system of the Earth's orbital plane.</note>.

These three positions, reduced to the same year 1590 and the month of October by the precession of the equinoxes <note>The slow, constant shift in the orientation of Earth's axis that changes celestial coordinates over time.</note>, are as follows:

ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS
<meta>Catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER 41.</margin>
It appears that the aphelion <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> is closer to the eighth degree of Virgo than to others, because its distance there is longer. Therefore, according to what was demonstrated in chapter 25, *let $\alpha$ be the center of the SOLAR body. From it, let $\alpha\vartheta, \alpha n, \alpha \chi$ be drawn in that proportion as the distances are produced here in numbers: and let all the points be connected. And let the angle $\chi\alpha\vartheta$ be $114^\circ 2' 12''$, which is the distance from $14^\circ$ Aries to $8^\circ$ Virgo. Likewise, let $\chi\alpha n$ be $27^\circ 5' 17''$, which is the distance from $8^\circ$ Virgo to $1^\circ$ Libra; and $n\alpha\vartheta$ is composed of both. For the SUN is assumed to be the center of the zodiac.*

->*Now it is necessary to investigate the circle,*<-
->*which passes through $n, \chi, \vartheta$: so that $n, \chi, \vartheta$ are three*<-
->*locations of the PLANET.*<-

In the PTOLEMAIC form, $\alpha$ will be the EARTH, the center of the zodiac: $n, \chi, \vartheta$ are the three locations for the attachment point of the epicycle. The rest remain the same.

Therefore, in the triangle $n\alpha\vartheta$, with the angle and sides given, the angle $\alpha\vartheta n$ is found to be $20^\circ 26' 13''$. Similarly, in $\chi\alpha\vartheta$, the angle $\alpha\vartheta\chi$ is given as $35^\circ 16' 17''$. When $\alpha\vartheta n$ is subtracted from this, it leaves $n\vartheta\chi$ as $14^\circ 44' 4''$. Let $\gamma$ be the center of the sought circle. Let the line $\gamma \epsilon$ be drawn from it and continued to $\epsilon$, the aphelion, and $\delta$, the perihelium <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun.</note>: and let $n$ and $\chi$ be connected with $\gamma$.

Since, therefore, the angle $n\vartheta\chi$ stands at the circumference, and $n\gamma\chi$ is at the center, over the same arc $n\chi$, then $n\gamma\chi$ will be double the angle $n\vartheta\chi$, namely $29^\circ 28' 8''$. And in a system where $n\gamma$ is $100,000$, $n\chi$ will be $50,868$—which is double the sine of half the angle $n\gamma\chi$.

Now, in the triangle $n\alpha\chi$, with the angle and sides again given, $\chi n\alpha$ is found to be $78^\circ 44' 1''$. Through this, $\chi n$ is found to be $77,187$, where $n\alpha$ is $163,100$. Therefore, in the system where $\chi n$ was previously $50,868$ and $n\gamma$ was $100,000$, $n\alpha$ becomes $107,486$. And because $n\gamma\chi$ is $29^\circ 28' 8''$, $\chi n\gamma$ will be half the remainder of $180^\circ$ (two right angles), because $n\gamma$ and $\chi\gamma$ are equal <note>As radii of the same circle.</note>. Thus $\chi n\gamma$ is $75^\circ 15' 56''$. From this, subtract $\chi n\alpha$. The remainder is $\gamma n\alpha$.

In the triangle $\gamma n \alpha$, therefore, the angle and the sides are given. From this, $n\alpha\gamma$ is known to be $38^\circ 15' 45''$. And because of this (since $\alpha n$ is at $1^\circ 24' 21''$ Libra), the line of apsides <note>term: line of apsides; the line passing through the center of the orbit, the Sun, the aphelion, and the perihelion.</note> $\alpha\gamma$ will be at $27^\circ 8' 36''$ Libra. Through the angle $n\alpha\gamma$, the eccentricity <note>The distance between the center of the Sun and the center of the orbit.</note> $\alpha\gamma$ is also found to be $9,768$, where $n\gamma$ is $100,000$. Finally, in the measurement where $\alpha n$ is $163,100$, $n\gamma$ will be $151,740$. However, the semi-diameter of the annual orbit <note>Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> was also $100,000$ parts. Thus, the proportion of the orbits would be as $100,000$ to $151,740$.

You will gather how faulty <note>original: "vitiosa"</note> all this is from the fact that whenever you use another distance in place of one or more of the used distances $\alpha\vartheta, \alpha n, \alpha\chi$ (distances that belong to another place on the eccentric) and find it by an equally certain and irrefutable argument, all these results come out differently every time.

And in the following chapter, that which is roughly $100,000$ to $152,640$ will be found with complete certainty. The eccentricity is $9,264$ where the radius is $100,000$. The aphelion in the year 1590, on the 31st of October, was found above in chapter 16 to be in the 28th degree and 53rd minute of Leo, which will be confirmed in the following chapter within 11 minutes of arc.

PART FOUR.

## CHAPTER XLII.

### To seek the most certain location of the aphelion, the correction of the mean motion, the genuine eccentricity, and the proportion of the orbits, through several observations outside of the acronychal position, with MARS being near aphelion, and likewise several others with MARS near perihelion.

**N**ow you have seen, reader, that we must begin anew: for you saw that the three eccentric positions of Mars, and just as many distances from the Sun brought under the law of the circle, denied the aphelion <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> (which was established above with no small certainty). From this, a suspicion arose in us that the path of the PLANET is not a circle. Therefore, the remaining distances cannot be learned from any three. Thus, the distance of any given position must be constructed from its own specific observations—most of all the aphelia and perihelia <note>The points furthest from and closest to the Sun, respectively.</note>, from the comparison of which we learn about the genuine <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>.

Let $\alpha$ be the center of the world, $\alpha\beta$ the <term>line of apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit.</note>, and the eccentric circle be centered at $\beta$: $\iota$ is the aphelion, and $\vartheta$ is the perihelion. From chapter 41, and even better from chapter 16, we understand that when MARS was near $\iota$, the nearest observations were these:

I. In the Year 1585, on the 17th of February at 10:00, the PLANET was seen at $15^\circ 12' 30''$ of Leo, with a Northern latitude of $4^\circ 16'$.

II. In the Year 1586, on the 27th of December at 4:00 in the morning, it was at $29^\circ 42' 40''$ of Virgo, with a latitude of $2^\circ 46' 36''$ North.

And in the Year 1587, on the 1st of January at 7:08 in the morning, it was at $1^\circ 4' 36''$ of Libra, with a latitude of $2^\circ 54'$ North. And on the 9th of January in the morning, it was at $2^\circ 51' 30''$ of Libra, with a latitude of $3^\circ 6'$ North.

In the Year 1588, on the 10th of November at 6:30 in the morning, the distance between Mars and <note>original: "Cor ♌"</note> Regulus (the Heart of the Lion) was $31^\circ 27'$. The Northern declination of MARS was $3^\circ 16' 15''$. Therefore, Mars was at $25^\circ 31'$ of Virgo, with a latitude of $1^\circ$.

<margin>CHAPTER XLII.</margin> North latitude 1° 46' 43" B. <note>Kepler uses 'B' for 'Borea' (North) and 'D' for 'Dextra' or 'Descendens'.</note> On the 5th of December in the morning at 6:00: between Mars and the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "Cor Leonis"; the star Regulus</note> 45° 17'. Southern declination 2° 5'. Therefore Mars was in 9° 19 1/2' of Libra; latitude 1° 53 1/2' North. However, these observations are not confirmed by the following fixed stars.

In the Year 1590, on the 6th of October, at 4:45 in the morning, Mars was observed at an altitude of 12 1/2 degrees from the Tail of the Lion <note>original: "cauda Leonis"; the star Denebola</note> and the Heart of the Hydra <note>original: "corde Hydræ"; the star Alphard</note>, with its declination. But because neither of the fixed stars was aligned in a straight line in longitude from MARS, it happened that the <term>right ascensions</term> <note>The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note>, constructed from both sides and through the declination, differed by 6 minutes. This can easily happen if the declination is off by even the smallest amount. Indeed, the observers seem not to have fully trusted the declination, as they measured MARS from the Tail of the Lion, which is at the same longitude, with the entire distance extending in latitude, so that they might know the latitude of MARS more certainly from this than from the declination. But retaining the declination of Mars at 14° and the distance from the Heart of the Hydra at 34° 33 1/2', its right ascension would be 168° 56 1/4'. Thus the position is 17° 16 1/2' of Virgo; latitude 1° 16 2/3' North. The table of <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes stars appear higher than they are.</note> for fixed stars shows 4 minutes at this altitude; the refraction table for the SUN shows more. And Virgo rises steeply. Therefore, it must be projected about 3 minutes further forward (or a bit more according to the solar refractions) into the succeeding signs, to where it was displaced from by refraction. The <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations.</note> was very small. It therefore subtracted little from the refractions. Let it be in 17° 20' of Virgo.

In the Year 1600, March 5/15 at 8:30 PM: in 29° 12 1/2' of Cancer. Latitude 3° 23' North. And March 6/16 at 8:15 PM: in 29° 18 5/6' of Cancer; latitude 3° 19 3/4' North.

The method for reducing the observations to the proper times is this: Since in the Year 1587 the daily motions of MARS are decreasing, as appears both in Maginus <note>Giovanni Paolo Magini, an Italian astronomer and contemporary of Kepler.</note> and in the observation itself over three days, I have used the daily motions thus: 17, 16, 16, 16, 15, 15, 14, 14, 13, 13, 13, 12, 12.

In the Year 1588, on the 10th of November, the observation is 39 minutes less than Maginus’s position at the meridian. On the 5th of December, it is 33 minutes less. And our moment is in between. Therefore, we will also use the intermediate difference of 36.

In the Year 1590, the observation was neglected and was in itself poorly handled, as appeared; however, the daily motion in Maginus is constant at 37 minutes over several days.

# PART FOUR

CHAPTER XLII.
</margin>

On July 17, [Mars] was more advanced in the calculation by about 1° 16' than in the tables of Magini. Now, on September 26, it is still more advanced by 0° 53'. Thus, in 70 days, the difference decreased by about 23 minutes. If we also argue proportionally, on September 19, this difference will be larger by about 2 minutes. Therefore, we believe that Mars at our hour was at 14° 20' Pisces.

In the year 1594, Mars moves away from its station <note>The point where a planet appears to stop moving against the stars before reversing direction</note>. And since on July 30, at the following midnight, the position of Mars differs from Magini's meridian by 3° 25' 1/2, and on August 10 by 3° 59' 1/2—so that the difference increases, though gradually less and less—I assumed the difference on August 6 to be 3° 46', so that it is at 1:15 AM after the following midnight at 16° 52' Pisces, with a daily motion of 10 minutes. Our time is ahead by 8 hours and 30 minutes, to which about 4 minutes of Mars's retrograde motion are due. Therefore, at our time, it was at 16° 56' Pisces. It is certain that (on this account at least) we do not stray more than one minute <note>original: "scrupulum"</note> one way or the other.

He was not observed more often in <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where the planet is closest to the Earth</note>. For in the year 1595, his arrival in perigee fell in the middle of summer, with the twilight lasting through the night in Denmark <note>Making precise nighttime observations impossible</note>. In the year 1597, Tycho Brahe was on a journey. Near the Sun, however, the planet lies hidden for a long time in the winter semicircle, due to a speed not much less than the Sun's.

Let the eccentric position of Mars be $\vartheta$ in the diagram. Let the positions of the Earth be $\zeta, \mu, \eta$.

| | $\zeta$ | $\mu$ | $\eta$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

Now, therefore, the positions of $\alpha \vartheta$ have been made too close to each other, and there is more error here in being too close than there was before in being too far. Wherefore, the truest length of $\alpha \vartheta$ will be about 138,430.

The plane here is inclined (as also before at the opposite location) by 1° 48', and the secant exceeds the radius by 49 units. As 100,000 is to 138,420, so these 49 are to 68. Therefore, the corrected length of the radius is very nearly 138,500, derived from these far-reaching observations.

<margin>CHAPTER LXII.</margin>

Previously, however, we similarly took an observation from the year 1588, on the 22nd day of November, at 9 hours, 11½ minutes, at 29° 26' 12" Leo.

Since, therefore, from the year 1588 on November 22 at 9:11½ to the year 1589 on November 1 at 6:10, there are 344 days minus 2 hours and 52½ minutes; and a full revolution relative to the same fixed star <note>A sidereal year, or the time it takes for the planet to return to the same position relative to the stars</note> takes 686 days minus 28 minutes: it is clear that our interval is just a few hours short of half the return time. Behold:

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 343 Days | 11 Hours | 46 Minutes | Half period |
| 343 Days | 21 Hours | 52½ Minutes | * Our interval |
| **Excess** | **10** | **6½** | |

---

And since from the location of the previous time (29° 26' 12" Leo) to the location Mars held at the later time (29° 54' 53" Aquarius), there are 180° 34' 41"; and after subtracting 48" for <term>precession</term> <note>The very slow shifting of the stars' positions due to the Earth's wobbling axis</note>, the remainder is 180° 33' 53". Therefore, if those 10 hours and 6½ minutes corresponded to the daily motion of Mars on its <term>eccentric</term> <note>An orbital path whose center is not the Sun</note> near its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun</note>, then these remaining 33' 53" above a half-circle would imply that the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun</note> is at 29 degrees, 20 minutes, 12 seconds of Leo.

We know, however, the daily motions of Mars on the eccentric around the <term>apogee</term> and <term>perigee</term> from the distances already found, and from what was demonstrated in Chapter XXXII. For the daily motions are very nearly in double proportion to the distances <note>An earlier rule Kepler used: if a planet is twice as far, it moves half as fast, though he later refined this</note>. For at apogee, the daily motion is about 26' 13", and at perigee, it is 38' 2", while the average daily motion is 31' 27".

Consider then, that if Mars, moving from the point of apogee, takes half of its return time, it would be at the point of perigee at the end of this time, having completed exactly 180 degrees. But if this span of time is considered to begin one day after it was at apogee, it will therefore begin its course 26' 13" away from apogee and finish at 180° 38' 2". Thus, in half the time, it will run more than half the path by 11' 49". The opposite would happen if it began one day before apogee.

Since our time interval has also shown a larger arc, our <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun</note> must also be moved forward. Then the PLANET would have begun at 5 minutes 16 seconds before the aphelion—which is thus placed at 29° 25' 28" Leo—and arrived at 8 minutes 1 second after the perihelion, a distance of travel of 13 minutes 17 seconds beyond 180 degrees. But it was discovered that the journey was 33 minutes 53 seconds above 180 degrees. Therefore, it is still faster by 20 minutes 36 seconds. Since one day is required to increase the journey by 11 minutes 49 seconds, or a movement of the PLANET from the aphelion by 26 minutes 13 seconds, how much will the PLANET be moved from the aphelion until the journey is increased by 20 minutes 36 seconds?

And so the rule of proportions shows 1 day, 17 hours, 54 minutes, or a distance from the aphelion of 45 minutes 42 seconds. Therefore, the aphelion must be moved backward <note>original: "in antecedentia" — in the direction opposite the signs of the zodiac</note> by 45 minutes 42 seconds from the location we had just given it at 29° 25' 28" Leo. It is uncertain which investigation of the aphelion should be given more trust. For it could easily happen that, in the positioning and assumption of the lines $\alpha\iota$ and $\alpha\vartheta$, we have erred by 4 minutes due to the difficulties of the observations—two minutes here and two there—which is enough to accumulate from conspiring errors so that the aphelion could be altered by 11 minutes. Here, however, it is right for us to trust the present operation.

### Correction of the mean motion

Once the location of the aphelion is changed, the <term>mean motion</term> <note>The theoretical average speed of the planet if its orbit were a perfect circle</note> is also changed. For if at the time when, by the previous investigation of the aphelion, Mars <note>original: ♂</note> is thought to fall into the aphelion, stripped of its <term>equation</term> <note>The mathematical correction used to adjust the "average" position to the "actual" observed position</note>, it has at that same time already passed the aphelion by 11 minutes; it therefore has a subtractive equation of 4 minutes. And so, by its mean motion, it has passed that former mean location by 4.

### Investigation of the eccentricity

First, let the distances previously found be corrected if necessary, on the grounds that they may differ slightly from the <term>apsides</term> <note>The two points—aphelion and perihelion—where the planet is at its maximum and minimum distance from the Sun</note> just found: the aphelia by 40 minutes, the perihelia by 75 minutes. And yet, nothing changes noticeably at such close proximity to the apsides.

The difference is 18, which is clearly of no importance. You see how precisely the eccentricity of the <term>equant point</term> <note>An imaginary point used in ancient astronomy to account for the observed changes in a planet's speed</note> must be bisected in MARS to establish the distance between the center of the eccentric and the center of the world [the Sun]. And this I took up as a foundation above in Chapter 32, and deferred its demonstration to what followed. That has now indeed been performed.

# CHAPTER 43.

## Concerning the deficiency of the equations, which are constructed by the bisection of the eccentricity and by triangular areas; assuming the orbit of the PLANET is perfectly circular.

Having most certainly demonstrated these points concerning the bisection of the eccentricity of MARS—which we likewise proved in the third part regarding the theory of the SUN—it would now finally be time that, fortified by full confidence in this matter, we should proceed to the physical speculations of chapter 32 and those following, as these will be common to all PLANETS. Had it not seemed right to me, by a specific plan, to put those first, it was because in that place the method for calculating <term>equations</term> <note>In historical astronomy, an "equation" is the difference between a planet's average position and its actual position as seen from Earth.</note> from physical causes had to be completed for the theory of the SUN or the EARTH with every kind of perfection. I also knew that when that **METHOD** of establishing equations had to be applied to the theory of MARS, much more difficult speculations would follow.

For once the truest shape of the orbits has been found, it is necessary that the equations of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>An off-center circle used to explain why planets seem to speed up and slow down.</note> follow from that same source; until now, those equations have only served the "vicarious hypothesis" investigated in chapter 16. We shall, therefore, explore this on this occasion.

Therefore, according to the things demonstrated in chapter 40 (all of which are to be understood as repeated here individually), let the orbit of the PLANET be a circle according to common opinion, even though chapter 41 has already commanded us to doubt it: *Therefore, at an <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>An angle used to define the position of a planet along its circular path as measured from the center of that circle.</note> of 90°, the eccentricity of 9264 found in chapter 42 will be the tangent; this will show the <term>optical part of the equation</term> <note>The component of the planet's movement that is an optical illusion caused by the observer's position being off-center.</note> as 5° 17' 34". And because at an eccentric anomaly of 90° the area of the triangle is right-angled, by multiplying the radius by half the eccentricity (namely 4632), the area of the triangle results in 463,200,000. As the area of the circle (31,415,926,536) is to 180 degrees (or 1,296,000 seconds), so is this newly found area of 463,200,000 to 19,108, or 5° 18' 28", which is the <term>physical part of the equation</term> <note>The component of movement caused by the planet's actual physical acceleration or deceleration.</note>. Thus, the total equation is 10° 36' 2", so that a <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The hypothetical position of a planet if it moved at a constant speed.</note> of 95° 18' 28" corresponds to an adjusted anomaly of 84° 42' 26". But according to the* **METHOD** *of chapter 18, the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> <note>Kepler’s highly accurate but purely mathematical model that predicted Mars's position without yet knowing the physical shape of the orbit.</note> (reliable enough in longitude) shows us that for the same mean anomaly of 95° 18' 28", the adjusted anomaly should be 84° 42' 2". The difference is 24".*

*Let us now take our eccentric anomaly at 45° and 135°. And as the whole sine is to the sines of these angles, so is the area of 19,108 (from the maximum equating triangle) to the area of this place, 13,512 or 3° 45' 12". And so, since it is certain that to our vicarious [hypothesis]*

...that so great an error could not be attributed to [chance], it was necessary for me to believe that this method of equating is even now imperfect.

And indeed, in Chapter 19, when I attempted the bisection in the case of **MARS**, and calculated the <term>equations</term> <note>In historical astronomy, an "equation" is the difference between a planet's average position and its actual position as seen from Earth.</note> through an immobile point of the <term>equant</term> <note>A mathematical point used by Ptolemy to account for the observed speeding up and slowing down of planets.</note> in the **PTOLEMAIC** manner, a difference of about 45' was found at the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle used to define a planet's position along its circular path.</note>—almost as great, yet in the opposite direction. For in the upper quadrant, the **PLANET** approached the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> more than was right, and in the lower quadrant it approached the <term>perihelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note> more than was right; here, in the upper quadrant, it departs further from the aphelion, and in the lower from the perihelion, than is right. Thus, above the aphelion it is too fast, and below the perihelion likewise. Therefore, it will be slower than is right in the middle longitudes <note>The "middle longitudes" refers to the parts of the orbit halfway between the closest and furthest points from the Sun.</note>.

<margin>Refutation of false causes for this imperfection.</margin>
I believe it has now occurred to the reader whether perhaps the cause of the errors is that which was mentioned in Chapter 40: that a flaw underlies this operation using areas, because areas are not exactly equivalent to distances, which govern the speed and the <term>delays</term> <note>The "mora" or delay is the amount of time a planet spends in a specific part of its orbit.</note>. Yet the present error cannot arise from this. First, the excess of the sum of the distances over the area of the circle is small—namely, the tiny space between the <term>conchoids</term> <note>A shell-like geometric curve; Kepler is comparing the shape of the orbit's path to a circle.</note> is very small. Second, the area indeed represents all distances as shorter than is right, especially those in the middle longitudes. Therefore, if any error flows from this, it is in the fact that we do not make the **PLANET’S** delays long enough in the middle longitudes. But the errors we have now detected go in the opposite direction: for we have made the **PLANET’S** delays too long in the middle longitudes.

The same can be objected against anyone who wishes to conceive a suspicion that, having dismissed the double <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used by Copernicus to explain non-circular motion.</note> of **COPERNICUS** and **TYCHO** (which makes the **PLANET’S** orbit oval), we have for the present adopted the perfect **PTOLEMAIC** circle. For it was stated at the end of Chapter 4, that the **COPERNICAN** orbit does not curve inward toward the center (which would be of use to us here), but curves outward from the center by 246 units, which would here rather increase the error, since we are now following the rule that delays are as the distances.

<margin>Estimation of the space between the two conchoids.</margin>
In order that the very small space of the conchoid in Chapter 40 might be visible to the eye, consider that the <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric ratio representing the distance from the center of a circle through a point on its edge.</note> of the angle 5° 19' (the maximum optical equation) is 100432, namely the line E A. From this excess of 432, therefore, which is the little line B A (a part of the line E A), we can almost learn the accumulation of all these excesses—consider Q A, R B, A B, S A, L A—in this manner.

<margin>A shortcut for summing the sines quickly.</margin>

*Therefore, if all our remaining excesses from the maximum 432 were as the sines on both sides of the semicircle to the semidiameter, then as 100,000 is to the sum of the secant and tangent of the 89th degree (namely to 11,458,869), so 432 would be to 49,934, the sum*

By what proportion the excesses of the distances of the points of the circle from the eccentric point grow, or the width of the space between the conchoids <note>A "conchoid" is a specific type of geometric curve; Kepler uses this term to describe the non-circular, "shell-like" path he is starting to observe.</note>.

...[the sum] of nearly all the excesses for every degree of the semicircle. *For by as much as the excesses of the distances in the upper quadrant are longer than these secant excesses, by just as much are they nearly shorter in the lower quadrant.*

However, the excesses $QA, RA, SA, etc.$ are not yet related to each other as the <term>sines</term> <note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of a side of a right triangle to the hypotenuse; in Kepler's time, these were calculated as lengths within a circle of a fixed radius, usually 100,000.</note> of various degrees are; rather, they roughly follow a double proportion of sines. *As the sine of 90 degrees is double the sine of 30 degrees.* Already the <term>Optical equation</term> <note>The adjustment to the planet's position required because we view it from a specific point (the Sun or Earth) rather than the center of its orbit.</note> for 90 degrees is $5^\circ 19'$. Half of its sine gives an arc that is also nearly half of the former, namely $2^\circ 39' 15''$ for the Optical equation of an <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle measured from the center of the orbit used to locate the planet's position on its path.</note> of $30^\circ$, whose <term>secant</term> <note>A geometric line starting from the center and cutting through the circle to a tangent line; here it measures the distance from the Sun to the planet's position on its circular path.</note> is 100107. And this 107—the excess of the secant over the total sine <note>original: "sinum rectum"; here meaning the radius of 100,000.</note>—is nearly a fourth part of the former 432; whereas the sine of 30 degrees was half of the sine of 90 degrees. Let some Geometer see whether this proposition is demonstrable. For me, it suffices for the present that the smallest details with which I am occupied are answered.

Therefore, parts are accumulated up to 432 that are not proportional to the sines, but are always smaller; at 45 degrees or thereabouts, they are only halves; before that, less than half; so that around 30 degrees they are only quarters, and finally they become imperceptible.

Thus (as experience testifies, having calculated all distances individually and cast them into one sum), from a total sum of 49,934 we retain only a seventh part, which is about 7,000.

And because one distance of 100,000 is worth 60 minutes <note>Kepler is converting linear distance units into angular measurements of arc on the sky.</note>, no more than $4\frac{1}{5}$ minutes will be due to this small sum. Of these, however, some portion is scattered throughout the entire circuit; so that this tiny error around $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$, where it is greatest, becomes imperceptible even in **MARS**.

Wherefore we must seek another cause for this discrepancy.
