But if anyone should wish to attribute this difference to the slippery luck of observation, that person surely cannot have attended to or perceived the force of the demonstrations used so far; and they will impute to me a most wicked fraud of grossly corrupted observations by **BRAHE**. Therefore, I appeal to the observations of the following years, provided that skilled observers perform them. For if I have indulged my own desire on one side, it will grow into a much greater error on the other side. But there is no need for this. It is to you I speak, experts in astronomical matters, who know that the sophistical excuses so common in other disciplines are open to no one in astronomy. I call upon you. You see in $\kappa$ a small defect from the circle; in $n$ and $\vartheta$, on both sides indeed, a very large one—so large that we cannot excuse it by the uncertainty of observation (for which I put about 200 or at most 300 units in doubt in Chapter 42).

What then is to be said? Is this what was said above in Chapter 6: that by shifting assumptions from the mean to the apparent motion of the **SUN**, another eccentric is established which exceeds on the side of the Sun's apogee? Not at all. For by as much as it exceeds here, it approaches there. Here, however, you see on both sides the **PLANET** approaching the center from its circular orbit. This is attested to by many other observations, some of which follow in Chapters 51 and 53.

Therefore, it is clearly this: The orbit of the **PLANET** is not a circle, but entering inward on both sides little by little, and returning again to the width of a circle at the peri- <note>original: "in peri-" — the text continues on the next page, likely as "perihelion" or "perigee."</note>

<margin>
Second argument.

...exiting at the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the central body.</note>. They call this type of travel path an **oval**.

And this same point is also proven from the preceding Chapter 44. In that chapter, it was established that the area of a perfect <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the Sun is not at the exact center.</note> is approximately equivalent to all the distances from the source of motive power <note>The Sun</note> for any number of equal parts of that eccentric circumference; thus, the parts of the area measure the "delays" <note>The time spent</note> which the **PLANET** spends in the corresponding parts of the eccentric circumference. Therefore, if that plane, around which the **PLANET** marks its limit, is not a perfect circle, but is narrowed at the sides from the width it possesses at the line of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the points of greatest and least distance from the Sun.</note>; and yet this plane, bounded by an irregular orbit, still measures the delays which the **PLANET** makes in its whole circuit and in its equal parts: then the narrowed plane measures an equal amount of time as the previous, non-narrowed plane. Consequently, the parts of the narrowed plane nearest the <term>aphelion</term> and <term>perihelion</term> <note>The points furthest from and closest to the Sun, respectively.</note> will measure a greater time, because the narrowing there is slight; but the parts in the middle longitudes will measure less time than before, because the greatest narrowing of the whole plane occurs there. Now, if we use this narrowed plane to regulate the <term>equations</term> <note>The mathematical corrections used to determine the planet's position.</note>, the **PLANET** will become slower around the aphelion and perihelion than in the previous faulty form of the equations, and faster around the middle longitudes, because the distances here are reduced. Thus, the delays subtracted from here toward the aphelion and perihelion—after a compensation is made upward and downward—will be accumulated, just as if someone were to squeeze a fat sausage in the middle; by that compression, the stuffed filling is squeezed out from the belly and forced toward both ends, which protrude above and below the hand.

But if opposites are cured by opposites <note>original: "contraria contrariis medentur," a classic medical principle</note>, this is clearly the most suitable medicine for purging the defects with which our Physical hypothesis was found to labor in Chapter 44 above. For the **PLANET** will be faster in the middle longitudes, where it was previously found to be slower than was right; and it will be slowed down above and below near the apsides, where previously its excessive speed harmed the equations, which were overflowing into the "eighths of the times" <note>Small segments of the orbital period where Kepler's previous models failed.</note>.

This, therefore, is the second argument by which it is demonstrated that the orbit of the **PLANET** most truly deviates from the established circle, and moves inward at the sides toward the center of the eccentric.

Moreover, this argument was not of such great importance to me that I could think of the **PLANET’S** deviation based on it alone. For having sweated a very long time in reconciling the equations of this form, and being finally deterred by the absurdity of the measurement, I abandoned the whole business—until I was taught about the deviation by the distances, in the manner done in Chapter 41. Afterward, I took up this business of the equations again.

**AND** from this also it is demonstrated, as I promised I would do above in Chapters 20 and 23: that the orbit of the **PLANET** is not a circle, but of an **oval** figure.

## On the natural causes of this deflection of the PLANET from the circle: the first opinion examined.

<margin>CHAPTER XLV.</margin>

AS SOON AS I was taught in this manner by the most certain observations of BRAHE <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used.</note> that the Orbit of the **PLANET** is not exactly circular but fails at the sides; I immediately thought I knew the natural cause of this deflection. For I had exercised myself intensely on this subject in Chapter XXXIX. And I advise the reader, before proceeding further here, to diligently read through that entire chapter again. For since in that chapter I had attributed the cause of the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> to some power which resided in the body of the **PLANET**; it followed that the cause of this deflection from the eccentric circle should also be attributed to that same body of the **PLANET**. However, it happened to me as they say in the proverb: *the hasty bitch brings forth blind pups.* <note>original: "canem festinum cæcos parere catulos." A proverb meaning that haste leads to errors or incomplete results.</note> For since I had labored intensely on that matter in Chapter XXXIX, because I could not state a sufficiently probable cause for why a perfect circle was made from the **PLANET'S** orbit (for certain absurdities always had to be attributed to that power which has its seat in the body of the **PLANET**); now having discovered from **OBSERVATIONS** that the **PLANET'S** orbit is not perfectly circular, I immediately yielded to a great impulse of persuasion. I came to believe that those things which were called "absurd" in Chapter XXXIX for the purpose of constructing a circle, once transformed into a more probable form, would result in a just orbit for the **PLANET** that was consistent with the **OBSERVATIONS**. If I had proceeded along this path a little more considerately, I could have reached the truth of the matter immediately. But since I was blind with desire, and did not look back at each and every member of Chapter XXXIX, clinging to that thought which first offered itself—which was wonderfully probable due to the uniformity of the <term>epicyclic</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one; a common tool in older astronomy to explain complex motions.</note> motion—I fell into new labyrinths, from which we must struggle out in this Chapter XLV and the following ones up to the L.

*Let the diagram of Chapter XXXIX therefore be repeated. The poorer opinion in that chapter was that the **PLANET**, in order to describe a perfect circle, strives by an innate force to move in an epicycle, and thus unfolds its body from the ray of power emanating from the **SUN**: As if the ray of power from the **SUN** were AC, and it proceeded at an unequal pace from AC into AY, while the **PLANET** was initially at C. Since this "conspiracy" <note>original: "conspiratio," meaning the breathing together or agreement of different data points.</note> brought such an admirable force of persuasion, I immediately concluded that this inward movement of the **PLANET** at the sides happens because the power moving the **PLANET** (and managing the distances according to the law of the circle) anticipates the power of the **SUN**. However, the solar power, acting through its various degrees, would receive the **PLANET** across different intervals and promote it unequally—more slowly when it is high. The result would be that the distances of equal arcs of the epicycle would be "piled up" toward the aphelion $c$ and the <term>perihelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note> F, and would be more spread out around the middle longitudes. Thus, all the distances would be pulled "upward" (becoming shorter) from their proper proximity to the perihelion into the place of longer distances.

Thus, that error began to be confirmed in me—the one I had fortunately begun to refute above in Chapter 39: that it is the property of the **PLANETARY VIRTUE** <note>The internal force or "soul" Kepler initially thought guided the planet.</note> to lead the body of the **PLANET** around in the path of an epicycle.

## CHAPTER XLVI.

### How the line of the PLANET'S motion can be described, according to the opinion of chapter XLV, and what kind of line it is.

In the previous chapter, the cause was indeed stated by which it can happen that the **PLANET** deviates from a circular orbit: but the geometric drawing of the path cannot be carried out through that diagram. For the epicycle is inclined according to the length of the distances: however, the multitude and length of the distances in turn depend on the rotation of the epicycle. *And because the sum of the distances is contained in the plane of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the Sun is not at the center.</note>, as demonstrated in chapter XL; therefore, that sum cannot be found unless this epicycle is transformed into an eccentric. However, it was demonstrated in chapter II, and repeated in chapter XXXIX, and utilized in chapter XL, that if a concentric circle is drawn from center α with a radius equal to βδ itself, and an epicycle is drawn in it with radius αβ; then, an eccentric δη is drawn from center β with eccentricity αβ. Afterward, if the circumferences, both of the epicycle and of the eccentric δη, are divided into similar parts: the distances of the points of division (of both the epicycle and the eccentric) from the chosen point α will result in the same length on both sides. This being established—since in chapter XL, by the supposition of an eccentric, we provided an easy and plain demonstration and a method for computing distances—here too we can view the distances in the eccentric, even if we assume that they are managed by the uniform motion of the* **PLANET'S** *epicycle. In this way, the road seems open to us for the geometric description of the* **PLANETARY** *path, which follows from the hypothesis of chapter XLV. So much does the range of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one; here Kepler uses it to explain the planet's changing distance from the Sun.</note> make such departures from $\alpha$, as if it were describing equal arcs in equal times on the circumference of a perfect <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the center is not the same as the center of the Earth or Sun.</note> $\delta \lambda$ (let this be the semicircle defined by the straight line $\lambda \alpha \delta$): suppose these are $\delta \epsilon, \epsilon \zeta, \zeta \eta, \eta \theta, \theta \iota, \iota \kappa, \kappa \lambda$. These are drawn so that the angles at $\beta$ are equal, and $\beta$ is the point of equality in this specific case where distances are being sought. Let the points of division be connected with $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Therefore, this eccentric semicircle is purely fictitious, drawn only for the purpose of calculating a certain sum of distances. But if the **PLANET** were moved by the **SUN** with an equal degree of power both at $\delta$ and at $\lambda$—just as the epicyclic rotation itself is always assumed to strive for uniformity—then it would truly complete these equal parts of the eccentric (from which we took the distances) in equal times. Furthermore, the distances of the times marked by the signs of division would be these very lines $\alpha \delta, \alpha \epsilon, \alpha \zeta, \alpha \eta, \alpha \theta, \alpha \iota, \alpha \kappa, \alpha \lambda$, not only in their quantity but also in their identical positions. In a word, the Planet’s path would be the circle $\delta \eta \lambda$.

<margin>In this place, when we compute nothing but the distance $\alpha \epsilon$, which is $\alpha \mu$, the angle $\delta \beta \epsilon$ measures the time, whose genuine and physical measure is elsewhere the area $\delta \alpha \mu$, as will appear below.</margin>

But because the **PLANET** itself represents the named distances in terms of quantity (due to the uniform rotation of the epicycle), but is moved by the **SUN** unequally in equal times—less at $\delta$ and more at $\lambda$—it follows that in the time * marked and measured by the angle $\delta \beta \epsilon$, it does not complete the space $\delta \epsilon$. Nevertheless, it attains the length of the distance $\alpha \epsilon$. And in the time measured by the angle $\lambda \beta \kappa$ (which is equal to angle $\epsilon \beta \delta$), it completes more space than $\kappa \lambda$, yet it attains the length of distance $\alpha \kappa$. Therefore, the **PLANET** reaches the length of distance $\alpha \epsilon$ before it is truly moved to point $\epsilon$, and it reaches the length of distance $\alpha \kappa$ before it is moved to point $\kappa$. Conversely, by the time it is moved to $\epsilon$ or $\kappa$, the distance was already $\alpha \epsilon$ or $\alpha \kappa$, and because of this, the actual distance will now be somewhat shorter. The **PLANET**, therefore, at points $\epsilon, \kappa$, and all such markers, is closer to point $\alpha$ than to the circumference at $\epsilon, \kappa$. Thus, the **PLANET** moves inward from the established width of the circle $\delta \lambda$ toward a point near the center $\beta$, and it never falls upon this circle except at the points $\delta$ and $\lambda$. The logic for this inward movement is the same in the opposite semicircle.

Because, therefore, the plane <note>Kepler uses the word "plane" to mean the area of a sector of the orbit, which he discovered relates to the time the planet takes to travel.</note> $\delta \alpha \epsilon, \delta \alpha \zeta,$ etc., contains within itself the sum of all distances of the points on the arc of the epicycle (which is similar to arc $\delta \epsilon$ by Chapter 40), and since the Planet describes unequal arcs of its genuine path in equal times (now measured by $\delta \epsilon, \epsilon \zeta$)—short arcs when it is far from the **SUN** at $\alpha$, and long ones when it approaches close to the Sun—so that the arcs of the Planetary journey traversed in equal times are in the inverse proportion of the distances (per Chapter 32): it therefore generally happens that by as much as the area $\epsilon \alpha \delta$ exceeds the sector $\epsilon \beta \delta$ (the measure of which is angle $\epsilon \beta \delta$ or arc $\epsilon \delta$), by that much the arc $\epsilon \delta$ (here the measure of time) exceeds the arc of the completed journey, which we call $\mu \delta$.

Second, the aforementioned proportion is not perfectly geometric. For even if individual distances are in inverse proportion <note>original: "proportione conversâ"</note> to the individual arcs of the **PLANETARY** journey compared to the mean arcs, the proportion of the sum of several distances to the sum of as many mean distances does not remain the same as the inverse proportion of the sum of as many arcs to the sum of the mean arcs. You will see this in an example. Let there be two distances, 12 and 11, with the mean being 10; let the mean arc also be 10. It follows that as the distance 12 is to the mean distance 10, so the mean arc 10 is to the arc of distance 12, which is $8 \frac{1}{3}$. Likewise, as the distance 11 is to 10, so 10 is to an arc of $9 \frac{1}{11}$. Combine the distances 12 and 11 into one sum, which is 23. The sum of the two mean distances is 20. The sum of the two arcs is $17 \frac{14}{33}$. Here, 10 was indeed the <term>geometric mean</term> <note>original: "medium proportionale"; a value that represents the central tendency of a set of numbers using their product.</note> between 12 and $8 \frac{1}{3}$, and likewise between 11 and $9 \frac{1}{11}$. But now the sum 20 is not the geometric mean between 23 and $17 \frac{14}{33}$, but rather between 23 and $17 \frac{19}{23}$, which is larger.

However, this ratio holds true in an <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>original: "medietate Arithmetica"; the standard average found by adding numbers and dividing by the count.</note>. *For example*, let 10 be the arithmetic mean between 12 and 8; likewise between 11 and 9. Combine 12 and 11 to get 23; combine 8 and 9 to get 17. Therefore, 20 is again the arithmetic mean between 17 and 23. And since it was demonstrated in Chapter XXIX that there is a small difference between the arithmetic and geometric mean in this matter, it will therefore be very close to the truth, even though it is denied to be true in every respect here.

Third, even if the area $\epsilon\beta\delta$ were precisely the geometric mean between $\epsilon\alpha\delta$ and $\mu\beta\delta$, it still could not be established geometrically. For the sector $\epsilon\beta\mu$ ought to be equal to the triangle $\alpha\epsilon\beta$. But geometers still lack a method for cutting a given angle in a given proportion <note>This is a reference to what is now known as "Kepler's Equation," which relates the area of a sector to the angle at the center; it cannot be solved with a simple compass-and-straightedge construction.</note>.

<margin>
Is it necessary? <note>original: "Op.e?"</note>
A <term>sector</term> is properly a part of a circular plane cut off by two straight lines from the center. It is therefore used improperly for any plane other than one that is perfectly circular.
</margin>

Fourth, if none of the above hinders us, the circular sector $\mu\beta\delta$ is still not the same as the sector (so to speak) of an oval plane $\mu\beta\delta$. Thus, even if the arc $\mu\delta$ were defined as if on the circumference of a circle, nothing would follow from this regarding $\mu\delta$ as an arc of the **PLANET’S** journey, which is not a circle. Therefore, although this is a help to those who wish to use numbers—because they know that $\epsilon\beta\delta$ is the mean between $\epsilon\alpha\delta$ and $\mu\beta\delta$—for us, who seek a geometric path, no passage is open this way.

Therefore, we shall try **OTHER** things. In the true journey of the **PLANET**, the plane interjected between the arcs of the journey and the **SUN** is likewise truly the measure of the time in which the **PLANET** is engaged in the arc placed above it, according to Chapter XL. Therefore, let lines be projected from point $\alpha$ of the diameter, enclosing spaces equal to $\epsilon\beta\delta$ and $\zeta\beta\delta$ themselves: so that the space $\epsilon\eta\beta$, which departs from space $\epsilon\beta\delta$, is equal to space $\eta\alpha\beta$, which is added to the same $\epsilon\beta\delta$. Let these be $\alpha\mu, \alpha\nu$. And with center $\alpha$, at distances $\alpha\epsilon, \alpha\zeta$, let arcs $\epsilon\mu, \zeta\nu$ be drawn, intersecting these lines at $\mu$ and $\nu$. Would the points $\mu, \nu, o, \pi$, etc., drawn in this manner, then be correctly placed so that the **PLANET** reaches them in times $\delta\epsilon, \delta\zeta, \delta\eta, \delta\iota, \delta\kappa$? This is indeed very close to the truth; yet three things are still missing here. First, as above, the plane does not exactly equal the sum of the distances. ## CHAPTER XLVI.

...to cut from a given point of the diameter along a straight line, in a given proportion. Third, it is not known whether for any plane μ α δ, ν α δ, etc., it decreases in proportion due to the deflection of μ, ν from the circumference, as much as for the others in their own proportion. Nevertheless, even these things will be useful to those who, with the aid of numbers, wish to proceed by the smallest increments, contrary to the custom of Geometry.

<margin>A third attempt and method for describing the oval arising from Chapter XLV.</margin>
**SINCE THEREFORE** Geometry fails us; yet so that we may have some description of the line that arises for us from the speculation of chapter <term>XLV</term>; come, let us seek help from <term>lack of art</term> <note>original: "ατεχνία" (atechnia); Kepler means an empirical or non-geometric shortcut where rigorous proofs are currently unavailable.</note>, summoning our "vicar" <note>Kepler's "vicarious hypothesis" was an earlier model that predicted the planet's direction perfectly but failed on its distances.</note> from chapter <term>XVI</term>, which places the lines α μ, α ν, etc., in which the **PLANET** exists, at the correct times in the correct places of the zodiac; and let us blend it with this current fictitious eccentric δ θ λ, from which the speculation of chapter <term>XLV</term> is convinced that the correct lengths of the lines α ε, α ζ—that is, α μ, α ν—are drawn.

It is indeed pleasing, for the sake of clarity, to compare two other hypotheses with one another, fused into a single diagram—both indeed deceiving in some places, but each useful for investigating individual truths (as far as could be known until now): by which diagram many things said thus far are brought under a single view.

Let **A** be the center of the **EARTH** (*or* **SUN IN COPERNICUS**), **AI** the line of apsides <note>The axis connecting the farthest and closest points of the orbit.</note>, **AD** the eccentricity of the <term>equant point</term> <note>original: "puncti æquantis"; the point from which the planet's motion appears uniform in speed.</note>. *Although indeed in chapter* **XIX** *it was denied that point* **D** *could remain stable and* **AD** *remain the same: that is only to be understood if* **DA** *is bisected. But if the division of* **DA** *is left free to us, as in chapter* **XVI**, *then this point can remain stable.* Let **AD** therefore be divided in that proportion which was found in chapter <term>XVI</term>. Let the division be **C**, and **AC** 11,332, **CD** 7,232. And with center **G**, and a distance **CH** of 100,000, let the eccentric circle, marked with dots, be drawn through **H**. This, then, will be the hypothesis of chapter <term>XVI</term>. For having assumed any known angle of the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>original: "anomaliæ mediæ"; a measure of the time elapsed since the planet was at its farthest point.</note>, let a dotted straight line be drawn from **D**, the center of the equant, to the circumference; let this be **DH**, encompassing with the line of apsides the required angle, <margin>This is, in the vicarious hypothesis of chapter XVII, the proper measure of time; because in it, the point D of the equant is placed according to the opinion of the ancients.</margin> *namely, the measure of the proposed time. <margin>CHAPTER XLVI.</margin>
<margin>* This is true by reason of the shape, since the path of the Planet is not a circle, as was imagined here. But by reason of the position and the center B, it is not fictitious, but true: by which name it is opposed to the previous version described from center C; this one is described from B.</margin>
By bisecting at B, so that a truer eccentric *I L* may be written with center B, though it is not a perfect circle. Now let another hypothesis be delineated. Let *AD* be bisected at *B*, so that *AB* is 9282 (or according to the numbers in chapter XLII, 9264) and with center *B* and the interval *CH*, let another eccentric *IL* be written. In this chapter, I have also called this *fictitious*, as it was described for the sake of calculating the correct distances. It is, however, the same as the one in the second-to-last diagram, $\delta\vartheta\lambda$, described from center *B*. And let the mean anomaly <note>The planet's position calculated as if it moved at a constant speed.</note> (which was previously proposed to us by means of time) be transferred from *D* to *B*, with a straight line *BF* drawn from *B* which is parallel to the previous line *DH*. And let point *F*, the intersection of the new eccentric, be connected with *A*.

Therefore, through what has been said in this chapter XLVI, *AF* will be the distance from the center of the **SUN** at *A* (which the hypothesis of chapter XLV requires the **PLANET** to have at *F*). But the angle *BAF* is false, and the location of *AF* beneath the zodiac is false. For the **PLANET** is not found at *AF* at the assumed time and mean anomaly. Previously, however, the true line of the **PLANET** was *AH*, but the length of *AH* was false. (Therefore, with center *A* and interval *AF*, let an arc *FG* be drawn, intersecting *AH* at *G*). The line *AG* will therefore be constituted by two manifestly false hypotheses, yet it is true in its position beneath the zodiac, and consistent in its length with the hypothesis of chapter XLV.

Thus, by means of the **Vicarious Hypothesis** of chapter XVI—which consists of points *A, C, D* and the eccentric *H*—we have supplied the defect of Geometry, which was unable to show us the position of line *AG* (I mean, where the correct distance *AF* is to be transferred) as required by the hypothesis of chapter XLV.

<margin>A fourth method of description rejected.</margin>
**SOMEONE MIGHT ASK**, whether we could not equally in the former diagram as in the latter, cut off a point of equality $\gamma$, and from it draw lines $\gamma\mu, \gamma\nu, \gamma\omicron, \gamma\pi, \gamma\rho$ parallel to $\beta\epsilon, \beta\zeta, \beta\vartheta, \beta\iota, \beta\kappa$ and draw arcs $\epsilon\mu, \zeta\nu, \vartheta\omicron, \iota\pi, \kappa\rho$ intersecting these parallels? And by these points of intersection, understand the determined locations and positions of the distances?

**THE ANSWER IS**, no. For in this way we will err somewhat, transferring the distances too high up, as is easily apparent from the latter diagram. For in it, the line *AH*, which receives the true distances *AF*, is always lower than the line *DH* drawn from the equant point *D* parallel to *BF*.

<margin>What kind of oval is born from these descriptions. Dürer.</margin>
In whichever of the stated ways the line possessing the body of the **PLANET** is drawn, it now follows that this path—marked by points $\delta. \mu. \nu. \omicron. \pi. \rho. \lambda.$—is truly an **oval**, not an **ellipse**, a name which <term>mechanics</term> <note>Kepler refers here to artisans and practical geometers like Albrecht Dürer.</note> misapply to an egg-shape. For an egg is seen to be tapered with two vertices, one however blunter and the other sharper, and with sloping sides. I say that we have created such a figure. For because the **PLANET** is fast at $\lambda$ and slow at $\delta$, and more or less fast there than it is slow here; because the long distances exceeding the semi-diameter are more numerous than the short ones (for they are longer up to 92 1/2°; thereafter they are shorter through 87 1/3° degrees, which can be demonstrated according to the doctrine of chapter XXIX); and moreover, those more numerous long ones are crowded upward into a narrower arc of the eccentric by the translation; while these fewer short ones are spread out into a wider one: so that the mean anomaly of 92 2/3° \*, by which the distances of 92 2/3° are completed, corresponds to an eccentric anomaly of about 87 1/3°: the remainder of the mean anomaly, 87 1/3°, with as many shorter distances...

<margin>\* This is valid only in this erroneous opinion of chapter XLV, by which we are carried here.</margin>

Therefore, the short distances near the perihelion <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun.</note> are more widely spaced from each other than the long distances near the aphelion <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note>. And so, even if there were the same proportion between two neighboring perihelion distances, the segment of the circle would still be narrowed more around parts ε, μ, δ than around parts ς, η, λ, because in the shorter space at δ, the short [distances] are shifted into the place of the longer ones more so than at λ. It is therefore necessary that the conchoid be thinned into a point at the bottom by greater intervals through a shorter space than at the top: and those greater intervals are moreover compared to shorter lines. Therefore, the proportion is increased on both counts. With so many causes converging, it appears that the segment of our eccentric circle is much wider below than above, at an equal distance from the apsides <note>The highest and lowest points of the orbit.</note>. This is easy for anyone to investigate either with numbers or by a **mechanical drawing**, assuming some evident eccentricity. <margin>* This type of figure is found in the little book on the spheres and the commentaries of Reinhold on the theories of Purbach, in the theory of Mercury.</margin> *

### Attempted quadrature <note>The process of calculating the area of a shape.</note> of the egg-shaped plane, which chapter 45 brought forth, and which we were busy describing in chapter 46: and through it, the METHOD of equations.

<margin>
Sight <note>original: Όψις (Opsis)</note>.
What is the Optical part of the equation, and what is the Physical.
</margin>

**WE HAVE ACCOMPLISHED NOTHING**, if we have not constructed just equations <note>In this context, "equations" refers to the mathematical adjustments needed to calculate the planet's position.</note> no less than distances, from the adopted hypothesis and physical causes of chapter 45, which we follow here as true. However, since an equation is composed of the parallax of the points of the eccentric and the "delay" <note>The time the planet spends in a specific part of its orbit.</note>; the former of which I am accustomed to call the **Optical** part of the equation, and the latter the **Physical** part: and since the "delay," if anything else, is certainly measured most concisely (though not most perfectly) by the plane <note>The area</note> circumscribed by the journey of the **PLANET**: we are therefore turned back to the measurement of the eccentric oval <note>original: ooidis</note> plane, the rules for drawing which were set out previously. For even if we are missing a little something to establish this as the genuine measure of time (namely, that the lines which [mark] the parts of the circumference are inclined even more toward the oval circumference than toward a circular one...

...they connect with the source of power; and thus also those lines which are drawn from the center of the eccentric to those same parts of the oval <note>original Latin: ooidis</note>; whereas otherwise radii from the center to the circumference of a perfect circle are entirely straight lines: whence it follows that neither is the sum of the distances measured exactly by the plane, nor are the arcs of the oval exactly proportional to the distances. All of this will be clear from a re-reading of chapters 40 and 32. However, how small that error will be can be conjectured from chapter 43.

But how can we otherwise measure this plane, compare it to the plane of a circle, and divide it into the required parts, unless we find a square equal to the segment or the <term>lunule<note>A crescent-shaped area formed by the intersection of two circles or a circle and an oval.</note></term> cut away? Here, therefore, we must summon a <term>god<note>original Greek: θεὸς</note></term> from a tragedy—or rather <term>some word/reason<note>original Greek: λόγος τις</note></term>—<term>from the machine<note>original Greek: ἀπὸ μηχανῆς. <margin>
An ellipse is a regular figure resulting from the section of a cone through the axis. Others call it an oblong circle.
</margin>

If our figure were a perfect ellipse, the business would have been finished by **ARCHIMEDES**, who in his book *On Spheroids*, propositions 6, 7, and 8, demonstrates that the area of an ellipse is to the area of a circle (which shares the major diameter with the ellipse) as the rectangle of the diameters (or the figure of the section) is to the square of the circle's diameter.

But let this figure be a perfect ellipse; for it differs very little. Let us see what follows from that.

I say, therefore, that the lunule $\delta o \lambda \vartheta$ cut from the semicircle will be insensibly larger than a small semicircle whose semidiameter is the <term>eccentricity<note>The distance between the center of the orbit and the Sun.</note></term> itself, 9264, or $\alpha \beta$. For let $\alpha \beta$ be bisected at $\sigma$ (as in chapter 29), and from $\sigma$ let the perpendicular $\sigma \tau$ go out to $\alpha \beta$. And let the points $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be connected with $\tau$. Let $\gamma \phi$ proceed parallel to $\beta \tau$, and let the points $\beta \phi$ and $\alpha \phi$ be connected. And with center $\alpha$ and interval $\alpha \tau$, let the arc $\tau \psi$ be drawn, cutting $\alpha \phi$ at $\psi$, and $\beta \phi$ at $\xi$.

<margin>
What "mean length" means to the Arabs. Today we use the term "mean length" abusively for the point on the circumference that has the mean distance—that is, the point distant by a moderate measure from the center of the world.
</margin>

Since, therefore, the point $\tau$ is equally distant from $\alpha$ and $\beta$, we are therefore (to speak most properly with the Arabs) at the <term>mean length<note>The average distance between the planet and the Sun.</note></term>—that is, at the moderate distance of the **PLANET** from the **SUN** $\alpha$. And because $\gamma \phi$ is parallel to $\beta \tau$, therefore, by the diagram of the preceding chapter, the point $\chi$ of the line $\alpha \phi$ itself is the genuine and truest place of the translation of $\alpha \tau$ into $\alpha \psi$. Thus $\xi \psi$ is the point of the moderate distance of the **PLANET**. Wherefore the small part of the line $\beta \psi$ which lies between $\psi$ and the circumference measures the width of the lunule around the mean length; but the small line $\xi \phi$ is larger than this width by some insensible amount.

Let a perpendicular be dropped from $\beta$ to $\alpha \tau$, which shall be $\beta \nu$. I say that $\xi \phi$, part of the line $\beta \phi$, is double $\alpha \nu$.

For let $\tau \phi$ be connected. And from $\tau$ onto $\beta \phi$ let the perpendicular $\tau \lambda$ fall; likewise from $\xi$ onto $\alpha \tau$ the perpendicular $\xi \omega$. Since, therefore, the straight line $\alpha \gamma$ falls upon the parallels $\gamma \phi$ and $\beta \tau$, the angles $\beta \gamma \phi$ and $\alpha \beta \tau$ will be equal. Moreover, $\gamma \beta$ is equal to $\alpha \beta$ by construction. But also $\beta \phi$ is equal to $\alpha \tau$. For each is equal to the same $\beta \tau$ by construction. Therefore, triangle $\gamma \phi \beta$ is congruent to triangle $\beta \tau \alpha$. Wherefore $\gamma \phi$ will also be equal to $\beta \tau$. However, they are parallel by construction.

Therefore, $\beta\gamma$ and $\tau\phi$, which connect equal parallels at their ends, will be parallel and equal on the same side. But $\beta\gamma$ is equal to $\alpha\beta$. Therefore $\alpha\beta$ and $\tau\phi$ are equal and parallel. Thus $\beta\phi$ and $\alpha\tau$ will also be parallel. And because the angles at $\lambda, \upsilon$ are right angles, and the base $\tau\phi$ is equal to the base $\beta\alpha$, and the angle $\beta\alpha\tau$ or $\beta\alpha\upsilon$ is equal to the angle $\tau\phi\beta$ or $\tau\phi\chi$: therefore $\alpha\upsilon$ and $\chi\phi$ will be equal; and thus also the perpendiculars $\beta\upsilon$ and $\tau\chi$.

Again, because $\tau\chi$ and $\xi\omega$ are equal and parallel between parallels, and $\beta\tau$ and $\alpha\xi$ are equal, and the angles at $\chi, \omega$ are right angles: the remaining sides of the triangles $\beta\chi$ and $\alpha\omega$ will therefore be equal; and $\beta\xi$ and $\upsilon\omega$ will be equal and parallel between the parallels $\beta\upsilon, \xi\omega$. Therefore, when the equals $\beta\xi$ and $\upsilon\omega$ are subtracted, the remainders $\xi\chi$ and $\alpha\upsilon$ will be equal. But previously $\chi\phi$ and $\alpha\upsilon$ were also equal: and therefore $\xi\phi$ is double $\alpha\upsilon$.

Having demonstrated these things, we will come closer to our proposition. And because the straight line $\tau\chi$ falls perpendicularly from point $\tau$ on the circumference onto $\phi\beta$, the diameter of the circle (which is understood to be continued to the other circumference): therefore, as $\phi\chi$ is to $\chi\tau$, so $\chi\tau$ is to the remainder of the diameter. Thus, the rectangle formed by $\phi\chi$ and the remaining part of the diameter is equal to the square of $\tau\chi$.

And because the square of $\tau\phi$ (that is, $\alpha\beta$) equals the squares of $\tau\chi$ and $\chi\phi$: when equals are added, the rectangle formed by $\chi\phi$ and the whole diameter is equal to the square of $\alpha\beta$.

And because $\phi\xi$ is double $\phi\chi$: therefore the rectangle formed by $\phi\xi$ (which is <note>By "insensibly," Kepler means the difference is so small it cannot be perceived or measured.</note> insensibly longer than the width of the lunule $\psi\phi$) and the semidiameter $\phi\beta$ equals the square of $\alpha\beta$.

<margin>
*Almost, I say. For if $\beta\xi$ were the shorter diameter of the ellipse, and $\xi\phi$ the excess of the longer: then clearly the same proportion would exist between the planes of the circle and the ellipse. But $\beta\xi$ is not exactly the very same shorter diameter.
</margin>
But the rectangle formed by $\xi\phi$ and $\phi\beta$ is the difference between that formed by $\xi\beta$ and $\beta\phi$ and the square of $\beta\phi$. And the <term>lunules<note>The crescent-shaped areas between the circle of the orbit and the actual elliptical path.</note></term> are also the difference between the planes of the ellipse and the circle. And as the rectangle under $\xi\beta$ and $\beta\phi$ is to the square of $\beta\phi$: so almost* the plane of the ellipse is to the plane of the circle. Therefore also, as the square of $\beta\phi$ is to the rectangle $\xi\phi, \phi\beta$ (that is, to the square of $\alpha\beta$): so almost the plane of the circle is to the plane of the two lunules. And conversely: as the square of $\beta\phi$ is to the plane of the circle, so the square of $\alpha\beta$ is almost to the plane of the lunules.

But as the square of $\beta\phi$ is to the plane of the circle whose radius is $\beta\phi$; so the square of $\alpha\beta$ is almost to the plane of the circle whose radius is $\alpha\beta$. Therefore, the plane of the circle whose radius is $\alpha\beta$ exceeds each cut-away lunule $\psi\phi$ by an insensible amount; it certainly equals the lunules $\xi\phi$, which are a little wider than is right, because $\xi\phi$ is insensibly longer than $\psi\phi$ itself, as was *stated at the beginning.*

<margin>
This demonstration has its use even in the most true physical hypothesis.
</margin>
With these things granted which we have posited—namely, that the plane of the ellipse differs insensibly from the plane of our <term>egg-shape<note>original Greek: ooidos</note></term>, because there is a compensation between the upper excesses of the egg-shape over the ellipse and the lower deficiencies—with these granted, I say, we have squared our <term>crescent shapes<note>original Greek: menoides, meaning moon-like or crescent figures.</note></term>, and thus also the egg-shaped ones; or, to speak properly, we have "circled" them. For ARCHIMEDES teaches the proportion of the circle and the square.

# PART FOUR

<margin>CHAPTER XLVII.</margin>

Now we shall apply these things to practical use in this way. Because the area of the <term>oval</term> <note>original: "ooidis"; Kepler uses this term for the egg-shaped path of the planet before he fully concludes it is a perfect ellipse.</note> is less than the area of the circle by the area of a small circle described by the eccentricity; let the area of that small circle therefore be calculated. *Now, the ratio of the areas of planes is the duplicate ratio of the diameters <note>In the geometric language of the time, a "double" or "duplicate" ratio refers to the square of the ratio. Here, the area of a circle is proportional to the square of its diameter.</note>. And because as $\beta \phi$ (100,000) is to $\beta \alpha$ (9,264), so $\beta \alpha$ is to $\xi \phi$ (858); the ratio between $\beta \phi$ and $\xi \phi$ is therefore the duplicate of the ratio between $\beta \phi$ and $\beta \alpha$. Therefore, as $\beta \phi$ (100,000) is to $\chi \phi$ (858), so the area of the circle (31,415,900,000) is to the area of the small circle (269,500,000).*

Therefore, having subtracted the area of the small circle, there remains the area of the oval, 31,146,400,000, which is equivalent to 360 equal parts of the time of a full revolution.

What has been said so far is indeed consistent with the opinion expressed in Chapter 45. However, for their use, it is not enough merely to know the total size of the oval's area. We must also understand the method for dividing it, from the center $\beta$ or the point $\alpha$, in a given ratio. *For example, in the previous diagram, let point $\vartheta$ be taken, and let the <term>PLANET</term> be viewed on the line $\alpha \vartheta$, having moved back from the circumference $\vartheta$ toward the <term>SUN</term> $\alpha$. Therefore, given the eccentricity $\alpha \beta$ and the angle $\vartheta \alpha \beta$, and assuming the <term>PLANET</term> is at point $\vartheta$ on the circumference, the angle $\vartheta \beta \delta$ will be given. Consequently, both the sector of the perfect circle (that is, $\vartheta \beta \delta$) and the area of the triangle $\vartheta \beta \alpha$ will be given—that is, the entire area $\vartheta \delta \alpha$, which (except for those things mentioned above in Chapter 40) ought to have been the measure of time as the <term>PLANET</term> traveled from $\delta$ to $\vartheta$, if the <term>PLANET</term> had moved in a perfect circle $\delta \vartheta$. But because it described an interior oval and did not encompass the entire area of the perfect circle, just as we recently needed knowledge of the area of the whole oval, so now we also need to know how great a portion of the oval is intercepted by the lines $\delta \alpha$ and $\alpha \vartheta$. That is, how large a portion of the area of the <term>lunule</term> <note>original: "lunulae"; the crescent-shaped sliver between the circle and the oval path.</note> $\delta \vartheta$ is compared to the area that measures both lunules, namely the area of the small circle of eccentricity. For when this is subtracted from the portion of the circle cut off by the lines $\alpha \vartheta$ and $\alpha \delta$, the remaining portion will be the portion of the oval cut off by those same lines $\alpha \vartheta$ and $\alpha \delta$; and thus finally the whole oval-shape will be correctly compared to its part $\delta \alpha \vartheta$, for the purpose of learning the time, or the delay, that the <term>PLANET</term> makes between the lines $\alpha \delta$ and $\alpha \vartheta$.*

Where is there now another <term>Geometer</term> <note>A mathematician specializing in geometry.</note> to teach us this? Let the last diagram of Chapter 40 be repeated, in which $CD$ is a semicircle stretched out into a straight line and divided into equal parts; and $D \varepsilon$ is a quadrant. *And on the line $\varepsilon A$, let a line be extended from $\varepsilon$ toward $A$ which is to the longest line $\beta A$ (on the line $CA$) as that $\beta A$ is to $BC$. In this way, let the remaining lines $\zeta \mu, H \nu, I \pi, K \rho$ be established in their proper quantity, having the width of the lunule at any given place, such that $\zeta \mu$ is a little shorter than $\kappa \rho$, and $H \nu$ shorter than $I \pi$ (even though they are at equal distances from $C$ and $D$), according to the demonstrations in Chapter 46. Thus the lunule will be delineated and unfolded part by part into a straight line, insofar as it shortens the distances.*

Now, if the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>An auxiliary angle used to relate the uniform motion of a circle to the non-uniform motion of the planet.</note> $\delta \beta \delta$ were $90^{\circ}$ (which I am assuming as a guess), its sector $\beta \beta \delta$ would be 7,853,981,670. Therefore, we guessed well that the angle $\delta \beta \delta$, or the eccentric anomaly, is $90^{\circ}$. # CHAPTER XLVIII.

## The method of computing the equations of the eccentric by the
## measurement and numerical division of the circumference
## of the oval described in Chapter 40.

Since the <term>calculus</term> <note>original: "calculus"; here meaning the method of computation rather than modern calculus.</note> used in the previous chapter was abandoned by Geometry for so many reasons, and was therefore suspected regarding the fault of the excesses and deficiencies which we detected in the equations of the eccentric in that chapter: I finally fled to arithmetic enumerations, by which I attempted to avoid those inconveniences which hindered us in Chapter 46 as we were about to describe the path of the **PLANET**. 

First, because the plane was not an exquisite measure of the sum of the distances, I dismissed the plane and instead computed the distances themselves for each of the equally divided parts of the circumference. Second, because the proportion did not remain the same when some terms of geometric proportions were added, I therefore consulted the proportions of each of the individual distances to their own smallest arcs separately. Third, because the sum of some distances in Chapter 46 could not be established geometrically, I established it here arithmetically; for nothing hindered me. Fourth, in doing this, I had no business with the <term>sectors</term> <note>The wedge-shaped areas of a circle or ellipse.</note> of either the circle or the oval: and so even this could not hinder me, that those sectors differed among themselves.

Yet we are not destitute of a certain geometric guidance for making a good guess about the length of the oval. *For let it be that as BD is to BA, so BA is to DH, which is extended from D toward B. Therefore, because (through the things demonstrated in Chapter 46) that which is under the width of the <term>lunula</term> <note>The crescent-shaped area between the circular path and the oval path.</note> and the semidiameter of the circle is almost equal to the square of the eccentricity; wherefore, through the 17th proposition of the sixth book of <term>EUCLID</term>, the eccentricity is the mean proportional between the width of the lunula and the semidiameter. But here the same thing happens from the law of declination. Therefore, DH is the width of the lunula.*

*Let half of HD also be taken, and extended from B toward D, and let it be BI: and with center I and distance ID, let circle DK be drawn, touching the eccentric at D. Let there also be drawn, with center B and distance BH, a circle HK, touching the former at K. It is manifest that circle HK is smaller than DK, and circle DGR is larger than DK. And because circular circumferences are to one another as their semidiameters: therefore, as BD is to DI and IH, so the larger circle DG is to the smaller ones DK and KH. But DI is the arithmetic mean between DB and HI, because BI is half of HD itself. Therefore, circle DK, touching the smaller and larger ones described from the same center B, is also the arithmetic mean between those circles which it touches.*

*If the path of the Oval is continued, by assumption it will itself touch the larger circle at the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> D and the <term>perihelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun.</note> R, but the smaller circle HK at the middle longitudes,*

...as it happens, the larger [part] corresponds to the smaller circle HK, and the smaller [part] to the larger circle DR. It is therefore consistent that the oval circumference is not far from the length of the circular circumference DK.

However, the following demonstration suggests it is a little larger.

Let the <term>geometric mean</term> <note>The square root of the product of two numbers; here used to find a middle value between the long and short axes.</note> between BH and BD be taken, which shall be BO, and with center B and distance BO, let the circle OP be described. Therefore, according to Book V of Archimedes' *On Conoids and Spheroids*, the area of this circle OP will be equal to the area of the ellipse whose longer semi-diameter is BD and shorter is BH. But because the circle is the most capacious of <term>isoperimetric</term> <note>original: "isoperimetron"; figures having the same perimeter length.</note> figures, conversely, therefore (by common knowledge), the circle will have the shortest perimeter of capacious figures. Since, therefore, the ellipse having diameters DB and BH, and the proposed circle OP, are equally capacious <note>i.e., they have the same area.</note> according to what was just cited, the circumference of the ellipse will be longer than the circumference of the circle OP. 

Furthermore, BO is imperceptibly smaller than ID, because BO is defined as the geometric mean between those same terms, while ID is the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The simple average of two numbers.</note>. For by the doctrine of Euclid's Book V, because BO is the geometric mean between HB and BD (as the smaller HB is to the larger BD), so also the excess of the mean HO is to the deficit of the mean OD. Thus, since HB is smaller than BD, HO will also be smaller than OD. But BI is equal to half of HD. Therefore, BI is greater than HO and smaller than OD. Consequently, unequal amounts are added to the common semi-diameter HB of the smallest circle HK: namely, less than half of DH in the case of BO, and exactly half of DH in the case of DI. Therefore, DI is greater than BO. Thus, circle DK is greater than circle OP. This is, however, imperceptible, since DH is less than a hundredth part of DB. 

Therefore, even if we generously assume these circles to be equal, and assume that the oval is a perfect ellipse: the oval circumference will be a little longer than circle DK, and certainly longer than circle OP. And since above in Chapter 47, DH was 858 where DB was 100,000; therefore, let half of DH, which is 429, be subtracted from DB 100,000. There will remain 99,571. Therefore, as 100,000 is to 99,571, so, very nearly, will the circumference of the circle be to the sought circumference of the oval. And since the circumference of a circle has 180 degrees (or 10,800 minutes, or 1,296,000 seconds), a small portion will fall away, amounting to 55' 60" or 9' 2" 40". And from the semi-circumference of the oval, 4' 6" 20" must be removed—or even less, if the oval exceeds circle DK, which we used as a measure. 

Indeed, I found—not through demonstration, but through the most laborious and persistent calculation—that the deficit of the oval semicircle is 4' 45": so that where a perfect semicircle is 180 degrees, the oval would be 179° 14' 15".

And because this shortening of the oval circumference is necessarily equal to the opposite optical amplification (for this oval, although shorter, nevertheless appears under an amplitude of 2 right angles, or precisely 180 degrees, and is judged to be that long), the reader might rightly wonder whether it is necessary in this process first to shorten the whole oval, and then through...

For from the diagram it seems to appear that the shortening occurs there at its maximum, where the approach to the center B is also at its maximum, and vice versa.

If these two variations proceeded in tandem, this method of calculating the <term>equations</term> <note>In 17th-century astronomy, an "equation" is a correction applied to a planet's mean (average) motion to find its true position.</note> would be born to us:

*The <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance from aphelion the planet would have if it moved at a constant speed in a circle.</note> would first be GBD, from which the distance GA would be computed, which, when added to AD (the distance of the other preceding terminus from GD, which is always 1) and the sum halved, would constitute the uniform distance of the arc CD (of all its points, that is). And then we would say: as the length of the semicircle is to the sum of all distances in the semicircle, so is this distance of the arc GD to the length ED—that is, to the appearance of CD from A. Now, from ED, as if from the measure of angle CBD, and from AC and AB, we would seek the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The planet's true position after corrections for its elliptical path and non-uniform speed are applied.</note> CAD by a shorter route than before.*

But let the reader know that these two variations do not "walk with equal step" <note>original: "non ambulare pari passu"; they do not change at the same rate.</note>. For the optical amplification, which arises from the approach of the path DC to the center B, occurs most powerfully around the mean longitudes <note>The points 90 degrees away from the farthest and closest points of the orbit.</note>; there is almost none at <term>aphelion</term> and <term>perihelion</term> <note>The farthest and closest points to the Sun, respectively.</note>. But on the contrary, the "shortening" <note>original: "decurtatio"</note> of the oval path, which arises from the planet’s entry toward the center, is almost equal all around. For since two opposite distances in the mean longitudes of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The circular path from which the planet's actual path deviates.</note> equal two joined together near the line of <term>apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the farthest and closest points of the orbit.</note>—one near the aphelion, the other near the perihelion—the arcs of the oval circumference are in a permuted proportion of the distances. Therefore, two such arcs in the mean longitudes will be equal to two arcs, one near the aphelion and the other near the perihelion. If the arcs of the oval path themselves are equal, then the diminution of these arcs in all four places will also be nearly equal. The matter has been proven by experiment. For if the deficit of the oval semicircle is 45' 15", the deficit of one-180th part of the oval near the aphelion will be about 14 seconds. Yet the amplification from the approach of the oval does not even equal one second near the aphelion.

Therefore, as far as the cited visual estimation of the diagram is concerned, it is not simply as this objection previously stated—that the shortening of the oval and its optical amplification compensate for each other. It would indeed be so if all arcs of the oval path were presented directly to the center B. But this happens only in the mean longitudes. Toward the apsides, however, these arcs approach their termini unequally. For this reason, they do not become as much larger through proximity and appearance as they were made shorter through physical contraction.

Therefore, following this **METHOD**, I constructed the equations of **MARS** for every degree of the eccentric, and did so three times. For at first, I had assumed an <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how far the Sun is from the geometric center of the orbit.</note> that was not large enough (9165), thinking I had made it certain through the treatment of planes. Then, I had also placed more than 180 in the rule, when I ought to have placed less.

And so, since here the final operation showed more than 180, which...

### CHAPTER XLIX.

### A critique of the previous METHOD of equations, and a more elegant METHOD based on principles forming the oval path according to the opinion of Chapter 45.

**S**O THAT YOU may see the cause of the <note>original: "ἀτεχνίας"</note> clumsiness of this already completed method, consider on what foundations it rests. It is assumed that the planet moves uniformly on an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note>, and is carried nonuniformly by the Sun in proportion to its distances. From these two principles of motion, an oval path is born. But it is impossible to know by this method what portion of the oval path corresponds to any given time, even if the distance of that portion is known—unless the length of the entire oval is known from the start. However, the length of the oval cannot be known except from the measure of the planet's entry from the circumference of the circle toward the sides. But neither is the measure of this entry known before it is known what portion of the oval path is traversed in any given time. Here you see a <term>begging of the question</term> <note>Latin: "peti principium." A logical error where the starting assumptions depend on the conclusion one is trying to prove.</note>; and in our operation, we had first assumed that which was sought—namely, the length of the oval. Nor is this fault merely one of our understanding, but it is utterly alien to the original Ordainer of the planetary courses themselves; for we have not yet found such an <note>original: "ἀγεωμέτρητον"</note> un-geometrical anticipation in any of His other works. Therefore, either another way must be entered upon for calling the opinion of Chapter 45 to the calculations, or if this cannot be done, the opinion itself—being suspect because of this begging of the question—will falter.

A complication has arisen for us here because we have cut the composite oval path into unequal parts, using an equal measure of time; and so

CHAPTER XLIX.

We have measured out the unequal parts of this composite oval, which are nonetheless equalized again by the compensation of distances, all around the planet's path in the usual manner. And yet, in our presuppositions, we held that at least one of the two powers—the one originating from the <term>SUN</term> <note>Kepler believed the Sun physically pushed planets with an "immaterial species" or motive power.</note>—is intensified in proportion to the distances; but that the planet’s own power is not. Yet here in this work, we make both forces somehow subject to this proportion of distances, because we give the oval—the combined work of both forces—to the planet to be traversed according to the measure of the distances.

Even if, therefore, we have approached very close to the truth in the result of this method, we still have nothing to boast about in terms of having expressed the opinion of Chapter <term>XLV</term>, if we are destitute of a rational foundation. It seemed, therefore, that we would act more rightly if, having dismissed the way of the composite oval and the squaring of its plane—the subject matter of Chapters <term>XLVI, XLVII, and XLVIII</term>—we turned our calculation back to the very principles of the oval path assumed in Chapter <term>XLV</term>. *Let Chapter <term>XLV</term> be re-read; and with the <term>CENTER</term> at the body of the <term>SUN</term>, at the distance <term>AD</term>, let the circle <term>DG</term> of the center of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> be described; and another, with center <term>A</term> and distance <term>AB</term>, the circle of the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note>; in which <term>AGB</term> is the line of apsides; and let the <term>Planet</term>, when it is at the <term>aphelion</term> <note>original: "ἀφήλ." Therefore, to know the angle <term>DAB</term> during the time <term>CDE</term>, consider that the <term>Planet</term> has arrived from <term>B</term> to <term>E</term> by two powers: one which made it closer to the <term>Sun</term>, and which at the same time also led it out of the line <term>AC</term> or <term>AD</term> in which it had been before (when <term>AC</term> was at <term>AB</term>); and another, by which it moved forward with the epicycle, so that the center of the epicycle <term>D</term> would be on the line <term>AC</term>, whereas it was previously on <term>AB</term>. That power, indeed, which drives the center of the epicycle around, in a time designated by 360, moves through 360 degrees, or four right angles around <term>A</term>, on account of the sum of the 360 distances. Therefore, given the sum of some distances from the time <term>CDE</term> as we have done so far, the angle <term>DAB</term> will also be given. For whatever impression the <term>SUN</term> makes on the body of the Planet through the mediating distances <term>AB</term> and <term>AE</term>, it is also posited to make that same impression on the center of the epicycle <term>GD</term>: because the Planet, if it had not meanwhile extricated itself toward <term>B</term> from the virtuous ray <note>The physical line of force radiating from the Sun.</note> <term>AB</term> or <term>AC</term>, but had only descended toward the Sun, would then still be on <term>AC</term>, and at its point \* <term>F</term>, on which line the center of the epicycle <term>D</term> itself also resides.*

CHAPTER XLV

*Because if anything in the proportion is disturbed, the planet does it (according to the opinion of this Chapter XLV) by its own descent in the circumference of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient and Renaissance astronomy to explain variations in speed and distance.</note>. For if the planet had remained at the highest point of the epicycle, and had endured the same force of motion from the* **SUN**, *represented by AB and AE—suppose an unequal force (which indeed cannot happen simultaneously, for while the distance of the planet from the Sun remains the same, the strength of the motion from the Sun remains the same)—then it would have traced a perfect arc of a larger circle BC, of which the proportion to the whole BC is the same as the proportion of arc GD to the whole GD.*

*I know indeed, if the planet is assumed to be in a narrower circuit—namely, that of the center of the epicycle DG—it would be far swifter. But a swifter motion is not for that reason to be assigned to the center of the epicycle. For the center of the epicycle is supposed to move, not for its own sake, since it is not a body, but for the sake of the planet. Therefore, assuming that the planet itself transports its body from the rays of the* **SUN** *by an epicyclic law, and uses certain powerful rays from the* **SUN** *according to its location (which were rejected in Chapter XXXIX, but resumed and somewhat changed in Chapter XLV, and are retained here to explain my attempts), the reasoning of the calculation is sound thereafter, whatever its effect may be. For here too an oval exists no less than before, because DE and AB do not remain parallel. For by as much as the long distances AB and AE exceed the mean distances AG and AD, by so much shorter has the arc DG (or the angle DAG) been made than the angle CDE by the measure of time. Thus, DE nods toward B.*

*Therefore, it enters from the circumference of the circle toward BA. For by Chapter 11, if DE had remained parallel to AB, then E would have been on the circumference itself.*

**THEREFORE**, *this method* **IS BORN**. *Let the distances be sought for all whole degrees of the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The hypothetical position of a planet if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant speed; essentially a measure of time.</note>. You have the method above in Chapter XXXIX, which we also used in the previous Chapters XLVII and XLVIII. For first, the distances of the non-whole degrees of the mean anomaly, or CE, are found. Afterward, they are referred proportionally to the whole degrees of CE itself. If you are weary of this detour, and if a longer labor by the direct path delights you—finally, if you wish to see everything before your eyes in one diagram—you shall act thus:*

*Time, or the artificial name for time, which astronomers call the mean anomaly, count it in the epicycle CE, from its <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> C, against the sequence of the signs. Therefore, the angle ADE (or the complement CDE) is given in some whole degrees of the mean anomaly. The radius AD of 100,000 is given, as is the radius of the epicycle DE of 9,264. Therefore, both the part of the <term>equation</term> <note>The angular correction needed to find the planet's true position.</note> DAE and the distance AE will be given. Record both of these in a catalog, with their mean anomaly CE written down, for future use. In this way, let all the distances AE be collected and added; and the sum will be found to be about 36,075,562. For this sum was found from some <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measurement of how far the orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> very little different from our present one, which is 9,264. A three-hundred-sixtieth part of this is worth 100,210, and the total part of four right angles is one degree. As, therefore, all the distances in order are to the distance 100,210, so is the arc of this distance 100,210 (60 minutes) to the arcs corresponding to the other distances: because the proportion is inverse, as was often warned in Chapters XXIX, XLVII, and XLVIII. Therefore, having multiplied 60 minutes or 3,600 seconds by 100,210, and having divided the product 180 times by all the distances of the semicircle,*

# CHAPTER 50.
## On six other ways of constructing the equations of the eccentric that were attempted.

**F**rom this threshing, how great a heap of grain have we collected? ### The process of the first and second methods was this.

<margin>
O 295.
What is the distance-based anomaly?
* Although it holds a middle quantity between the others, beware of calling it the "mean," for "mean" is properly a name for time.
</margin>

First, with an <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measurement of how far the Sun is from the center of the planet's circular or elliptical path.</note> of 9165, which is a little less than the correct amount, I sought all the distances according to the doctrine of chapter 29, which corresponded to the whole degrees of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angle used to track a planet's position in its orbit.</note> that sits in the middle between the mean and the truly equated anomaly. Although I sometimes call this the "equated" anomaly, I add the condition that it is intended only for distances. Therefore, I call it the **distance-based anomaly**. *In the other diagram of chapter 46, it is angle FAB; in the following diagram, it is CAD.*

Second, I sought <term>third proportional</term> <note>A geometric term: if A is to B as B is to C, then C is the third proportional to A and B.</note> lines, such that each would be to its distance as that distance is to the radius 100,000.

A problem proposed to Geometers.

AD, *so AD is to AD as AD is to AG; thus, as AH is to AC, so AC is to AF; finally as AK is to AL, so AL is to AM: and so for all the rest. I say, let the geometer demonstrate that the last 360 [segments] joined together—say* AG, AF, AM—*are equal to the first 360 joined together—say* AI, AH, AK.

AND SO, in the first method using the sums of distances, I intended one thing but performed another. For I collected not the arcs, nor the angles, nor the paths, but the <term>delays</term> <note>Latin: 'mora'. Kepler’s term for the amount of time a planet spends traversing a particular part of its orbit.</note> in the unequal arcs of the planet's path. And in the rule of proportions, I said: as the sum of the <term>mean distances</term> <note>original: 'mediarum'. These are the distances from the sun when the planet is at the "sides" of its orbit, halfway between its closest and furthest points.</note> AD, AE, AL—specifically 35,914,252—is to the delay [time] of 360 [degrees], so is any sum of distances to its own delay in the space that encompassed these distances. *Let* A *be the Sun, B the center of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the Sun is not at the center.</note> CD, and BC the semi-diameter. Here, the distances CA were fitted to whole degrees of the angle CAD, and therefore to unequal arcs of the circle CD, which had deceived me.* <note>Kepler realized he was measuring distances from the perspective of the Sun (A) rather than along the physical path of the planet (CD).</note> *Therefore, let CAD be 45°. But because the planet is slower in arc CD, due to its long distance from A [the Sun], and because the distances are the measure of this delay: I therefore collected, for the anomaly CAD of 45°, forty-five distances at the start of the arcs (the longer ones); the sum was 4,869,307. I also collected the 45 shorter ones at the ends of the arcs—subtracting the longest distance AD (109,165) from the sum of 46 distances (4,975,577); 4,866,412 remained. And the value that was intermediate between both sums—4,867,852—I converted into degrees, of which 35,924,252 equal 360, or of which 99,790 equal 1°. By this method, 48° 46' 51" was produced. And this should have been the time corresponding to the angle CAD. But the arc CD (or angle CBD) had been found to be nearly that much, namely 48° 42' 51". This is absurd, and against the hypothesis, which requires the planet to be slower in CD. Immediately, therefore, the cause of this absurdity became clear: namely, that to know the delay in CD, it would have been proper to consult distances corresponding to equal arcs of CD itself, whereas these distances already employed correspond to unequal arcs of CD, and arcs that are larger the longer the distances are, according to Chapter 32. Therefore, these distances were too few in number.*

<margin>I say "mean," not from the quantity between three things, but from the uniform motion and the mean of the time which it measures here, insofar as the same distances are sought.</margin>
But nonetheless, so as not to waste this labor in vain, I subtracted the excess of the number of this delay over the number of the angle CAD from CAD, so that EAD remained 41° 13' 9", and AC and AE were equal. Here it was assumed that in the time CBD, the planet completes an angle EBD around the center of the eccentric B equal to CAD itself; and therefore, for the equal arcs ED of that eccentric, as many distances from A are collected as we found here in the equal degrees of CAD itself. Thus, however much of them was dispersed through the unequal and (in this place) large parts of CD in our calculation, that same amount should be understood as gathered within the narrowness of ED and its equal parts. Here, then, the angle CBD would be the distance-based mean anomaly, giving the angle CAD for seeking the distances CA, from which distances the angle CAE—the physical retardation and translation of CA into EA—is derived.

## Third and Fourth Methods.

Since this method also did not stand up to reason, and I had learned in that other one that distances corresponding to whole degrees of the angle CBD (or equal arcs of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The circular path around a center that is not the Sun.</note> CD) were to be sought, I approached those as well.

Sixthly, using the same distances as before, I sought their proportionals—those which have the same ratio to the distances as the distances have to the radius of 100,000. But this was not necessary. However, I wanted to be prepared for every eventuality.

Seventh and Eighth, I again added the individual values, both the distances AD and AC, and their proportionals AG and AF. The sum of the distances themselves came to 36,075,562. Or, for the sake of convenience, reversing the reasoning: if the angle CAB is sought for an angle CBD of whole degrees (such as 45°), and the 45 correct distances are picked out. I say these things are done demonstratively. But again, as before, in this way CAD becomes the truly equated anomaly. Therefore, CA remains in its place, and the orbit DC will be a perfect circle. Since this is false, as shown in Chapter 44, it is therefore necessary that the distances used here at the mean longitudes are too long; thus the delays become more prolonged than they should be, and shorter at the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in the orbit closest to and farthest from the Sun.</note>.

And this method will be almost exactly equivalent to the former one using proportionals. ## Fifth and Sixth Methods.

Since, therefore, I had achieved nothing with these four methods, at that time with the <term>mean anomaly</term> and the distances assigned to it (in the fifth operation), I moved to the table of the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> from Chapter 16 and the <term>true equated anomaly</term>. Eleventhly and twelfthly, I added each within their classes, and the sum of the distances was 35,770,014, while the sum of the proportionals was 35,692,048. For since there are now more of the short distances than of the long ones (because through this translation of distances, we have pulled all the long ones upward and made few of them; establishing large arcs IG of the oval path above at the <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>, and thus assigning individual distances to each degree of the anomaly—not FAB as in the first method, but HAB, that is, the <term>truly equated anomaly</term>; of which degrees there are no more in the upper <term>semicircle</term> than in the lower): hence it happens that not only does the sum of the 360 distances turn out smaller than 360 <term>semidiameters</term><note>The radius of the orbit.</note>, but even the sum of the proportionals turns out smaller than the sum of the distances themselves was.
