CHAPTER 50.
</margin>

Regarding the fifth method and the sums of the distances themselves, reason again cries out against the method of equations <note>The "method of equations" refers to the calculation used to find the difference between a planet's average position and its true position.</note> relying on it. Let the diagram proper to this chapter be repeated, and let what was said about the first method be recalled to mind. For in that method, the <term>equated distance anomaly</term> <note original="anomalia distantiaria coæquata">The angle of the planet as viewed from the Sun.</note> CAD was divided into equal degrees. From this, it happened that the arc CD was cut into unequal and large parts, and held too few distances. Then, seizing upon a sort of accidental remedy for the error, we gathered from the sum of the distances on CD that a shorter arc ED corresponded to those distances, so that AC was transferred into AE; thus ED, cut into equal parts, could be considered to have one distance assigned to each of its degrees. 

But here, the translation of AC into AE has already been made and perfected—not from the sum of the distances found in CD, but from a mixture of the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> <note>Kepler’s earlier, highly accurate but physically "incorrect" model used as a mathematical benchmark.</note> with the hypothesis of distances established in Chapter 46. And the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note original="anomalia media">The angle representing the planet's uniform motion over time; effectively, a measure of time.</note> (which we counted on arc CD to find the distance CA or EA) was assigned the arc ED; yet in such a way that BE and AC are no longer precisely parallel as they were in the first method. I say that this, having already been done through the mixture of hypotheses, does not need to be done again through calculation as in the first method. Instead, this alone is asked: do the few distances AC and AE, collected into a single sum by this fifth method, produce the same physical equation as those assigned artificially by the two mixed hypotheses?

<margin>
Note in what respect "mean" is used here. See the upper margins.
</margin>

Consider how the distances accommodated in this last instance behave. The angle EAD, whose boundary E is distant from the Sun by the distance AC, is divided into equal degrees in this last instance, and one distance is assigned to each. By this reasoning, the arc ED of the oval path standing over that angle EAD now goes into unequal parts and obtains too few distances. Therefore, the mean anomaly already conceived from the vicarious hypothesis cannot be obtained from the sum of the distances in EAD.

<margin>
In this fifth method, there is indeed a third anomaly EAD, and its mean anomaly (the first in order) CD or CBD, and also the same distance-measure of the distance CA or EA itself. But the plane CAD measures some sum of distances EA, DA, which is foreign to this equated EAD, namely the corresponding measure of time for the arc DN itself and the equated DAN. Again, therefore, a monstrosity.
</margin>

Just as above in the first method—when CD obtained fewer distances than was right when angle CAD was divided into equal degrees, and we substituted the suitable arc ED for those distances—so in this fifth method, since ED obtains fewer distances than is right when angle EAD is divided into equal degrees, if one wished to accept an unscientific remedy again, we would substitute ND for ED, to which those distances correspond. *Suppose that for the purpose of seeking the distance* CA, *the mean anomaly* CBD *is 48° 44'. Given the angle* B, and sides CB and BA, CA *is given as 105784, and angle* CAB *as 45°.* The vicarious hypothesis requires that AC be transferred to AE. And we now divide ED, which the vicarious hypothesis indicates is 41° 22', into equal degrees; and through those, we collected no more than 41 distances and part of a 42nd. But these, cast into a sum, will produce a mean anomaly that is by no means equal to the DC first assumed, but rather another, DO, which shows that the distance AO must be transferred to AN. **A wine-jar began to be formed; as the wheel turns, why does a pitcher come out?** <note original="Amphora cœpit institui, currente rota cur urceus exit?">A quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, used by Kepler to describe a process that starts with a grand design but ends in a botched or inconsistent result.</note> For this was being asked: whether all the distances that are in the equal degrees of ED, when cast into a sum, would show the mean anomaly DC. But the operation answered me concerning ND and the anomaly DO.

<summary>Kepler demonstrates that the fifth method for calculating the planet's position fails because summing distances over an equally divided angle does not produce the expected time-measure (mean anomaly), leading to what he calls a mathematical "monstrosity."</summary>

# PART FOUR.

<margin>
This sixth method, with a very slight correction of those errors where the opinion in Chapter 45 still fails, can also be applied to the truest Physical hypothesis; it is both succinct and clear.
</margin>

Finally, let us turn to the sixth method and the proportional values, which are suited for the demonstration in Chapter 32. For those arcs that appear equal from the center of the Sun, their true quantities in the orbit are in the proportion of their distances: such that as much as *a e* is longer, so is *e d*.

But for arcs in the orbit that are truly equal, the delays <note>original: "morae"; the time spent by the planet in a specific section of its orbit.</note> are likewise in the proportion of the distances. For by as much as *e d* is more distant from *a*, by so much longer does the Planet remain in the arc *e d*.

Therefore, the delays which the Planet links together in those arcs that appear equal from the center of the Sun are in the double proportion <note>In the mathematical language of the time, "double proportion" often refers to the square of the ratio (i.e., $distance^2$).</note> of the distances.

But in this way, the radius *a f* is also to *a h* in the double proportion of the distance *a c* or *a e* itself to the mean distance *a h*. Therefore, the measures of the delays which the Planet links in equal degrees of the angle *e a d* are the lines *a g* and *a f*, which are the appropriate proportionals for that same angle *e a d* of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note original="anomalia vere coæquata">The planet's actual angular position relative to the Sun, after accounting for its eccentric orbit.</note>, corresponding to whole degrees or equal parts.

Let these proportional distances, therefore, be tested against the equal degrees of the equated anomaly, just as other distances were tested earlier in this chapter. Since the sum of all 360 distances (35,692,048) corresponds to the total 360 equal parts of the angle at the Sun, and is worth a total delay of 360, what is the just and corrected sum worth for any given degrees of the equated anomaly?

->It is found in this manner:<-

| for equated anomalies | Mean anomalies | Which the vicarious <insert>model</insert> produces | Difference |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 41 | 48. 24. 3 | 48. 19. 2 | 5 + |
| 81 | 91. 30. 39 | 91. 34. 8 | 3 1/2 -- |
| 91 | 101. 28. 10 | 101. 34. 7 | 6 --- |
| 131 | 138. 28. 5 | 138. 39. 28 | 11 -- |

->This coincides with those in Chapter 49.<-

<margin>
In this Sixth method, the third anomaly is *E A D*, the second is *E D*, and the First is the sum of the lines *A G* and *A F*, where *A F* or *A C* is understood to be transferred into *A E*. Nonetheless, in calculating the distance *A E* (which is *A G*, from which *A F* flows), *D C* or *D B C* is also the first. Thus it is depicted twice here, because two things are investigated: time and distance.
</margin>

Once again, the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much the orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> is argued to be smaller than it should be. When this is corrected, the difference above at 41 will be about 8 +, and below about 7 1/2 ---. Thus, here too, the Planet does not become fast enough near the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in the orbit where the planet is closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the Sun.</note>; consequently, there is more distance than is right around the apsides, and therefore less than is right at the middle longitudes. But it approaches the truth very nearly indeed, and clearly coincides with the method of Chapter 11. For if you consider it well, the same thing was done here as was done in Chapter 11. There, however, we calculated the Optical part of the <term>equation</term> <note>The correction applied to the mean motion to find the true position.</note> separately, and the Physical part likewise separately. Here, however, we calculate both together. There, we had introduced fictitious "virtuous rays" <note>Kepler's earlier conceptualization of the Sun's motive force acting like a set of rotating spokes.</note> so that we could assign to the <term>epicycle</term> its own work of extricating itself from those fictitious rays (for in truth, no rays revolve with such slowness as the center of the planetary epicycle moves, as was said in Chapter 39). And yet, as far as the effect is concerned, we left all the Physical power of moving the Planet to the Sun, so that the epicycle merely moderated the distances. Here, we have used the same virtue of the Sun for the Physical translation; but we have likewise calculated the distances from the epicycle, and given its equal parts to equal times—that is, to equal degrees of the mean anomaly, as the opinion of Chapter 45 requires. Even though we eventually took as many distances in any part of time as there are degrees of the equated anomaly, those distances were nevertheless derived from the distances of the mean anomaly, and are the same in length. And this form is so much more convenient.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>Chapter 50</margin>
...form, so that we can here set aside that other persuasion concerning the epicyclic motion of the Planet, and move one step closer to the truth of the physical cause. We leave to the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; here, Kepler is reducing it to a simple back-and-forth motion.</note> nothing but an oscillation along a diameter, though even this is still flawed, as appeared even from these equations. For as was noted a little earlier regarding the second method, this preoccupation with epicyclic motion is excessive, showing distances that are too short in the middle longitudes; from which it happens that the Planet at that place exceeds the proper measure of velocity, and at the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the Sun.</note> it falls short of that measure. But it is enough for us to express the opinion of Chapter 45 by calculation. Wherefore, even if someone should object here, based on Chapter 32, that this proportion of daily motions cannot be constant because the parts of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The circular path of the planet which is off-center relative to the Sun.</note> near the apsides are directly opposed to the Sun, while the intermediate parts are seen obliquely—so that they appear differently than if they were directly opposed—if anyone, I say, should object to this, I will respond as I did in Chapter 49: this obliquity of the intermediate parts is added by the Planet on its own account and is brought about through its descent; it is therefore not to be imputed to the moving cause from the Sun, nor is that cause disturbed by it.

You have therefore, studious Reader, out of so great a number of chapters and methods, only two methods of equating which agree with the opinion in Chapter 45. One is based on a physical hypothesis mixed with an epicycle ordered in longitude, which is in Chapter 49; the other is in this chapter, specifically its sixth method, representing a purer physical hypothesis, where the epicycle provides nothing but the descent toward the Sun ☉; or if one wished to order it in latitude, it would be perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic. And each of these, by different ways, agrees in a single effect. Thus you may more safely trust them in examining the opinion of Chapter 45.

> And thus far, with the empty confidence of having found the true physical causes, let there be a fresh triumph over Mars. Now, I know not what rumor excites me to new tumults and new labors.

**W**hile I triumph over the motions of <term>Mars</term> in this manner, and bind him in the prisons of Tables and the shackles of eccentric equations as if he were utterly conquered, it is reported from various places that the victory is futile and the war is breaking out again with full force. For at home indeed, the enemy, though treated with contempt as a captive, has broken all the bonds of the equations and burst out of the prisons of the tables. For no method administered geometrically according to the prescription of the opinion in Chapter 45 was able to match the proximity of the numbers of the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> <note original="hypothesin vicariam">Kepler’s earlier mathematical model from Chapter 16 which, while physically "false," produced very accurate predictions of the planet's positions.</note> in Chapter 16 (which has true equations arising from a false cause). Abroad, truly, scouts stationed throughout the entire circuit of the eccentric—I mean the genuine distances—have routed my physical causes summoned from Chapter 45.

### PART FOUR

X 4

<margin>CHAPTER 51</margin>
...forces, and they have shaken off their yoke, having resumed their liberty. And now it was nearly the case that the fugitive enemy joined forces with his own rebels, driving me to despair; had I not quickly sent in new reinforcements of <term>Physical reasoning</term> <note>Kepler refers to his "Physical" theories—the idea that the Sun's power actually pushes the planets—to help explain the data where pure geometry failed.</note>, the old ones having been routed and scattered; and had I not, having been informed with all diligence where the captive had escaped, followed in its very tracks without any delay. I will narrate both matters in order, as they happened, in the following several chapters.

And to speak of the first beginning, I shall first seek the distances of several <term>eccentric positions</term> <note>Specific points along the off-center circular path Kepler was testing.</note>, so that the credit of the matter might be more full. Let it therefore be our intention to explore the distances around the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The position of a planet in its orbit if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle.</note> of 90 and 270 degrees.

<margin>At mean anomaly 87.</margin>
In the year 1589, on the 6th day of May, at 11:15 PM, **Mars** was observed at 27° 7' 30'' in Libra with a latitude of 0° 6' 30'' North. At that time, the true position of the **Sun** is gathered to be 25° 48' 40'' in Taurus, and its distance <term>FROM THE EARTH</term> <note>original: "A TERRA"</note> was 101361. The mean longitude of <term>Mars</term> was 7 signs, 26° 0' 36'', and therefore its <term>eccentric place</term> <note>The position of the planet on its orbital path as viewed from the Sun.</note> was 15° 32' 13'' in Scorpio. But our "substitute hypothesis" from Chapter 16 did not attain the true or observed position of **MARS** in the <term>acronychal</term> <note>When a planet is at opposition—directly opposite the Sun in the sky, rising at sunset.</note> position within 2.5 minutes; thus, in this subtle business, it is not permitted to trust the computation of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The planet's position corrected for the eccentricity of its orbit.</note>. Therefore, to the Method of Chapter 27, 28, or 42, I will add another observation, though using a freer Method. But as I warned above in Chapter 12, the planet was not often observed twice in this place. We must therefore be content with two observations.

<margin>Shortcuts for finding the longitude of a Planet given its distance from a fixed star of known latitude, when the Planet lacks latitude.</margin>
For to the one already stated, another is joined from the year 1594, on the 28th day of December, on the morning of which day at 7:15, the mean longitude of Mars is gathered as 7 signs, 26° 13' 39'', exceeding the former by a few minutes. Then, therefore, **Mars**, at an altitude of eight or nine degrees, was observed to be 50° 34' distant from **Spica Virginis** <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo.</note>. *Since it stood very close to the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The path the Sun follows across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</note>, in the right triangle between Spica, its ecliptic place, and Mars, the base is given as 50° 34' and the side between Spica and the ecliptic as 1° 59', namely the latitude of Spica. Therefore, the remaining side is 50° 32' 18''. Because Spica was at 18° 11' Libra, Mars fell at 8° 43' 18'' Sagittarius. This place declines from the equator by 21° 50' 20''.*

However, **Mars** was found to decline by 21° 41'. Therefore, it displayed a very small Northern latitude, namely 9' 20''. It also had a Northern latitude of 3' on the following 4th of January, 1595. By which our observation is confirmed. Even if you assume this exact latitude for Mars, its ecliptic position will not be sensibly altered; so you may safely pronounce its position to be 8° 43' Sagittarius. And because **Mars** was near the **Sun**, it was therefore very high from the Earth, and in a <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in a planet's position depending on the observer's location on Earth; it is smaller for more distant objects.</note> much smaller than the Sun, which we shall neglect. But we cannot similarly neglect <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light through the atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear slightly higher than they actually are.</note>; which I will now remove.

<margin>Method for separating refractions in length and breadth.</margin>
For the position of the **Sun** was 16° 47' 10'' Capricorn, its distance from Earth 98232, the right ascension of which is 288° 12'. Therefore, 306° 37' of the equator was rising, and with it 29° Sagittarius, whose angle between the ecliptic and the horizon was 26°, and the complement 64°. And because the refraction of altitude from the table of Fixed Star refractions is shown as 6' 30'', and from the Solar tables as 11', at a height of the Star of 8.5 degrees; therefore, 5' 51'' or 9' 53'' are owed to the latitude. The latitude there was 3' 29'' North: here 0' 53'' South. And the refraction of longitude was 2' 39'' or 4' 34''.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>
The use of parallax in calculating latitudes.
</margin>

**Chapter 51.** [The latitude] was seen as $6 \frac{2}{3}'$ North. Because Mars is near the Earth, and the angle at the Sun [☉] is $10^\circ 17'$ and at the Earth $28^\circ 41'$, this latitude therefore requires an inclination of $2^\circ 30'$. Thus, in our later observation, the inclination of Mars [♂] will be $2^\circ 30'$, and a little bit less because we are 8 minutes closer to the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note>. *With an assumed inclination of $2^\circ 30'$*, since this angle at the Sun [☉] is $61'$ and at the Earth $38'$, it must follow that the latitude is $1^\circ 50'$ South, roughly, as shown by our <term>Parallax table</term> <note>Kepler used these tables to account for the difference in the planet's position as seen from the Earth versus from the Sun.</note>. But by taking into account the <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light through the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear slightly higher than they actually are.</note> of the Fixed Stars, the latitude left to us was $3^\circ 29'$ North. By taking into account the solar [parallax] adjustment, we were reduced by $0^\circ 33'$ to the South. Therefore, in our case, more than the correct amount was assumed for refraction on one side, and less on the other. The correct intermediate refraction would thus be $3^\circ 36'$. Consequently, Mars is placed for us at $8^\circ 46 \frac{1}{2}'$ in **Taurus [♉]**.

Let **the Sun [☉]** be the Sun, B and A be points on the orbit of the Earth, A being the Earth's location in the first observation, B in the later one, and M be Mars. Let the lines be connected. Although Mars did not return precisely to the same place, in both positions it is represented by the line ☉M. Therefore, the angle AM☉ is $28^\circ 41' 14''$ and A☉ is $101365$. Let the distance of Mars from the Sun, M☉ (*which is what we are looking for here*), be assumed as if known, and let it be $154200$. Therefore, ☉M will fall at $15^\circ 31' 3''$ in **Scorpio [♏]**. 

Now, if ☉M is assumed to be $154200$ in the first observation, it must be assumed to be shorter in the later one. One degree at this location on the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The off-center circular path Kepler was testing for Mars.</note> changes the distance by 240 units, regardless of which method you use to construct the distances. Therefore, since the <term>mean longitudes</term> <note>The position of the planet assuming it moved at a perfectly uniform speed.</note> here differ by 13 minutes, and after subtracting the measure of <term>precession</term> <note>The slow, continuous shift in the orientation of Earth's axis which changes the coordinate system of the stars.</note>, by only eight; the proportional part of 240 is 32. Therefore, in the second observation, we assumed ☉M to be $154168$. But the angle ☉MB is also known, namely $38^\circ 0' 40''$, and ☉B is $98232$. Thus, the angle ☉MB is given as $23^\circ 6' 11''$. Therefore, ☉M is at $15^\circ 40' 9''$ in **Scorpio [♏]** the second time, differing from the first eccentric location by 9 minutes. 

It should have differed a little more. For the <term>mean anomalies</term> <note>The angle measuring the planet's progress around its orbit from its perihelion (closest point to the Sun).</note> differed by $8' 3''$, to which $7' 49''$ correspond in the equated anomaly of the eccentric at this location. Add to these the intermediate precession of the equinoxes, $4' 48''$. Thus, $12' 37''$ are accumulated. Therefore, it should have fallen at $15^\circ 43' 40''$ in **Scorpio [♏]**. Therefore, we must suspect slightly different distances for ☉M, and they must be altered so that the lines represented by ☉M move away from each other by about $2 \frac{1}{2}$ minutes more. For when the Earth is at A, ☉M must move in <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "antecedentia"; moving "backward" against the order of the zodiac signs.</note>; and when the Earth is at B, it moves in <term>direct motion</term> <note>original: "consequentia"; moving "forward" through the zodiac.</note>. This happens if you increase ☉M: so that in the first position it is $154400$, and the second time $154368$. Then ☉M falls first at $15^\circ 29' 34''$ in **Scorpio [♏]**, and the second time at $15^\circ 42' 18''$ in **Scorpio [♏]**.

Moreover, the mean anomaly is $87^\circ 9' 24''$ at the first time, and $87^\circ 16' 30''$ at the following. And these are at the first mean longitude.

<margin>
At 87 degrees, the complement of the mean anomaly.
</margin>

For the other mean longitude, we will use the observation from the year 1615 in the month of December, well-supported by the agreement of several consecutive days; and there the <term>Proxy hypothesis</term> <note>original: "Vicaria hypothesis"; Kepler's name for his earlier, highly accurate mathematical model that didn't yet account for physical causes.</note> also represented the <term>acronychal</term> <note>A planet is at its "acronychal" point when it is directly opposite the Sun from the Earth's perspective.</note> position of Mars perfectly in the preceding October. For the sake of agreement, we will also add October of the year 1617. In other years, it was not observed at this location on the eccentric. For the eccentric location falls at $10^\circ$ in **Taurus [♉]**. Thus, Mars being at this location in the year 1580 in November, was observed for the last time.

#### PART FOUR.

<margin>CHAPTER 51.</margin>
First, his arrival at this location fell in October 1582, when the zeal for observation was not yet burning hot. In September 1584, July 1586, June 1588, April 1590, and March 1592—at these times, because of the shortness and brightness of the nights in Denmark, [Mars] was neglected while it was near the Sun; they were instead intent upon the fixed stars, the Moon, and the remaining planets whenever an opportunity arose. At the end of 1593 and the beginning of 1594, when it was in <term>quadrature</term> <note>An aspect where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart.</note> with the Sun [☉], the observation was not continued beyond this aspect, because astronomers are particularly accustomed to looking for this quadrature. Therefore, on December 17, 1595, at 7:06 in the evening, the planet was seen at 11° 31' 27" **Taurus [♉]**, with a northern latitude of 1° 46' 44". The position of the Sun was 5° 39' 3" **Capricorn [♑]**. Its distance from the Earth was 98,200.

->From this, the <term>mean longitude</term> <note>The position the planet would have if its orbit were a perfect circle and its speed constant.</note> of MARS is gathered as 2 signs, 2° 4' 22".<-

And because the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> is at 4 signs, 28° 58' 10", the distance of the position from the aphelion is 8 signs, 53' 48" backward from **Cancer [♋]**. Previously, the distance forward was almost the same, namely 87° 9' 24". Therefore, these two positions are almost equally distant from the aphelion. Now, according to our <term>Vicarious Hypothesis</term> <note>Kepler's earlier mathematical model that predicted longitudes accurately but failed on distances.</note>, the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance from aphelion, adjusted for the planet's varying speed.</note> corresponding to this simple anomaly is 76° 25' 48", which, when subtracted from the position of the aphelion, leaves 12° 32' 22" **Leo [♌]** as the <term>eccentric position</term> <note>The planet's position on its orbital path as viewed from the center of the orbit rather than the Sun.</note> of Mars.

Let **A** be the *Earth*, **o** the *Sun*, and **M** *Mars*. The distance **AO** is given as 98,200. And because **OM** is at 12° 32' 22" **Leo [♌]**, while **AM** is at 11° 31' 37" **Taurus [♉]**, the angle **AMO** is 31° 0' 55". And because **AO** is at 5° 39' 3" **Capricorn [♑]** but **AM** is at 11° 31' 27" **Taurus [♉]**, the complement angle **OAM** is 54° 7' 36". From this—because the ratio of the sine of angle **AMO** to side **AO** is the same as the sine of angle **OAM** to side **OM**—the distance **OM** comes out to 154,432. And because this position is 15 minutes closer to the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point farthest from the center of motion.</note> than the one in the year 1589, and at this place in the eccentric orbit one degree equals 240 units, 60 units must be subtracted for the 15 minutes (since distances from the aphelion are shorter in more distant places), so that 154,372 is produced. Conversely, because the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane.</note> is around 16° 20' **Cancer [♋]**, and the eccentric position is at 12° 32' **Leo [♌]**, it is 26° 12' distant from the Node. The maximum inclination of the planes is 1° 50'. Therefore, the inclination of this position is 48' 32". Its <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric function used here to calculate the diagonal distance from the Sun to the planet's position above or below the ecliptic plane.</note> exceeds the radius by 10 parts, which in our dimensions is 15 1/2. Thus, the distance of that point in the orbit of Mars from the Sun is 154,387. Previously, at this very same distance from the aphelion, it was found to be approximately 154,400 away from the Sun. Therefore, the eccentric distances of these points from the Sun are equal "to the fingernail" <note>original: "ad unguem"; an idiom meaning "exactly" or "to a hair's breadth".</note>. For the 13 units that are missing in the latter case are negligible. I shall be happy if I can remain within an uncertainty of 100 units everywhere.

Now I will also add the year 1597, not so much to confirm the previous points—which are certain enough in themselves—but to provide the reader an opportunity to compare TYCHO'S observations with those of others; by which means he may finally understand how great a benefit that man has bestowed upon us. There are indeed observations by the same author from the last days of October 1597, but they were taken with a <term>radius</term> <note>A cross-staff; an instrument for measuring the angle between two stars.</note> in a foreign place and were not recalculated by the author himself, who knew how to correct distances taken by the radius using a certain table for the <term>parallax of the eye</term> <note>A correction for the fact that the observer's eye is not at the exact center of the instrument.</note>, as he advised in his *Progymnasmata*. Since, therefore, very different distances were recorded for the same moment (perhaps because the corrected ones were placed next to the observed ones), they should be set aside. However, I myself, while absent in Styria, observed at that same moment—and this is a marvelous thing to say—through the eyes of TYCHO BRAHE, who was staying on the shore of the Baltic Sea. Here is the series of observations. "Hold back your laughter, friends." <note>original: "Risum teneatis amici"; a quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica* regarding something absurd or unexpected.</note>

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER 51.</margin>
In the year 1597, on Saturday, November 8 (or October 29 <note>Kepler provides both the New Style (Gregorian) and Old Style (Julian) dates.</note>), in the morning, Mars was not yet on the line from the 12th star of Gemini to the 4th. On the following day, it had already passed that line: it was closer to the 9th star than the 12th, and precisely on the line from the 11th to the 9th; likewise, it was precisely on the line from the 1st to the 5th, or perhaps just a very little bit further east. And the 5th star was midway between the 1st and Mars.

From these observations, the position of Mars can be derived, assuming the very certain positions of the stars from the catalog of <term>TYCHO BRAHE</term> <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used to derive his laws.</note>, which I now claim to have seen with my own eyes. But because the Ninth star is not recorded in <term>BRAHE’S</term> catalog (for in its place at the ninth position is another star, distant from the <term>PTOLEMAIC</term> <note>Referring to the star catalog of Claudius Ptolemy from the 2nd century AD.</note> position by more than 3 degrees, and smaller than all the others), we will therefore call upon the latitude of Mars for consultation; for a moderate knowledge of it is sufficient for us.

*The mean longitude of Mars is found to be, for the morning of October 29 at the fifth hour (probable, since I did not record the exact hour), 1 sign, 29° 10' 43". Therefore, the <term>eccentric position</term> <note>The position of the planet on its orbital path, regardless of the observer's viewpoint.</note> is at 9° 43' **Gemini [♊]**, distant from the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note> by 23° 20'. The <term>inclination</term> <note>The angle between the orbital plane of Mars and the ecliptic.</note> is therefore 43' 52". The Sun, however, is at 15° 40' **Scorpio [♏]**, and the seen position of Mars is estimated in advance to be around 12 1/2° **Cancer [♋]**. Therefore, the latitude is 1° 36' 24". Let it be calculated what the longitude of the point on the line from the twelfth star to the fourth would be, having a northern latitude of 1° 30 1/2'.*

*Since, therefore, the fourth star is at 9° 54' **Cancer [♋]** with a northern latitude of 7° 43', and the twelfth is at 12° 56' **Cancer [♋]** with a southern latitude of 0° 13 1/2', the longitude of our point will be proportionally 12° 16' 17" **Cancer [♋]**. Mars, however, was not yet here on October 29; and on the 30th it had already passed it. Its daily motion was not greater than 5 minutes, half of which is 2 1/2, so that on the morning of the 30th it would have been at 12° 18 1/2' **Cancer [♋]** in the completed year 1600; but in the year 1597, it was at 12° 16' **Cancer [♋]**. Three minutes of error in latitude can hardly produce one minute of error in longitude. Therefore, the position is sufficiently certain.*

*If you also explore by the first and fifth stars, the point on that line whose latitude is 1° 30 1/2' falls at 12° 9' **Cancer [♋]**. And Mars was further east—that is, further along in the sequence of signs—namely at 12° 16' approximately, or a little before, being also in the middle. Therefore, the latitude computed by us is confirmed; for it must itself be very nearly in the middle, and indeed it is. For between the latitude of Mars at 1° 3 1/2' and the fifth star at 5° 42 1/2', the difference is 4° 12'; between this and the first star at 10° 2', the difference is 4° 20' in the middle.*

Therefore, let Mars be at 12° 16' **Cancer [♋]**. In the year 1617 <note>original: "MDCXVII". This is likely a typographical error in the original text for 1597 (MDXCVII), as the observation context and the following calculations match the 1597 date.</note> on October 30 at 5:00 in the morning, the position of the Sun is found to be 16° 38' 8" **Scorpio [♏]**. The distance is 98,820. The mean longitude is 1 sign, 29° 42' 10". The <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> is at 4 signs, 28° 57' 10". The complement of the mean anomaly is 89° 15'; the equated anomaly is 78° 43' 23", and the eccentric position is 10° 13' 47" **Gemini [♊]**. Therefore, from this, the distance is derived as 153,753.

But because we are 2° 6' deeper from the aphelion than before, we will add twice 240 (the sum of parts due to one degree):

<margin>At 43 degrees, the complement of the mean anomaly.</margin>
BUT LET US ASCEND even higher, toward the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note>, and explore those places where, from what was demonstrated in Chapter 6, the warping of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The off-center circular path previously used to model orbits.</note> through the permutation of the Sun's mean motion with its true motion can happen most evidently; namely, in the Sun's <term>apogee</term> <note>The point where the Sun is furthest from Earth.</note> and the sign of Cancer.

In the year 1596, on the 9th of March, at 7:40 in the evening, when the position of the Sun was 29° 31' 24" Aries; its distance from the Earth was 99,764; the mean longitude of Mars was 3 signs 15° 35' Taurus; the aphelion was at 4° 28' 58" 31"'; the complement of the <term>mean anomaly</term> to a full circle was 43° 23' 31"; the <term>coequated anomaly</term> <note>The mean anomaly corrected for the orbit's eccentricity.</note> was 36° 46' 2"; the eccentric position from the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> <note>Kepler's earlier "placeholder" model that accurately predicted longitudes but failed on distances.</note> was 22° 18' 29" Cancer: the planet was seen at 15° 49' 12" Gemini. The latitude was 1° 47' 40" North. Therefore, the angle at the Earth was 76° 17' 48", and at the planet 36° 29' 17". Thus, the distance of Mars from the Sun was 162,994—or more accurately, the distance of the point in the plane of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> that lies perpendicularly beneath the body of Mars.

But for the sake of certainty, let another observation be added to this one. Mars was in precisely the same place among the fixed stars in the year 1584, on the 25th of November, at 10:20 PM, when the Sun was in 14° 6' 3" Sagittarius, at a distance from the Earth of 98,318. The mean anomaly did not differ sensibly from the previous one, because the motion of the aphelion is only a little faster than the motion of the fixed stars. Therefore, the eccentric position is the same, if you subtract the <term>precession</term> <note>The slow wobble of Earth's axis that shifts the positions of stars over centuries.</note> of 9' 45", namely 22° 8' 44" Cancer. However, the planet was seen on the 11th of November at 1:25 AM in 23° 14' 5" Leo with a northern latitude of 2° 12' 24". On the following 20th of November, at 6:30 PM astronomically, it appeared in 26° 6' 30" Leo. And so, in 9 days and 5 hours, it moved through 2° 46' 25"; according to <term>Magini</term> <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini, a contemporary astronomer whose tables Kepler used for comparison.</note>, it moved through 2° 48'. Since our time follows by another 4 days and 15:49 hours, to which a motion of 1° 28' corresponds from Magini's tables, we will add 1° 27' by analogy with the former. Thus, Mars could have been seen at approximately 27° 27' 30" Leo. Therefore, the angle at the Earth was 73° 27' 27", and at the planet 35° 18' 46". Thus, the distance of Mars from the Sun here is 163,051, exceeding the previous one by 57 units, which are absorbed by the slightest change in the eccentric position, showing that the vicarious hypothesis is not faithful down to a single minute here. But even in the application of the observation, some very slight error could easily have been made.

**Thirdly**, let the same thing be investigated by us below the mean longitudes, toward the <term>perihelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note>.

<margin>At a mean anomaly of 113 degrees.</margin> In the year **1591**, on the night following the **14th** of May at 1:40 AM, when the Sun was at 2° 8' 43" of Gemini; its distance from the Earth was 101,487; the mean longitude of Mars was 8° 22' 18' 4"; the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its aphelion.</note> was 113° 24' 4"; the equated anomaly 103° 15' 48"; wherefore the eccentric position from the vicarious hypothesis was 12° 9' 48" of Sagittarius (or by analogy with the nearby 26° of Sagittarius just mentioned, 12° 8' 3/4" of Sagittarius). Because of this, the distance of Mars (or the point on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>) from the Sun is 147,802 or more truly 147,683. Here you see that by an error of a single <term>scrupulum</term> <note>A small unit of measure, here a minute of arc.</note> in the eccentric position, we lose 120 units of our measurement, because of such great proximity between Mars and the Earth, and such closeness to the position of the Sun's opposite point. Therefore, the smallest details are not to be pursued here. Furthermore, this observation is well-supported by others from surrounding days, right up to the day of <term>opposition</term> <note>When a planet is directly opposite the Sun in the sky.</note> with the Sun. Since it is 12° 10' of Sagittarius from the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note>, about 26 1/2 parts; therefore the <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric ratio used to calculate distances in a triangle.</note> of the inclination of this place exceeds the radius by about 11 units, which in our dimension are about 15 or 16, so that the distance of **MARS** from the **SUN** here becomes as nearly as possible 147,820 or 147,700.

In the similar anomaly <note>In historical astronomy, 'anomaly' refers to the angular distance of a planet from its aphelion—the point where it is farthest from the Sun.</note> of the descending semicircle, there is only one observation available, but it is sufficiently certain. For in the year 1593, on the night following the 29th of June at 1:30 AM, when the Sun was at 17° 25' 42" of Cancer at a distance of 101,760 from the Earth, the longitude of Mars was 18° 10' 1" 29. The anomaly was 161° 5' 29", and therefore the calculated position of Mars was 6° 10' 5". It was observed at 13° 37' 22" of Capricorn, at a latitude of 4° 37' South. From this, the complement of the angle at the Earth was 56° 11' 46", and at the planet—that is, the parallax <term>parallax: the apparent shift in a planet's position when viewed from the Earth versus the Sun</term> of the annual orbit—it was 37° 27' 23". From this, the distance of Mars from the Sun is found to be 139,036. Previously, at an anomaly of 161° 45' 28", where Mars is 40 minutes of a degree further from the aphelion than here, the distance was found and established as 139,000. And these 40 minutes at this location on the eccentric <note>original: "eccentrici loco." The 'eccentric' is the circular path of the planet which is shifted so its center is not at the Sun.</note> produce 52 units of distance. Therefore, by the analogy of our anomaly, at an anomaly of 161° 45 1/2, the distance would result in 138,984—an admirable and certainly suspicious degree of agreement. For all things can hardly be so certain and exquisite. However, the distances must be increased slightly on both sides because of the maximum inclination of the eccentric at this location.

From this very long induction <note>A logical conclusion drawn from a series of specific observations.</note> through many locations of the eccentric, it appears that those distances of Mars from the Sun are equal to each other whose points on the orbit are equally distant from the aphelion, which we investigated in Chapters 16 and 42. This is clear evidence that the aphelion is correctly positioned, according to the seventh proposition of the third book of Euclid. <note>Kepler cites Euclid's geometry to prove that lines of equal length from a point (the Sun) to a circle's edge must be equidistant from the circle's diameter (the line of apsides).</note>

At the same time, the distances of the Sun from the Earth are confirmed. These were constructed above in Chapter 29 and have now been used here in various ways; no great discrepancy in the numbers has arisen that could testify to any defect in them.

Therefore, regarding the conclusions from the observations in this chapter and the distances found through them, which contribute to the shaping of the planetary path (the reason we produced them in this chapter), we shall defer explaining them until Chapter 55. For first, in the following Chapter 52, something else must be demonstrated from these findings, and in Chapter 53, still more observations must be brought forward as testimony.

-># ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS<-

<margin>CHAPTER 52.</margin>

Since I have constructed the eccentric of Mars upon the body of the Sun itself, it is necessary that the Planet is also truly at its farthest distance from the Sun in those parts which are around 29° Leo <note>29 degrees of the zodiac sign Leo.</note>. However, in both semicircles, those parts that follow this 29° Leo at equal intervals are at equal distances from the Sun, but at unequal distances from the point that acts as a substitute for the Sun. For Tycho Brahe, this point is the center of the Sun's epicycle; specifically, the distances are smaller in the descending semicircle. Having established this, it follows naturally that the parts around 24° Leo are not at the greatest distance from either the body of the Sun or the Copernican center of the world (which for Brahe is the center of the Sun's epicycle, and likewise the center where the planetary system is attached). Furthermore, parts moving away from 24° Leo by an equal arc in either semicircle will be at unequal distances from both the Sun and from that substitute point.

*For let the center of the Sun be represented by **A**, the line of apsides <term>line of apsides: the line passing through the points of an orbit where the planet is closest to and farthest from the center</term> of Mars by **AC**, the eccentricity by **AC**, and the eccentric orbit by **ED**, with its center at **C**. Let **F** be a point above **AC**, which is the equant point <term>equant point: a mathematical point used to account for the observed speed changes of planets</term>. Let **G** be the aphelion <term>aphelion: the point in the orbit farthest from the Sun</term>. Let the angles **GFE** and **GFD** be equal, and let **EA** and **DA** be connected; these will be equal, as has already been demonstrated. Let a line **AB** be drawn through **A** toward <unclear>Jupiter</unclear> <note>The symbol ♃ in the text usually represents Jupiter, used here as a directional marker</note>; and let **AB** be extended from **A** toward <unclear>Jupiter</unclear> by a quantity of 1800, where **AC** was 14140 in Chapter 42, and **AE** and **AD** were 154400. Let the center of the Earth's orbit be **B**. Therefore, because **BA** tends toward 5 1/2° Scorpio and **AE** toward 15 1/2° Scorpio, the angle **EAB** is about 50' and acute, while **EBA** is obtuse; for this reason, **EA** is longer than **EB**. Similarly, while **BA** tends toward 5 1/2° Scorpio, **AD** tends toward 12 1/2° Gemini; therefore, angle **BAD** is 157°, and **ABD** is quite acute; for this reason, **AD** (or **AE**, which is equal to it) is shorter than **BD**. Therefore, **BE** is much shorter than **BD**, and this is clearly perceptible. For how can we ignore a difference of 1800 and more, when observations cannot tolerate an error of even 200? Therefore, the parts of the eccentric in opposite semicircles that are equally distant from **G** (namely **E** and **D**) are not equally distant from any points outside the center, except from points on the line **CA** which passes through the body of the Sun.*

*BUT YOU MAY SAY that by connecting **BC** and continuing the line, a new line of apsides is formed where the line cuts the circle; and that point **D** is closer to that line of apsides than **E** is; is it therefore no wonder that **BD** is longer? I ANSWER: Whatever lines are drawn, **AE** and **AD** always remain as they are, because they have been demonstrated from observations in a triple form of hypotheses. For this demonstration, absolutely nothing has been assumed that could be disputed. Therefore, while **AE** and **AD** remain, let **BC** indeed be drawn, as has been proposed against me. However, that line **BC**, as I demonstrated in Chapter 6, in no way produces a hypothesis fit for the observed <gloss>acronychal positions</gloss> <note>original: "ἀκρονυχίοις"; observations made when a planet is in opposition to the Sun</note>. Instead of **BC**, in order to save the acronychal observations, we must draw a line through **F** parallel to **CB**, namely **FH**, passing through **F** and **H**, the centers of equality <note>The points of uniform motion</note> for Mars and the Sun. Once this is done, the center of the eccentric is simultaneously transferred from **C** to **I**, and more than a semicircle tends toward **E** and less toward **D**. **AE** and **AD** are not left as they were; rather, **AE** is lengthened and **AD** is shortened. If these lines are changed, the observations made outside of the acronychal position will never be saved, because these observations testify to the equality of the lines **AE** and **AD**. I do not think there is a need for further calculation. If, however, anyone delights in this labor (although it is a crime for an Astrono—)*

He has an example above in Chapter **24**, where I computed the distances of the Earth from **H**—the point of the Earth's equality of motion <note>The equant point, where the planet appears to move at a constant speed</note>—and the distance of Mars from that same point **H** in the same operation and using the same observations. Later, in Chapter **26**, I computed the distances of that same Earth and Mars from **A**, the center of the Sun.

For the nature of the method I used is such that it teaches how—once any point is assumed in the plane of the Earth's circle that has a described and determined position relative to the body of the Sun, both in zodiacal longitude and in distance from the Sun—one may learn the distance of both the Earth and Mars from that chosen point through several observations. This is possible even without knowledge of the equated anomaly of the eccentric <note>original: "anomaliæ eccentri coæquatæ"; the angular position of the planet on its path adjusted for its irregular speed</note> adapted to that point, which I used in Chapter **26** only for the sake of brevity.

**B E S I D E S**, one may argue by another reason. It was demonstrated above in Chapter **44** that the orbit of a Planet is not a circle but an oval, such that its diameter (which is called the line of apsides <term>line of apsides: the axis connecting the points of an orbit closest to and farthest from the center</term>) is the longest. Now, in Chapter **51**, it is demonstrated that parts equally distant from **G**, the point of the aphelion <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit farthest from the sun</term>, also curve inward equally at the sides. Therefore, the genuine position of the oval is around the line **AC**, and not around the line **FH**. And whoever computes the various distances of Mars from point **H** by the method already commended will discover a great irregularity of distances, which can by no means be enclosed by a circle or by any probable figure arranged around **FH**.

**A N D S O**, I have again fulfilled the pledge I made in Chapter **6** and throughout this work, without any "begging of the principle" <note>A logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</note>; I have shown that the eccentric of Mars cannot be referred to anything but the Sun itself. Consequently, not only reason but even the observations themselves stand on my side, while I weighed the observations of Mars—freed from the "mean motion" <note>The theoretical average position of the sun used by previous astronomers like Ptolemy and Copernicus</note> of the Sun—against the actual apparent motion of the Sun.

...to explore by several methods. Let $\alpha$ be the Sun, $\beta$ the location of the Earth before the opposition of Mars <note>symbol: ♂</note> with the Sun <note>symbol: ☉</note>, and $\alpha$ $\beta$ $\delta$ the angle of vision or the curved elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between two celestial bodies as seen from the Earth</term> of $\delta$ from the Sun. Similarly, let $\gamma$ be the location of the Earth after opposition, and $\alpha$ $\gamma$ $\delta$ the angle of vision: so that at the first time the Planet is on the line $\beta$ $\delta$, and at the second on the line $\gamma$ $\delta$, and it truly completes the path $\vartheta$ $\eta$. Therefore, given the time of the two observations, the angle $\vartheta$ $\alpha$ $\eta$ will also be given quite precisely, at any place on the eccentric, from the vicarious hypothesis <note>Kepler’s "vicarious hypothesis" was an intermediate model that accurately predicted the planet's longitudes but used an incorrect physical center</note>. *But if the two times are not far apart, or if the Planet is positioned near the apsides <note>the points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the Sun</note> or the mean longitudes, the difference in the lengths of the lines $\alpha \vartheta, \alpha \eta$ will also be known reasonably well. Indeed, we already have so much in our prior knowledge that no difficulty remains here.*

*If, therefore, we assume $\vartheta \alpha$—and consequently $\eta \alpha$—to correspond to the angles $\vartheta \beta \alpha, \eta \gamma \alpha$ given from observation, and the known distances $\beta \alpha, \gamma \alpha$ from the third part of this work, it is clear that if this assumption is longer than it should be (such as $\varkappa \alpha, \iota \alpha$), then the resulting angle $\iota \alpha \varkappa$ will be smaller than is correct; but if it is shorter than it should be (such as $\zeta \alpha, \varepsilon \alpha$), the resulting angle $\varepsilon \alpha \zeta$ will be larger than is correct. Therefore, those distances must be assumed which establish for us the correct angle of the eccentric motion.*

In the same way, any remaining error in the eccentric position will also be revealed here. For let it be that $\vartheta \alpha, \eta \alpha$ hold their correct places; then let $\vartheta \alpha$ be moved forward <note>original: "in consequentia"; moving in the direction of the signs of the zodiac</note> by mistake by the angle $\vartheta \alpha \delta$: and let $\eta \alpha$ similarly be moved forward by an equal angle $\eta \alpha \varepsilon$. You see that instead of $\alpha \vartheta$, the resulting $\alpha \delta$ will be quite long, and instead of $\alpha \eta$, the resulting $\alpha \varepsilon$ will be very short, contrary to what is known beforehand from the hypothesis. However, the angle $\gamma \alpha \beta$ must not be altogether tiny, lest even the smallest error of observation, turning toward opposite parts of the sky (as can happen), introduce something significant. Thus, by this method, we must proceed through the years 1582 in Cancer, 1585 in Leo, 1587 in Virgo, 1589 in Libra, 1591 in Scorpio, 1593 in Sagittarius, and 1595 in Aries. For in all these places, sufficient observations are at hand.

But if one wishes to investigate demonstratively which elongation of the Earth from the line through the Sun and the Planet allows a mistake in the distance of Mars from the Sun to be perceived most clearly, let Chapter 6 be consulted. For from that, we will define an angle at the Sun so great that the proportion of its sine to the radius nearly equals the proportion of the excess of Mars's distance from the Sun over the sine of the complement of the angle, to that very distance.

*For let $\alpha$ be the Sun, $\vartheta$ the Planet, $\upsilon \xi$ the orbit of the Earth. From $\vartheta$ let the straight line $\vartheta \mu$ be erected, perpendicular to $\vartheta \alpha$. And on $\vartheta \mu$ let several centers be taken, from which circles are described through $\vartheta$, until one of them touches the orbit of the Earth at $\nu$. The point $\nu$ will be where the deficiency of $\alpha \vartheta$ itself in $\vartheta$ appears most clearly—that is, where it subtends the greatest angle. Let $\nu o$ be drawn from $\nu$ parallel to $\mu \vartheta$, cutting $\alpha \vartheta$ at $o$. I say that as $o \vartheta$ is to $\vartheta \alpha$, so $o \nu$ is to $\nu \alpha$. For as $\nu \mu$ (which is $\vartheta \mu$) is to $\mu \alpha$, so is $o \nu$ to $\nu \alpha$. But $\nu \mu$ is to $\mu \alpha$ as $o \vartheta$ is nearly $\xi \vartheta$ to $\vartheta \alpha$. Therefore, etc.*

*Let $\alpha \vartheta$ be 161,000. $\xi \vartheta$ will be nearly 61,000. And as 161 is to 61, so 100,000 is to 37,882. This sine shows the angle $\nu \alpha \vartheta$ to be 22° 15'. And it would be greater if you now take $o \vartheta$ instead of $\xi \vartheta$.*

# PART FOUR.

<margin>CHAPTER 53.</margin>
Therefore, until the anomaly of commutation <term>anomaly of commutation: the angular distance of the Earth from the planet’s opposition, which determines the parallax</term> varies by $22 \frac{1}{4}$ degrees, many days—nearly 45, in fact—pass, after or before which the position at $\delta$ <note>the position of Mars</note> is far from another. Thus, at aphelion <term>aphelion: the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun</term>, this angle of commutation is about 28 degrees; at perihelion <term>perihelion: the point in a planet's orbit closest to the Sun</term>, it is about $18 \frac{1}{3}$ degrees.

Having found these limits of most evident error, should any arise from a faulty distance of Mars from the Sun, it is now easy for us to select suitable observations where they are available in abundance.

We shall begin from the opposition of the year 1582, from which year we shall select these observations.

| YEAR 1582 Nov. 24, 4:00 AM | Dec. 26, 8:30 PM | Dec. 30, 8:10 PM | Year 1585 Jan. 26, 6:15 AM |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Observed in 26° 38' 30" ♋ | 17° 46' 30" ♋ | 16° 6' 30" ♋ | 8° 20' 30" ♋ |
| Observed latitude 2° 49' 10" North | 4° 7' 0" North | 4° 8' 0" North | 2° 52' 12" North |
| Sun in 11° 40' 40" ♐ | 15° 4' 12" ♑ | 19° 8' 31" ♑ | 16° 33' 20" ♒ |
| $\alpha\beta$ dist. ☉ from Earth 98345 | $\alpha\beta$ 98226 | $\alpha\gamma$ 98252 | $\alpha\gamma$ 98624 |
| Mean Anomaly 67° 28' 13" | 49° 39' 10" | 47° 51' 35" | 34° 8' 15" |
| Eccentric position 0° 43' 34" ♋ | 16° 7' 10" ♋ | 17° 57' 32" ♋ | 0° 9' 46" ♌ |
| In the ecliptic $\alpha\delta$ 0° 42' 42" ♋ | 16° 6' 23" ♋ | $\alpha\eta$ 17° 56' 45" ♋ | $\alpha\eta$ 0° 9' 30" ♌ |
| Resulting $\alpha\delta$ 158920 | 163082 | $\alpha\eta$ 158842 | $\alpha\eta$ 164116 |
| Via latitude 158960 | 163147 | 158907 | 164196 |

The two middle values differ by 4240. And indeed, the latter $\alpha\eta$ is shorter, when it ought to have been longer by 336. Therefore, the sum of both is 322054. From this I subtract 336, and add it again. The halves of the established values are 160859, which is $\alpha\delta$, and 161363, which is $\alpha\eta$. Mars <note>symbol: ♂</note> at $\alpha$ would then be at 16° 5' ♋, and at $\alpha\eta$ at 17° 55' ♋. Thus, here the vicarious hypothesis <note>Kepler’s earlier model which was accurate for longitudes but physically incorrect</note> would lose $1 \frac{1}{2}$ minutes.

Yet these distances themselves, because that angle is so small, are **unreliable**. For if the angle of Mars varies by one minute through an error of observation, which easily happens, we will go astray by a thousand parts in any distance.

Let us therefore take the two more remote observations, which are found to differ by 5235. But we know in advance they ought to differ by about 5570. Thus, having performed the operation as before, more true values come forth: $\alpha\delta$ 158792, and $\alpha\eta$ 164364; so that $\alpha\delta$ is at 0° 41' 0" ♋, and $\alpha\eta$ is at 0° 8' 30" ♌. And it becomes certain from the observations of these four days that in this place, about $1 \frac{1}{2}$ minutes must be taken away from the eccentric positions derived from our vicarious hypothesis.

The distances previously found, on this side and that side of opposition, which resulted in a mean measure between these, are also moderately confirmed; except that analogy indicates they ought to be a little longer.

At the same time, it is clear that if the angle ♂ $\delta$ $\eta$ <note>the angle between the Sun, Earth, and Mars</note> is corrupted by one minute, each distance is corrupted by about 50 parts, not more. In these distances, therefore, barely a hundredth part of the previous uncertainty can be erred.

Now, if any chosen length of distances satisfies the observations of these four days, it will likewise express the observations of the intervening days; namely, November 25, 26, 27 of the year 1582; December 3, 17, 27, 28, 29 of 1582; and January 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22 of the year 1583.

The two middle values differ by 118. They ought to have differed by 187 in the opposite direction: such that the distance from the Sun to Mars <note>original: "a ♂"</note> would be 166,226, and the distance to the second point <note>original: "an"</note> would be 166,412. Therefore, the distance to Mars falls at 18° 48' 47'' Leo, and the second distance at 23° 34' 48'' Leo. Thus, even with such a negligible change in the eccentric position, the Vicarious Hypothesis <term>Vicarious Hypothesis: Kepler's early, highly accurate mathematical model for Mars's longitude, which he later discovered was physically impossible</term> is confirmed in this instance. But we understand from this that an error of a single minute in observation in this location is liable to corrupt both distances by approximately 100 units <note>Kepler usually calculates in "parts" where the radius of the Earth's orbit is 100,000</note>.

Therefore, by consulting more distant observations, their difference is found to be 1022. According to the preliminary knowledge of a mediocre hypothesis, the difference ought to have been greater, namely 1275. Doubtless, the fourth degree of Leo is near the eighteenth degree of Cancer, where something previously had to be subtracted from the eccentric position of the Vicarious Hypothesis. If you subtract one minute in the 4th degree of Leo, you will already make the distance from the Sun to Mars shorter by 100 units; and if you subtract $1 \frac{1}{2}$, you will make it approximately 164,934—so short, indeed, that the second distance can also retain this length of 166,206. Furthermore, the final observation from the year 1583, which showed a length of 164,364, could be reconciled with this one. For they ought to have differed by 488, according to the hypothesis of distances (which is certain and known enough for this purpose), whereas they actually differ by 750.

However, that change of $2 \frac{1}{2}$ minutes in the eccentric position can be transferred from the midpoint into the observations. For if either one of these erred by one minute, it could cause 50 units of error in each distance.

It would be tedious to repeat the same method in so many words through all the years of the oppositions. Therefore, in the following table, I have placed the observations themselves which I consulted, and I have added what resulted from the computation. The hypotheses for the calculation are these: The position of the Sun is taken from Tycho Brahe. The distances of the Sun and Earth are from Chapter 30. The aphelion <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit furthest from the Sun</term> of Mars for the completed year 1600 is at 29° 0' 30'' <note>original: "29. 0 1/2"</note>. The mean motion for the same time is 1s 7° 14' 34'' <note>This notation indicates 1 sign (30 degrees) plus 7 degrees, etc.</note>. The eccentricity and the proportion of the orbits are as in Chapter 54. To these I have added the distances of Mars from the Sun as if they were already known. Thus, if we equate the proposed observations by means of these distances, these distances will be correct; which was my purpose to investigate in this chapter.

Therefore, the distances investigated by the method of this chapter from the observations set down here will come out as these very ones. However, the apparent positions, when Mars is moving in its <term>eccentric</term> <note>the circular path around the Sun that is offset from the center</note> in Cancer, will come out about 4 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupulis", referring to minutes of arc</note> earlier, and in Sagittarius and Capricorn by just as many further ahead. Nor do these small errors arise from faulty distances; for they would not be in opposite regions of the same quality, but of contrary quality. I think they can be reconciled by a change of the Sun’s <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</note> by one degree, which is easily permitted by the observations of <note>Tycho</note> Brahe. Yet I define nothing for the present. For the correction of both this apogee and the entire hypothesis is reserved for the *Work of the Tables* <note>Kepler refers to his forthcoming "Rudolphine Tables", his definitive astronomical calculations</note>.

## CHAPTER 54.

### A more accurate examination of the proportion of the orbits.

In Chapter 42, we indeed established the proportion of the orbits from observations taken outside of the acronychal position <note>The "acronychal position" is when a planet is in opposition to the Sun, appearing in the sky all night. Observations "outside" this position are harder to use for calculating distances.</note>, but those observations did not entirely agree with one another to our full certainty <note>original: *plerophorian*</note>. Furthermore, by the nature of the thing itself, even if the most exact observations are provided, this business cannot be brought to a certainty within 100 small parts. We must, therefore, proceed by the "votes" and number of the observations. And since in Chapter 28, at a mean anomaly <term>mean anomaly: the position of a planet along its orbit calculated as if it moved at a constant speed</term> of 11 signs 37 minutes—that is, after the correction from the preceding Chapter 53, at an anomaly of 11 signs 52 minutes—the distance of the point on the ecliptic onto which a perpendicular line from the body of Mars descends was found to be 166,180 or 166,208; and since this place is 23 degrees away from the northern limit: the inclination will be about 1° 4 ½'; the excess of the secant <note>A trigonometric value used here to calculate the difference between the distance measured along the orbital plane and its projection onto the ecliptic.</note> is 45 parts, which in our dimension are about 70. Therefore, the distance of Mars from the Sun is 166,250 or 166,278.

Now we shall also compare the observations from Chapter 51, so that we may be supported by a moderate consensus. In the year 1586, at the remainder of the mean anomaly of 10° 9' 41'', which is 8° 54' 41'' after correction, we found 166,311. But by subtracting 1 ½ minutes from the position shown by the "vicarious hypothesis" <term>vicarious hypothesis: Kepler's earlier mathematical model that accurately predicted a planet's direction but was physically incorrect regarding its distance</term>, we found 166,208. Therefore, two degrees (minus 3 minutes) lower, about 95 should be taken away, so that it becomes 166,113. Again, 80 should be added because of the latitude, making it 166,193. Similarly, in the year 1588, when the remainder of the anomaly was 8° 2' 51'', which is correctly 7° 47' 51'', by subtracting 1 ½ from the position of the Vicarious hypothesis, we found the distance to be 166,396. Thus, 4 degrees and 4 minutes lower, it will be shorter by about 102, namely 166,204; and because of the latitude it becomes 166,284—whereas it was 166,193 from the year 1586. The average of these is 166,238. In the descending part of the orbit, however, from five observations, we had found 166,250 or 166,278. Although the difference is imperceptible, let us nevertheless take the mean value of 166,260; thus we place more trust in the descending semicircle, as it is better confirmed by the observations.

Therefore, let this be certain: at a mean anomaly of 11 signs 52 minutes, the distance is 166,260. Wherefore, no matter how roughly you pre-conceive the hypothesis (which is to be confirmed shortly), it follows that in units where the radius is 100,000, the aphelion <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> distance cannot increase by more than 164 parts—even less if you use the hypothesis of a perfect circle. Those parts, reduced through the pre-conceived proportion of the orbits as established in Chapter 42, produce about 250; and these added to 166,260 make 166,310. However, above in Chapter 42, we found 166,780 from weaker observations—a difference of 255 parts.

We shall proceed in the same way with the perihelion distance <note>The point in a planet's orbit closest to the Sun.</note>, which in Chapter 42 was found to be 138,500 from observations that were not sufficiently firm.

Now, in Chapter 51, at a residual anomaly <term>anomaly: the angle measuring a planet's position from its aphelion</term> of 160° 45 1/2', which is 160° 36 1/2' after correction, we found the distance to be 139,000 or 138,984 without the correction for latitude. Let us assume 139,000 at 21° Pisces. Since this location is 35 degrees away from the limit <note>the "limit" refers to the point of maximum northern or southern latitude</note>, and therefore the inclination is 1° 31 1/2'; the excess of the secant <note>a trigonometric value used to adjust for the tilt of the orbit relative to the ecliptic</note> will be 35 1/2, which is worth 49 units in our dimension. Therefore, the true distance of Mars from the Sun is 139,049. But if the radius is 100,000, the perihelion distance <note>perihelion: the point in the orbit closest to the Sun</note> is 575 parts shorter than that at an anomaly of 161 1/2°, which makes 876 units in our dimension—less, if you were using a perfect circle. And these, subtracted from 139,049, leave 138,173 for the perihelion distance. This is a difference of 327 from the 138,500 found in Chapter 42.

According to this method, therefore, it is found:

| **Aphelia** <note>the distance at the furthest point from the Sun</note> | 166,510 | Of which, however, 152,342 |
| **Perihelia** <note>the distance at the closest point to the Sun</note> | 138,173 | becomes 100,000, and 14,169 |

But nevertheless, because our observations, especially at perigee <note>perigee: the point where Mars is closest to the Earth</note>, do not support such a large difference; and because it is possible that the "vicarious" hypothesis <note>Kepler's "vicarious hypothesis" was a mathematically accurate but physically "false" model used in earlier chapters to fix the planet's longitudes</note>, being inherently false, might admit some error into the eccentricity; before a certain conclusion is reached, all "votes" <note>Kepler often refers to the consensus of multiple observations as "votes"</note> should be collected.

Therefore, let us adapt the aphelion distance found here, say 166,510, to the eccentricity of Chapter 42, which was 9,265. Thus, as 109,265 is to 90,735, so 166,510 is to 138,274, where the radius is approximately 152,400.

Indeed, manifold experience has also taught that the truest eccentricity, and that which is most consistent with physical equations, is between 9,230 and 9,300—that is, this very one from Chapter 43, namely 9,265.

So that we neither abandon too much the perihelion found in this chapter (138,173), nor trust too much the aphelion (166,510), let us conclude the truest aphelion is 166,465 and the perihelion is 138,234, where the radius is 152,350.

# CHAPTER LV.

## It is demonstrated from the observations of Chapters 51 and 53, and the proportion of the orbits in Chapter 54, that the hypothesis adopted in Chapter 45 is faulty, and makes the distances in the middle longitudes shorter than is right.

I began to say this indeed in Chapter 51. But because more observations, and more suitable ones, had to be prepared through Chapter 53 to give testimony—from which something else was simultaneously inferred in Chapter 52—the full demonstration of the matter had to be deferred until now.

Z

He then begins Chapter 55 by announcing that his previous hypothesis (from Chapter 45) incorrectly shortened the distances at the middle longitudes.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from Chapter 54, where Kepler adjusted the dimensions of Mars's orbit, he now compares his previous "oval" model against Tycho Brahe's observations to see if the theory matches reality.</meta>

->## ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS<-

<margin>Chapter 55.</margin>
No words are necessary. For the mean anomalies <term>mean anomaly: the angle representing a planet's position if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle</term> of all the examples that occur throughout Chapters 51 and 53, let the distances be computed according to the hypothesis of Chapter 45 and the proportion of the orbits in Chapter 54, using the method I employed from Chapter 46 through Chapter 50. Then, let those be compared to the distances in Chapters 51 and 53, which were found from infallible observations. It will then appear that the further we descend from the apsides <term>apsides: the two points in an orbit, aphelion and perihelion, where the planet is furthest from or closest to the Sun</term>, the more the calculated distances fall short of the observed distances. Thus, the opposite happens of what we observed above in Chapter 44. There, the distances computed according to the law of a circle were longer in the middle longitudes <note>the points halfway between the furthest and closest points to the Sun</note> than those observed; here, the distances produced by that hypothesis—which creates an oval orbit for the planet—become too short.

Therefore, it is clear that the path of the planet is neither a circle, nor does it curve inward at the sides as much as that oval does (which arose from the opinion in Chapter 45 and was described in Chapter 46). Instead, it proceeds by a middle path. And conversely, if you use the distances from Chapter 45 to calculate the observed positions of Mars—especially those which surround the opposition from a distance in Chapter 53—the planet will fall too far in *consequentia* <note>original: "in consequentia"; moving forward in the direction of the zodiacal signs</note> before the opposition, and too far in *antecedentia* <note>original: "in antecedentia"; moving backward against the order of the signs</note> after the opposition. This is most evident in the years 1589 and 1591 in the descending semicircle, and in the years 1582 and 1595 in the ascending semicircle. For in those places, that Oval from Chapter 45 errs by 660 parts in deficit, just as the perfect circle errs by the same amount in excess; these can cause a difference of 20 minutes and more in the apparent position.

And so, David Fabricius <note>a German astronomer and correspondent of Kepler</note>, using his own observations, was able to prove this error of distances being too short in the middle longitudes in my hypothesis from Chapter 45 (which I had shared with him as true). He wrote to me at the very same time that I myself was laboring with renewed care in investigating the true hypothesis. He came very close indeed to beating me to the discovery of the truth. Since the perfect circle errs by the same amount in the opposite direction, we rightly argue from this that the truth lies in the middle of the two.

The equations <term>equation: in this context, the correction needed to account for the difference between mean and true motion</term> computed from physical causes in Chapters 49 and 50 also testified to the same thing: namely, that the *lunula* <term>lunula: a crescent-shaped area (literally "little moon") representing the difference between a circle and the actual oval path</term> which is cut away from the perfect semicircle ought to have only half the width of what the opinion in Chapter 45 cuts away. Therefore, nothing prevents us from saying that the matter has been most certainly demonstrated: namely, that the opinion of Chapter 45, while it cures the excess of the perfect circle, falls into the opposite fault of deficit.

Thus, the physical causes of Chapter 45 go up in smoke.

# PART FOUR.

<header>PART FOUR.</header>

<margin>CHAPTER 56.</margin>
**I**n Chapter 46, the width of the crescent <term>lunula: a crescent-shaped area representing the difference between a perfect circle and the planet's actual path</term> was discovered, which the opinion in Chapter 45 produced for us and taught should be cut away from the semicircle. This, I say, was found to be 858 parts, where the radius of the circle is 100,000. Therefore, since I gathered clearly from the two arguments I provided in Chapters 49, 50, and 55 that only half the width of that crescent should be assumed—namely 429, or more correctly 432 (and in the dimension where the semi-diameter of Mars's orbit is 152,350, it is nearly 660)—I began to think about the causes and the method by which a crescent of such width could be cut away.

While I was anxiously engaged in this thought, reflecting that absolutely nothing had been said in Chapter 45 <note>referring to his realization that his previous physical theory was incomplete</note>, and thus that my *triumph over Mars* had been futile; by pure chance I happened upon the secant <term>secant: a trigonometric ratio representing the distance from the center of a circle through a point on its edge to a tangent line</term> of the angle 5° 18', which is the measure of the maximum optical equation <term>optical equation: the correction needed for the planet's position due to the observer's perspective from an eccentric point</term>. When I saw that this secant was 100,429, here, as if waking from a sleep and seeing a new light, I began to reason as follows. In the middle longitudes <note>the points halfway between aphelion and perihelion</note>, the optical part of the equation becomes greatest. In those same middle longitudes, the crescent or the reduction of the distances is greatest; and it is exactly as large as the excess of the secant of the maximum optical equation (100,429) over the radius (100,000). Therefore, if the radius is used instead of the secant at the middle longitude, the result is exactly what the observations suggest. And in the diagram of Chapter 40, I concluded generally that if you use HR instead of HA, VR instead of VA, and substitute EB for EA—and so on for all the others—the same thing will happen in the other places of the eccentric as happened here in the middle longitudes. And by equivalence, in the small diagram of Chapter 39, $\alpha\kappa$ will be taken for lines $\alpha\delta$ or $\alpha\iota$, and $\alpha\mu$ will be taken for $\alpha\epsilon$ or $\alpha\lambda$.

<margin>Diagram illustrating the geometry of the orbit and the oscillation (libration) of the planet.</margin>

Therefore, let the reader run through Chapter 39 again. He will find there that it has already been discussed from natural causes—which the observations here now spontaneously attest to—that it seems consistent for the planet to perform a certain libration <term>libration: a back-and-forth oscillation or swaying motion</term> on the diameter of a kind of epicycle <note>a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; Kepler uses this here as a geometric tool</note> which perpetually points toward the Sun. He will also find that nothing fought more against this opinion than the fact that, at the time when we were assuming a perfect circle had to be represented, we were forced to make the parts of the libration $\gamma\iota$ and $\lambda\mu$—the top and bottom parts (which correspond to equal arcs of the eccentric)—unequal, making the top parts short and the bottom parts long. Now, therefore, having denied the circular path for the planet, and having used $\kappa\alpha$ and $\mu\alpha$ instead of $\delta\alpha$ and $\epsilon\alpha$ (that is, instead of $\iota\alpha$ and $\lambda\alpha$, as was said), it follows spontaneously that those parts of the libration, namely $\gamma\kappa$ and $\mu\zeta$, are equal. Thus, what had tormented us for a long time in Chapter 39 now yields to us as an argument for the truth we have discovered.

But concerning the fact that the middle parts $\kappa\mu$ are still larger than the extremes...
