### PART FOUR

<margin>CHAPTER 57.</margin>
**I**t appears, therefore, from the most certain observations, that the path of the Planet in the ethereal air is not a circle, but of an oval shape, and that it oscillates <term>libration: a back-and-forth movement along a straight line, used here to describe how the planet moves toward and away from the Sun</term> on the diameter of a small circle in this manner: if, after equal arcs of the eccentric, the Planet completes the diametral distances γα, κα, μα, ζα for the sake of the circumferential distances γα, δα, εα, ζα (which is to say, γα, ια, λα, ζα, upon which the perfection of the circle rests); where it is obvious to the eye that a crescent-shaped piece <note>original: "lunula"</note> of such great width is cut away from the perfection of the eccentric semicircle, as is <margin>Definition. What is circumferential distance, and what is diametral:</margin> the difference of the various distances at any place, such as ικ or λμ. This having now been obtained—not by *a priori* reasoning <note>Reasoning based on theoretical principles rather than observation</note>, but by observations, as I have already said—physical speculations will now proceed more correctly than they have until now. *** For this oscillation accommodates itself to the space completed in the eccentric; not indeed in some rational or mental way—as if the mind of the Planet <margin>*** The principle of this oscillation is proven to be natural.</margin> numbered the equal arcs of the imperfect eccentric **CD, DE, EF** to the equal parts of the oscillation γκ, κμ, μζ (for these are unequal)—but in a natural way. This way is based not on the equality of the angles **DBC, EBD, FBE**, but on the **strength of the angle <margin>** What may be the genuine and justified <note>original: "ἀπο-λόγητος"</note> measure of this oscillation: or the cause why the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly measures this oscillation.</margin> DBC, EBC, FBC**, which is constantly increasing. This strength nearly follows what Geometers call the <term>sine: a mathematical ratio used here to measure the planet's varying distance from the Sun</term>: where the ascent, by a continuous lessening, is gradually changed into a descent, more probably than if the Planet were said to suddenly turn its prow around; which indeed we said in Chapter 39 was most clearly repugnant even to the evidence of observations. Since, therefore, the measure of this oscillation points to a very natural "finger" <note>An indicator or signpost</note>, the cause will also be natural; namely, not the mind of the Planet, but some natural, or perhaps corporeal, faculty.

And since we established in Chapter 39, by the best reasons among our presuppositions, that a Planet cannot make the transition from place to place by the naked exertion of its own inherent forces unless those forces are helped or informed by an <margin>Natural examples of oscillations of this kind</margin> external force; we must therefore consider whether, in some way, we might also attribute this oscillation in part to the Solar power itself. In attempting this, we shall be referred back to our **oars** <margin>In the Oars.</margin> already introduced above in Chapter 39. For let there be some circular river **CDE. # ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER 57.</margin>
...[like a] sailor, who turns an oar once in twice the periodic time <note>The time it takes for a planet to complete one full orbit</note> of the Planet, by an inherent and most uniform force: so that at point **c**, the line of the oar, relative to the line from the Sun, is a straight line, directing now the prow and now the stern into the following signs <note>In the direction of the zodiacal signs</note> in alternating returns. At point **f**, however, the line of the oar becomes part of the line from the Sun; in other places, the inclinations are intermediate. Therefore, the river flowing over the oar at **d** and **e** will depress the ship toward **a**, but at **c** only very little, because it is only slightly inclined there. The same happens at **f**, because at this point, the river strikes the oar directly. At **d** and **e**, however, the force is stronger, because here the oar is much more disposed to this approach by its inclination. The opposite occurs in the ascending semicircle. For the river, brought under the oar at **g** and **h**, will drive it away from the Sun (☉).

At the same time, this will also occur: other things being equal, the impulse at **c** is slower than at **f**, because our river is weak at **c** and strong at **f**. And this also fits our desire, because our oscillation <note>original: "libratio"</note> followed equal spaces of the eccentric, in the upper parts of which the Planet lingers longer than in the lower parts.

<margin>
Defects of the example.
</margin>
This example only teaches the possibility of the thing. For it is somewhat foreign to itself: first, because the restoration of the oar and the river are completed not in the same time, but in double the time; and because the faces of the Planets would seem to need to change for those looking from the Earth. Yet the face of the Moon—which participates with the Planets in that motion we are discussing here—does not change in its monthly circuit; rather, it is perpetually turned toward the Earth, from which its eccentricity is computed. Add to this that while the force of a river is material (for water there acts with weight and material impetus), the force of the Sun is immaterial. Therefore, the condition of the Planets must be different; nor will they need an oar, a physical instrument, to receive the force of weights (since that moving species <note>Kepler's term for the "force" or "influence" radiating from the Sun</note> of the Sun lacks them). Certainly, we do not even deem the stars worthy of a physical oar, so long as we establish that they are round.

<margin>
The example of the Magnet.
</margin>
But from this very refutation, another example is born, which will perhaps be more suitable. As is the river, so is the oar. The river is an immaterial species of magnetic virtue in the Sun. Why, then, should the oar not also have something of the magnet? What if, therefore, the bodies of all the Planets are certain immense and round magnets? Regarding <term>Earth</term> (one of the Planets, according to Copernicus), there is no doubt. <term>WILLIAM GILBERT</term> has proved it.

<margin>
William Gilbert's Magnetic philosophy.
</margin>
<margin>
A certain magnetic disposition in the body of the planet itself seems to be the cause of this oscillation.
</margin>
But this virtue must be described more precisely: namely, that the globe of the Planet has two poles, with one of which it pursues the Sun, and with the other it flees from the Sun. Let us imagine the axis of this kind to be a magnetic needle, and let its tip seek the Sun; let it be held, however, against its magnetic nature which seeks the Sun, so that in the translation of the globe it remains perpetually parallel to itself—except insofar as, with the passing of centuries, it shifts its aim from one set of Fixed Stars to another...

# PART FOUR

<sig>Z 4</sig>

...transfers [the axis], and thus causes the progression of the aphelia <note>The "aphelion" is the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun; Kepler is explaining why this point slowly shifts over centuries</note>. I admit that either of these could nonetheless be the work of a mind <note>original: "mentis opus"</note>; as if a mind were sufficiently equipped by an animate faculty for this motion, since it is a motion not of the whole body from place to place (a motion which was correctly denied to the motive cause innate in Planets above in chapter 39), but of its parts around the center of the whole, which remains as if at rest.

<margin>Example of the Earth.</margin>
Behold again in the globe of the <term>EARTH</term> <note>original: "TELLVRIS"</note> an example of this kind of directional axis from <term>COPERNICUS</term>. For while the axis of the <term>EARTH</term>, during the annual revolution of its center, remains nearly parallel to itself and to all its positions, summer and winter are produced; * insofar as the long centuries incline it,
<margin>* That the precession of the equinoxes is similar to the progression of the aphelia.</margin>
the Fixed Stars are thought to move forward, and the equinoxes to recede.

Why then do we hesitate to attribute to all the Planets—in order to account for the appearance <note>original: "phantasiam"</note> of eccentricity—what has been observed to exist in one of them (namely, the <term>EARTH</term>) from the appearance of the precession of the equinoxes and the annual revolution of the rising and setting Sun?

In this, just as <term>COPERNICUS</term> was deceived, thinking that a specific principle was needed to balance the Earth annually from North to South and back again so that summer and winter occur—and by whose effort, measured against the revolution, the equality of the return of the tropical and sidereal years results (to the extent that they are almost equal)—when, however, all those things are obtained by a single constant direction of the <term>EARTH'S</term> axis, upon which the daily motion occurs. No external causes are needed, except for that single, very slow precession of the equinoxes. So here too, no plan <note>original: "consilio"</note> will be needed by the movers of the Planet so that its body is carried around the Sun while remaining in a parallel position, and simultaneously completes its oscillation <note>original: "librationem"</note>. For the one will naturally depend on the other. It remains only to consider the very slow progression of the aphelia.

<margin>The cause why the oscillation is fastest in the middle.</margin>
For when the pointer <note>original: "lingula," likely referring to the magnetic needle or the planet's axis</note> is at **c** and at **f**, there is no reason why the Planet should approach or recede, since it presents its ends to the Sun at equal intervals. It would surely turn its tip toward the Sun if it were allowed by that force which holds its axis straight and parallel. As the Planet leaves point **c**, its tip gradually approaches the Sun, and its tail moves away. Gradually, therefore, the globe begins to "sail" toward the Sun. After **f**, the tail gradually approaches, and the head moves away from the Sun. Gradually, therefore, the entire globe, by a natural "hatred" <note>original: "odio"; Kepler uses this to describe magnetic repulsion</note>, flees from the Sun. In the region of **A** itself, however, when the length of the axis is extended directly toward the Sun, there the approach is strongest, and here the flight is strongest. Indeed, this was previously required by our presuppositions derived from observations, where from the parts of the oscillation $\gamma \kappa, \kappa \mu, \mu \xi$, which correspond to equal arcs of the eccentric, the middle parts $\kappa \mu$ were the longest, and thin toward $\gamma, \xi$.

<margin>The cause why the oscillation is slower at the top, faster at the bottom.</margin>
But this also agrees with what the observations require: that $\gamma \kappa$ and $\mu \xi$ are equal, even though their arcs $\gamma \delta, \epsilon \xi$—or rather **CD, EF** in the eccentric—are equal but completed in unequal times, with **CD** taking longer; so that the part of the oscillation $\gamma \kappa$ is completed more slowly than $\mu \xi$, which is equal to it. For in this way, <term>magnets</term> <note>original: "magnetes"</note> also approach each other more slowly from a greater distance, and more quickly and rapidly from a shorter one.

He explains that the planet's approach and recession (libration) toward the Sun is a natural consequence of its axis remaining parallel while orbiting.</summary>

## ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>
That the active axis of the Planet is kept in a parallel position by a natural force.
</margin>
Indeed, we can even transfer that very force which keeps the magnetic axis in a parallel position—distinguishing the direction of the axis toward the Sun from the "possession" of Mars (to which we had briefly granted it earlier)—over to the duties of nature. For although it seems an obstacle that nature acts in one and the same way, while this retentive force seems to struggle differently at different times; <margin>With an exception, however.</margin> specifically, that the nodding of the axis toward the Sun (which it is designed to prevent) vanishes at the middle longitudes, but is strongest at the aphelion <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun</note> and perihelion <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun</note>: yet what prevents this force of retention from being many times stronger than the nodding of the axis toward the Sun? Thus, it would be exhausted little or not at all by such a weak adversary. <margin>A magnetic example.</margin> Let us again take an example from the magnet. In it, two powers are most clearly mixed: one of direction toward the pole, the other seeking iron. Thus, if a single compass needle is directed toward the pole, but iron approaches from the side, the needle declines a little from the pole and inclines toward the iron; in this way, it indulges somewhat in its "familiarity" with the iron, yet still grants most of its allegiance to the pole.

<margin>
The cause of why a magnet declines somewhat from the pole.
</margin>
From this, **GILBERT** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), the English physician whose work on magnetism, *De Magnete*, deeply influenced Kepler’s physics</note> thinks it happens that the small tongue of the needle declines from the pole toward continents of great size; thus, the cause of this magnetic declination lies in the stretches of land, according to whether higher, larger, and more powerful tracts are nearby to the right or the left.

<margin>
What the cause of the motion of the aphelia is.
</margin>
And so, by the same logic, we can allow both natural faculties an equal operation; and by the balancing of both, show a cause for the shifting of the aphelia that is neither obscure nor, by heaven, in vain. For suppose that this force of directing the axis toward the Sun detracts somewhat from the retentive power, according to the measure of its proportion to it. In the semicircle of the aphelion, as at **c**, the tip will nod slightly toward <term>H</term>, which is in the preceding direction <note>original: "in antecedentia"; moving backward or westward against the order of the zodiac signs</note>, while the tail will turn away from the Sun, slightly overcoming the retentive force. Thus, the aphelion will become retrograde <note>Moving backward</note>. But in the semicircle of the perihelion, as at <term>F</term>, that same tip will nod toward <term>G</term>, which is in the following direction <note>original: "in consequentia"; moving forward or eastward with the order of the zodiac signs</note>, again overcoming the retentive force in the opposite direction. Then, therefore, the aphelion will become direct and swift. Because **AF** is shorter than **AC**, and the Sun is closer to **F** than to **c**, the force of the magnetic axis turning toward the Sun is stronger at **F** than at **c**. More will therefore be detracted from the retentive force at **F** than at **c**. Thus, the perihelion nod in the following direction does not just compensate for the aphelion nod in the preceding direction, but actually exceeds it. <margin>Why the aphelia do not recede.</margin> And so the cause is clear why the apsides <note>The points of greatest and least distance in an orbit</note> move forward and do not recede. Thus, the aphelion found by us will be valid only at the equated anomaly <note>A measure of the planet's position in its orbit</note> of 90 and 270 degrees, when the active axis is stretched toward the Sun itself, which is its proper position. And the motion of the aphelion will be a spiral, as will be clear below in Chapter **LXVIII**, regarding the motion of the precession of the equinoxes existing for another cause. Therefore, the direction of the magnetic axis into a parallel position—or the force that guards it—will not look to these or those Fixed Stars, but only to the position of its own body, just as it is at any time. And when the matter is simply considered, because this direction is more like rest than motion, it is sought with better right in the matter and in the disposition of the body than in some Mind.

<summary>Kepler uses William Gilbert’s magnetic theories to explain why a planet's orbit (the apsides) slowly rotates forward. He argues that this happens because the Sun's magnetic-like pull on the planet's axis is stronger when the planet is closer to the Sun, causing a net forward shift over time.</summary>

# PART FOUR.

<margin>What kind of oscillations a rightly arranged magnet is expected to perform.</margin>
Now, let us follow this similarity of planetary <term>libration</term> <note>libration: from 'libra' (scales); refers to the back-and-forth movement of the planet toward and away from the Sun.</note> with the motion of a magnet more closely, and by a most beautiful geometric demonstration: so that it may appear that magnets possess such a motion as we detect in a Planet. Let $DFA$ be either a round magnet or the body of *Mars* itself: let $DA$ be the line along which the magnetic <term>virtue</term> <note>virtue: 'virtus' in Latin, referring here to a physical power or force inherent in the object.</note> is stretched: $D$ is the pole seeking the Sun: $A$ is the pole fleeing from the Sun. First, you will note that in this investigation, it is the same whether we consider the whole globe of the magnetic body, or a single physical line of its power parallel to $DA$.

<margin>*Blind paths you mark for sailors on the sea, O Magnet:*
*What wonder if the Wanderers move at your nods?*
<note>original: "Cæca mari signas Nautis vestigia Magnes : Quid mirum, Errones nutibus ire tuis?" The 'Wanderers' refers to the planets.</note></margin>

->*Of which* *I am*<-

Since this magnetic power is corporeal and divisible with the body, as proven by Gilbert the Englishman <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), whose book 'De Magnete' influenced Kepler's physical theories.</note>, Giambattista della Porta, and others; certainly, because a globe consists of what are essentially infinite physical lines parallel to $DA$, whose power is extended in a straight line toward one region of the world, the judgment concerning the quality of motion will be the same for each individual line as it is for all of them joined together, and vice versa. Therefore, in place of the whole body and all its filaments, let the middle axis $DA$ be proposed for investigation. Let $DA$ be bisected at $B$, and let $FBI$ be drawn perpendicular to $DA$. Thus, when the Planet is positioned so that $BI$ points toward the center of the Sun, there will be no approach. For the angles $DBI$ and $ABI$ are equal, and therefore equally strong; the former for approaching, the latter for fleeing. This, therefore, is like an equilibrium in mechanics. Thus, the center $B$ of *Mars* is situated in this way at the <term>apsis</term>, say, at the aphelion <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>, most remote from the Sun. Now, let some arc $IC$ be taken, measuring the angle of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>A technical term for the planet's angular position in its orbit as seen from the Sun.</note>, and let $BC$ be drawn and extended to $K$. Let the Planet be positioned so that $BC$ points toward the Sun, which is understood to be at $K$.

<margin>What the measure of the speed of oscillation is at any given point.</margin>
First, the measure of the strength of the Planet’s approach is sought. For the approach occurs because the seeking pole $D$ is inclined toward the Sun $K$ by the angle $DBK$. However, the fleeing pole $A$ refuses it by the angle $ABK$. Since, therefore, that strength of the angle is natural, it will be in the ratio of a <term>statera</term> <note>statera: a Roman balance or steelyard scale.</note>.
<margin>This oscillation [libration] has the ratio of a balance, consistent with its name.</margin>
But when a perpendicular $CP$ is drawn from $C$ to $DA$, the ratio of the balance will be between $DP$ and $PA$. For a balance suspended from the fulcrum $KB$, with the arms remaining, at the angle $DBK$, the weight of arm $BD$ would be to the weight of arm $BA$ as $DP$ is to $PA$; so much so that if the arms were suspended from $CP$ at $P$, and the weight $BA$ were adjusted to $PD$, and the weight of arm $BD$ to $PA$, then $DA$ with the hanging balance $CP$ would make right angles. What the measure of the space completed through libration is up to a given moment.

For since the sine of any arc is the measure of the strength of that angle, the sum of the sines will be roughly the measure of the sum of the strengths or "impressions" through all equal parts of the circle: the common effect of all of these is the total libration completed. <margin>
Application of the magnetic libration now demonstrated to the observed libration of the Planet.
</margin>
Since it has therefore been demonstrated that—with a certain magnet arranged in such a way as we assume the bodies of the Planets are arranged in the heavens relative to the Sun—the libration of the magnetic body would be such as is measured by the <term>versed sine</term> for the purpose of the space covered; and since observations truly testify that the body of the Planet librates in that same measure of the <term>versed sine</term> of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term>: it is therefore highly probable that the bodies of the Planets are <term>magnetic</term>, disposed toward the Sun in the manner we have described.

# PART FOUR.

<margin>The proportion between the <term>versed sines</term> <note>original: "sinus versos"; the versed sine ($1 - \cos \theta$) represents the horizontal distance covered as one moves around a circle, which Kepler uses to measure the planet's radial approach to the Sun.</note> of the eccentric anomalies is the same as that between the sums of the <term>right sines</term> <note>original: "sinuum rectorum"; the standard sine function.</note> of the <term>equated anomalies</term> <note>The angle of the planet as seen from the Sun.</note> corresponding to those eccentric anomalies; and this is very precise.</margin>

I must now show that it was not a great mistake that I took the arcs *i c* and *i γ* as the same. When I say that the arc *i c* on the body of the Planet is the measure of the equated anomaly, I am speaking strictly; and then *c N* is the genuine measure of that strength which belongs to the Planet when it has the Sun on the line *B K*. But when I say that *i γ* is the measure of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>An auxiliary angle used in Kepler's calculations to relate the planet's position to a perfect circle.</note> which corresponds to the equated anomaly *i c*, I am speaking loosely, making use of the circle of the Planet's body to represent the eccentric. However, since in the descending semicircle of the eccentric, a larger arc of the eccentric anomaly corresponds to a smaller equated anomaly—namely, *i γ* to *i c*—we certainly collect more sines in *i γ* than in *i c*: and this is by right. For since a sine measures the strength, and the strength acts according to the proportion of time and according to the proportion of proximity to the Sun (for magnets are stronger up close), which is, to be brief, according to the proportion of the arc *i γ*; it follows that exactly as many sines are to be established in *i c* as are found in *i γ*.

<margin>The slower the Planet is in any given arc, the smaller the parts of the equated anomaly must be made, so that the collected sines of those parts can be the correct measure of the power spread through that equated anomaly.</margin>

The only way we err in this is that we take those many sines to be longer than they should be; just as *G H* is longer than *c N*.

But this excess is, in itself, first of all slight and imperceptible. For at the beginning of the quadrant, the arcs *i c* and *i γ* differ very little, and the sines are small: at the end of the quadrant, when the equation of the eccentric *c γ* is at its maximum, the sines differ very little . .

<margin>The lack of proportion, which we established between the versed sine and the sum of the right sines, is compensated for by an opposite error, in that we collect right sines that are too long from the eccentric anomaly instead of the equated anomaly.</margin>

Furthermore, this error is to our advantage. For the sums of the sines always give a little more than the versed sines; having been commended by experience, we now strive to accommodate and reconcile the principles of the balance and of magnetism to them. Therefore, our present error, which accumulates long sines instead of short ones, is avoided if we use simple versed sines instead of the sums of right sines; since the sums of the sines do not match the versed sines exactly, but rather exceed them by the effect of the <term>libration</term> <note>The back-and-forth radial motion of the planet.</note>.

Therefore, we have brought the matter within the reach of the senses by the best of reasoning. Let us conclude that the body of the Planet, like a magnet, approaches and flees according to the law of the balance on an imaginary diameter of an epicycle tending toward the Sun; and that the virtuous and real diameter of the body *D A* is extended into the middle longitudes—namely, *B D* at this time in 29° of Taurus ($\succ$), and *B A* in 29° of Scorpio ($\mathfrak{m}$). For the <term>aphelium</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> is in 29° of Leo ($\Omega$).

<margin>The magnetic power inherent in the bodies of the Planets is excited and brought into action by a similar power in the body of the Sun.</margin>

In this way, that oscillatory movement is completed without any mental effort <note>Kepler is arguing against the idea that planets are moved by "souls" or "intelligences" that must calculate where to go; instead, it is a physical, magnetic response.</note>, through a magnetic power that is indeed inherent and solitary, yet whose definition depends on the external body of the Sun. For it is defined as a power seeking the Sun, or fleeing from it. And even if this power between magnets, which joins them, ought to be mutual: I indeed denied the attractive power of the Planets in Chapter 39 regarding the Sun. However, that was understood only as a purely attractive force, as is clear from the argument used there. But here it is posited as both attractive and, in another orientation, repulsive. Or let it even be posited thus: that the Sun, like iron not yet magnetized, is merely sought, and does not in turn seek; since the Sun's "filaments" <note>Kepler imagined the Sun's force as circular fibers or filaments that sweep the planets along.</note> were previously said to be circular, while those of the Planets are here posited as straight.

<margin>The difficulty and imperfection of this example of the magnet.</margin>

It is enough for me to have demonstrated from this example of the magnet the possibility of the thing in general. As for the specifics of the matter, I am in doubt. For as far as the Earth is concerned, it is certain that its axis, by its uniform and equidistant di-

As stated in Chapter 39, this mind, from the contemplation of the Sun's increasing diameter, may come into a knowledge of the distances it covers; and it may preside over a faculty, whether animal or natural, to so arrange its globe in a parallel position that it is impelled in the proper manner by the Solar power and is balanced with respect to the Sun. > The versed sine of the { **eccentric** / **equated** } anomaly measures { **the Libration of the Planet** / **the Increase of the Sun's diameter, as it would appear to a spectator on the body of the planet: and vice versa.** }

These things being so, I say it will also follow that the increments of the Sun’s diameter at α—observed from γ, κ, μ, and ζ—are accumulated by the same measure as the <term>versed sine</term> <note>The versed sine ($1 - \cos\theta$) was a common trigonometric function in historical astronomy, used here to describe the radial distance a planet moves along its orbit's radius.</note> of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The "equated anomaly" is the angular distance of a planet from its perihelion or aphelion, adjusted for the eccentricity of the orbit.</note> increases. Therefore, at $c$, the equated anomaly is zero; the versed sine is zero; and the Sun, viewed from γ, appears at its smallest, so that the portion of its increment is likewise zero. Similarly, at $F$, the equated anomaly is 180. The versed sine is equal to the entire diameter, 200,000, and the Sun, viewed from ζ, appears at its largest, so that its entire increment has been added.

Therefore, for an equated anomaly of 90 degrees, let the perpendicular AM be erected from A to CF. And let MB be connected. Also, from α, let a tangent to the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; Kepler uses this geometric device to model complex movements.</note> be drawn at ν, and let the point of contact ν be connected to the center β. Hence νβα and ABM are equal. Let the perpendicular νo fall from ν onto γζ. Because νoβ is a right angle, it is equal to MAB; and νβo was equal to MBA; the triangles are therefore similar; and as νβ is to βo, so MB is to BA, and vice versa. And since νβ, βγ, βζ and MB, BC, BF are equal, then νβ and βo joined (that is, γo) are to oζ as MB and BA joined (that is, GA) are to AF. Therefore, since CA is the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly CBM, and is assumed to measure the part of the <term>libration</term> <note>The "libration" refers to the planet's oscillation or movement along the radius of its orbit, changing its distance from the Sun.</note> corresponding to it, γo will be that part. Thus, in this eccentric anomaly CBM, or the equated anomaly CAM of 90 degrees, the planet will be at $o$.

But for an equated anomaly of 90 degrees (namely CAM), the versed sine is half of the whole diameter, namely 100,000. I also say that the visible size of the Sun's diameter at α, seen from $o$, will be halfway between the size seen from γ and from ζ, so that half of the increase will have been added while the planet is positioned at $o$ below.

For let the diameter of the Sun's body be αξ, and the angles of vision be εξα, ξoα, and ξγα, with the point ξ connected to the points ζ, o, and γ. For the sake of greater clarity, this is also partially evident from the following. Let the straight line **BL** be erected from **B** perpendicular to **GF**: and with center **A**, and a distance equal to **BC**, let an arc be drawn intersecting **BL** at **L**: and let **AL** be joined. Since, therefore, the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle measured from the center of the circular orbit, rather than from the Sun.</note> **CBL** is 90°; the versed sine **CB** will be 100,000, half of the total diameter; wherefore the <term>libration</term> $\gamma \beta$ is also half of the total $\gamma \zeta$. And accordingly, the distance will be $\beta \alpha$. Indeed, by construction, **AL** is equal to it. Therefore, the planet will be at **L**. And because **AL** is equal to **BC** or **BM**, and **BA** is a common side, and angle **LBA** is a right angle, as is **MAB**: therefore the triangles **BMA** and **ALB** are congruent. Thus, **BL** is equal to **AM**. But **AM** is equal to $\alpha \upsilon$ as shown above; therefore **BL** is also equal to it. But $\alpha \upsilon$, namely the line extending to the right angle $\alpha \omicron \upsilon$, is longer than $\alpha \omicron$, which subtends the acute angle $\alpha \upsilon \omicron$. Therefore, **BL** is also longer than $\alpha \omicron$. And **AL** is longer than **BL**. Therefore, **AL** is much longer than $\alpha \omicron$. Consequently, the Sun appears smaller at distance **AL** than at distance $\alpha \omicron$. However, the distance $\alpha \omicron$ just now appeared to be the mean between the maximum and minimum. Therefore, at distance **L**, the Sun appears smaller than the mean. Thus, in **L**, although half of the eccentric semicircle is completed, nevertheless less than half of the increment has been added to the diameter of the Sun. Clearly, this is because the equated anomaly **LAC** is less than half of 90°. And this is that very thing <note>original: "quod cap: xxxix nos torserat"</note> which had tormented us in Chapter 39, as was said in the preceding Chapter 56. For if the orbit of the planet had been a perfect circle, the increase in the diameter of the Sun ($\odot$) would have measured the increases in the versed sines of the eccentric anomaly: the observation of which is further from the "mind" of the planet than the observation of the equated anomaly, as we shall now hear. See, therefore, from the opposite perspective, how conveniently this measure is assigned to the planet and how plausibly.

<margin>The planet cannot have knowledge of the eccentric anomaly.</margin>

If we were to suppose that the measure of this libration is to be perceived by a Mind <note>Kepler often explores whether planets have a "soul" or "mind" (species immateriata) that directs their motion based on celestial geometry.</note>, namely the versed sine of the eccentric anomaly, which observations recommend; then the mind of the planet would be destitute of this means of the variable diameter of the Sun: because it does not accommodate itself to the versed sines of this eccentric anomaly. For the path of the planet is not a circle. And the mind of the planet would understand the parts of the libration, or the spaces to be traversed by themselves, without a sign <note>Meaning a physical marker or reference point in space.</note>. This we have already categorized among the absurdities. It would also understand the eccentric anomaly, which is the angle between two straight lines projected from the center of the eccentric, one through the point of the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note>, the other through the center of the planetary globe. In the diagram, this is **DBC** (or the line **DK** projected from **D** parallel to **BC**; then **KDB** is the complement of that same eccentric anomaly.) If, therefore, the mind perceives the angle **KDB**, it is necessary that it perceive the three points **K, D, B**. Concerning point **D**, there is no doubt, because this is the center of its own globe. Concerning **K**, I do not doubt much. For **BC** and **DK**, due to the infinite distance of the Fixed Stars, eventually coincide at the same

Regarding the Sun **B**, it is denied that its perception belongs to the mind of the planet, because **B** is not clothed in any body <note>Kepler is likely referring to the center of the eccentric circle—a mathematical point—rather than the physical Sun, which he usually denotes with a different letter or symbol in these proofs.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Kepler's investigation into the physical and "mental" causes behind planetary motion. Having established that the planet's distance varies according to a specific geometric rule (the versed sine), he now questions how the planet—or its guiding intelligence—actually perceives and follows this rule.</meta>

<page-num>279</page-num>
<header>PART FOUR</header>

# PART FOUR

<margin>CHAPTER 57.</margin>

Furthermore, if the cause for looking at point <term>B</term> <note>Point B represents the center of the circular eccentric orbit, a mathematical point rather than a physical body.</note> is removed, the effect is also taken away. But point <term>B</term> must be looked at if the circle <term>CD</term> is to be completed. However, the orbits of the planets are not perfectly circular, as was proven from observations in Chapter 42. Therefore, the planets do not even aim toward <term>B</term>. And so, this point <term>B</term>, as a center, is something that exists only after the path <term>CD</term> is made. If it were truly looked at by the planet, it would have to exist prior to the journey itself.

For these reasons, therefore, I deny that the <term>versed sine</term> <note>The versed sine ($1 - \cos\theta$) is a trigonometric function Kepler uses to measure the planet's radial distance from the Sun.</note> of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle of the planet measured from the center of its orbit.</note> provides the planet with the measure for its <term>libration</term> <note>The back-and-forth radial movement of a planet toward and away from the Sun.</note>; not because this is not the measure, but because even if it is, it is not perceived by the mind of the planet.

<margin>That the planet is able to have knowledge of the equated anomaly.</margin>
But if we propose the increasing and decreasing diameter of the Sun as a means or aid by which the planet, through its librations, reaches its correct and inherently imperceptible distances; and if we give a rule and measure for this varying diameter of the Sun—to be perceived by the planet's mind—based on the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>Also called the true anomaly, this is the planet's angle as seen from the Sun.</note> in the diagram <term>DAC</term>, or rather <term>KDA</term>: then we stand on firmer ground. For both signs are perceptible: on the part of the libration, the increasing and decreasing size of the Sun's diameter; and on the part of the measure or angle, three points embodied by physical objects. For the Sun is at <term>A</term>, the planet is at <term>D</term>, and a fixed star, acting as the indicator of the <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>, is at <term>K</term>.

Perhaps, therefore, it should be said (as we already embraced above in Chapter 39, assuming the case that the forces of Nature are not sufficient on their own for administering the celestial motions) that the planet has been granted a sense of the light of the fixed stars and the Sun. By the meeting of these radiations at the center of the planetary body, it may estimate this angle of the equated anomaly.

<margin>Since the planet's mind focuses on the angle of the equated anomaly, not on the magnitude of its arc, but on the sines.</margin>
ONE single difficulty remains to be cleared up. Why is it not the angle itself that becomes the measure for the planetary work—which is here to increase the Sun's diameter by approaching the Sun—but rather the <term>versed sine</term> of that angle? * And by what means does the planet perceive the sine of the equated anomaly? Does it also perform geometric reasoning in the manner of humans? Yet, up to now, no task of administering celestial motions has been found to suit the planet's mind that could not be performed without any reasoning, through a divine instinct extending from the first creation of things down to the present.

<margin>* Just as a little while ago the <term>sine</term> of the eccentric anomaly (I meant the corresponding equated anomaly) was the index of the strength of the libration, while the <term>versed sine</term> of the eccentric anomaly was the index of the completed libration; so here, the sine of the equated anomaly itself is the index of the speed at which the Sun's diameter increases, while the versed sine of the equated anomaly is the index of the increase already attained through all the preceding speeds.</margin>
We must therefore repeat what was said a little above: that the sine of the equated anomaly is the index of the "strength" of the angles <term>KDA</term>. Aristotle writes of these in his *Mechanics*, as mentioned earlier in this chapter. For two arms joined at an obtuse angle are directed more easily than at a right angle, and this is in the proportion of the sines. Conversely, two arms joined at an acute angle are more easily forced into a single straight line, with their ends joined, than if they were joined at a right angle. Repeat the demonstration itself from what was set forth just before.

<margin>The way in which the planet could come to know the versed sine.</margin>
Thus, in one way, if it is established that the planet has a sense of the strength of angles, there will be nothing absurd if we say (according to our human concept) that the sines of the angles become known to it. But why would it sense the natural strength of angles? To be sure, we are returning to natural principles. For let there be, as before, certain tracts of the planetary body in which a magnetic force is inherent, directing it toward the line that tends toward the Sun. However, let this now belong not to the nature of the body, as before, but to the animal faculty, or that which rules the body of the planet...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 57 of Kepler's "New Astronomy." Following the previous page's discussion on how a planet might "perceive" its distance from the Sun, Kepler here explores the tension between a planet's "animal faculty" (an internal guiding intelligence or soul) and its "magnetic faculty" (a physical, quasi-magnetic interaction with the Sun).</meta>

<header>ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER 57.</margin>

...intrinsically, this gift: that while it is swept along by the Sun, it perpetually directs that magnetic axis toward the same fixed stars; except insofar as it inclines it slightly with the passage of centuries. Therefore, a conflict will arise between the <term>animal faculty</term> <note>From the Latin "anima" (soul); Kepler refers to an intelligent guiding force or soul within the planet.</note> and the <term>magnetic faculty</term>, with the animal faculty emerging victorious. This is no different from what we said in Chapter 34: that the bodies of the planets naturally desire to remain at rest, but are moved by an external force from the Sun <note>original: "$\odot$"</note>.

Or take a more fitting example. The natural weight of the human arm tends downward toward the center of the Earth; but the animal faculty <note>The human will or life-force.</note> enables a flag-bearer to extend it above his head and move it in a circle. In this case, the animal faculty overcomes the natural weight, and would overcome it perpetually, if the body of the flag-bearer and all its faculties were not created mortal.

These things being established, the Mind of the planet—through the struggle of the animal faculty (which seeks to retain the magnetic axis) against the magnetic power of direction toward the Sun—will be able to understand and perceive the strength of the angles.

And this method seems to be confirmed even by the example of the Moon, which it is certain is more strongly incited in the diametrical line of the Sun and Earth, perhaps because of this very strength of the angles.

<margin>A model of celestial motions, if a mind participates in them.</margin>

Therefore, the final sum of the matter will be this: A planet positioned at <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> strives not at all toward the Sun, but is carried forward according to its distance from the center. From this advancement, the angle $kDA$ follows. According to the proportion of this angle’s strength, the planet itself increases the diameter of the Sun <note>That is, it perceives the Sun as larger by moving closer.</note> by approaching the Sun. By this approach, it lessens the distance, such that it becomes $AD$. With the distance decreased, it is carried forward more swiftly. Therefore, the angle $kDA$ changes more quickly. Consequently, the planet (all else being equal) increases the Sun’s diameter more quickly. In this way, a perennial circulation is achieved—not in intervals, such as those we establish in our thoughts and calculations (disregarding errors that are imperceptible), but in a manner that is clearly continuous.

<margin>Comparison of the mental principle with the magnetic one.</margin>

I have said these things up to now on the condition that the <term>libration</term> <note>The back-and-forth movement of the planet toward and away from the Sun.</note>—of which observations testify—cannot be performed by some magnetic power inherent in the bodies of the planets, and if it were absolutely necessary for us to take refuge in the idea of a Mind. However, if one wishes to compare that natural motion with this mental motion: the natural motion indeed stands by itself, needing nothing; whereas this mental motion (no matter how you equip it with an animal faculty for moving the body) seems to bear witness to that magnetic motion and to summon its assistance. For first, the mind itself can do nothing to a body. It is therefore necessary to join to the mind a faculty for executing its duties in librating the body of the planet. That faculty will be either animal, or natural and magnetic. It cannot be animal; for an animal faculty cannot transport its own body from place to place (as is required in this libration) without the power of another supporting body. It will therefore be a magnetic faculty—that is, a natural consensus between the bodies of the planet and the Sun. Thus, the mind calls nature and magnets to its aid.

<summary>Kepler compares the "animal faculty" (the planet's guiding soul) to the "magnetic faculty" (physical force), arguing that even if a mind directs the planet's motion, it must rely on physical magnetic properties to move the planet's mass.</summary>

Next, this Mind—at the halfway point of its rule or its <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The angle measuring the planet's position from its perihelion (closest point to the sun) as seen from the sun.</note>—while it completes half of its work (which consists of increasing or decreasing the apparent diameter of the Sun), completes a larger part of the <term>libration</term> <note>A swinging or oscillating motion used here to describe the planet's movement toward or away from the sun.</note> above $\gamma$ $o$, but a smaller part below $o$ $\zeta$. Nor do $\gamma$ $o$ and $o \zeta$ correspond to equal parts of time. For more time is consumed in $\gamma$ $o$ than the excess of it over $o \zeta$ required. Nor are the parts continuously increased from $\zeta$ toward $\gamma$, but at $\gamma \kappa$ they are smaller, as they are also at $\alpha \zeta$. Yet the works of a Mind are usually constant.

For this reason, it was necessary for us to furnish that Mind with an animal faculty as well as a magnetic one, and to devise a struggle between the two. By this struggle, the Mind might be reminded of its duty, of which it could not be reminded by the equality of time nor of the spaces traversed. And so, once again, we have sought the aid of the <term>lens</term> <note>Kepler often uses the term "lens" or "lentil" to describe the shape of the area carved out by the planet's non-circular path.</note> from nature.

On the other hand, all these modifications are in truth inherent in the work of the Sun’s external magnetic power, and the magnetic power joined to it, which is innate to the planet itself, as explained above. If, therefore, these magnetic powers perform their duty by themselves, what need is there for them to have a director of the Mind?

And although we have remained uncertain regarding the magnetic force innate to the planetary bodies themselves—by contemplation of the Earth's axis, which is different from the <term>line of apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit.</note> of the Sun—this difficulty is common to both sides. For even if the Mind is posited, we are nonetheless forced to admit such an axis as we require in the Earth; by means of this, the Mind may perceive the strength of the angle, or its <term>versed sine</term> <note>A trigonometric function ($1 - \cos\theta$) used in early astronomy to measure distances from a diameter.</note>. Conversely, likelihood strongly urges us to ascribe this libration of the planets—which beyond controversy follows the laws of Nature—entirely to Nature, in whatever way it may be present in the bodies of the planets.

And so, as for this sensitive perception of the Sun and the fixed stars, which I accept cautiously and allow to the Mind of the planet, I do not know whether I have sufficiently proved it to the philosophical reader.

There is also the fact that even in those very methods which we have prescribed for the Mind—the most approved of all that can exist—there seems to be involved a certain Geometrical uncertainty; I do not know whether this would be rejected by **GOD** himself, who has hitherto always been found to proceed by a demonstrative way. For if the planet, as it approaches the Sun partly by its innate force, comes into different and varied degrees of the external power from the Sun (as indeed it does), and if these different degrees reciprocally intensify the planet's own power of approaching while they increase the angle (which is set as the rule for the approach, or the increase of the Sun's diameter): then the planet's own effort will finally become, in part, a measure for itself. In the planet's intention, the "before" and "after" occur simultaneously; since it is unequal throughout its parts, it required a measure for this very reason. In this way, the discovery of how to balance the strengths of both powers—so they may clear themselves in the same time and in the same rotation of the body—will be given not by demonstration, but as if by the <term>rule of false</term> <note>A mathematical method of finding a solution through trial and error or approximation, rather than direct proof.</note>.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>Assuming a Mind is present, what then follows as the cause for the advancement of the aphelia.</margin>
<margin>Concerning **interception** <note>original Greek: αντιφράξει (antiphraxis). This refers to one body physically blocking the force or "virtue" of another.</note> once again.</margin>
Unless someone wishes to suspect that an occasion for the advancement of the aphelia might be found from this very <term>non-geometric</term> <note>original Greek: αγεωμετρήτω (ageometreto). Kepler uses this to describe motions that do not perfectly conform to simple Euclidean geometry.</note> measurement. But we left it in suspense above in Chapter 35, whether this kind of motion could not exist from another cause—namely, from **interception**; just as an iron plate intercepts the power of a magnet from an iron needle, so might the bodies of the planets mutually intercept their own specific magnetic virtues by which they beckon to the Sun. For, lest this should happen with the Solar virtue—lest, I say, the Solar virtue, which is common to all, be intercepted from one by the intervention of another—we distinguished between the essence of the Solar body and that of the planetary bodies. Since, therefore, we have not distinguished between the bodies of the planets themselves, this appears to be left as a possible cause. Indeed, it could not be resolved unless the truest arrangement of the planet's magnetic body, by which its <term>libration</term> <note>The oscillating, back-and-forth motion of a planet toward and away from the sun.</note> is governed, were discovered.

<margin>Interception does not shift the aphelia, nor does it act by the way of Nature.</margin>
But let this be an example of the reasoning: Suppose the magnetic arrangement of the planet were as we introduced a little while ago (and later denied concerning the Earth). In that case, an impediment from **interception** has no place. For because the effect of the magnetic virtue was to tend toward the Sun and flee from the Sun, and meanwhile to keep the fibers of the magnetic seat straight; if, therefore, another planet, intervening between the Sun and the planet, hinders this navigation toward the Sun or this flight (while the common motion from the Sun is not hindered), the planet will therefore navigate or flee less than is proper. And thus the width of the circuit would change along with the periodic time over the course of centuries, and would again be corrected by opposing eclipses; but the aphelion would not be shifted by this interception. Therefore, the cause of the motion of the aphelia previously brought forward by us still reigns alone, without a partner or rival.

<margin>Nor [is it shifted] by the supposition of a Mind.</margin>
Furthermore, even if a Mind presides over the libration in the manner described, **interception** will do no harm. For the Mind would use as its rule, as has been said, the increasing of the Sun's diameter and the angle of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its perihelion as seen from the sun.</note>; and even if it were deprived of its perception for a short time (because the Sun was covered), it could, if it please the gods, compensate for what it had neglected once the Sun emerged again and brought the equated anomaly back into view. For the Mind, if such exists, dominates the animal faculty, and uses it unevenly at other times as the situation requires. Why then should it not also use it here outside the normal order to remove this discrepancy between the measure (the equated anomaly) and the thing measured (the Sun's diameter) which had crept in through an eclipse of the Sun? What of the fact that there are also other such slow motions, like the **precession of the equinoxes**, which arises from the direction of the Earth's axis toward various fixed stars, and not toward the Sun? In that case, the turning away of the Solar light can accomplish nothing, since even the presence of the same light does not bring it about.

<margin>What a Physicist might say to deny interception.</margin>
Therefore, so that we may escape the inconveniences of magnetic **interception** even in the specific librations of the planets (no less than we did in Chapter 35 regarding the common rotation driven by the Sun), it must be said that the bodies of the planets may indeed be similar because of their magnetic arrangement; but either they are removed further from one another than allows the spheres of the planets' virtues to meet mutually, or the virtue emanating from the Sun is stronger (no less that which calls the planets' own virtues into action than that which carries them in their orbits) than can be hindered at all by the opposition of a weaker little body; but

He argues that physical magnetic forces or a presiding "Mind" would both be resilient to such temporary obstructions.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER 57.</margin>
...to pass through, just as light passes through a globe of water; or that the bodies of the planets are of such thinness that they have no effect; and that the Sun is never completely blocked from any of the planets moved by the Sun by another planet, just as the Sun is never completely blocked from the Earth by the Moon <note>Kepler is comparing planetary "shadows" to optical ones, suggesting that if gravity or magnetic virtue is like light, it might not be fully obstructed.</note>. For although the entire Sun can indeed be covered by the Moon for several hours, the Moon is not balanced toward the Sun, but toward the Earth, of whose sight it can never be deprived, since no body comes between the Moon and the Earth.

<margin>Under what conditions, assuming a mind is present, could the motion of the aphelia be assigned to the <term>anomaly</term>? <note>original Greek: ἀνωμαλίᾳ (anomalia). In astronomy, this refers to the irregular or non-uniform movement of a planet.</note></margin>
But if it seems plausible to anyone that the shift of the apogees is instantaneous and arises from this cause—the eclipsing of the Sun—let him say, if he pleases: so that the <term>libration</term> <note>The back-and-forth oscillating motion of a planet toward and away from the Sun.</note>, interrupted during the eclipse (while the planet has meanwhile been moved by the Sun into a different angle and a different strength of its power), does not allow a sudden jump in speed once the eclipse is over, this jump in the angle is compensated for by the planet itself. This is done by a tilting of its axis toward the Sun after the eclipse, making it as it was at the start of the eclipse. In this way, a shift of the aphelia will be obtained, but one made in leaps, remaining in the same place among the fixed stars for many years until another darkening of the planet occurs.

<margin>Another cause for the movement of the aphelia, assuming a mind is present.</margin>
But that first cause for the shifting of the aphelia, arising from the deviation of the libration from its circuit under the fixed stars, because of the <term>non-geometric</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγεωμέτρητον (ageometreton). This refers to a relationship that cannot be expressed by simple whole-number geometry.</note> connection of one to the other, would be more in favor of a uniform shifting of the apogees.

<margin>Third [cause].</margin>
Finally, if neither of these causes is sufficient, let the mind, equipped with an animate faculty that oversees the constant direction of the magnetic axis, also have this task of tilting it over the course of centuries. But let us not rest upon any of these causes, nor even upon a "Mind" standing over the universe; let us rest in nature. For nature, just as she has provided for everything else, has also shown a clear occasion for the motion of the aphelia.

## CHAPTER 58.

### How, while the libration demonstrated and discovered in Chapter 56 remains, an error might nevertheless be admitted in the reverse application of the libration, by which the path of the planet is made "puffy." <note>original: "buccosum." Kepler uses this colorful term to describe an orbit that "puffs out" like a cheek, departing from a perfect circle to form an oval.</note>

> GALATEA PELTS ME WITH AN APPLE, THE PLAYFUL GIRL,
> AND FLEES TO THE WILLOWS, YET WISHES TO BE SEEN FIRST. <note>A quote from Virgil's *Eclogues* (3.64-65). Kepler uses this to describe how Nature seems to play hard-to-get with the scientist.</note>

TRULY, I sing this truth about Nature from the mouth of **VIRGIL**. For the closer one comes to her, the more petulant are the games she plays; she escapes through many twists and turns just as one is about to grasp her and is already holding on. Yet she does not cease to invite one to catch her, as if she delights in my errors. Throughout this entire work, my aim has been to find a physical hypothesis that would produce not only distances consistent with observations but also equations that are likewise correct, which until now I have been forced to derive from the "substitute" hypothesis of Chapter **16**.

<margin>CHAPTER 58.</margin> ...we must borrow: attempting the same thing even through this most true hypothesis, but by a false method, I began again to tremble for the whole of the matter. *In the <term>line of apsides</term> <note>The line connecting the points in an orbit where the planet is closest to and farthest from the Sun.</note>, with centers* **A** and **B**, *let equal circles* **G D** and **H K** *be drawn. And let* **A B** *be the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance the center of the orbit is shifted away from the Sun.</note> of circle* **G D**. *Moreover, let the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>original: "anomalia eccentri." An angle used to define the position of a body moving along an elliptic or circular path.</note>, or the number of its degrees, be the arc* **G D** *or* **H K**, *by the equivalence shown in Chapter 3. Therefore, with center* **K** *and a distance* **K D** *which is equal to* **A B**, *let the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; a standard tool in ancient and Renaissance astronomy.</note>* **L D F** *be drawn, which will cut the circle* **G D** *at point* **D**, *by the equivalence of Chapter 3. Let* **A K** *be drawn and continued until it cuts the epicycle at* **L**, *so that* **L D** *is an arc similar to the eccentric anomaly* **G D** *or* **H K**. *And let* **B** *be connected with* **D**. *Then, from point* **D**, *let perpendicular lines be dropped to* **G A** *and* **L A**, *which shall be* **D C** *and* **D E**.* Wherefore, by what was demonstrated up to this point in Chapter 56, **A E** will be, beyond controversy, the correct distance for this eccentric anomaly, for which it is asked how much time is consumed in it. And since its <term>versed sine</term> <note>original: "sinus versus." A trigonometric value defined as 1 minus the cosine.</note> **G C**, or after multiplication, **L E** subtracted from **G A**, produced the correct distance **A E**: from these indications I was persuaded that the other end of this **A E** should be sought not on the line **D C** (which was nevertheless the most true way), but at point **I** on the line **D B**: so that if I drew the arc **E I F** with center **A** and distance **A E**, it would cut **D B** at **I**. Therefore, according to this persuasion, **A I** would be the correct distance in both position and length; and **I A G** would be the truly equalized anomaly. It is manifest, however, that the arc **E I F** cuts the line **D C** at a higher point, namely at **F**. Thus the angles **I A G** and **F A G** differ by the quantity **I A F**.

I erred, therefore, by using the line **A I** instead of **A F**. I first detected this error through experience. For when I had explored the quantity of the area **D A G** both through all the distances and through the small area **D A B**, and had afterward matched the angle **I A G** (**NOT** **F A G**) to this area **D A G** converted into time; I then found that in the upper part of the semicircle I collected 5 ½ minutes too much, and in the lower part 4 minutes too little, compared to what the <term>vicarious hypothesis</term> <note>Kepler’s earlier, highly accurate but purely mathematical model that predicted the planet’s position without explaining its physical cause.</note> (which is certain enough) gave. Therefore, with the equations disagreeing with the truth, I began again to blame the most true distances **A E** and the <term>libration</term> <note>The oscillating, back-and-forth motion of the planet toward and away from the Sun.</note> of the planet **L E** for a crime of which my false method, which looked at **I** instead of **F**, was actually guilty. Why say more? Truth itself and the Nature of things, though rejected and ordered into exile, snuck back in through the back door, and was received by me in a different guise. Having dismissed, I say, the librations of the diameter **L E**, I began to call back the **ellipses**, believing entirely that I was following a hypothesis far different from the librations; when in fact they plainly coincide, as will be demonstrated in the following chapter: except that the errors I had previously committed in my method were corrected by this reasoning, and **F** was used instead of **I**, just as it should have been.

My reasoning was such as it was in Chapters 49, 50, and 56. The circle in Chapter 44 fails by excess; the ellipse in Chapter 45 fails by deficiency. And that excess and this deficiency are equal. Between the circle and the ellipse, there is nothing...

But if the planet's path were an ellipse, it was sufficiently clear that *i* could not be used instead of *f*; because if this is done, the planet's path is made **bulging** <note>original: "buccosum," literally "puffy-cheeked." Kepler used this term to describe an oval that bulges out too much to be a true ellipse.</note>. For let the angles *G B D* and *H A K* be equal below *Q B P* and *S A R*: and with center *x*, let the epicycle *P T* be drawn again, equal to the former one: and from *P*, the intersection of the epicycle with the eccentric, let the perpendiculars *P V* and *P M* fall onto *B Q* and *A R*: and let *P* be connected with *B*. And with center *A* and the distance *A M*, let the arc *M N* be drawn, cutting *P V* at *O* and *P B* at *N*. It is therefore analogous to the things above, that if we use *i* for *f*, we now use *n* for *o*; and let us think that *A N*, as it is the correct distance in length, so also is it correct in position. But the points *i, n* and similar ones make the planet's path **bulging**. For the arcs *G D* and *Q P* are equal, and *B D* and *B P*, projected from the common center, cut the sectioned crescent. But *D I* and *P N*, the widths of the crescent extended toward the center, are unequal; and *D I* is smaller, while *P N* is larger. For since *E D* and *M P* are equal, and the angles *E D I* and *M P N* are right, and the circle at *E* is larger (as if with a longer radius *A E*) and the circle *M N* is smaller (as if with a shorter radius *A M*), *P N* will certainly be larger, and *D I* smaller. Therefore, the sectioned crescent is thinner above at *D*, and wider below at *P*. But in an ellipse, this crescent is of equal width at points equally distant from the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the center of motion.</note> *G* and *Q*. It is clear, therefore, that the path is **bulging**, and thus not an ellipse. And since the ellipse provides the correct <term>equations</term> <note>In this context, "equations" refers to the mathematical corrections needed to predict a planet's position.</note>, it is right that this bulging path provides incorrect ones.

Nor was there any need to compute the equations anew from the ellipse. I knew they would perform their duty of their own accord. I was only worried about the distances, lest perhaps those taken from the ellipse might cause me trouble. But although this happened, I had a hiding place ready: an uncertainty of 200 parts in the distances. So even here I did not hesitate much. But by far the greatest **scruple** <note>A source of doubt or hesitation; Kepler often uses this word when his data and his theory don't quite match.</note> was that, considering and looking around almost to the point of insanity, I could not find why the planet—to which a <term>libration</term> <note>original: "libratio." A back-and-forth oscillation. Kepler realized that a planet moving back and forth on a diameter while that diameter rotates creates an ellipse.</note> *L E* in the diameter *L R* was attributed with such great probability and such agreement with the observed distances—would rather want to go on an elliptical path, as indicated by the equations. **O, how foolish of me!** As if libration in a diameter could not be the way to an ellipse! Therefore, this knowledge cost me no small effort: that an ellipse exists by way of libration. This will become clear in the following chapter, where it will also be demonstrated that no figure of the orbit is left to the planet except a perfectly elliptical one; with the physical reasons derived from principles conspiring together with the experience of observations and the "proxy hypothesis" cited in this chapter.

# PRELIMINARY THEOREMS.

-> I. <-

**If an ellipse is described within a circle, touching the circle at its vertices at opposite points; and a diameter is drawn through the center and the points of contact; then from other points on the circumference of the circle, let perpendiculars be drawn to this diameter: all of these will be cut by the circumference of the ellipse in the same ratio.**

*From Book 1 of <term>Apollonius</term>'s <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BC), known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conic sections.</note> Conics, page 21. <term>Commandino</term> <note>Federico Commandino (1509–1575), a mathematician who translated and commented on the works of Archimedes and Apollonius.</note> demonstrates this in his commentary on the fifth proposition of <term>Archimedes</term>'s On Spheroids.*

*For let the circle be **AEC**. In it, let there be an ellipse **ABC** touching the circle at **A** and **C**. Let a diameter be drawn through the points of contact **A** and **C**, and through the center **H**. Then, from the points on the circumference **K** and **E**, let perpendiculars **KL** and **EH** descend, cut at **M** and **B** by the circumference of the ellipse. The ratio of **BH** to **HE** will be the same as the ratio of **ML** to **LK**, and so it is for all other perpendiculars.*

-> II. <-

**The area of an ellipse thus inscribed in a circle has the same ratio to the area of the circle as the aforementioned lines.**

*For as **BH** is to **HE**, so is the area of the ellipse **ABC** to the area of the circle **AEC**. This is the fifth proposition of <term>Archimedes</term>'s On Spheroids.*

-> III. <-

**If from a certain point on the diameter, lines are drawn to the intersections of the same perpendicular with the circumferences of the circle and the ellipse, the areas cut off by them will again be in the ratio of the divided perpendicular.**

*Let **N** be a point on the diameter, and **KML** a perpendicular. Connect the points **K** and **M** with **N**. I say that as **ML** is to **LK** (or, by the first theorem, as the shorter semi-diameter **BH** is to the longer **HE**), so is the area **AMN** to the area **AKN**. For the area **AML** is to the area **AKL** as **ML** is to **LK**, according to the assumptions of <term>Archimedes</term> for the fifth proposition of On Spheroids, which <term>Commandino</term> demonstrates in his commentaries on this proposition at letters **c** and **D**. Furthermore, for the right-angled triangles **NLM** and **NLK**, the height **NL** is*

### IV.

**When a circle is divided into any number of equal arcs by perpendiculars of this kind, the ellipse is divided into unequal arcs; those arcs located at the vertices have the greatest ratio, while those in the middle positions have the smallest.**

*For near the vertices, the ratio of the arcs is very close to the ratio of the perpendicular segments to which they are most closely aligned in length; yet it is less. Near the middle positions they become nearly equal; however, the elliptical arc is smaller because it is less curved than the circular one. This is self-evident.*

### V.

**The total circumference of an ellipse is approximately the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The simple average, calculated by adding two values and dividing by two.</note> between the circle of the longer diameter and the circle of the shorter diameter.**

*For it was proved above in chapter 48 that the circumference is longer than that of a circle whose diameter is the <term>mean proportional</term> <note>Also called the geometric mean; the value where the first diameter is to the mean as the mean is to the second diameter.</note> between the diameters of the ellipse—which is the circle whose area, according to the 7th theorem of <term>Archimedes</term>'s <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC), the greatest mathematician of antiquity, whose work on the measurement of circles and spheres Kepler relies on here.</note> On Spheroids, equals the area of the ellipse. But the arithmetic mean is also longer than the mean proportional. Therefore, these two are very nearly equal.*

### VI.

**The <term>gnomons</term> <note>A gnomon is the L-shaped area remaining after a smaller square is removed from the corner of a larger square.</note> of proportionally divided squares are to each other as the squares themselves.**

*Let there be two squares, PL and SH. Let their sides, KL and EH, be divided proportionally at points M and B. Let the gnomons KOQ and CRE be drawn. Therefore, because ML is to LK as BH is to HE, it follows that OL is to LP as RH is to HS. But gnomons are the differences between squares. Therefore, just as LP is to its gnomon, so is HS to its own; and by permutation, as PL is to HS, so is gnomon KOQ to gnomon CRE.*

### VII.

**If from the end of the shorter semi-diameter, on the circumference of the ellipse, a line is extended equal to the longer semi-diameter so that it terminates on that longer semi-diameter: the distance between this point and the center <term>is able to</term> <note>Kepler uses the Latin term "potest" in the classical geometric sense, meaning that the square of this distance is equal to the area mentioned.</note> the gnomon which the square of the longer semi-diameter forms around the square of the shorter semi-diameter.**

->VIII.<-

**If a circle is divided into any number of parts, or even an infinite number, and the points of division are connected with some point other than the center within the circle's bounds, and likewise connected with the center: the sum of those lines from the center will be less than the sum of those from the other point.**

**And two lines near the line of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit closest to (periapsis) and farthest from (apoapsis) the center of motion.</note>, drawn in opposite directions from the eccentric point, will be very nearly equal to the two drawn from the center in opposite directions; however, the two in the intermediate positions will be much greater than those drawn from the center at the same locations.**

<margin>Demonstrated in chapter 40.</margin>

Therefore, this excess does not increase equally with the number of lines, much less with the sines. For the differences of the sines vanish at the ends; whereas the differences of the said excesses are greatest at the ends. And since the area of circle $KNA$ grows equally—the part $KHA$ with the number of lines, by construction; and the part $KNH$ with the sines of the arcs to which the lines belong, multiplied by $HN$, according to chapter 40—the area of the circle is therefore not suitable for measuring the sum of the distances of its circumference. <note>This is a pivotal moment in Kepler's discovery process: he realizes that simply summing the distances from an eccentric point does not perfectly match the area of a circle, which led him to refine his "Area Law" for planetary motion.</note>

<margin>CHAPTER 59.</margin>

*For let any point on the circumference of the circle be chosen, which we shall call K; and from K through H <note>Point H is typically the center of the eccentric circle in Kepler's diagrams.</note> let a straight line be drawn to the opposite part of the circumference, I. From N <note>Point N usually represents the sun's position at the focus.</note> let a perpendicular fall onto KI, which we shall call NT. Then KH and HI joined together are equal to KT and TI joined together. And any sum of the pairs KH and HI equals an equal sum of the pairs KT and TI. However, since the sum of the lines AN and KT—as many as are found in the arc AK at equal intervals—increases partly with the number of lines HA and HK, and partly with the <term>sines</term> multiplied by HN, it therefore increases equally with the area KNA, by the preceding proposition. Therefore, the area of the circle and its parts KNA measure the sums of the diametral distances.*

### X.

Regarding the distances drawn from the eccentric point of the ellipse to equal arcs of the ellipse: the ratio is no less contrary than that of the circle in Theorem VIII; the ratio is contrary to the mutual ratio of the arcs of the circle and ellipse explained in Theorem IV. For the pairs drawn from the eccentric point in opposite directions exceed the pairs drawn from the center in opposite directions in the smallest proportion, and clearly not at all around the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the sun.</note>. But at the mean longitudes, they exceed them in the greatest proportion.

This appears in chapter 40. Therefore, again as in Theorem VIII, the area of the ellipse is not suitable for measuring the sum of the distances of equal arcs of its own elliptical circumference.

### XI.

With these things thus premised, I will now set forth the demonstration.

If in an ellipse divided by perpendiculars dropped from equal arcs of the circle (as described above in Theorem IV), the points of division of the circle and the ellipse are connected with the point that was found in Theorem VII: I say, those lines that are drawn to the circumference of the circle are circumferential distances; while those drawn to the circumference of the ellipse are diametral <note>Kepler distinguishes "circumferential" (to the auxiliary circle) from "diametral" (the actual distance to the planet on its elliptical path).</note>. These are established at an equal number of degrees from the apsis of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one; here Kepler uses it to describe the components of planetary motion.</note>.

*From point I, which is opposite to K across the center H, let a perpendicular IV fall onto AC, cutting the elliptical circumference at Y. And from point N, found by Theorem VII, let the sections NK and NM be drawn to K and M, and NI and NY to I and Y, these being sections made on both sides by the same perpendicular. Let the diagram from chapters 39 and 57 also be recalled.
