I say that NK is the circumferential distance (as demonstrated in Chapter 2) and NM is the diametral distance $\alpha \kappa$.*

*First, the square of KN equals the squares of KL and LN. Similarly, the square of MN equals the squares of ML and LN. <note>Kepler uses the term "potest" (is able) to mean the square of a line, a common Euclidean phrasing.</note> Let LP be the square of LK, and LO the square of LM. Therefore, if the square of LN and the square of LM (that is, the square LO) are taken away from both sides as common elements, there remains the <term>gnomon</term> KOQ, <note>A gnomon is the L-shaped area left over when a smaller square is removed from the corner of a larger square.</note> by which the square of KN exceeds the square of MN. Now, as KL is to EH, so KM is to EB, according to the first part of this proof. Therefore, just as KQ (the square of KL) is to EC (the square of EH), so is the gnomon KOQ to the gnomon ERC, by the sixth part of this proof. But just as here in the eccentric circle KL (the <term>sine</term> of arc AK) is to EH or AH (the <term>total sine</term>), so also in the epicycle, the perpendicular $\delta \kappa$ (drawn from point $\delta$ of arc $\gamma \delta$, which is similar to AK, onto the diameter of the apsides $\beta \gamma$) is to the semidiameter of the epicycle $\beta \gamma$. For this reason, as the gnomon KOQ is to the gnomon ERC, so is the square of $\delta \kappa$ to the square of $\beta \gamma$. But HN is equal to this $\beta \gamma$. And the square of HN equals the gnomon ERC, by the seventh part. Therefore, the square of $\beta \gamma$ also equals the gnomon ERC; and accordingly, the square of $\delta \kappa$ (the perpendicular from the point on the epicycle mentioned just now) will equal the gnomon KOQ. But the square of that perpendicular $\delta \kappa$ is the excess of the circumferential distance $\delta \alpha$ over the diametral distance $\kappa \alpha$. Therefore, the gnomon KOQ, being equal to it, is also the excess of the square of $\delta \alpha$ over the square of $\kappa \alpha$. But KN is equal to this $\delta \alpha$. Therefore, the square of KN exceeds the square of $\kappa \alpha$ by the gnomon KOQ. But the square of MN also exceeds it by that same gnomon. Therefore, MN and $\kappa \alpha$ are equal diametral distances. Which was to be demonstrated. A similar proof will show that NY equals $\alpha \mu$, provided that $\zeta \eta$ is similar to CI. And so it is for all of them.*

### XIII.

But here a doubt arises: If the area AKN is equivalent to all the distances from N of the elliptical arc AM, consisting of as many points as we suppose to be in AK, then what exactly is that elliptical arc—that is, where does it end? For it seems it should not be terminated by the perpendicular line KL. The reason is this: because in this way, by the fourth [proposition] of these, unequal elliptical arcs correspond to equal [arcs] of the circle. Thus, the smaller arcs are around the <term>vertices</term><note>The points A and C, where the ellipse is most sharply curved; its "ends".</note> A and C, and the larger ones around B. Yet it seems necessary that equal arcs of the elliptical orbit be taken, if indeed we wish to estimate and compare the <term>delays</term><note>original: "moras". Kepler uses this to mean the duration of time a planet spends traveling through a specific segment of its path.</note> of the planet in them. And specifically, because it is certain that the end of this arc must be at distance MN from N; therefore, as in Chapter 58, with center N and distance NM, the arc MZ being drawn shows a point somewhere terminating that arc of the ellipse, and it seems that point will not be M, but Z, where the arc intersects the line KH, so that the arc of the orbit is AZ.

->The answer is: the arc of the ellipse whose delays the area AKN measures must absolutely be divided into unequal parts, and those which are near the <term>apsides</term><note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the sun.</note> must be smaller.<-

For let us suppose that the planet's path ABC itself is divided into equal arcs. Because the planet spends more time in arc A than in arc C in proportion to how much longer NA is than NC; and since NA and NC together equal the longer diameter of the ellipse, and HB is the shorter <term>semidiameter</term><note>The radius of the minor axis of the ellipse.</note> of the ellipse; the delay of the planet in the arc at B and the opposite arc joined together will also be shorter than in the equal arcs A and C joined together. Thus, in order for the delay around A and C to become shorter, and around B and the opposite longer, so that the combined delay of two opposite arcs always becomes equal, it is necessary for the arcs at A and C to be made smaller, and at B and its opposite larger. This, however, is accomplished by the perpendiculars KML, as is clear from the objection itself.

But by this solution we have only established that there must be very short arcs around A and C. Whether these very arcs, determined by the perpendiculars KML, are the most exact ones, is not yet established. This will now become clear in the following manner.

### XIV.

If someone were to divide the ellipse AMC into any number of equal arcs and assign to each of them its own distance from N, but instead of the sums of the distances...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 59 of Johannes Kepler's "Astronomia Nova," where he is refining the "Area Law" for planetary motion. He is demonstrating that if one calculates the time a planet spends in a portion of its orbit using the area of an ellipse rather than a circle, certain geometric errors introduced in earlier models (like Chapter 40) are naturally corrected.</meta>

-># ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANET MARS<-

<margin>CHAPTER 59.</margin>

In [the arcs] AM, AB, and ABC, if one were to use the areas AMN, ABN, and ABCNA, they would encounter the same error according to the tenth <term>preliminary theorem</term><note>original Latin: "protheorema." Kepler uses this term for the geometric lemmas he provides at the start of chapters to build his proofs.</note> that occurred above in Chapter 40. This happened when we attempted the same thing with a perfect circle as is now proposed for the ellipse: namely, that the two lines MN and NY, belonging to two points M and Y opposite the center H, would be taken in place of the shorter line MHY.

But if that same person were to divide the ellipse AMC into the same number of unequal arcs—contrary to the tenth preliminary theorem—by this rule: first, the circle AKC is divided into equal arcs, and then from the endpoints of each arc, perpendiculars KL are drawn to the diameter AC, intersecting the ellipse AM into arcs as well; and if the elliptical area is used for the distances of these arcs from N: then the error committed will be remedied, and a most perfect compensation will occur.

I shall prove this regarding the starts of the quadrants A and C, their ends B, and the intermediate progress.

*In the beginnings of the quadrants* A and C, *if two lines* NA and NC *are used for the line* AHC, *there is no error. At the end, however, if I use* BH *for* BN (that is, for EH), *the maximum error or deficiency occurs, in the amount of* BE, *according to the tenth preliminary theorem. And according to the seventh preliminary theorem of this chapter, as* HE *is to* EB, *so is the required length to the error committed at this location. If, therefore, the total sum of all distances took its measure from something that fails by being too small—namely, the area of the ellipse—then when that deficiency is distributed among the individual distances by the power of our operation or calculation, it will result in* NA *and* NC *being taken as too short relative to this measure of the whole. This measure misleads us into thinking all lines fail equally in deficiency, even though* NA *and* NC *do not fail at all. They contributed a correct measure to this sum, but when the sum was redistributed in turn, they did not receive a correct amount back, because other lines around* B *defrauded the sum.*

SEE NOW how we may remedy this error in the same proportion.
For by the fourth preliminary theorem of this chapter, the smallest arcs AK and AM around the <term>apsides</term><note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to (perihelion, A) or farthest from (aphelion, C) the sun.</note> A or C are in the proportion of KL to LM, which is the same as EH to HB. The straight line around B previously failed in deficiency by this same proportion. Conversely, around B, the smallest arcs of the circle and the ellipse (say, KE and MB) are equal; just as before, the straight lines AN and NC joined together were equal to the line AHC. ...at *B*, the middle lengths. And so, where the distances are too short in respect to their faulty sum—within the erroneous area of the proposed ellipse—there the arcs are small in respect to their average size, as at *a* and *c*. Conversely, where the distances are too long, there the arcs are too long, as at *B*. Thus, the less "delay" <note>Kepler uses the term "delay" (*mora*) to refer to the time a planet spends traversing a specific arc of its orbit, which he realized is proportional to the area swept out by the planet.</note> we accumulate in the calculation through a very short distance near the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the Sun.</note>, the more distances are applied to such an arc (since it is cut into small parts, and each such part is assigned its own distance). And in turn, the more delay we accumulate beyond what is due through individual distances in the calculation around the middle lengths *B*—while we have transferred part of the defect inherent in this location to the innocent apsides *a* and *c*—the fewer distances the calculation collects, as if they were begged from the large parts of the arc. In the former case, at *a* and *c*, what the individual distances cannot provide due to their shortness in the calculation, they provide through their frequency, so that they accumulate the proper delays. In the latter case, the fact that they would err by the length they acquired in the calculation is corrected by taking it away from those distances that are spread out more widely and loosely.

I have spoken concerning the beginning and the end: that the arcs of the circle begin to differ from the elliptical arcs at *A* and *C* in the same proportion as *EH* is to *HB*; and the correct distances differ in the same proportion from those which the area of the ellipse collects at *B*, and the opposite. They also cease to differ in that same proportion—namely, the proportion of equality—for the arcs at *BE*, and for the distances at *A* and *C*.

We must now say the same concerning the intermediate progress.
For the lines *NA* and *NC*, from small beginnings and through rapid increases, exceed the lines *AHC* by some notable amount. Conversely, where they exceed them most (as *BN* exceeds *HB*), there the increments gradually die away: they are greatest in the middle, around an <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>An angle used to define the position of a planet moving along an elliptic orbit.</note> of 45°.

This is evident from the angle of the equation and the secants. For as much as the <term>secant</term> <note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side of a right triangle.</note> of the angle of the <term>optical equation</term> <note>The "optical equation" is the difference between the planet's mean position and its true position as seen from the Sun, caused by the observer's perspective.</note> differs from the <term>total sine</term> <note>In the trigonometry of Kepler's time, the "total sine" refers to the radius of the reference circle, often set at 100,000.</note>, by nearly that much does *BN* differ from *BH*; the opposite angles of the equations assist each other toward this proportion. But the increments of the secants of the optical equation are nearly at their maximum around 45°, being slow at the beginning and end of the quadrant. See the end of Chapter 43 regarding these matters.

And the increments of the elliptical arcs, distinguished by the perpendiculars *KL*, proceed in the same proportion. For at the beginnings *A* and *C*, the arc *AK* (always starting from *A*) is to its increment as *LK* is to *KM*. But the total arc itself is small. Therefore, the increment is also small. At the end, around *B*, the proportion of *AE* to *AB* is reduced almost to equality, even though the arc *AB* is large, being near the quadrant; thus, the increment is again small. Therefore, the increment of the arcs is most evident in the middle, around 45°.

It is clear, therefore, that the ratios are equal even in their progress, as far as can be determined by subtle consideration.

This demonstration, while most certain, is nonetheless <term>unartful</term> <note>original Greek: ατεχνος (atechnos); meaning it lacks a formal, systematic method</note> and <term>un-geometrical</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγεωμέτρητος (ageometretos)</note>, at least as far as this part concerning the progress of the intermediate increases is concerned. I would wish, as with the rest, that this small part also be settled geometrically and <term>artfully</term> <note>original Greek: ἐντέχνως (entechnos); with technical skill</note>, so that even the followers of <term>Apollonius</term> <note>Apollonius of Perga, a Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections (including ellipses).</note> might be satisfied. In the meantime, until someone else finds and polishes this, we must be content with this.

## The arc of the ellipse, whose delays the area <term>AKN</term> measures, must be terminated at <term>LK</term>, so that it becomes <term>AM</term>.

For up to this point, we have been occupied with this fiction: if anyone had so much leisure that they wished to compute the area of an ellipse, it would follow that by using the elliptical area <term>AMN</term>, in place of as many distances of <term>AM</term> as there are equal arcs in <term>AK</term>, they would not wander from the mark. Let this stand for us as the major premise demonstrated thus far.

*I shall now subjoin the minor premise from the third pre-theorem of this chapter, in which it was shown that just as the area <term>AKC</term> is to the area <term>AMC</term>, so also is the area <term>AKN</term> to the area <term>AMN</term>. It is concluded, therefore, since the proportion of equimultiples is the same, that the area of the circle <term>AKN</term> itself also measures the sum of the diametral distances (such as <term>KT</term>, <term>TI</term>) or elliptical distances of <term>AM</term>, numbering as many as there are parts in <term>AK</term>. From this it is clear that the more crowded distances are correctly assigned to the parts of the ellipse around <term>A.C.</term> <note>A.C. refers to the apsides, the points nearest and farthest from the sun.</note>, specifically as many as are established in that section by the perpendiculars <term>KL</term>, coming from equal arcs of <term>AK</term> itself.*

Lest anyone doubt the truth of the matter, distrusting the subtlety and complexity of the argument, the thing itself first became known through experience in this manner. I established for each degree of the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle used to define the position of a planet moving along an elliptical orbit, measured from the center of the orbit.</note>, in place of the distances from <term>N</term>, the diametral lines <term>KT</term> and <term>TI</term>. I also added each one in order to the sum of the previous ones. When all were collected, the sum was 36,000,000, as is right. Then, comparing the individual sums with the total, just as (in the rule of proportions) the sum 36,000,000 was to 360 degrees (the technical name for the total time of restoration <note>Original: "nomen artificiale temporis totius restitutorii." ## IV.

### The angle of the Planet's approach from the circumference of the circle to the diameter of the apsides is the same in the eccentric anomaly at the center of the eccentric as it is in the equated circular anomaly, with the same number of degrees, at the center of the Sun.

And the [angles] **FDH** and **IGN** are equal. Therefore, **FHD** and **ING** are also equal. And **H** is the center of the eccentric, while **N** is the center of the Sun. ## V.

### The genuine and truest measure of the angle by which the fictitious equated [anomaly], which relies on a circle, differs from the true equated [anomaly], which relies on an ellipse, is the product of the sine of the fictitious equated anomaly and the sine of the complement of the true equated anomaly.

In the same diagram, by multiplying the sine of angle **AHD** by the sine of angle **VFD**, the genuine measure of angle **FHD** was going to be produced through [Theorem] III. But through [Theorem] IV, the sine of the equal angles **VHD** and **XNG** is the same, and likewise, the sine of **VFH** and **XIN** is the same. Therefore, by multiplying the sine of angle **XNG** (the fictitious equated anomaly) by the sine of angle **XIN** (the complement of **XNI**, which is the true equated [anomaly]), the genuine measure of angle **FHD** is produced; that is, through [Theorem] IV, the angle **ING**, which is the difference between **XNG** and **XNI**.

## COROLLARV.

Because the difference **ING** is small, and nowhere greater than 8 <term>minutes</term> <note>A minute is 1/60th of a degree.</note>, the difference between the rectangles formed by the sine of **XIN** and the sine of **XGN** will be even much smaller in effect.

This page contains the famous "Kepler’s Problem": the realization that there is no simple geometric way to calculate the planet's position directly from the time elapsed because the math involves both a circular arc and a straight line (the sine).</meta>

PART FOUR

From here, this practice will be made. <margin>Given the <term>equated anomaly</term><note>The angle of the planet as seen from the Sun.</note>, find the corresponding <term>eccentric anomaly</term><note>An auxiliary angle used to relate the planet's motion in an ellipse to a perfect circle.</note>.</margin> Given the angle of the true equated anomaly, let its <term>sine</term><note>A trigonometric function representing the vertical side of a right triangle.</note> be multiplied by the <term>sine of the complement</term><note>original: "sinum complementi"; this is the modern cosine.</note>. Let the double of the product, discarding the last five digits, be multiplied by the maximum angle of entry at an anomaly of 45 degrees. The angle of entry for the given anomaly will be produced. When this is added to the true equated anomaly *XNI*, it gives the fictitious anomaly *XNG*. Through this angle, and the known sides *NH* and *HG*, the eccentric anomaly *AHG* is found, along with the value of the triangle *HGN*, as has been done until now.

To seek the maximum angle at an anomaly of 45 degrees is not <margin>* And the mean anomaly.</margin> difficult. Let *VHD* be 45°. Therefore, as the <term>total sine</term><note>The radius of the calculation circle, here set to 100,000.</note> is to 70,711, so is 429—or more correctly 432, the maximum entry, namely the maximum width of the <term>lunula</term><note>The "little moon" or crescent-shaped area representing the difference between the circle and the ellipse.</note>—to *FD* 315. And since at 45° the lines *HV* and *VD* are equal, subtract *FD* 315 from *VD* 70,711. The remainder is *VF*, 70,396. This, with *HV*, gives the angle *VHF* 44° 52' 19", which differs from 45° 0' 0" by only 7' 41". And this is the maximum angle *ING*.

THERE FOLLOWS another method through <term>Analysis</term><note>Here meaning algebra.</note>, the foundations of which are these. In the diagram for Chapter 59, given the angle *MNL*, the proportion of the lines *MN* and *NC* is given: and I know that *MN* and *LN* are composed of known parts and a swapped proportion. For in *MN* is the total sine, which is known; in *LN* is *HN*, the known <term>eccentricity</term><note>The distance between the center of the orbit and the Sun.</note>. The ratio of the remainder of *MN* to the remainder of *LN* (that is, to *LH*) is the same as the ratio of the eccentricity *AN* to the total sine. See also, if you prefer, the diagram for Chapter 58. Therefore, let *MN* be 100,000 + 1 <term>æ</term><note>Kepler uses "æ" (from *æqualis*) as an algebraic symbol for the unknown root, similar to our modern "x".</note>; from the angle *MNL* of 30°, let *LN* be $\frac{86,603,000,000 + 86,603}{100,000}$ æ, and *NH* be 9,265 or $\frac{926,500,000}{100,000}$, so that *HL* is $\frac{7,733,800,000 + 86,603}{100,000}$ æ. But as *HN* 9,265 is to 1 æ, so 100,000 is to *LH*. Therefore, *HL* a second time is $\frac{100,000}{9,265}$ æ, which is $\frac{1,079,310}{100,000}$ æ; previously it was $\frac{7,733,800,000 + 86,603}{100,000}$ æ. Removing the denominators and things that can be removed equally from both sides, there remains 992,717 æ equal to the number 7,733,800,000. Thus, one root is 7,744, and *MN* is 107,744. And because as *HN* is to this root, so is the total [sine] to *LH*, *LH* will therefore be 83,583, which is the sine of *KE* 56° 42', the complement of the eccentric anomaly *AK* 33° 46'. Having found this, now, as just before, the area *AKN* is found, which is the measure of time or the <term>mean anomaly</term><note>The angle a planet would have if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant speed.</note>. In the diagram of Chapter 58, these things are very clear. Let *GQ* be the eccentric, *AB* the eccentricity, *GD* or *LD* the eccentric anomaly, *FAC* the equated anomaly, and *FC* or *EA* the distance. Therefore, as *AK* is to *AB*, so is *BC* to *KE*: and in the equated anomaly *CAO*, as *AR* is to *AB*, so is *BV* to *RM*. Therefore, *EK* or *RM* is set to be one Root. The rest as above.

But given the mean anomaly, there is no geometric <margin>Given the mean anomaly, find the eccentric anomaly and thus the equated anomaly.</margin> method of reaching the equated anomaly, namely the eccentric anomaly. For the mean anomaly is composed of two parts of an area: a sector and a triangle. The former is measured by the arc of the eccentric; the latter by the sine of that arc multiplied into the value of the maximum triangle...

<summary>Kepler provides a trigonometric and algebraic "practice" for converting between different types of orbital anomalies. He famously concludes that there is no direct geometric method for finding a planet's position from the time elapsed (Kepler's Problem).</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the mathematical demonstration from the previous section. Kepler has been explaining that while one can calculate the "mean anomaly" (time) if the "eccentric anomaly" (position on the circle) is known, the reverse—finding the position if you only know the time—is not possible through standard geometry. He is now summarizing this difficulty and issuing a formal challenge to the mathematicians of his day.</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER 60.</margin>
...multiplied, with the last digits cut off. But the proportions between arcs and their sines are infinite in number. Therefore, when the sum of both is proposed, it cannot be said how large the arc is, or how large its sine is, that corresponds to this sum; unless we first explore, given the arc, what area results: that is, unless you have constructed tables and work from them afterwards.

**This is my opinion.** The less this seems to possess of geometric beauty, the more I urge geometers to solve this problem for me:

## Given the area of a part of a semicircle and a given point on the diameter, find the arc and the angle at that point; by the legs of which angle and by which arc the given area is contained. Or: To divide the area of a semicircle from any point on the diameter in a given ratio.

It is enough for me to believe that it cannot be solved <term>a priori</term><note>Latin: "from the cause." In logic, it means to prove something from first principles rather than from experience or trial-and-error.</note>, on account of the <term>heterogeneity</term><note>original: "ἑτερογένειαν" (heterogeneian). Kepler is referring to the "different natures" of a straight line (the sine) and a curved line (the arc), which cannot be easily solved together in a single algebraic equation.</note> of the arc and the sine. To whoever shows me the way out of my error, he shall be to me a great <term>Apollonius</term><note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – 190 BC) was a Greek geometer famous for his work on conic sections; Kepler is saying he would consider such a person a mathematical genius.</note>.

<summary>Kepler defines the famous "Kepler's Problem," admitting that there is no direct geometric method to determine a planet's position from the time elapsed because arcs and sines are mathematically "heterogeneous." He challenges other mathematicians to find a solution, concluding that he must rely on numerical approximations and tables in the meantime.</summary>

# CHAPTER LXI.
## Examination of the position of the Nodes. <note>A <term>Node</term> is one of the two points where a planet's tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic). Finding these points is essential for calculating a planet's latitude—its distance north or south of that plane.</note>

Since the proportions of the orbits of **MARS** and **EARTH**, the eccentricity of both, and the shape of their paths have been found with the greatest certainty in the preceding parts, it is now easy for us to perfect those things which we investigated above in chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14 with a coarser approach. <note>original: "craſſiori Minerva," a Latin idiom meaning "with a rougher hand" or "using simpler methods."</note>

Let us begin with the Nodes. In the year 1593, on the 10th day of December at 7:00 PM, Mars was seen at 4° 44' of Taurus, with a southern latitude of 1° 15', without considering parallax; its altitude <note>Altitude here refers to height above the horizon.</note> was 35½°, which is free from refractions. After 687 days—a full revolution of **MARS**—on the 28th day of October in the year 1595 at 11:30 PM, Mars was found at an altitude of 51° in 18° 35' of Taurus, with a southern latitude of 4½', without considering parallax. And again, 687 days before [the first observation], specifically on the 23rd of January 1592 in the evening at 10:00 PM, it again had a southern latitude of 2 minutes, at an altitude of 25 degrees. Finally, subtracting another 687 days so that we arrive at the 7th of March in the year 1590: on the 4th day of March at 7:00 PM, at an altitude of 14 degrees, Mars was seen to have a southern latitude of 3' 20". This would have appeared greater, had not Mars appeared too high due to refraction at this low altitude. <note>Atmospheric refraction bends light, making objects near the horizon appear higher than they actually are. This can distort measurements of latitude.</note> For the refraction at this altitude is 3½ minutes; of which about 2 minutes apply to the latitude, so that the observed southern latitude would have been 5'. Since, however, we are anticipating the day corresponding to the others by three days, in this space of time—moving toward the Node by 1½ degrees—three minutes are worn away from the inclination. When these are converted into latitude, they produce a little bit less, so that for the 7th of March there remain 2½ minutes of latitude, and perhaps a little less if the refraction were smaller, for its quantity is not entirely constant.

Let the latitude in the year 1590 be 1 minute; in 1592, 1½ minutes; in 1593, 2½ minutes; and in 1595 at 6:00 PM, 4½ minutes—even if we admit an error of one minute in the opposite directions here and there. From these latitudes, an inclination of 1½ minutes will be shown to us, which can correspond to about 40 minutes of distance from the Node. This is for the sake of agreement only.

But we shall achieve what we want more accurately through the year 1595. For since on October 28 at 12:00 PM the southern latitude was 4½', and on the following November 3rd, at the same hour (six days later), the latitude was 19' 45" North. Therefore, in six days, the latitude changed by 24 minutes; thus, it changed by 4 minutes daily. And since on October 28 at 12:00 PM the eccentric position <note>The position of the planet on its own orbital path, rather than as seen from Earth.</note> was 16° 8½' of Taurus, and the remaining 4½ minutes of latitude are completed in one day and an eighth part, after which time 31 minutes [of longitude] are added to **MARS**: Therefore, the Node will be at 16° 45½' of Taurus at the beginning of November, 1595.

Observations concerning the other node were not so frequent.

<summary>Kepler calculates the precise location of Mars's orbital node (16° 45½' Taurus) by comparing observations separated by Mars's 687-day orbital period, accounting for atmospheric refraction.</summary>

# CHAPTER LXII.
## Examination of the inclination of the planes.

**I**N THE YEAR 1593, on August 25, at 17 hours 27 minutes, Mars was seen in <term>opposition</term> to the Sun <note>The "acronychal" position, where Earth is directly between the Sun and Mars.</note> at 12° 16' of Pisces. On the 23rd, the latitude was 6° 7' 30''. On the 24th, it was 6° 5' 30''. On the 29th, it was 5° 52' 15''. Therefore, over five days, the latitude decreased by 13' 15''. But in the single day before the opposition, it decreased by 2'. According to this analogy, if the latitude at the day and hour of opposition is set at 6° 2' 30'', there will not be an error of even half a minute.

These latitudes were observed at an altitude for Mars of 22 degrees, which is now considered to free the fixed stars from refraction. <note>Kepler is noting that at this height above the horizon, the bending of light by the atmosphere—refraction—is negligible enough not to skew the data.</note> Since, therefore, the <term>equated anomaly</term> was 166° 36', the distance of Mars from the Sun was 138,556 units, and the Earth from the Sun was 100,666 units. From this, in the diagram of chapter 14, if **A** is the *Sun*, **B** is *Earth*, **C** is *Mars*, and **AB** is 100,666, **AC** is 138,556, and angle **EBC** is 6° 2' 30'', then **BAC**, the declination of the orbit from the ecliptic at this location, is calculated to be 1° 37' 22''. And since the node is at 16° 43' of Taurus, I subtract 12° 16' of Pisces from this. <note>original: "hinc aufero 12. 16'. x." Kepler is calculating the angular distance along the zodiac between the planet and its node.</note> An arc of 64° 27' remains. And as the sine of that arc is to this inclination of 1° 39' 22'', so the whole sine is to the inclination of 1° 50' 10'' at the Southern limit.

But because this location is a little further away from the limit, so that every handle for suspicion may be cut off; come, let us consult observations outside the acronychal position, where Mars is closer to the limit. By this labor, I will also simultaneously provide a demonstration of the proportion that exists between the inclination and the seen latitude, more universally. In the year 1593, July 21, at 14 hours astronomically, the planet was seen at 17° 45 ¾' of Pisces, with a Southern latitude of 5° 46 ¼'. At this hour, the eccentric position of Mars is found to be 28° 1 ½' of Aquarius, and the position of the Sun is 8° 26' of Leo.

</margin>

*In the present diagram, let* **EA** *be at* 8° 26' Leo, *and* **KA** *at* 28° 1 ½' Aquarius. *The angle* **EAK**, *of true <term>commutation</term>, will be* 11° 35 ½'. <note>The "angle of commutation" is the angle at the Sun between the Earth and the planet.</note> *Let* **EK** *also be at* 17° 45 ¾' Pisces. *I say that, as the sine of* **AEK** *is to the sine of* **EAK**, *so is the sine of the inclination of* **K** *itself to the sine of its seen latitude. For let the inclination of* **K** *itself be understood as a straight line dropped from the body of the Planet perpendicularly into the ecliptic. It will be, therefore, as the distance* **EK** *is to the distance* **AK**, *so is the sine of the appearance of line* **K** *from* **A**, *to the sine of the appearance of the same from* **E**. *But as the sine of* **EAK** *is to the sine of* **AEK**, *so is the distance* **EK** *to the distance* **AK**. *Therefore, as the sine of* **EAK** *is to the sine of* **AEK**, *so is the sine of the appearance of line* **K** *from* **A**, *to the sine of the appearance of the same from* **E**.*

*The minor point is known from the doctrine of Triangles, and specifically from Number XIV of the third book of* LANDSBERG'S *Triangles.* <note>Philippe van Lansberge (1561–1632) was a Dutch astronomer whose works on trigonometry were standard references for Kepler.</note> *The major point requires proof.*

<margin>
<note>Geometric diagram showing the relationship between sines and distances with points v, p, q, m, l, r, n, o</note>
</margin>

*Let there be a straight line* VO, *from two points of which,* P *and* M, *two perpendicular and equal lines are raised,* PQ *and* ML. *And let the endpoints,* Q *and* L, *be connected with the point of the line* VO, *which is* O. *With center* O *and distance* OL, *let an arc be drawn, cutting* QO *at* N. *And from* N, *let a perpendicular* NR *be dropped onto* VO. *It will therefore be that as* PQ *is to* QO, *so* RN *is to* NO. *But* ML *is equal to* PQ. *Therefore, as* ML *is to* QO, *so* RN *is to* LO. *Now,* ML *is the sine of angle* LOM, *by which the quantity* PQ *or* LM *is viewed from nearby, so that* LO, *which is the shorter distance of the endpoint* L, *is the* <term>total sine</term> <note>original: "sinus totus"; in historical trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle used to calculate the sine table, here acting as a reference value.</note>. QO *is indeed the longer distance of the quantity* ML, *or rather the endpoint* Q *of* PQ. *And* RN *is the sine of angle* NOR, *by which* LM *or* PQ *is viewed from further away, so that again* NO—*that is,* LO—*is the total sine. Therefore, as the sine of the appearance from nearby is to the longer distance, so the sine of the appearance from far away is to the shorter distance. And by permutation and conversion: as the shorter distance is to the longer, so the sine of the appearance from far away is to the sine of the appearance from nearby. And in the present business, and thus universally: as the distance of Mars from the Earth is to its distance from the Sun, so is the sine of the latitude to the sine of the inclination of the planes. And conversely, as the distance from the Sun is to the distance from the Earth, so is the inclination to the latitude. Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Since these things are certain, and since the line marked by* $\kappa$ <note>Referring to a specific point in a diagram from a previous chapter.</note> *appeared from Earth at* 5° 46 ½', *by multiplying this sine by the sine of* EAK, *and dividing the product by the sine of* AEK, *there results the sine* 3188, *the arc of which is* 1° 49' 37''. *And this is the inclination of that point* $\kappa$, *as it would appear from the Sun. But since Mars is at 20° 1 ½' of Pisces, the <term>Node</term> is at 16° 43' of Aries, and thus the elongation of Mars from the Node is 86° 42': As the sine of this elongation is to the total sine, so the sine of 1° 49' 37'' is to the sine of the maximum inclination, 3200. Therefore, this again comes out as before to be 1° 50' 2'' to the South.*

*For the Northern inclination in the year 1585, on the 31st day of January following midnight, at an altitude for Mars of 53°, the already decreasing Northern latitude of Mars was 4° 31'. The true <term>opposition</term> <note>When Mars and the Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth.</note> occurred 16 hours earlier, at 21° 36 ½' of Leo. It is then consistent that the latitude was 4° 31' 10''. Since the complement of the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance from the planet's furthest point from the Sun, adjusted for the orbit's eccentricity.</note> of Mars was 7° 6' 23'', its distance from the Sun was 166,334, and the distance of the Sun from the Earth was 98,724.*

This, being subtracted from* EBC, *leaves* BAC *as 1° 50' 20''. But because we are 5 degrees away from the <term>limit</term> <note>The point of maximum latitude.</note>, the inclination of the limit will therefore be about 2'' seconds greater, namely 1° 50' 45''. The mean of these is 1° 50' 25'', a most exact inclination, which was also found above in Chapter XIV through various methods and operations, which I wish to be repeated here.*

In the first case, the observation for that specific day was missing, as you saw in Chapter 15. In the second, there was an uncertainty of three <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupulorum"; Kepler uses this term for minutes of arc ($1/60$th of a degree).</note> in the observation, because they sometimes used a polar altitude of $34^\circ 7'$, when it was actually $34^\circ 5 \frac{1}{2}'$. The third case serves as our foundational reference. The fourth agrees perfectly, provided you ignore <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations.</note>, by which the observed latitude is incorrectly adjusted to $3^\circ 41'$, as you saw in Chapter 15. In the fifth, we are missing 2 minutes; these are likely in excess in the observation due to <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light through the atmosphere, which is stronger when a planet is low on the horizon.</note>, because Mars was no higher than $22 \frac{1}{2}$ degrees, as recorded in Chapter 15. In the sixth, you may recognize a small deficit of about two minutes. However, one should not place too much trust in the exact quantity of refraction; for what if it were two minutes greater? The seventh was again a foundational reference for us. The eighth undoubtedly had a faulty declination, because at the 8th hour, Mars was not on the Meridian. Armillary spheres, with which declination is observed outside the Meridian, are more prone to error than <term>Quadrants</term> <note>An instrument used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies.</note>. However, the analogy of the surrounding days (as seen in Chapter 15) shows the latitude to have been $0^\circ 50'$ North, just as we calculated. The ninth observation is not worthy of trust. However, the calculation for December 10th, accurately examined, almost reaches the latitude of $3^\circ 23'$ observed by **FABRICIUS** <note>David Fabricius (1564–1617), a German astronomer and correspondent of Kepler.</note>; it gives $3^\circ 21 \frac{1}{2}'$ North. The tenth comes very close to the calculation. The eleventh, once refraction is excluded, corresponds perfectly. The twelfth is barely 2 minutes greater than the calculation. I believe this is because there is that much error in my own instruments; for in my one-and-a-half-foot quadrant, two minutes are not easily discerned. 

We therefore hold the <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: "acronychias"; refers to the position of a planet when it is exactly opposite the Sun in the sky.</note> latitudes with sufficient precision throughout the entire circuit of the orbit, based on this inclination of $1^\circ 50' 30''$. 
I leave the examination of the remaining latitudes—those found frequently in this book from observations outside the acronychal position—to more diligent researchers.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER LXIII.</margin>

**I**t was stated in Chapter 57 that if the diameter of the body or globe of Mars is assumed to possess a magnetic force, and to be extended toward the mean longitudes <note>Kepler refers here to the line of apsides, the long axis of the orbital ellipse</note>, and is held in that position parallel to itself throughout its entire circuit, the physical hypothesis of eccentricity would be complete.

This assumption is all the more probable because now the explanation of latitude is also settled by an entirely similar speculation: if indeed a certain diameter of latitude is assumed in the body or globe of Mars, which is extended toward the location of the limits <note>The "limits" are the points of maximum northern and southern latitude, 90 degrees from the nodes</note> among the fixed stars, and remains parallel to itself in this position throughout the entire circuit. The ratio of this power to the former is the same as that found in our magnets, between the direction toward the pole and the attractive force for iron.

For that former force seeks or flees the Sun; this one <note>the force governing latitude</note> does not seek those places under the fixed stars where the limits of latitudes are achieved by sailing toward them or fleeing them (just as a magnet does not swim toward the region of the pole, even if it floats freely), but it is merely directed toward those places, as a magnet is directed toward the pole.

Indeed, the excursion of the planet from the plane of the ecliptic toward either side follows this direction, toward which this axis of inclination is directed by the part which leads in the motion of the body. Let <term>CBAD</term> <gloss>the ecliptic</gloss>, <term>A.C.</term> be the Nodes, and <term>B.D.</term> the limits. Let the axis of latitudes in the body of the planet be <term>GNH</term>, <term>EAF</term>, <term>LOM</term>, <term>ICK</term>.

Since we assume, therefore, that this axis remains parallel to itself throughout the entire circuit, it will happen that when the body is moved from the ascending Node <term>c</term> to the Northern limit <term>B</term>, this axis of the body <term>IK</term>—which at the beginning and in the Node <term>c</term> was, as it were, touching the circle of the circuit imagined through <term>CNAO</term>—finally at the limits <term>N. O.</term> cuts the same at right angles, pointing toward the center of the world <term>s</term>, that is, toward the Sun. And that which hitherto, because of some declination from the royal road <note>original: "itinere regio"; Kepler uses this term to refer to the Sun's path or the ecliptic</note> <term>CBA</term>, had enticed the body of the planet so that it would rush out in the same direction, namely into the region <term>N</term>, toward which it had turned its leading part <term>K</term>; now at the limits, although it remains inclined to the plane of the ecliptic <term>CBS</term> (for we said that in every position it remains parallel to itself; thus, once inclined to the plane of the ecliptic, it will always be inclined), yet from the royal road itself, that is, from the circumference of that plane <term>CBAD</term>, it no longer declines when situated at <term>G H</term>. For it nods neither forward toward <term>A</term>, nor backward toward <term>c</term>; it only nods away to the side, or toward the pole, in a direction where it has no path. Therefore, as the planet is moved beyond <term>B</term>, now the other part of the axis <term>G</term>, which turns toward the South, leads the way, and in that manner leads the planet from the maximum Northern inclination <term>N</term>, through the descending Node <term>A</term>, to the maximum Southern inclination <term>O</term>.

And this axis of inclination is a kind of oar: for what sailors achieve with oars to cross from one bank to another, this the planet achieves through this axis of inclination, crossing from the North to the

# PART FIVE

...and in turn, by the flow—that is, the immaterial species <note>Kepler’s term for the radiating power of the Sun that moves the planets</note> of the Sun—moving along the straight path CBAD.

<margin>CHAPTER LXIII.</margin>

As far as the geometric dimension is concerned, words are hardly necessary. A straight line, moved parallel to itself along a straight path, creates a plane by its motion. This axis itself is a straight line, and in whatever direction it inclines—*noting that "inclining" presupposes a straight path*—it is carried along that way. Therefore, it describes a plane. If this plane is extended, it cuts the sphere of the Fixed Stars in the form of a great circle, as seen in the diagram of Chapter 13, FEGH: because it cuts the plane of the ecliptic DG at the center of the world, or of the Sun, A. To be more certain of this, consider that the intersections or Nodes, as you see in the diagram, are in positions opposite one another from the center of the Sun A, as experience testifies (see Chapter 62).

Therefore, since there is a plane that is traversed by the orbit of Mars, its inclination to the plane of the regular ecliptic will be regular. For if two equal circles are drawn—one, DC, in the plane of the ecliptic, and the other, FE, in the plane of the orbit of Mars—from the common center A of the Sun (that is, in one and the same sphere of the Fixed Stars, concentric with the Sun): then as the sine BD of the arc between the intersection of the circles and any point of the circle of Mars (say D) is to the total sine <note>original: "sinum totum"; in historical trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle, usually set to 1 or 100,000</note>, so the sine of the inclination DF of point F is to the sine CE, of the maximum inclination, at the Limit E. It was proven in Chapter 14, through the ingenious treatment of observations, that the declinations of all points of the circuit from the plane of the ecliptic are indeed ordered by this same measure. Thus, no objection can be raised against our hypothesis.

FURTHERMORE, two difficult questions must be resolved. One concerns the condition of this inclination of the axis; the other concerns the axis itself. It is asked, first: is this inclination of the axis natural or rational—is it the work of a corporeal nature or of an angel? Second: is this axis of inclination numerically the same as the magnetic axis that seeks the Sun? And if they are different, how do they exist in the same spherical body of the planet? These two questions are intertwined.

I would have almost believed it to be NATURAL, because of the similarity of its power to that which is natural in the Magnet itself: were it not for the subsequent transposition of the Nodes <note>the gradual movement of the points where the orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, which seems entirely to be the work of reason—if not discursive <note>reasoning step-by-step</note>, then certainly instinctive. For remaining in a parallel position is less strange, and closer to Nature, than what we previously saw in the matter of eccentricity. There, we said the Sun was sought by the "virtuous" axis; here, the axis seeks a location under the furthest distant Fixed Stars. There, by the force of this magnetic power, the axis would have had to be turned as the body was carried around, and would not have remained parallel to itself unless it were held back by an animal force <note>an "anima" or soul-like vital force</note>, whether bare or in some way capable of reason. Here, by the force of our directing power itself, that parallelism of the axis follows without any necessity of animal or reasoning force. Unless, perhaps, someone also attributes this to a mind: that this diameter, which effects the latitudes when the planet is at the limits...

By this argument I also asserted above, in Chapter 39, the Planet’s orientation toward the Sun. Yet not every orientation toward the Sun proves a concomitant reason <note>Kepler uses "reason" or "mind" here to mean a conscious, soul-like guiding force, rather than just a blind physical law.</note>. It is certainly true that he who first arranged the celestial motions directed this axis in such a way that it would look toward the Sun (in the stated position); and therefore he used counsel and the highest reason. And yet I would judge both to be joined, rather than positing the rational force alone. Let the magnetic force obey; let reason preside, governing it, as we also stated before in Chapter 57 regarding the seeking power of the Sun.

This question being thus dispatched, another follows. For if this directing power is from magnetic, corporeal, and natural forces, its subject will be a body. <margin>
Principle <note>original Greek: "Θεμις" (Themis). Used here to denote a fundamental law or "the right way" to understand the geometry.</note>: It is one thing, the diameter which causes eccentricity; another, the <term>libratory diameter<note>An imaginary axis used to calculate the "back and forth" or "up and down" swinging motion of the planet's latitude.</note></term>. The former is something real; the latter is imaginary, for the sake of visualizing its effect. Wherever the former stands, it is extended perpendicularly to the line of apsides, or into the place of mean longitudes under the Fixed Stars; the latter, as was said in Chapter 39, is always extended into the body of the Sun itself.
</margin>

For it was said in Chapter 58 that the diameter which causes eccentricity is extended toward the mean longitudes; but it has now been said that the diameter which causes latitude is extended toward the limits <note>The points of maximum distance from the ecliptic.</note>. Therefore, if the limits were joined to the mean longitudes, each diameter would be extended to the same place; and so they would coincide in location, and nothing would prevent them from being the same thing. But the Nodes, or the true intersections of the ecliptic, do not meet in the apsides. In *Mars*, the northern limit is 12 degrees before the aphelion; in *Jupiter*, the northern limit and the aphelion precisely coincide; in *Saturn*, the Node follows the aphelion by 24 degrees; in the *Moon*, because of the brevity of its circuits, all things are exchanged with all things. For the Node is sometimes at the apogee, sometimes at the mean longitude, and sometimes at the perihelion. Since, therefore, these two powers differ in time and place, it follows that they are not one and the same.

Yet nothing prevents both from residing in one and the same Planetary body, as in a whole, except for the motion or rotation of the globe. Thus, if the Planets move like the Moon—which does not rotate on its own axis, but shows the same face to us from every direction—nothing prevents us from asserting that both powers are interwoven with each other, just as the <term>weft is interwoven with the warp<note>A metaphor from weaving: the "warp" are the stationary lengthwise threads, and the "weft" are the threads woven through them. Kepler is suggesting these physical forces are fundamentally entwined.</note></term>. For then the whole...

### PART FIVE

with the body of the Planet maintaining the same position with respect to the Fixed Stars while it is carried around the Sun, all the straight-line segments within it, including those two diameters, will maintain that same orientation toward the Fixed Stars. However, if we are dealing with the globe of the Earth—which, besides being carried around in its annual period, is also rotated every single day—then we are left in great doubt, no less than we were above in Chapter 57. For if a body is rotated, only one single "effective" diameter, which is parallel to the axis of the rotational motion, remains constant and equidistant to itself. Even if you were to say that another diameter is woven into the first to cause the latitudes—a power of a different kind—that diameter would observe the same regions as the axis of rotation; for it describes a cone around that axis, passing through every one of its regions. Thus, by nodding now to the right and now to the left, it eventually brings the body into a middle region, which the axis of conversion faces.

</margin>
Therefore, if the globe rotates, then the subject of this <term>declinatory virtue<note>The physical power or "quality" that causes the planet's orbit to tilt or deviate from the main path.</note></term> is either not a body but something spiritual, or it is not the same body. If it is something spiritual, how does it preserve the regions of the world, which is a material thing? And how does it introduce this kind of motion (a deviation from the <term>royal road<note>original: "via regia"; the ecliptic or the main path of the Sun's apparent motion.</note></term>) into a physical body? Is it perhaps easier for a body to be tilted and to exit the "royal road" (while having an external cause for its translation from the Sun) than it is to be moved from place to place by the force of its own mover? If instead we prefer a physical subject, something mechanical will be born for us, similar to those spherical lamps which, even when thrown and rolled about, do not spill their oil. For a vessel is enclosed within them which, being pulled downward by a weighted bottom and thus held in place, does not follow the rolling motion of the sphere surrounding it.

Could there then be some interior globe within this globe of the Earth, into which the daily motion of the outer Earth does not penetrate, but which is held by a very strong inclination toward certain places of the Fixed Stars, so that it does not follow the rotated outer body? For we shall hear in Chapter 68 that this question also pertains to the Earth; where we shall also see whether, by proposing some mean <term>ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun through the stars; the reference plane for planetary latitudes.</note></term> for the six Planets, it might be possible (as we required a little earlier) for the nodes of each to coincide with their own <term>apsides<note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest to or farthest from the Sun.</note></term>.

Or is it rather to be believed that there can be certain modes of celestial motions which, although they themselves are corporeal like <term>magnetic virtues<note>Kepler’s theory that planets act like giant magnets to maintain their orientation.</note></term>, can nevertheless be understood by no one on Earth due to a lack of examples? Just as if we lacked the example of the magnet—as it was once unknown—we would be ignorant of many of the causes of celestial motions.

Those who defend <term>solid spheres<note>The traditional Aristotelian view that planets are carried by physical, transparent crystal shells.</note></term> easily explain everything according to what was said in Chapter 13. For they will assign an inclination to the plane of the <term>eccentric of Mars<note>The off-center circular path Mars was thought to follow in older models.</note></term> F E relative to the plane of the ecliptic D C—not a swinging one, but a fixed and constant one—resting on the diameter of the intersection B A, drawn through the center of the world A (<term>BRAHE<note>Referring to Tycho Brahe, whose observations Kepler was analyzing.</note></term> places it through the center of the Sun). This intersection, they will say, is rotated around that center A beneath the ecliptic D C over the course of centuries.

# CHAPTER LXIV.
## ->Investigation of the parallaxes of Mars through latitudes.<-

THEREFORE, in Chapter 61, both <term>Nodes<note>The two points where a planet’s tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note></term> were found in precisely opposite locations with a wonderful consensus—one that excludes all <term>parallax<note>The apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations; Kepler is arguing that Mars is so far away that this shift is too small to measure with his tools.</note></term>.
        For let us suppose that the parallax of Mars were at least 2 and 1 minutes when it was at <term>opposition<note>original: "opposito Solis"; when Mars is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, making it closest to us.</note></term> to the Sun and thus closer to the Earth than to the Sun; the first time being in the year 1595, when it was about 38° from the <term>zenith<note>The point directly overhead.</note></term>, and the second time in the year 1589, when it was about 66° from the zenith. Thus, in the year 1589, when it was thought to be in the Node, it would have still been nearly 2 minutes to the North; therefore, it would still have been one degree before the Node. The Node would therefore be not at 16° 46' Taurus (♉), but at 17° 46' Taurus. On the other hand, in the year 1595, it would have had 1 minute of parallax. Therefore, on the day it was thought to be in the <term>ascending node<note>The point where the planet crosses from south of the ecliptic to north.</note></term>, it would truly have already had a latitude of 1 minute. Consequently, it would already be about 36 minutes beyond the Node. The ascending node, then, would be not in 16° 46' Taurus, but in 16° 16' Taurus.
        Behold: the <term>descending node<note>The point where the planet crosses from north of the ecliptic to south.</note></term> would be at 17¾° Scorpio (♏) and the ascending node at 16¼° Taurus, if you assume even the slightest parallax. Let us conclude, therefore, along with Chapter 11, that the <term>diurnal parallax<note>The parallax caused by the Earth's rotation, changing the observer's position throughout the day.</note></term> of Mars is clearly imperceptible, provided that both observations of latitude are accurate to within 2 minutes.
        A similar argument for there being no parallax will also arise for us from the investigation of the truest inclination of the planes set forth in Chapter 62, unless <term>refraction<note>The bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, which can make stars appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note></term> should disturb anything.
        For suppose that Mars had a parallax in the year 1593 at an altitude of 22° of at least 2 minutes, but in the year 1585 at an altitude of 53° of nothing. The observed Southern latitude would therefore be smaller; thus, the inclination would also be smaller than the Northern one. But just a little while ago, it appeared smaller even without parallax—as much as can be attributed to a flaw in observation or to some refraction at an altitude of 23°. Therefore, if parallax were applied, the observation would be accused of a greater error; and conversely, if the observation stands, parallax is destroyed. This is true insofar as the orbit of Mars is arranged in a perfect plane, which plane intersects the ecliptic at the very center of the Sun.

But the same thing is proved much more certainly from the latitudes observed in the remaining <term>acronychal<note>Referring to the position of a planet when it is in opposition to the Sun, rising as the Sun sets.</note></term> positions: especially those which the conditions of the observation or <term>refraction<note>The bending of light by the Earth's atmosphere which makes celestial objects appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note></term> did not make doubtful. This began to be discussed in Chapter 15, but until now could not be completed. For in the year **1587**, when Mars was 55 degrees from the <term>zenith<note>original: "vertice"; the point directly overhead.</note></term>, if it had possessed a <term>parallax<note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations. Kepler is arguing that Mars is so distant that this shift is nearly impossible to measure.</note></term> of 4 minutes, the latitude would have been changed from 3° 37' to 3° 41'. Truly, in the year **1589**, at a distance of 64 degrees from the zenith, if the parallax of Mars (based on a horizontal solar parallax of 3 minutes) had been 5 1/2 minutes; then the Northern latitude, instead of the observed 1° 7', would have been 1° 12 1/2' when cleared of parallax. In the year **1602**, however, when using the assumed parallax, the observed latitude was found to be 4° 10'; but neglecting it, it was 4° 7 1/2': we calculated 4° 7 4/7', which is quite precise. Thus in the year **1604**, we did not entirely reach the quantity of the observed Northern latitude. Therefore, we would complain even less that it was increased by the subtraction of parallax.

By these three ways, we have proved the uncertainty of the parallax of Mars; however, we have not entirely demonstrated its total lack of perception, because the business of refraction eludes us, and sometimes observations do not descend within 2 or 3 minutes of precision. And so, if anyone wishes to assign to Mars a maximum parallax in latitude of 2 or 2 1/2 minutes, these <term>Brahean<note>Observations made by Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), whose data Kepler used to revolutionize astronomy.</note></term> observations will not strongly refute him. For the inclination will also be adjusted, and it will become 1° 51' 0".

If, however, by the opposite reasoning, the <term>apogee<note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note></term> of the Sun is joined to the <term>perihelion<note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note></term> of Mars, the maximum Northern latitude in opposition comes out to $4^\circ 44' 12''$, and in conjunction $1^\circ 9' 32''$. The Southern latitude in opposition would be $6^\circ 26' 56''$, and in conjunction $1^\circ 3' 32''$.

And these things would be so if the <term>apsides<note>The collective term for the apogee and perihelion, the far and near points of an orbit.</note></term> and the <term>limit<note>The "limit" refers to the point of maximum latitude, where the planet is furthest north or south of the ecliptic.</note></term> had been joined in former times; whether this will happen before the fall of the whole **Cosmic Machine** <note>original: "Machinæ"; Kepler views the universe as a physical, interconnected mechanism.</note> is uncertain. Certainly, **Ptolemy** attributed equal motions to the apsides and the <term>nodes<note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note></term>; if that were the case, that conjunction would never occur. And although today they seem to move at different rates, the observations of the ancients are not so certain, nor is the difference in these motions so great—even in modern astronomy—that we can conclude with absolute certainty how many tens of thousands of years separate such conjunctions of the apsides and the limits.

Let us therefore return to our own age, which extends between **us** and **Ptolemy**. But here, a manifold *impasse* <note>original: "ἀμηχανία" (amēchania); a Greek term for a state of being at a loss or facing a lack of means.</note> awaits the one seeking geometric determinations.

First, the apsides of the Sun and Mars are not joined. Second, the orbits of the planets are not perfect circles. Therefore, even if we draw a new line of apsides through the centers of the circles of Mars and the Earth (as in the diagram of Chapter 52 through $B$ and $C$), it could still happen that the greatest proximity of the celestial bodies occurs somewhere other than on this line.

Finally, even if the place of greatest proximity were established, the location of the Northern and Southern limits is different. For example, the limit is at $16^\circ 50'$ of Leo. But the straight line $BC$ projected through the centers of the circles extends into about $24 \frac{1}{2}^\circ$ of Leo and Aquarius; namely, in the same direction where the line $HF$ of his apsides is projected by **Brahe**, to which our $BC$ runs parallel, since both eccentricities are bisected—$AF$ at $C$, and $AH$ at $B$.

And I had already chosen the midpoint between $17^\circ$ Leo and $25^\circ$ Leo, specifically $21^\circ$ Leo. But the year **1585** held me back, in which year at $21^\circ 36'$ Leo the latitude observed was not quite at its maximum. For since the <term>opposition<note>When the Earth is directly between the Sun and the planet.</note></term> occurred on the night following January 30th, on the preceding 24th day the latitude was observed to be $4^\circ 31'$, having increased up to that point; but on January 31st, sixteen hours after opposition, the latitude was again seen to be $4^\circ 31'$. It appears, therefore, that if the opposition had been at that place of the <term>eccentric<note>The off-center circular path used in traditional astronomy to model planetary motion.</note></term> on the 24th day, a greater latitude than $4^\circ 31'$ would have been seen, for two reasons: first, because the star would be closer to the Earth than it is outside of the <term>acronychal<note>Referring to the position of a planet when it is in opposition to the Sun.</note></term> position; second, because Mars would have been further from its apogee and thus lower.

<summary>Kepler calculates the theoretical maximum Northern and Southern latitudes of Mars and discusses the historical difficulty in aligning the orbital apsides with the points of maximum latitude. He uses Tycho Brahe's 1585 observations to show that the planet's highest latitude does not perfectly coincide with its closest approach to Earth.</summary>

Let the maximum latitude therefore occur around 19° <term>Leo<note>The zodiac sign Leo, represented by the symbol ♌.</note></term>, where Mars was on the 24th of January. Since the complement of the <term>equated anomaly<note>The angle measuring the planet's position in its orbit, adjusted for its elliptical path.</note></term> is 18°, the distance of Mars will be 166,200, and that of the Sun 98,670. For the maximum Southern latitude, an equated anomaly of Mars of 170° gives us a distance of about 138,420; and the Sun in 19° <term>Libra<note>The zodiac sign Libra, represented by the symbol ♎.</note></term> is at a distance of 101,280. From this, the maximum Southern latitude is calculated as nearly 6° 52' 20"; which in conjunction appears as 2° 4' 20".

# CHAPTER LXVI.

->That the maximum excursions to the sides do not always occur at the opposition of the Sun.<-

Regarding the maximum latitude that can occur in any single period of Mars, defining its specific locations geometrically is a much more perplexing business. It involves that great paradox which I found emphasized in these words, written in <term>Tycho Brahe's<note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise planetary observations provided the data Kepler used to discover the laws of planetary motion.</note></term> own hand among the observations of the year 1593:

> It is worthy of consideration that Mars, around the tenth day of August, held its maximum Southern latitude; and afterwards it decreased; so that on the 24th, at opposition, it was rendered nearly a quarter of a degree closer to the <term>ecliptic<note>The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun; the "path" the Sun appears to follow through the stars.</note></term>. Yet the Tables, even with the position of maximum latitude corrected to 18° of Aquarius, do not show this at all, regardless of how the maximum latitude there is assumed. The cause of this matter must be studiously investigated.

Later, when I had come to him in Bohemia and had frequently asked about the logic of the latitudes—and he had recounted many things to me, such as that the <term>nodes<note>The two points where a planet's tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note></term> are in opposite places, and that the intersection passes through the point of the Sun's mean position, or through the center of its <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; an older astronomical concept Kepler was moving away from.</note></term> (concerning which in the following Chapter 67), and many other things—being reminded of this business by this mention, he said: "This is wonderful, that the latitudes become greatest before or after the oppositions with the Sun." Mention of this matter was also made above in Chapter 15.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS
<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

<margin>**CHAPTER LXIII.** <note>Note: The chapter numbering in the original source appears to jump back to LXIII or is a misprint for LXVII, as it follows the logic of the preceding Chapter LXVI.</note></margin>
The true hypothesis of latitude established in this fifth part certainly contains the cause of the matter; but you will not investigate the limits of the maximum latitudes geometrically any more easily than **APOLLONIUS OF PERGA** <note>A Greek geometer (c. 240–190 BCE) famous for his work on conic sections and planetary "stations."</note> investigated the limits of the stations.

<margin>*On the points of the stations.*</margin>
<margin>*On the points of the maximum latitudes.*</margin>
For just as in this business of stations, a certain mark can be described by which the location of the stations is known (this occurs when the line of sight to Mars, as the Earth moves, remains parallel to itself); yet from that mark, without a complex calculation, the location of the station cannot be demonstrated *a priori* <note>Known beforehand through theoretical reasoning rather than observation.</note> due to the confusion of many causes. So the matter also stands regarding the latitude, which is at its maximum at any given time. For then the latitude is at its maximum when the distance of Mars from the Earth increases or decreases in the same proportion as the lines of Mars's inclinations <note>The tilt of the orbital plane.</note> increase or decrease; and the latitude is increased when the proportion of the distance decreases more than the proportion of the lines of inclination, or when the latter increases while the former decreases. Conversely, the latitude is diminished either when the distance of Mars from the Earth increases more than the lines of inclination do, in their respective proportions, or when those lines are diminished while the distance increases.

These things happen indiscriminately, sometimes at <term>opposition<note>When a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note></term>, sometimes before, and sometimes after, depending on whether the opposition falls exactly on the <term>limit<note>The point of maximum orbital tilt.</note></term>, or before or after the limit.

My <term>Ephemerides<note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies.</note></term> prove that these results follow from the hypothesis of this work. In the year 1604, around February 25 or March 6, the maximum *Northern* latitude occurred, even though the opposition followed a full month later. Conversely, on September 27 or October 7, the maximum *Southern* latitude occurred while Mars was positioned between the <term>quintile<note>An aspect of 72 degrees.</note></term> and <term>sextile<note>An aspect of 60 degrees.</note></term> of the Sun. Again, at the end of the year 1605, the maximum *Northern* latitude occurred while the Sun was moving from the quintile to the <term>quadrate<note>An aspect of 90 degrees, also called a "square."</note></term> of Mars. And conversely, at the end of July in the year 1606, the maximum *Southern* latitude occurred while the Sun was in <term>trine<note>An aspect of 120 degrees.</note></term> with Mars. Indeed, in the year 1607, the maximum *Northern* latitude happened a little after the <term>conjunction<note>When Mars and the Sun are in the same direction from Earth.</note></term> of Mars with the Sun.

The **CAUSE** why these things seem strange in the old astronomy is chiefly this: that **PTOLEMY** and others who imitated him fabricated extremely intricate motions of *inclinations*, *deviations*, and *reflections*. For since **PTOLEMY** was stuck in the imagination of the <term>epicycle<note>A small circle on which a planet was thought to move, while the center of the circle moved around a larger orbit.</note></term>, as soon as he saw that at opposition with the Sun (when the planet is visible) it moves out into one region, he immediately indulged in conjecture, asserting that at conjunction with the Sun (when it is not visible) it moves out into the other region; or, in general, that it does the opposite of what he sees it doing at opposition. He did this, of course, so that there might be some compensation and equality of restoration and a coherence with the Sun. But this is not to find the truth by observing, but to fashion observations according to a falsely conceived imagination—though he is to be forgiven, as he had few observations. See also *Chapter XIV* on this matter.

But come, let us see if our calculation returns the latitude observed on the day of August 10. For we are already certain about July 21 and August 25 of that year. For the calculation presents the very same things as those observations upon which it rests.

<summary>Kepler explains that Mars reaches its maximum latitudes at varying times relative to the Sun (not just at opposition) because of the changing ratio between the planet's distance from Earth and its orbital inclination. He critiques Ptolemy for inventing complex orbital mechanics like epicycles to force a symmetry that does not exist in nature.</summary>

Therefore, the hypothesis established in this work provides this very thing; the cause of which **BRAHE** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the preeminent observational astronomer whose data Kepler used</note> had warned should be diligently investigated, and which **ancient astronomy** <note>Kepler refers here to the geocentric system of Ptolemy, which relied on complex secondary circles called epicycles</note> with so much apparatus cannot provide. It provides this, I say, by its own simplicity, while a constant inclination or obliquity is given to the plane of the eccentric, and that tilt is variously increased or decreased: not in reality, but by **optical reasoning** <note>Kepler argues that the "wobble" in planetary tilt observed by earlier astronomers was actually a perspective shift caused by the Earth's own motion</note>, according as our sight approaches it or recedes from it—whereas in Brahe and Ptolemy, that tilt itself was moved toward or away from our sight.

### CHAPTER LXVII.

# It is demonstrated from the locations of the **Nodes** <term>the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>, and the inclination of the planes of **MARS** and the **ecliptic**, that the **eccentricity** of **MARS** arises not from the point of the **mean position of the SUN** <note>An imaginary point representing the average position of the Sun if its motion were perfectly uniform</note> (or in **BRAHE'S** case, from the center of the Sun's **epicycle**) but from the **center of the SUN itself**.

<summary>Kepler uses specific observational data to demonstrate that his model of a fixed orbital tilt for Mars accurately predicts its apparent latitude. <margin>
CHAPTER LXVII.
</margin>

**T**HE final conclusions correspond with the first principles. I argued in the sixth chapter on Physics that, since solid orbs are rejected <note>Kepler believed planets moved through fluid space, not on physical crystal spheres as ancient astronomers thought</note>, the **eccentricities** <term>the amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term> of the Planets cannot arise from any point other than the very center of the Sun. I postponed the geometric demonstration of this matter, derived from observations, partly to chapters XXII, XXIII, and LII—at which places I believe I have satisfied even the most eagle-eyed readers—and I shall now settle the rest of it. First, by the locations of the **Nodes** <term>the two points where a planet's orbital path crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit</term>. It was demonstrated in Chapter LXI that once the eccentricity of Mars is constructed from the center of the Sun itself—or, what is the same thing, using **acronychal observations** <term>observations made when the planet is exactly opposite the Sun in the sky, which eliminates the distortion of the Earth's own movement</term> taken from the opposition of the Planet with the apparent position of the Sun—the Nodes fall into parts exactly opposite from the center of the Sun; that is, the **diameter of the apsides** <term>the line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit</term> and the diameter of the intersection of the planes of the ecliptic and Mars <note>the line of nodes</note> meet, or cut each other, at that same center from which the eccentricity is calculated: namely, in the center of the Sun.

The question is, if we use the **mean motion** <term>the idealized, perfectly circular average motion of the Sun/Earth</term> for the apparent motion of the Sun, will the Nodes still be in opposite locations relative to the point from which eccentricity is calculated? Not at all. *Let the Copernican diagram of Chapter VI be repeated. In it, let κδ be the line of limits <note>the line connecting the points of maximum latitude</note>, at 16 ½° of Leo and Aquarius <note>original symbols: ♌ and ♒</note> (not, as in Chapter VI, the line of apsides in 29° Leo). Therefore, the line perpendicular to κδ from κ will be the diameter of the Nodes. However, if we use the mean motion instead of the apparent motion of the Sun, then instead of κ we are given β, from which eccentricity is calculated. Therefore, from β, the perpendicular to κδ, which is βζ, will fall in locations exactly opposite from β, but it will not fall in the locations of the Nodes; because the former perpendicular through κ falls in the locations of the Nodes, which is higher than βζ by the distance κβ.*

<summary>Kepler uses the geometric alignment of the orbital Nodes to prove that planetary eccentricity must be measured from the physical center of the Sun rather than the mathematical 'mean Sun'. This further reinforces his shift from purely mathematical models to a physics-based astronomy.</summary>
