*It is helpful to investigate how great the angles at the circumference of the **eccentric** <term>the circular path of a planet which is off-center relative to the Sun</term> will be, when point x is connected with the intersection of the line $\beta$ s and the circumference of the eccentric. Since s is at 16° 45' of Scorpio by assumption, and $\beta$ is at approximately 5° 45' of Scorpio: the angle $\beta$ x s will be 41°. And since the angle $\beta$ s x is a right angle, x $\beta$ s will be 49°. And since x $\beta$ is the eccentricity of the Sun, 3600, where the orbit of the Earth or Sun is 100,000; just as the total sine of angle s is to $\beta$ x (3600), so the sine of angle $\beta$ is to x s (2717). In that same measurement, where the radius of the Earth's orbit is 100,000, the radius of the orbit of* Mars *is 152,350 according to Chapter LIV. Therefore, where the radius of the orbit of* Mars *is 100,000, x s will be 1790, which shows an angle of 1° 1' 33" in the sines.*

*Therefore, the **ascending Node** <term>the point where the planet crosses the ecliptic moving north</term> ought to have been that many degrees and minutes in a more forward position, and the descending node in a more rearward position, if I had wrongly chosen x, the center of the Sun, instead of the **PTOLEMAIC, COPERNICAN, or BRAHEAN** point $\beta$. Conversely, when observations are weighed according to the mean motion of the Sun, and thus point $\beta$ is assumed—if this were wrong and x should have been chosen—the ascending Node must be found in a more rearward position from $\beta$, and the descending node in a more forward one, such that the Northern semicircle is shortened by an arc of 2° 3' 6".* <note>Kepler is showing that if you use the old "mean Sun" model, the math for where the planet crosses the Earth's orbital plane doesn't match the physical reality of where the planet actually is.</note>

*Let us see if this actually happens. In Chapter XII, having weighed the observations roughly, it was thought that* Mars *was in the Node on October 28, 1595. Then the eccentric position was found, from the **BRAHEAN** equations which rely on point $\beta$, to be at 16° 48' 8" [of Scorpio]. Similarly, on the morning of May 9, 1589, we supposed* Mars *to have been in the other, descending Node. We then computed the eccentric position of* Mars *from those same **BRAHEAN** equations as 15° 44.5' ... It follows, therefore, exactly as was said it should. It is 1 degree and 3.5 minutes less in the Northern semicircle. But if the observations are inspected more accurately, as in Chapter LXI,* Mars *reaches the ascending Node one day and 15 hours later. Therefore, about 50 minutes are added to the eccentric position, so that the Planet falls at 17° 38' 8" in eccentric motion. Therefore, the shortening of the upper semicircle is 1° 53.5', which is very nearly equal to the calculated 2° 3'.*

*Thus point x stands firm in every way, and $\beta$ is rejected. For why should the diameter of the intersection of the planes not cut the diameter of the **apsides** <term>the line of the orbit's long axis</term> at the center, from which the eccentricity arises, just as above? What would be the cause of such a thing?*

*The same things are also demonstrated through the inclination of the planes demonstrated in Chapter LXII, and through the diagram in Chapter XX. The inclination found there—that is, the angle* lab, *by which the deviation of the Northern limit from the ecliptic is viewed from the* Sun (A)—*was 1° 56' 45". However, the angle* mad, *by which the deviation of the Southern limit from the ecliptic is viewed from the* Sun (A), *was found to be nearly equal to it, namely 1° 56' 8". From which it was concluded that, since the angles at* A *above and below are equal, and the line drawn through* A *to the locations of the ecliptic limits* B.D. *is a single line (because it is in the single plane of the ecliptic); therefore, the other line, cast from* A *to the limits themselves at* L.M., *is also a single line. And thus, that which is contained under the orbit of* Mars *is a single plane. But if* <note>Kepler's geometric logic here is that the orbit of Mars is a perfectly flat plane that passes directly through the physical body of the Sun, rather than being "wobbled" or centered on an empty mathematical point.</note>

# CHAPTER LXVIII.

## Whether the inclinations of the planes of Mars and the ecliptic are the same in this our age as in the age of PTOLEMY.
## Concerning the latitudes of the ecliptic, and the unequal circuit of the Nodes.

<margin>On the changed latitude of the Fixed Stars.</margin>
**I**t was stated in Chapter 14 that in any single period of Mars, the obliquity or inclination of the Martian plane to the plane of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> remains fixed. However, a doubt arises as to whether this obliquity is the same and fixed in all centuries. The cause of the doubt is this:

**BRAHE** demonstrated in the first volume of his *Progymnasmata* <note>original: "Progymnasmatum"; Tycho Brahe's "Introductory Exercises," a foundational astronomical text published posthumously in 1602.</note> on page 233 that the latitudes of the fixed stars today are different than they were in the time of **PTOLEMY**. The difference is that Northern stars near the summer solstice have increased their latitudes, while Southern ones have decreased them. Conversely, near the winter solstice, Northern stars have decreased their latitudes, while Southern stars have increased them. Moving from these boundaries toward the equinoctial points, the variation in latitude happens to be less, and thus near the equinoctial points themselves, there is almost none at all. We shall adapt this experience of our time to our principles established in Chapter 63.

It is well established that the sphere of the Fixed Stars is raised by an immense interval above the planets; therefore, it is fitting that it be free from those motions which are inherent to the planets. **COPERNICUS** simply assumes that the Fixed Stars are entirely...

# CHAPTER LXVIII.

<margin>What is the Ecliptic?</margin>
However, since the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year. In the Copernican system, this is actually the path of the Earth orbiting the Sun.</note> is the greatest circle in the sphere of the Fixed Stars, under which the Sun constantly appears to us from Earth, and which it seems to traverse annually: whether that motion belongs to the Sun or to the Earth, it belongs to one of the Planets in either case. Thus, the Fixed Stars do not contain the cause of the ecliptic within themselves, but it exists only because of the annual motion of either the Sun or the Earth around the center of the World.

<margin>The Ecliptic is transposed to other Fixed Stars.</margin>
And since it is found that the ecliptic has changed its position under the Fixed Stars: it is therefore not the Fixed Stars that have withdrawn from the ecliptic, but the ecliptic that has withdrawn from the Stars.

<margin>The cause of the changed ecliptic.</margin>
The cause of this shift is undoubtedly provided by our principles in Chapter 72, provided they are sound. For since the Sun, by its most rapid rotation within its own space—which for **COPERNICUS** is the center of the World—stirs the Planets by an <term>emitted species</term><note>Kepler's term for a physical force or influence radiating from the Sun that pushes the planets along their orbits.</note>, there will be certain poles of this rotation. In the last diagram of 
<margin>That there is some mean ecliptic.</margin>
Chapter 63, let the body of the Sun be **IO**, and the poles of its conversion be **A** and **E**. Corresponding to these in the Sphere of the Fixed Stars are the points **f** and **G**. Therefore, the greatest circle of the rotating Solar body **IO** will be aligned under some greatest circle of the Fixed Stars, which is **ML**. Since this is undoubtedly one and the same under the constant Fixed poles **F** and **G**, as required by the dignity of that body which first imparts motion to the others: the Planets are nevertheless found to traverse different circles inclined toward one another, according to those principles of nature explained in Chapter 63. Doubtless, therefore, the different circles of all the Planets respect this <term>Royal Circle</term><note>original: *circulum Regium*. This refers to the plane of the Sun’s equator, which Kepler sees as the governing "royal" reference for the entire solar system.</note> **ML**, described by the rotation of the Solar body around its axis **AE**: and yet each will maintain an inclination of a constant quantity; though it is subject to shifting, because we observe that the <term>Nodes</term><note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> are transferred.

Since, therefore, the ecliptic is also one of the planetary circles (namely, that of the Sun or the Earth), it is consistent that it too has a certain inclination to the Royal Circle **ML**, described among the Fixed Stars by the greatest circle of the Solar body **IO**. For what reason would there be why the other Planets should each decline from it differently, while only the ecliptic—standing over the Solar or Terrestrial path—should coincide precisely with this Royal Circle **ML**?

<margin>From the hypothesis of a mutable ecliptic follows every variety detected in the nutation of the latitude of the Fixed Stars.</margin>
Let it be granted, then, that the ecliptic properly so-called is inclined to that Royal Solar circle; and let it be represented to us by the circle **KH** drawn among the Fixed Stars; and let its poles be **B** and **C**. Having obtained these points, we easily find the occasion by which the latitudes of the Fixed Stars are changed; for these, by the very definition of the word, are calculated from the true ecliptic itself, and not from that Royal Solar circle, which has been hidden until now. For the ecliptic truly and properly so-called (because eclipses only happen under that line along which the Sun moves) will have its intersections or common Nodes with that circle **ML**—which we might call the <term>mean ecliptic</term>—transferred no less than the Nodes of the other Planets. Yet the maximum obliquity **MK** or **LH**, which is measured by the distance of the poles **FB** and **GC**, remains constant and fixed, as it does in the other Planets. *Namely, if with centers f and G, and the distances FB and GC remaining constant, the circle...*

Over the course of centuries, this will cause the <term>limit</term><note>The "limit" refers to the point of maximum latitude or tilt—the "peak" of the orbital curve.</note> of northern latitude to eventually be placed near the same Fixed Stars where the southern limit once was. In a shorter span of centuries, it will be thus: the limits **K** and **H**, having moved not far from their Fixed Stars, will change the stars' latitudes by an imperceptible amount. However, the <term>nodes</term><note>The nodes are the two points where the Earth's orbital plane intersects the reference plane (the "mean ecliptic").</note>, moving by an equal journey from their Fixed Stars, will change the latitudes of those stars more evidently. This is because the <term>sines of the inclinations</term><note>Kepler is explaining a trigonometric property: near the peak of a curve (the limit), the vertical change is very slow; near the crossing point (the node), the vertical change is very rapid.</note> increase by an imperceptible difference at the end of a quadrant (near the limit), but by a very noticeable difference at the beginning (near the nodes).

<margin>
Where the true
and mean
ecliptics
intersect.
</margin>
Since no change in the latitudes of the Fixed Stars is perceived near the equinoxes, but a quite notable change is seen near the solstices, we correctly gather that the limits of the ecliptic's latitudes are near the equinoxes, and the nodes are near the solstices. Therefore, the points **K** and **H** will be signs near the equinoxes. Similarly, we may also gather this: since the northern part of the true ecliptic moves away from the North—as the northern latitudes in Gemini and Cancer are increasing—the northern limit of the ecliptic must be either in Libra (if the nodes are advancing) or in Aries (if they are receding), which is more likely. For the Moon's nodes also recede, completing the zodiac in 19 years, while its <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> advances, completing the same in 8 ½ years.

And since the Sun’s apogee (or the Earth’s <term>perihelion</term><note>The point in Earth's orbit closest to the Sun.</note>) is in 5 1/6° of Cancer; therefore, according to Chapter 57, the <term>virtuous diameter</term><note>original: "diameter virtuosa". Kepler's term for a physical axis or "power" within the Earth's body that causes its orbital behavior.</note> that causes the <term>eccentricity</term><note>The "off-centeredness" of an orbit.</note> is stretched toward the body of the Sun when the Earth is at 5 1/6° of Capricorn. But according to Chapter 63, that same virtuous diameter which causes the latitude is also stretched toward the body of the Sun when the Earth is at the limit, which according to this Chapter 68 is in Aries. Therefore, according to that same Chapter 63, both powers can be produced by the same diameter of the Earth’s body. From this, one may probably reason that this "hidden" circle, or <term>mean ecliptic</term><note>A theoretical, perfectly stable orbital plane that Kepler is trying to identify as a universal reference frame.</note>, coincides with the true ecliptic known to us at 5 1/6° of Cancer and Capricorn.

<margin>
A probable
inquiry into the
mean ecliptic.
</margin>
If the <term>aphelia</term><note>The points in planetary orbits farthest from the Sun.</note> of all the planets were arranged in a single <term>great circle</term><note>A circle on a sphere that shares the same center as the sphere, like the equator on Earth.</note>, we could say that this very circle is the one we are seeking here. Indeed, it would then be possible for it to be true of all planets that the nodes (as here in the Earth's circuits) coincide with the <term>apsides</term><note>The two points in an orbit (aphelion and perihelion) where the planet is either closest to or farthest from the Sun.</note>. Thus, both variations—the eccentricity in height and the obliquity in width—would be produced by the same virtuous diameter. In this way, we would be freed from the great difficulties left to us in Chapter 63.

And indeed, the apogees of the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn agree reasonably well. For the aphelia of all three superior planets are in the same semicircle, and simultaneously in the same northern region. Thus, the southern limit of the true ecliptic would be in Libra, and the northern in Aries, which agrees with what was said above.

But the full consideration of this matter must be deferred until the motions of all the planets have been examined in relation to the true ecliptic known to us.

<margin>
What is the Equator or Equinoctial?
</margin>
...of the ecliptic, which is calculated from the equator: though we might more correctly call it the latitude of the equator from the ecliptic. Now, the <term>equator</term><note>The "equator" or "equinoctial" here refers to the projection of Earth’s equator onto the sky.</note> is the greatest circle of the body of the Earth, midway between the poles of the Earth's daily rotation about its axis. The same name, "equator" or "equinoctial," is also assigned to that tract of the sphere of the <term>Fixed Stars</term><note>The "Fixed Stars" were the distant stars thought to be embedded in a single sphere, serving as the backdrop for planetary movement.</note> which stands above the terrestrial equator in any given century. The name "poles" is likewise given to those points of the Fixed Stars that stand above the poles of the Earth in any century. This axis, therefore, and this great circle, are inclined to the ecliptic differently in different centuries. For as much as the northern latitude of the Fixed Stars in **Cancer** is greater today, and the southern latitude in **Capricorn** is greater, by that much is the latitude of the equator from the ecliptic smaller today than it was formerly, because this <term>obliquity</term><note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital path (the ecliptic).</note> is at its maximum in Cancer and Capricorn. Formerly it was indeed 23° 51½'; today it is 23° 31½'. The difference is 20', which is the same as the change in the latitude of the Fixed Stars.

It is consistent, then, that the equatorial circle with its axis and poles would have declined from the poles of this ecliptic *H K* by a perpetual, equal, and fixed distance if the true ecliptic were the primary circle of the world. But because the ecliptic has changed, the inclination of this axis (and likewise the equator, to which this axis belongs) to the ecliptic has also varied. Just as much as the ecliptic has moved away from the Fixed Stars in Cancer, it has approached the equator. Therefore, the equator seems to maintain a constant inclination toward some other circle. It must be, then, that there is a great cause and a great dignity belonging to this "hidden" circle. Thus, by all probabilities, there arises for us a certain **regal circle** *L O M* midway among the circles of the planets, toward which all the planets—and here even Mars—maintain a constant inclination.

Nor should we be disturbed by the example of the Moon, which has a constant inclination of 5 degrees to the ecliptic (and not to some other great circle), both formerly and today, even though the ecliptic has shifted. For there is a vast difference between the Moon and the other planets. The other orbits encompass the center of the world <note>original: "centrum mundi," referring here to the Sun as the center of the solar system.</note>. The Moon’s orbit alone (to speak roughly) is outside the center and is transported from place to place. The others collectively circle the Sun; the Moon circles the Earth. Their <term>eccentricities</term><note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> and their entire theories of longitude and latitude arise from the Sun, while the Moon's arise from the moving Earth. The Sun draws the others into a circle; the Earth draws the Moon. What wonder is it, then, if the Moon maintains the limits of its latitudes constant relative to the shifting ecliptic *H K*, under which the Earth’s circle lies, while the other planets look toward some other invariable circle, such as *L O I M*? Therefore, the Moon ought not to hinder us in any way from believing this.

<margin>
Whether the inclinations of the planes of Mars and the ecliptic vary.
</margin>
Once this is accepted—that the orbit of Mars is constantly inclined to some circle that remains constant under the same Fixed Stars, such as *L O I M*—it follows that this same orbit of Mars is inclined to the ecliptic *H K* differently in different centuries, as the ecliptic deserts its former Fixed Stars in some of its parts and passes to others. This follows, however, if we accept that the **Nodes** of Mars and the **Nodes** of the Earth (that is, the intersections these orbits make with that hidden circle *L O I M*) are not carried through the heavens at the same intervals, but that some are swifter than others. A genuine example of this matter has already been set forth.

He explains that the Moon is an exception because it orbits the Earth rather than the Sun directly.</summary>

For while the <term>equator</term><note>The projection of Earth's equator onto the sky.</note> maintains a constant inclination to this <term>hidden</term><note>original: "caecum." Kepler uses this term for a mathematical reference circle that is not directly observable but helps explain planetary motion.</note> circle **l o i m**, the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun, which is actually the plane of Earth's orbit.</note> **h k** has in the meantime been shifted: finally, the <term>declination</term><note>The angle of an object above or below the celestial equator.</note> of the equator from the ecliptic is found to be changeable.

<margin>
The Pole of the Earth does not move exactly along the small circle **B C E** itself, but along the spirals depicted at **E**, describing one such spiral each year, and the opposite pole describes a similar one, connecting one to another; from this connection arises the <term>precession</term><note>The slow "wobbling" of Earth's axis that causes the timing of seasons (equinoxes) to shift over centuries.</note> of the equinoxes and solstices. Moreover, each of these spirals is as large as the <term>Great Orb</term><note>The Earth's orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system.</note> is to Copernicus, or the Sun's orbit to others—that is, the proportion of this spiral to the surface of the sphere of the Fixed Stars is imperceptible. Therefore, they can be treated as the line **B C E**. To correctly imagine this motion, it should be noted that the axis of the terrestrial equator, continued in both directions to the Fixed Stars, describes a cylinder every year of the same width as one of these spirals, which has the body of the Sun in its center. But the same axis of the Earth, over the course of centuries, describes two cones with equal vertices in the Sun and a base at **B C E**. Thus, the cone is composed of many cylinders.
</margin>

> *Let **A** be the pole of the mean ecliptic, or the point upon which a straight line drawn from the center of the Sun through the pole of the Solar body falls. With **A** as the center and a distance of **AB**—23° 42', or something close to it—let a small circle be drawn. Let **B** and **c** be the locations of the North Pole of the world, or the points where the line drawn from the center of the Earth's body through the pole of the Earth's daily motion falls: **B** in the time of <term>Ptolemy</term><note>An influential 2nd-century astronomer; Kepler is comparing ancient data to his own.</note>, and **c** in <term>our time</term>. If the <term>Nodes</term><note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the ecliptic.</note> of the ecliptic also recede, the northern limit must be established among the Fixed Stars near the border of **Aries** and **Pisces**. For the latitude of the Fixed Stars in **Gemini** and **Cancer** has increased, as was said before. Let point **D** be taken as an intermediate between **B** and **c**, showing the location of the pole of the equator at an intermediate time; and let **A** and **D** be connected. Therefore, the circle **AD** continued will pass through the solstice of the intermediate time. Let **E I** be drawn from **A** at right angles to **A E**, which when continued will pass through the vernal equinox of the intermediate time. Therefore, near the line **AE** would be the pole of the circle under which the orbit and circuit of the Earth was formerly arranged. And because the northern limit is in **Aries**, let **E A** be produced toward **A**, and near that extension let point **i** be chosen below. The pole of the Ptolemaic ecliptic would therefore have been at **i**. With center **A** and distance **A i**, let a small circle be drawn in which another point **o** is taken, closer to **c** than **i** is to **B**. And let **c** be the pole of today's ecliptic, distant from **c** by 23° 31½', while **i**, the pole of the Ptolemaic ecliptic, is distant from **B** by 23° 51½'. This will be the Theory of the changed <term>obliquity</term><note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital plane.</note> of the ecliptic and the latitude of the Fixed Stars, except that we are not certain of the dimension of the small circle **o i**. For that quantity of 20 minutes of changed obliquity of the ecliptic can be produced in various ways.*

> *And because **o** is the pole of the modern ecliptic, and **o c** turns toward the beginning of **Cancer**: let **c p** be an eighth part of the circle, and **p** the middle of **Leo**, where today the northern limit of **Mars** is located. Let **p o** be continued beyond **o**; and let a nearly parallel line **G I** be drawn to it through **i**, though turning slightly <term>forward</term><note>original: "in consequentia," meaning in the direction of the signs of the zodiac (eastward).</note> (because formerly the limit of **Mars** among the Fixed Stars was a little further forward than it is today), and let it be continued beyond **i**. And let a small circle be drawn from **A** cutting **p o** at **F** and **G I** at **H**. Let the small circle be large enough so that **o F** is greater than **i H**. And let the pole of the circle under which the circuit of **Mars** is arranged be placed today at **F**, and formerly at **H**. The modern obliquity, or inclination of the Martian plane to the ecliptic **o F**, will be greater, and the Ptolemaic **i H** smaller; and yet the pole of the Martian orbit **H F** would have gone from **H** to **F** around **A** at a constant interval **A H**, **A F**.*

<margin>
The reason why the shifting of the Nodes of Mars is so slow?
</margin>

> *And since the pole of the Martian orbit has moved through a sufficiently large arc from **H** to **F**, whether forward or <term>backward</term><note>original: "in antecedentia," meaning against the order of the zodiacal signs (westward).</note>: yet because the pole of the ecliptic moved at the same time from **i** to **o** around the same point **A**, the pole of **Mars** would seem to have almost stayed still, because **i H** and **o F** are nearly parallel.*

For it is necessary that a great inequality in the motion of the Nodes follows if it is true that the poles of individual planets go around some common pole, but not at the same time.

I have said **WHAT** is consistent with the principles established in this Work, and by which hypotheses it can be achieved that the inclinations of the <term>planes</term><note>The flat geometric surfaces formed by the orbits of the planets.</note> are different in different centuries. Let us now look at the observations of **PTOLEMY**. For since the latitude of Mars is North with the <term>Heart of the Lion</term><note>original: "corde Leonis." The star Regulus.</note>, a Northern Fixed Star; and South with the Southern stars of Capricorn; it is consistent that the same thing happened to the maximum latitudes of Mars as to those stars, so that both increased, because their latitudes increased—namely, the Northern ones around the Summer Solstice, and the Southern ones around the winter. **PTOLEMY** therefore says the maximum Northern latitude of Mars observed was 4° 20', which today is 4° 32'. He thus confirms our opinion here; because the modern latitude shows it to be 12 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupulis." Arcminutes, where 60 minutes make up 1 degree of the sky.</note> smaller, with the <term>nodes</term><note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note> remaining at nearly the same distance from the <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> as they are today. But on the other hand, he makes the Southern latitude nearly 7 degrees, while even today it can be that much—specifically 6° 52 1/2'. Therefore, we are left in suspense by his observations. For as far as these 12 minutes in Northern latitude are concerned, it should be known that the smallest divisions of his instrument were worth 10 minutes, and frequently a quantity of one such division is found as an error by him. And among the Greek notations, the difference between those that signify 20 and those that signify 40 minutes is small and slippery, often neglected by translators; although the Arabic translator here renders it as 20.

Nothing else exists in **PTOLEMY** that could lead us by the hand to judge the ancient state of these matters. For the observation examined in the following Chapter 69 is proved to be in error. Since, therefore, we are destitute of suitable observations from antiquity, the very condition of the matter compels us to leave this dispute about the motion of the Nodes, like many other things, to posterity; if indeed it should please **GOD** to grant the human race a sufficient space of time in this world to learn these remaining things thoroughly.

### ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAPTER 69.</margin>
**PTOLEMY** preserved for us a <term>Chaldean</term><note>Relating to the Babylonian astronomers of ancient Mesopotamia.</note> observation made in the year 272 BC, on the 18th of January in the morning, when Mars <term>occulted</term><note>Passed in front of and hid from view.</note> the Northern star in the forehead of Scorpio. Again, no certainty of the exact hour was added here. **PTOLEMY** himself had the remaining four observations, having measured the star of Mars against the <term>Fixed Stars</term><note>The stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, as opposed to the "wandering" planets.</note> with an <term>astrolabe</term><note>A complex ancient tool used to solve problems relating to time and the position of the stars.</note>; however, he only records the location within the <term>zodiac</term><note>The band of the sky through which the Sun, Moon, and planets move.</note>, at the very moment of Mars's <term>opposition</term><note>The point when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note> with the mean motion of the Sun.

Arguments for the greatest matters must be taken from such few observations: or if they cannot be, Astronomy must be left imperfect. For first, through the four **PTOLEMAIC** observations, the <term>epoch</term><note>A reference point in time for astronomical calculations.</note> of the mean motion, relative to the Fixed Stars and suitable for **PTOLEMY'S** time, must be sought, and from its comparison with modern ones, the mean motion itself must be defined. Then, through the Chaldean observation, it seems possible to inquire whether the <term>eccentricity</term><note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Sun was truly greater in the past than it is today. Finally, through both this and the <term>Aristotelian</term><note>An observation mentioned by Aristotle.</note> observation, if the time were known, a trial could be made regarding the <term>latitude</term><note>The distance of a planet north or south of the Sun's path (the ecliptic).</note> of Mars at those times.

But what path shall we follow, **by the immortal God!** since we have almost nothing from **PTOLEMY** that we cannot rightly call into controversy before it becomes useful to us for proper precision.

->I.<-

<margin>How Astronomers investigate the beginning of the Zodiac or the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note>.</margin>
<margin>The suspected Ptolemaic observation of the equinox.</margin>
First, for the established times, the mean motion of the Sun comes forth from a calculation that relies on the observation of the <term>equinoxes</term><note>The two times of the year when day and night are of equal length.</note> and <term>solstices</term><note>The times when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, marking midsummer or midwinter.</note>. The Sun reveals the "beginning of Aries" <note>The first point of the zodiacal sign Aries, traditionally marking the spring equinox.</note> not by a finger pointed at the spot, but by a blind conjecture of time. For we say that the beginning of Aries is what the Sun held when the day was seen to equal the nights. What if **PTOLEMY** had wandered astray in the timing? We do not lack for conjectures. First, he does not reveal his method of observation. I wish he had observed the <term>meridian altitudes</term><note>The height of a celestial body above the horizon when it crosses the north-south line of the sky.</note>, from which, by making an <term>induction</term><note>A logical conclusion drawn from specific instances.</note>, the moment of the Sun's entry into the Northern hemisphere is obtained without error. But what if he himself observed with **ALEXANDRIAN ARMILLARIES** <note>Spherical instruments made of metal rings representing the great circles of the heavens.</note>, where <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes objects appear higher than they are.</note> could have harmed him? He himself provides manifest signs of this when he says that on those **ARMILLARIES** the equinox was observed twice on the same day. He attributes this to a fault in the instrument; I suspect a fault arising from refraction.

<margin>Difficulty in accepting the day of the equinox produced by Ptolemy.</margin>
Nevertheless, let us assume he observed by meridian altitudes. Another suspicion forces itself upon me with the greatest power against my will: that the moments of the equinoxes produced by **PTOLEMY** do not agree within a day and a half with the <term>analogy</term><note>The pattern or consistent relationship.</note> of the past observations of **HIPPARCHUS**, and the subsequent ones of **AL-BATTANI** <note>original: "ALBATEGNII." A famous 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> and **BRAHE** <note>Tycho Brahe, Kepler's predecessor and the most accurate observer of his age.</note>, all of which harmonize into a single uniformity; only the **PTOLEMAIC** equinoxes fly off course. This matter gave occasion to many very perplexed opinions about the heavens and gave birth to the motions of <term>trepidation</term><note>A discarded theory that the equinoxes "shook" or oscillated back and forth.</note> and <term>libration</term><note>A slow oscillation, real or imagined, of a celestial body.</note>: all of which are overturned once it is discovered that the observations following **PTOLEMY** agree consistently in uniformity with the very ancient ones of **HIPPARCHUS**.

<margin>In favor of Ptolemy's observation of the day of the equinox.</margin>
Yet **PTOLEMY** himself defends himself by the association of the vernal equinoxes with the autumnal ones. For if it had happened by a fault of the instrument that he pronounced the true equinox on the following day when it had been on the day before...

<margin>CHAPTER 69.</margin>
...if the autumnal equinox had been announced on the day before it actually occurred. Thus, by snatching two days away from the length of summer, a great change in the <term>eccentricity</term><note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Sun would have followed; yet Ptolemy leaves the eccentricity exactly as it had been found by **HIPPARCHUS** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BC) who is considered the father of trigonometry and discovered the precession of the equinoxes.</note> based on his own observations. Therefore, nothing remains but for us to follow the word of **PTOLEMY** and believe that the time when the Sun stood at the beginning of Aries <note>original: "$\gamma$ initio"; the symbol represents the first point of Aries, the vernal equinox.</note> was correctly observed.

# II.

<margin>
How the position of the Sun in the zodiac may be learned through observation; even if the position of the zodiac among the Fixed Stars is unknown.

The theory of the eighth sphere was difficult to grasp among the ancients, and inconsistent:

It is easy in Copernicus.
</margin>
Once the starting point and the <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term><note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its path around the Sun.</note> have been found through observation, it is no trouble, through the daily <term>declinations</term><note>The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the Sun, to declare its true distance from that point which the Sun held at the stated time of the equinox, wherever that point is placed or in whatever sphere it is established. For different people have assigned different spheres to this business; after the eighth and ninth spheres established by **PTOLEMY**, others established a tenth, and the most recent authors established an eleventh and twelfth through the most vain speculations. **BRAHE** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), Kepler’s mentor and a prolific observational astronomer.</note> vehemently rebuked this <term>busy meddling</term> <note>original: "$\pi o \lambda \upsilon \pi \rho \alpha \gamma \mu o \sigma \upsilon \nu \eta \nu$" (polypragmosynēn); Greek for over-refined or meddlesome complexity.</note>. But what he thought to substitute in their place, he never told me, nor did he leave it written anywhere. **COPERNICUS** indeed acted cleverly and agreeably (as the common people judge) and wisely (as I judge); he turned his eyes away from the heavens and sought that point on the globe of the Earth itself, which is overlooked by a fixed point in the sphere of the Fixed Stars in any given age, as was said in Chapter 68. But this is not the place to discuss those matters at greater length.

# III.

<margin>Were the solar equations larger in the past?</margin>
There follows the demonstration of the <term>equation</term><note>In this context, the "equation" is the mathematical correction needed to find the Sun's actual position compared to its average or "mean" position.</note>, which relies on the observed entries of the Sun into the beginnings of the <term>cardinal signs</term><note>Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn, which mark the start of the four seasons.</note>. For when the equation is subtracted from or added to the apparent position of the Sun, the <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical position of the Sun if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle.</note> of the Sun is established from that point which the Sun was seen to occupy at the time of the equinox. Here again, there is greater doubt regarding the magnitude of the equation than there was previously regarding the equinox or the beginning of the zodiac. For today, that equation appears smaller by 20 minutes than what **HIPPARCHUS** seemed to have demonstrated to himself, and which **PTOLEMY** retained. Nor is there a sufficiently just cause for us to say that the proportion of the orbits is different today than it was in the past. For a claim of such great importance requires the firmest testimony, which we lack. For those observations cannot be so accurate, especially regarding the entry into Cancer <note>original: "$\sigma$"</note> and Capricorn <note>original: "$\♑$"</note>. But if we substitute modern equations for **PTOLEMY**, we will not change his observations by so much that **PTOLEMY** himself would admit to perceiving it by observation: and something even greater could have harmed the **PTOLEMAIC** observations from the matter of <term>refractions</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note> itself. For <margin>The hours of the Ptolemaic equinox are uncertain.</margin> we can admit the day of the observed **PTOLEMAIC** equinox is certain, while in the meantime placing several hours of that day in uncertainty: where the alliance of the vernal and autumnal equinoxes does not defend itself against this small error (which we are dealing with) as it did before against that large one.

Certainly, that the equations in the age of **PTOLEMY** were equal to ours is argued by the constancy of the moderns. For it is almost the same as what **BRAHE** finds today, and what **ALBATEGNIUS** <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a central figure in Islamic astronomy.</note> and **ARZACHEL** <note>Al-Zarqali (1028–1087), an Andalusian Arab astronomer.</note> found some centuries ago.

Since, therefore, there is a suspicion that the solar equation used by **PTOLEMY** is faulty, having been deduced from faulty apparent positions of the Sun, and neither for the mean nor...

<margin>
CHAPTER 68.
</margin>
...nor to the opposition of the apparent Sun, Mars was led by <term>PTOLEMY</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated Western astronomy for over a millennium.</note>, without the risk of error.

This is a consolation, however: that we need the position of the apparent Sun, the understanding of which comes first.

<margin>
Modern solar equations may be retained by the good grace of Ptolemaic observations.
</margin>
We can, however, proceed by a twin path: either to believe <term>PTOLEMY</term> regarding the equinoxes, or to apply this correction to the <term>PTOLEMAIC</term> data based on modern <term>equations</term><note>In this context, "equations" refers to the mathematical corrections used to account for the difference between the average (mean) motion of a planet and its observed (true) position.</note>: namely, that the spring equinox occurred three hours later, and the autumnal equinox just as many hours earlier, than was recorded by <term>PTOLEMY</term>. Thus, on both sides, there would be an error of 8 minutes in the Sun’s <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note>. To be sure, <term>PTOLEMY’S</term> instruments were no more precise than those whose smallest markings represented 10 minutes. Even <term>HIPPARCHUS</term> treats one of these small divisions as being in doubt. For this reason, the times the Sun spends in the quadrants of the zodiac were not expressed with more precision than a quarter of a day. So much for the true length of summer and winter.

### IV.

<margin>
The Ptolemaic position of the Sun’s apogee is not certain within many degrees.
</margin>
But what shall we say now about the entry of the Sun into Cancer and Capricorn <note>These represent the Summer and Winter solstices</note>, upon which the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in the Sun's (or a planet's) orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> and the very arrangement of the equations depend? How easily could a single quarter-day be lost from the spring quadrant of the zodiac and added to the autumnal? For the entry of the Sun into Cancer is clearly imperceptible. Nor, indeed, can I be persuaded that <term>HIPPARCHUS</term> and <term>PTOLEMY</term> looked at the exact moment of this entry while neglecting the intermediate points. I believe it more likely that they were diligent throughout the whole summer in noting the Sun's declinations, always comparing two equal ones on either side of the Solstice, and taking the middle time between those moments of equal declination as the true entry of the Sun into Cancer. In this way, if the comparison was made at points near the Solstice, there would be little error; yet an error as large as a quarter-day could still be committed, in which 15 minutes of the Sun's motion pass away. Therefore, even if the equinoxes were perfectly certain, the Sun's position at the solstices could still be off by a quarter of a degree in either direction, and the apogee could then fall eight degrees further forward or backward. So much for the motion of the Sun.

### V.

<margin>
The Ptolemaic positions of the Fixed Stars in the Zodiac are not without suspicion of an error of about 20 minutes.
</margin>
Now, as for the observations of Mars itself, even if we grant that <term>PTOLEMY</term> aimed his <term>astrolabe</term><note>An ancient astronomical instrument used for measuring the altitudes of celestial bodies and solving problems of time and navigation.</note> at the Fixed Stars with the greatest certainty, the position of Mars in the Zodiac is still no more certain (just as we previously considered the position of the Sun) than the positions of those Fixed Stars themselves. If <term>PTOLEMY</term> committed an error in assigning a Fixed Star its degree of elongation from the equinoctial point, that same error will be committed in declaring the position of Mars. Yet not even the elongation of the Fixed Stars from the Sun (and thus from the point of Aries, from which the Sun's elongation is known by its declination) is free from the suspicion of error. Consider both the method of inquiry and the evidence of the error. In the 11th year of Antoninus <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius, around 138-139 AD</note>, <term>PTOLEMY</term> sought this through the <term>dichotomous Moon</term><note>The half-moon phase, where exactly half the Moon is illuminated.</note>. For he took the elongation of the Moon from the Sun, and of the "Heart of the Lion" <note>The star Regulus</note> from the Moon, using the astrolabe. Given * therefore

<margin>
* Point A is the "blind" equinoctial point <note>Invisible to the eye</note>. B is the Sun, C is the Moon, D is the Fixed Star; these are visible. BE is the Sun's declination. AB is obtained most conveniently by observing BE at midday. BC is obtained by instruments during the day, CD by instruments during the night. Thus, by combining AB, BC, and CD <note>The original text says AD, likely a typo for CD or the cumulative result</note>, the elongation of the Fixed Star D from point A is finally obtained—that previously "blind" point which is finally revealed once it is linked to the Fixed Star D. Afterward, planets are linked to the Fixed Stars by observation, and thus their elongation from the starting point of the zodiac, A, is known.
</margin>

### PART FIVE.

...[from the] Sun's distance from the point of the equinox, the distance of the Fixed Stars from the same point is given. Now, in measuring the distance of the Moon from the Sun, an error of half a degree seems to have been committed. For the measurement was begun at sunset. But the Sun, when setting, appears about half a degree higher than it truly is due to <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light by the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects near the horizon appear higher than their actual physical position.</note>. Therefore, the distance of the Moon from the Sun appears smaller than it truly is, and likewise the distance of the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "cordis Leonis"; the star Regulus</note> from the Sun and from the equinox. It seems, therefore, that half a degree must be added to the positions of the Fixed Stars in the time of <term>Ptolemy</term>.

<margin>
CHAPTER
69.
</margin>
Therefore, when <term>Ptolemy</term> thought Mars (connected by observation with the Fixed Stars) was at the point opposite the Sun's mean position, it would actually have been half a degree beyond this opposite point. Thus, whereas <term>Ptolemy</term> records these four observed positions of Mars: 21° 0' Gemini, 28° 50' Leo, 2° 34' Sagittarius, 1° 36' Aries; we ought to assume these: 21° 30' Gemini, 29° 20' Leo, 3° 4' Sagittarius, 2° 6' Aries. Yet <term>Ptolemy</term> protects himself against such audacity, asserting that he frequently investigated the distance of the Fixed Stars from the Moon, of the Moon from the Sun, and thus of the Fixed Stars from the Sun and from the equinox, and found it to be consistently the same. Therefore, although he provides only a single observation for the sake of demonstrating his method, it can be believed that he looked at many observations, both at sunrise and sunset, with the Sun or the Moon, and finally followed an average value <note>original: "intermedium"</note> found among many operations yielding different positions.

<margin>
In favor of Ptolemaic longitudes of the Fixed Stars.
</margin>
Even if this dispute over the 30 minutes seems to have no bearing on the mean motion of Mars (since on these four occasions Mars was observed from the Fixed Stars and can be referred back to them, neglecting the point of the equinox which is of uncertain distance—a method <term>I</term> used above in Chapter 17 to investigate the position of the <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> for <term>Ptolemy's</term> time), we are still bound by the fact that the seen positions of Mars must be reduced to the point opposite the apparent position of the Sun. This work never proceeds correctly unless the distance of both Mars and the Sun from the common point of the equinox is known beforehand; because only through these "elements," so to speak, is the arc of the true distance of Mars from the Sun learned.

<margin>
How far the uncertainty of the positions of the Fixed Stars in the zodiac affects observations of Mars.
</margin>
But if, at the moment when the true opposition of the stars is thought to have occurred, the planet appears thirty minutes beyond the true position of the Sun, then the planet is involved in the <term>second inequality</term><note>The apparent change in a planet's speed and direction caused by the Earth's own motion around the Sun.</note> and is not yet suitable for investigating the <term>first inequality</term><note>The variation in a planet's speed caused by the eccentricity of its own orbit, independent of Earth's motion.</note>. At the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth (or center of motion).</note>, these thirty minutes of the <term>prosthaphæresis</term><note>From the Greek for "addition or subtraction"; a correction used to calculate a planet's true position from its mean position.</note> of the orbit occupy a large arc of the <term>eccentric</term><note>The circular path of a planet that is off-center from the Earth or Sun.</note>, to which an even larger portion of time or mean motion corresponds. In the <term>perigee</term><note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth (or center of motion).</note>, the opposite happens. For that same correction occupies a small arc of the eccentric, to which a smaller portion of mean motion applies. Therefore, he who says that Mars on these four occasions was seen 30 minutes further along in the zodiac also says that the mean motion of Mars from the equinox point was earlier by many minutes at the apogee, and by few minutes at the perigee. And since the arc of the eccentric is smaller than this arc of faulty vision (which was 30 minutes), Mars had not even reached that far on the eccentric under the Fixed Stars as it seemed to have reached under them, by that quantity by which the arc of the eccentric differs from this 30-minute arc of vision. Since this arc is large at the aphelion, and differs little from the 30-minute arc of vision, but on the contrary at the perigee...

Finally, it follows that in <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Sun.</note> a little, and in <term>perihelion</term><note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the Sun.</note> more, must be subtracted from Mars's mean motion relative to the Fixed Stars, if we accept that the Fixed Stars are 30 minutes more advanced in the zodiac than recorded. In this way, not only does the <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical average speed of a planet, assuming it moved in a perfect circle at a constant rate.</note> become smaller (though by a much smaller amount than these 30 minutes, which are a defect of vision), but even the arrangement of the three <term>acronychal</term><note>Observations made when a planet is in opposition to the Sun, meaning it rises at sunset and is visible all night.</note> positions used by **Ptolemy** is displaced. From this, it is necessary for a different aphelion and a different <term>eccentricity</term><note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> to emerge. Although this latter point gives us no trouble; for we shall disregard it, even if the observations were to suggest something greater, or even without suspicion of error in the Fixed Stars, since it is certain that they do not possess such precision as those of **Tycho Brahe**. Therefore, we shall employ the form of the equations found from the Brahean observations, as if they remained the same for all ages.

Therefore, since three forks in the road have met us—concerning the Sun's eccentricity, the position of the Sun's <term>apogee</term><note>The point where the Sun is furthest from the Earth.</note>, and the position of the Fixed Stars and Mars in the Zodiac—there will be eight possible configurations of the mean motion and aphelion for those moments of observation, even if we disregard the zodiac and calculate only from the Fixed Stars.

## The first inquiry shall retain everything Ptolemaic regarding the Sun and the Fixed Stars.

Reduction of Ptolemy's observations to the Sun's apparent opposition.

Since, therefore, the positions of the Sun's mean motion were 21° 6’ [Scorpio], 7° 28’ 50” Cancer, and 2° 34’ Gemini; and the Sun's apogee was 5° 30’ Gemini; the apparent positions of the Sun were 21° 40’ [Scorpio], 7° 1’ 13” Sagittarius, and 2° 41’ Gemini—all three beyond the opposite point. Therefore, the true opposition precedes. And since the daily motion in 21° Gemini (today Cancer) is about 23 minutes, and the Sun's is 61, the sum is 1° 24’. Therefore, those 41 minutes will require 8 hours, when Mars was seen at 21° 8’ Gemini, opposite the Sun's apparent position. Likewise, in 29° Leo (today Virgo), the daily motion of Mars is usually 24, the Sun's is 59, the sum is 1° 23’. Therefore, a difference of 2° 23’ requires 1 day, 17 hours, and 21 minutes, when Mars was seen at 29° 31’ Leo. Finally, in 3° Sagittarius (today Capricorn), Mars's daily motion is 23, the Sun's is 57, the sum is 1° 20’, by which it is indicated that 7 minutes corresponds to 2 hours and 6 minutes, when Mars was seen at 2° 36’ Sagittarius.

PART FIVE.

<margin>
CHAPTER 69.
</margin>

...let the <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> of Mars be placed at 8° 41' Leo <note>original: "$\Omega$"</note>, and at other times slightly earlier due to the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term><note>The slow, westward shift of the equinoxes along the plane of the Earth's orbit, which changes the coordinates of stars over long periods.</note>. At the first time, let the <term>mean anomaly</term><note>The angular distance of a planet from its aphelion, calculated as if it moved at a constant speed.</note> be 46° 37', at the second 34° 21', and at the third 130° 37 ½'; and thus the longitude from the equinox at the middle time is 5° 4° 59' 20''. Then, by the modern hypothesis of equations, the star of Mars is related first at 21° 7' Gemini <note>original: "$\Pi$"</note>, second at 29° Leo <note>original: "$\Omega$"</note>, and third at 2° 37 ½' Sagittarius <note>original: "♐"</note>, by a chance precision. For there are no such foundations from which such great precision can be hoped. But if **Ptolemy** had recorded more <term>oppositions</term><note>Occasions when Mars is directly opposite the Sun in the sky, appearing at its brightest.</note> from his own time, we would undoubtedly experience greater difficulty. For with only three positions of the Sun, the matter is easily settled. Compare this aphelion with Chapter 17.

### Second, while keeping the Ptolemaic equation and the Sun's apogee, let 30 minutes be added to the Fixed Stars.

A slightly different result will emerge. For because Mars is half a degree beyond the opposition of the Sun, a corrected opposition will follow. The sums of the daily motions were 1' 24'', 1' 23'', and 1' 24 ½''. Therefore, for the remaining 30 minutes, nearly the same times emerge, to be added three times—namely, about 8 hours and 40 minutes. To these hours correspond 8 ½ minutes of the apparent motion of Mars, which must be subtracted from those 30 minutes. The remaining 21 ½ minutes will be added to the locations of the planet, so that it is at 21° 29 ½' Gemini, 29° 51 ½' Leo, and 2° 57 ½' Sagittarius. The intervals of both time and the locations in the Zodiac will remain nearly the same. Therefore, the distribution of the mean anomaly among these observations will also be the same as was just found. Only the aphelion will be moved by the same number of minutes, so that it is finally at 1° 2 ½' Leo. Thus, it must be moved back by 8 ½ minutes among the Fixed Stars. And the mean motion from the equinox will be 21 ½ minutes greater than the former, but 8 hours 40 minutes later. However, 11' 24'' of mean motion corresponds to these hours. Therefore, assuming the same time, the mean motion from the equinox will be only 10 minutes greater than before. But the locations of the Fixed Stars are 30 minutes further from the equinox. Therefore, the mean motion of Mars from the Fixed Stars has proceeded 20 minutes less than before.

### Third, with the Sun's apogee moved by 11 or 12 degrees, while keeping the longitude of the Fixed Stars the same.

In that case, at the first time, the Sun will be in its former place by 20 minutes; at the middle time, almost nothing will change; at the last time, it will be in its later place by 21 minutes due to the different <term>equations of the Sun</term><note>Corrections applied to the Sun's mean position to find its true position.</note>. Therefore, the first opposition will follow by 4 hours, and Mars will be in its former place by that many minutes. The last occurs 4 ⅓ hours earlier, with Mars in its later place by the same number of minutes.

From this, therefore, a double <term>epoch</term><note>A reference point in time used for astronomical calculations.</note> of motion is established for the times of **PTOLEMY**.

But what if we devise something suitable from the second and fifth cases, by which we might simply protect the Ptolemaic longitude of the Fixed Stars, so that we have no need to suspect this double epoch of the <term>mean motion</term><note>The average speed of a planet, calculated as if it moved in a perfect circle.</note> of Mars? For **PTOLEMY** explicitly asserts that in that observation of his, he found the distance of the Moon from the Sun to be 92° and 8 minutes, exactly as he had calculated from his hypothesis of the Moon's motions. Suppose **PTOLEMY** told the truth; that he was skillful enough in observing; and that he clearly perceived this distance on his instrument to be exactly what his hypothesis of the Moon's motions required (which was not inaccurate regarding the <term>quadratures</term><note>Positions where the Moon is 90 degrees away from the Sun, such as the first or last quarter.</note>). From this I argue as follows: If the Sun had been at 3° 5' Pisces, where **PTOLEMY** placed it according to his <term>eccentricity</term><note>The measure of how far the Sun's orbit is centered away from the Earth.</note>, the Moon could not have been seen by him to be at that correct distance of 92° 8' calculated from the hypothesis. This is because the setting Sun reaches the eye through <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light by the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects near the horizon appear higher than they actually are.</note>, and appears to be higher than it truly is (and thus 30 minutes further <note>original: "in consequentia" - meaning further along the zodiac in the direction of the signs</note>) than it actually is. However, because the arc observed from the Moon to the Sun was 92° 8', and in truth—due to refraction—it was 92° 38', the Sun was most truly not at 3° 5' Pisces, but at 2° 35' Pisces. This is consistent with the fifth case, where we said that **PTOLEMY'S** maximum additive equation (which applies at 5° Pisces), by the use of modern eccentricity, becomes 20 minutes smaller, thus placing the Sun at 2° 45' Pisces instead of 3° 5' Pisces. Therefore, assuming the universality of refraction in all places and times (as discussed in my *Optics*), and this observation standing as it is, an argument arises for us regarding a smaller eccentricity of the Sun than was thought by **PTOLEMY**.

Nor should it disturb you that I said the refraction was 30 minutes, while this decrease was only 20 minutes. For if you consider carefully, when 30° Taurus <term>culminates</term><note>Reaches its highest point in the sky.</note>, 1° Pisces is then setting at Alexandria; and thus the Sun at 3° Pisces had an altitude of two degrees, or perhaps more; therefore, the refraction was less than 30 minutes; nor was all the refraction simply extended along the longitude. Thus, these two causes were very nearly equal in magnitude, canceling each other out.

Ptolemy’s numbers for the locations of the Fixed Stars are not precise.

Even so, anyone who has worked with the Ptolemaic catalog of Fixed Stars will not think this ten-minute difference worth a word. ### On the mean motion of the Sun from the Fixed Stars, incidentally for future uses.

Since on the **9th** of Pharmuthi <note>A month in the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note> in the year of Christ **139**, which is February **24**, at sunset at 5:30 PM (at Hven 3:30 PM), the apparent position of the Sun was calculated at 3° 3' of Pisces; therefore the mean position was 0° 43' of Pisces. Therefore, the mean Sun preceded the heart of Leo by 5 signs, 11° 27' 49''.
In **1460** Egyptian years, 9° 40' 49'' are lacking.
We conclude that in so many years, by 17' 42'' less than what is given by the Prutenic Tables, the <term>epoch</term> <note>The reference point in time for astronomical tables.</note> at the root of CHRIST on January 1st at noon will be 7 signs, 16°, 8' from the heart of the Lion.

Ptolemy, while pretending that he proved this through another [observation], seems to have demonstrated it through this one: an erroneous proportion of the orbits through an erroneous observation.
</margin>
**Ptolemy**, relying on this observation because it was the most ancient of those he could lean upon, undoubtedly established that proportion of the orbits which we still find in his numbers, and as much as this observation seemed to require. For in the mean motion computed for this time, he does not differ from me by more than 20 minutes. The remainder, therefore, arises from the proportion of the orbits. For as for his pretending to investigate this proportion through an observation *three days distant from opposition*, he did so to make it seem as though he were proving different things from different observations. Because this observation was ancient, it had to be reserved for inquiring into the mean motions; he therefore substituted it for the inquiry into the proportion of the orbits, which had long since been found through this very observation. For it has already been said that it is absurd to attempt the proportion of the orbits through an observation so close to opposition as was the one by which **Ptolemy** pretends to have demonstrated this proportion.

<meta>catchword: Lest anyone</meta>

-># ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS<-

<margin>
CHAPTER 70.
</margin>
Therefore, let no one wonder that we differ by a degree and a half from the observation which <term>PTOLEMY</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Kepler is replacing</note> derived from antiquity; rather, let them inspect the proportion of his orbits, which is very different from that which modern observations prove; and consider how, in order to defend this observation, he [Ptolemy] corrupted the proportion of his own orbits.

<margin>
Ptolemy did not correctly understand the words assigned to the observation.
</margin>
As for the observation itself, of which these are the words: <note>original Greek: ἐφ' ᾧ ὁ τῆς Ἀρέως ἐδόκει προστεθικέναι τῷ βορείῳ μετώπῳ τοῦ Σκορπίου</note> "on which [day] the star of Mars seemed to have been placed toward the northern forehead of Scorpio," I believe an error was committed by <term>PTOLEMY</term>, who understood it to be the "first" star of <term>Scorpio</term>, while the observer meant the "fifth." This is proven by the words themselves. For the "forehead" of Scorpio has six bright stars. Of these, three are notable, being of the third or rather second magnitude; the remaining three are of the fourth, or in my estimation, third magnitude, one of which is higher than the three bright ones and more Northerly. Now if the observer called the "Bright star of the forehead" (which <term>BRAHE</term> <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used</note> correctly declares to be of the second magnitude, and which <term>PTOLEMY</term> understood him to mean) the "Northern forehead," did he not speak ambiguously? He said simply "Northern" for the "BRIGHTEST OF THE NORTHERN ONES," when it was not actually the most Northern star there. Therefore, I much more safely assume that the "Northernmost" star, which is fifth in number, was the one named by the observer.

Next, my computed longitude of Mars agrees with this star, not with the "Bright star of the forehead"; and this holds true while maintaining the hypothesis that modern Brahean observations have produced. For <term>BRAHE</term> places that Northernmost star at 29 degrees 3 1/2 minutes of Scorpio. Subtract the Heart of the Lion <note>The star Regulus</note> at 24 degrees 17 minutes of Leo. There will remain for it an elongation from the Heart of 94 degrees 46 1/2 minutes. Our calculation, however, reports Mars at an elongation from the Heart of the Lion of 94 degrees 49 1/2 minutes or 94 degrees 51 1/2 minutes. The difference is no greater than 3 or 5 minutes.

<margin>
Whether Mars could have covered the Fixed Star in latitude?
</margin>
I do not deny that a difficulty was presented to me by the latitude while I weighed the words <note>original Greek: ἐδόκει προστεθικέναι</note> "it seemed to have been placed toward," as if the observer were saying: "It seemed to have approached so closely that the two could almost be taken for one star," as if they seemed to touch each other. Although the Arabic translator rendered it as "to have covered" [obscured], as if the Greek had written <note>original Greek: ἐπιπροστεθικέναι</note> "to be placed over." Therefore, in my *Optics* <note>Kepler's 1604 work *Astronomiae Pars Optica*</note> page 304, I used the word "superposed." The Germans most fittingly say *drangesetzt* <note>placed right up against</note>. From this I shall reason thus: whether it ran underneath centrally, or grazed its Northern or Southern edge, it could not have been distant from it in latitude by any large amount. For latitudes are less uncertain than longitudes, because their principle is more constant and simpler, as has been demonstrated in this book. Now we know that the Node <note>The point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> recedes from the Fixed stars in the space of a Cynic year <note>A long cycle of approximately 1,461 years</note> by 4 degrees 15 minutes, as proven in Chapter 17. By <term>PTOLEMY</term>, the Northern limit was estimated to precede the Heart of the Lion by 3 1/2 degrees. For us, through the intervening 410 years, it will have receded one degree, so that at the time of the observation it was 2 1/2 degrees before the Heart of the Lion. Therefore, the Node was 87 1/2 degrees after the Heart of the Lion. But Mars is 56 degrees 35 minutes after the Heart of the Lion. Therefore, it is 31 degrees away from the Node, making an inclination of 57 1/2 minutes, which through the parallax of the orbit is made into 1 degree 7 minutes, the correct latitude.

<summary>Kepler resolves a discrepancy between his model and an ancient observation by arguing that Ptolemy misidentified which star in Scorpio Mars was near. By correctly identifying the star as the "Northernmost" rather than the "Brightest Northern," Kepler shows his modern calculations are highly accurate.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Tycho Brahe, Mars, Scorpio, Regulus (Heart of the Lion), celestial latitude, longitude, planetary nodes, ancient observations, star magnitudes</keywords>

PART FIVE.

# PART FIVE.

<margin>CHAPTER 70.</margin>
Now indeed, it is established from <term>BRAHE</term> <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), whose high-precision data Kepler used to build his laws of planetary motion</note> that the <term>latitude</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic</note> of the "Bright Star of the Forehead" is 1° 5' North, while that of the "Northernmost Star of the Forehead" is 1° 42'. Therefore, the latitude seemed to convince me, regarding the "Bright Star of the Forehead," that I should believe this one was covered by Mars, rather than the other.

But that coincidence of numbers is accidental. For <term>BRAHE</term> and <term>PTOLEMY</term> agree on the latitude of the "Northernmost Star of the Forehead," the former stating it as 1° 46', the latter as 1° 42'. In the latitude of the "Bright Star," they differ. <term>PTOLEMY</term> has 1° 20', <term>BRAHE</term> 1° 5'. But that equality of numbers is due to error; whereas this difference is rather a sign of agreement. For the latitudes of the Northern stars in <term>Scorpio</term>, <term>Sagittarius</term>, and <term>Capricorn</term> are smaller today than they were formerly by about 16 to 20 minutes; those of the Southern stars are larger by the same amount. This is because the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; its tilt relative to the stars changes very slowly over centuries</note> has shifted, and the <term>declinations</term> <note>The celestial equivalent of latitude</note> of the degrees of the ecliptic have changed by the same amount, as <term>BRAHE</term> demonstrated and we discussed in Chapter 68. Therefore, if it is true—as it is most true—that today the latitude of the "Bright Star" in the forehead of Scorpio is 1° 5', then in the time of <term>PTOLEMY</term> and <term>HIPPARCHUS</term> <note>An ancient Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BC) whose work laid the foundation for Ptolemy</note> it was no less than 1° 20', or rather greater. Since, therefore, Mars obtained a smaller Northern latitude than either of the said stars, and passed below both (for it is certain that even if we are off by a whole degree in the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, the latitude in the calculation is not distorted by more than three minutes. And it has already been shown above in Chapter 64 that it is most uncertain whether in ancient times Mars also had a greater Northern latitude in the Southern signs): I was therefore pointlessly subtle regarding the word <note>original Greek: προσέπεχεν, "approached" or "touched upon"</note>. Nor is that word to be explained otherwise than as the placing of stars at the same longitude; by which name the star I am referring to, with no impediment from its greater latitude, could just as well have been that "Bright Star."

<margin>The words of the observation have a common-sense meaning.</margin>
See whether this might be the meaning: that since in the Northern part of the forehead there are three stars in the shape of a triangle, Mars was seen in the middle of them, and was thus "placed toward" the Northern forehead of Scorpio; it surely became one of the number of those which are in the Northern part of Scorpio's forehead.

For this interpretation is also supported by the fact that the observer did not say "at the Northern [star] of the forehead" but "at the Northern forehead," which does not sound like one individual star but a part of the whole constellation.

Therefore, these two ancient observations do not help us at all in estimating either the latitude or the proportion of the orbits of that time.

-> **THEREFORE, SINCE** contrary observations do not hinder us, <-
-> but the overall likelihood of the matter confirms us: let us conclude that the <-
-> proportion of the orbits is the same today as it was formerly, <-
-> while the maximum latitudes are somewhat <-
-> changed today. <-

<unclear>How</unclear> it might have been moved during certain hours in <term>uniform motion</term> <note>The theoretical, perfectly circular motion astronomers used before Kepler proved orbits were elliptical</note>, as is known from the <unclear>position</unclear> of the Sun <note>original: *solis collimitantis*</note> marking the boundary: not in the same way.

For if it were in the same plane: it would be necessary that, just as formerly 70 years ago in Alpha <note>Likely a reference to a specific observation point or star in Kepler's diagrams</note>, and from then in the year 1591, it was in the opposite direction in the vicinity of <term>Capricorn</term>: so likewise now in the present motions which we are treating, it should have the same Latitude from the same <term>Longitude</term>. For if it was then Northerly <note>original: *Borealis*</note>, and is now Southerly <note>original: *Australis*</note> at the same longitude, it will be a sign that these are not in the same plane. <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>The Danish astronomer whose precise observations provided the data for Kepler’s laws</note> had conceived this reasoning from observations of smaller motions, and we are following in his footsteps. At this point, we will transcribe here, interpretatively and out of order (lest we soon become overwhelmed by the slow pace of the work itself, unless we scrupulously visit that which is in the calculation itself), this section intended for Chapter 62: so that Astronomy might also gain its mastery by another "Mars" <note>Kepler often uses a play on words: "Mars" refers to the planet, but in Latin, *Marte* also means "by force of arms" or "by struggle"</note>.
